articles.title: When Are Less Precise Predictions More Credible?
articles.authors: Eitan David Rude; Amin Shiri; Felipe M. Affonso; Hal Hershfield; Craig R. Fox
articles.abstract: People expressing uncertain values frequently offer point predictions or intervals of varying widths (e.g., “I’d say your investment will be worth $6,000” versus “I’d say your investment will be worth $5,000–$7,000”). Interestingly, prior research has drawn conflicting conclusions concerning the credibility of more versus less precise predictions. We resolve this inconsistency by identifying a key moderator: the perceived nature of uncertainty. Specifically, we find that under epistemic (“knowable”) uncertainty, predictions are seen as conveying experts’ degree of confidence, and more precise predictions are seen as more credible. Under aleatory (“random”) uncertainty, however, predictions are seen as conveying experts’ assessments of the degree of outcome variability, and less precise predictions are seen as more credible (provided they are within reasonable bounds). These results inform literatures on both the communication of uncertainty and the interpretation of confidence intervals.

articles.title: Preventing teacher and parental violence against children: A cluster-randomized controlled trial of a school-based intervention approach in Tanzanian primary schools
articles.authors: Eliud Kabelege; Katharina Mattonet; Lena Kolwey; Getrude Mkinga; Mabula Nkuba; Manuela Fritz; Faustine Bwire Masath; Katharin Hermenau; Janina Isabel Steinert; Tobias Hecker
articles.abstract:
Background: Violence against children (VAC) at homes and schools remains highly prevalent in low- and middle-income countries. We tested the effectiveness of a preventive intervention addressing teacher and parental violence simultaneously.
Methods: In this two-arm, cluster randomised controlled trial, 16 public primary schools in Morogoro, Tanzania, were randomly allocated (1:1) to receive either the Interaction Competencies with Children (ICC) programme or no intervention. Children (aged 8–15 years), their parents, and teachers were enrolled. The ICC intervention targeted teachers and parents focusing on non-violent behaviour management strategies and positive adult–child interactions. Interviewers at follow-up were blinded. The primary outcome was emotional and physical VAC, measured by children and adults’ reports at baseline and follow-up. All randomised participants were analysed. Missing data were estimated through multiple imputation. The trial was registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT#06369025).
Findings: In total, 410 and 427 children, 380 and 394 mothers, 253 and 246 fathers, and 244 and 235 teachers were assigned to the intervention and control condition, respectively. Participants were recruited between 15 April to 24 August 2024 for baseline and between 1 October 2024 to 21 February 2025 for follow-up assessment. Participants in intervention schools reported significantly greater reductions in emotional and physical violence by mothers (child report (CR): Cohen’s d = 0·227 for emotional violence (EV), 0·134 for physical violence (PV); adult report (AR): 0·343 for EV, 0·473 for PV), fathers (CR: 0·180 for EV, 0·215 for PV; AR: 0·222 for EV, 0·187 for PV), and teachers (CR: 0·089 for EV, 0·164 for PV; AR: 0·336 for EV, 0·607 for PV). No adverse events related to the intervention were detected.
Interpretation: By leveraging the infrastructure of public schools, ICC offers an effective and scalable multi-sectoral model for VAC prevention.

articles.title: Expertise Diversity Enhances Information Sharing in Wiki settings: Evidence from Sequential Collaboration
articles.authors: Maren Mayer; Joachim Kimmerle
articles.abstract: Online collaborative projects such as Wikipedia and OpenStreetMap rely on sequential collaboration, where contributors iteratively revise a shared product over time. While previous research has examined wikis for computer-supported collaborative learning and sequential collaboration for numerical judgment tasks, little is known about the cognitive mechanisms underlying information sharing in such settings. The present study bridges research on computer-supported collaborative learning, group information sharing, and cognitive models of sequential collaboration. Drawing on a computational model of sequential collaboration, we tested the prediction that higher variation in contributors' expertise facilitates the integration of information into a shared product. In an experimental study with 413 participants we demonstrate that information accumulation increased throughout the sequential chain but at a decreasing rate. Consistent with model predictions, higher expertise variation significantly increased the likelihood that information was incorporated into the shared text. Contrary to expectations, expertise variation did not affect the timing of information inclusion across chain positions, nor did it increase information deletions. These findings demonstrate that predictions derived from a cognitive model of numerical judgment formation generalize to information-sharing contexts. More broadly, the results suggest that diversity in contributors' knowledge can improve collaborative knowledge construction in sequential environments. This research adds to evidence that sequential collaboration is an effective mechanism for integrating distributed knowledge in online collaborative systems.

articles.title: Techno-Optimism Reduces Willingness to Address Climate Change
articles.authors: Jonas M B Haslbeck; Maien S. M. Sachisthal; Fabian Dablander
articles.abstract: Technological innovation is essential for mitigating climate change, but so are wider socio-economic transformations as well as lifestyle changes. Techno-optimism, the belief that technological innovation alone is sufficient to address climate change, may reduce public willingness to engage in climate action. Here we use a structural causal model to estimate the causal effect of techno-optimism on willingness to contribute 1\% of one's monthly household income to address climate change using a large, population-weighted sample from the Netherlands (N = 23, 395). We find that being a techno-optimist reduces the probability of being willing to contribute by 18.7% (95% CI: 15.6, 20.7). In addition, we find that the causal effect is much smaller for respondents on the political right, where overall willingness is already very low. We close by discussing the importance of adequately framing the role of technology when discussing climate change mitigation.

articles.title: Neural Racing Accumulator Model Estimation With Lightweight Monotonic Flows
articles.authors: Malte Lüken; Stefan T. Radev; Lourens Waldorp; Andrew Heathcote
articles.abstract: Race models describe speeded decision-making as a race between competing runners that accumulate evidence in favor of available choice options. Their parameters can be estimated through the model likelihood that combines the probability and cumulative density functions of each runner. However, estimating parameters of complex race models whose runners have intractable densities with (hierarchical) Bayesian inference has been challenging: Numerical density approximations tend to be slow and amortized neural posterior estimation methods require complex network architectures that can be expensive to train and, in classical settings, tie the trained estimator to a specific prior distribution and generative model. We propose a flexible neural estimation method that decouples training from the choice of prior distribution or model parameterization. We train a small neural network together with a monotonic neural spline flow to simultaneously learn the runners' conditional probability density and cumulative density functions. We then combine both functions to efficiently estimate race model likelihoods that can be used in combination with modern samplers. We demonstrate the utility of our approach on both tractable and intractable versions of the popular racing diffusion model. Based on our results, we argue that, when flexibility in choosing prior distributions or model parameterizations is needed, learning the model likelihood with lightweight neural density estimators is advantageous.

articles.title: Looking into the scientist’s mind: The effects of disclosing scientists’ rationale on students’ scientific reasoning and epistemic beliefs
articles.authors: Katharina Düsing; Vanessa van den Bogaert; Till Bruckermann; Hannah Greving; Julia Cathérine Thomas; Miriam Brandt; Anke Schumann; Daniel Lewanzik; Christian Voigt; Ute Harms
articles.abstract: This study investigated the effects of systematically developed video variations on students’ scientific reasoning (SR) and epistemic beliefs (EBs). Drawing on a novel video development framework, we evaluated four video variations that differed in (i.) how scientific practices were presented—either in a cookbook style (focusing on declarative “what” information) or in a scientific reasoning style (integrating declarative, procedural, and epistemic knowledge) and (ii.) how scientists’ thought processes were presented—either as science-in-the-making (concurrent think-aloud insights) or as ready-made science (post hoc reconstruction of thought processes). In a pre–post design, 512 secondary students each engaged with a digital learning environment in which one of the video variations was embedded. Multivariate analyses of covariance (MANCOVAs) that were conducted to control for pretest performance revealed significant main effects of the presentation formats. The scientific reasoning style fostered more elaborated EBs regarding the source of scientific knowledge compared to the cookbook style. Presenting scientists’ thought processes as science-in-the-making improved EBs (again, regarding the source), whereas ready-made science led to higher SR performance in planning and conducting investigations. These findings demonstrate that fine-grained design choices in video representations of scientific practices support SR and EBs to different degrees. We discuss the implications for future research and for education.

articles.title: fMRI hyperscanning reveals widespread neural coupling during natural conversations
articles.authors: Laetitia Mwilambwe-Tshilobo; Lily Tsoi; Sebastian Speer; Zaid Zada; Shannon M. Burns; Emily B. Falk; Diana Tamir
articles.abstract: Conversation is one of the most powerful tools that people have for building and maintaining social connections. How does conversation bring two minds together? Here we tracked the neural dynamics between dyads during real-time conversation using fMRI hyperscanning, where both people were scanned simultaneously, to explore whether and how conversation aligns brains. Dyads engaged in natural, free-flowing conversation as they co-constructed the content of their dialogue. In a control condition, partners read aloud scripted dialogue from another dyad’s conversation, preserving the turn-taking structure while removing the co-construction. To examine neural alignment, we compared whole-brain intersubject correlation between partners in each condition, assessing both synchronous and predictive neural dynamics. Results showed that naturalistic conversation led to significant widespread neural alignment across brain regions implicated in attention, audition, affect, executive control, and social cognition, compared to scripted conversation. Temporally refined analyses showed that during naturalistic conversation, relative to scripted conversation, both speakers and listeners anticipated each other within a short temporal window, with brain activity preceding their partner’s in the same neural systems. These findings show that live, turn-taking conversations align neural activity well beyond passive or asynchronous communication, providing a foundation for future research examining how spontaneous, co-constructed dialogue allows people to communicate effectively.

articles.title: Developing an adolescent self-report measure of social media experience: Insights from cognitive interviews
articles.authors: Jo Hickman Dunne; Louise Black; Jade Davies; Frederick Jones; Molly Anderton; Pratyasha Nanda; Felicitas Beissel; Lauren Burke; Reihaneh Farzinnia; Margarita Panayiotou
articles.abstract: Despite a rapid increase in research exploring the relationship between adolescent social media use and mental health, the field is hindered by poor quality tools that lack the validity and precision to assess this relationship. The current study presents findings from cognitive interviews that aimed to refine a multidimensional measure of adolescents’ social media experiences relevant to their mental health and wellbeing. We conducted 20 individual, paired or group interviews with 35 adolescents aged 11-16, across three rounds of interviews, testing 83 of a possible 107 items. Through iterative testing, issues relating to comprehension; inapplicability and assumptions within items; and items not addressing their intended experience, were identified and addressed. The interviews also highlighted two wider conceptual issues: (1) the impact of parental restrictions on adolescents’ experiences, and (2) difficulties in responding to items about abstract, identity-based experiences. In addition, the interviews supported an understanding of preferred response options and format. Findings from this study informed specific revisions to measure items to enhance validity, as well as broader considerations for assessing adolescent social media experience. Our study also reinforces the importance of cognitive interviewing in refining adolescent measures more broadly. We identify the need for the development of a set of general recommendations to guide item writing for adolescents, and further work to understand optimal response label options and wording for longer recall periods. Development of such guidance, alongside the greater use of cognitive interviews to pre-test measures, is crucial for improving instrument validity in the field of adolescent mental health.

articles.title: Understanding the role of generative artificial intelligence in mental health support: Survey of user experiences, engagement patterns, and perceived risks and benefits
articles.authors: Jake Linardon; Zoe McClure; Cleo Anderson; Claudia Liu; Olivia Marie Soliman; Mariel Messer
articles.abstract: Generative AI – especially ChatGPT – is increasingly used for mental health purposes, but users’ subjective experiences of these tools remain unclear. We characterized how individuals utilize ChatGPT for mental health support through a web-based survey completed by 308 adults (Mage=31.5, SD=5.3; 54% men) who reported prior use of this tool. Around half reported use of ChatGPT for mental health support more than once a week, 80% have used it for more than 3 months, and a third reported increased use over time. Depression (55%), anxiety (74%), stress (66%), and relationship conflict (49%) were the problems most frequently discussed with ChatGPT, with the severity of these problems typically rated as mildly or moderately severe. Endorsed reasons for use were its on-demand availability (71%), free cost (69%), and anonymous nature (54%), while common functions the platform served included obtaining advice (71%), providing a safe space for expression (63%), and to learn coping strategies (61%). Experiences were largely positive, with 8 in 10 agreeing that ChatGPT helped them feel understood, better process their emotions, and improve their mental health literacy. Concerns were also evident, with around half expressing worry about data privacy, and a quarter feeling overly reliant on the platform and reducing their motivation to seek help. Few indicated that ChatGPT had replaced professional help (7%) or discouraged help-seeking (12%). Findings shed light on how users are engaging with generative AI for mental health support and highlight the importance of rigorous research designed to evaluate its safety and long-term efficacy.

articles.title: Values and Political Preferences in Childhood
articles.authors: Christopher Johnston; Martín Opertti; Turgut Keskintürk
articles.abstract: Studies of youth political development focus primarily on political socialization and salient events, while paying relatively less attention to important individual differences among children themselves, such as values. We administer an original survey to a sample of 10-to-12-year-olds and show that children's value priorities strongly predict their political preferences, and that one dimension of value priorities continues to predict political preferences even after adjusting for parental values and political preferences. Taken together, our findings suggest that pre-teens already connect their domain-general value priorities to evaluations of political candidates and policies. Our work is consistent with a more agentic view of childhood political development, and lends support to the idea that personal values provide a foundation for the development of political belief systems.

articles.title: In AI Do We Trust? Comparing a Transformer-Based Natural Language Processing Model Against a Traditional Content Analysis Approach to Qualitative Research
articles.authors: Matthew Baron; Catherine Stein
articles.abstract:
Central to debates about the use of artificial intelligence (AI) models for qualitative
research are concerns about comparability and trust in AI generated findings. The present
methodological study compared findings from a transformer-based Natural Language Processing
(NLP) model, BERT, against a traditional content analysis approach to qualitative research using
the same text data. We examined claims that AI models generate findings that are identical or
similar to traditional qualitative approaches. The study assessed three aspects of comparability
between the BERT model solution and human-coded findings that included topic labeling,
classification overlap, and AI replicability. Results indicated broad similarity in the semantic
meaning of topic categories generated by the BERT model and themes from content analysis.
There was low overlap in the classification of individual participant responses between BERT
and content analysis categories, even for categories similar in semantic meaning. Running the
BERT model a second time on the same input data resulted in differences in topic categories and
document classification between the two approaches. Study implications and research
recommendations for the use of NLP models are discussed.

articles.title: Bodily Experience Shapes Evaluative Judgements and Attentional Engagement with Affective Touch in Art
articles.authors: Ionela Bara; Gianluca Saetta; David Crevillén Hernández; Cosimo Gentile; Emanuele Gruppioni; Emily S. Cross
articles.abstract: Affective touch plays a central role in social interactions by conveying emotion and interpersonal closeness. Yet little is known about whether differences in bodily experience following upper-limb amputation are associated with the emotional, evaluative, and attentional processing of observed affective touch. Across two pre-registered experiments, we examined the extent to which affective touch in art shapes emotional, aesthetic, and attentional engagement, and whether these responses differ following upper-limb amputation. In Experiment 1, artworks depicting touch evoked more positive and intense emotional responses than artworks not depicting touch, with little evidence for a difference in aesthetic appreciation. In Experiment 2, artworks depicting touch received higher ratings across all three measures compared to those not depicting touch, with the amputation group showing greater sensitivity to depicted touch in judgements of aesthetic appreciation than controls. Artworks depicting touch were also fixated later and viewed for less time than artworks not depicting touch, with comparable effects across groups. Furthermore, within artworks depicting touch, the upper region of paintings (depicting facial information) was fixated earlier and viewed for longer than the middle region of paintings (featuring more arm and torso information), suggesting preferential visual attention to socially informative body content. These findings demonstrate that observed affective touch in art carries emotional and aesthetic value beyond direct tactile experience. They further highlight that limb loss selectively reshapes the aesthetic evaluation of touch, rather than its emotional or attentional processing. Together, this work advances our understanding of observed touch by demonstrating that its social-affective meaning, aesthetic importance, and attentional prioritisation are partly dissociable, and that bodily experience selectively shapes its evaluation.

articles.title: Social Support among LGBTQ, Cisgender, and Heterosexual Undergraduate Students:  An Ego-Centric Social Network Study
articles.authors: Allyson Marie Blackburn; Nathan Todd; Nicole Allen
articles.abstract: While the population and acceptance of LGBTQ people are growing, there are persistent mental health disparities for LGBTQ individuals, especially for emerging adults. Social support is critical for the promotion of well-being. Yet, who receives support and the nature of the support provided can vary based on social identity, including sexual orientation and gender identity. In this study, we demonstrate the benefit of using ego-centric social network analysis (ESNA) to advance research about emotional support for sexual minorities. Using a sample of 1,215 undergraduate students (253 sexual minorities) from a large Midwestern university, we show that sexual minorities reported a greater proportion of LGBTQ people yet a lower proportion of family in their social network. We also show that sexual minorities reported that they were less likely to receive support but were more likely to be nominated by both heterosexuals and sexual minorities as network members who provide support. Finally, sexual minority participants relied more on friends than parents for emotional support, whereas the opposite was true for heterosexual students. These (and other) findings show how ESNA allows for testing hypotheses that capture the interconnected context of relationships. We discuss how findings advance the literature along with limitations and implications. Overall, we show that ESNA is a valuable tool to use to understand social networks as a critical context for development and well-being.

articles.title: Re. The influence of personality on the risk of myocardial infarction in UK Biobank cohort
articles.authors: Alexander Weiss
articles.abstract: Dahlén, Miguet, Schiöth, and Rukh1 used items from UK Biobank2 to construct “proxies” of the five domains of human personality—Agreeableness, Conscientiousness, Neuroticism, Extraversion, and Openness3. However, the items used came from an existing Neuroticism scale. In my analyses, I demonstrated that the discriminant validities of these proxies are poor, and so should not be used to study personality in UK Biobank or any other dataset.

articles.title: The Cultural Logic of Honor and Antisocial Punishment in Social Dilemmas: A Multi-Lab Study Across Three World Regions
articles.authors: Shuxian Jin; Dina Rabie; Jinkwon Lee; Jinkyung Na; Rania Miniesy; Vivian L Vignoles; Ayse K. Uskul
articles.abstract: Punishment can sustain cooperation by targeting free riders (prosocial punishment), but it may also backfire by triggering retaliation; and when punishment is directed at cooperators (antisocial punishment), it can lead to a decline in cooperation. Samples exhibiting greater antisocial punishment in previous research have tended to come from societies where honor is believed to play a stronger role in shaping social behavior. Here, we tested the role of honor in antisocial punishment through a preregistered multi-lab experiment conducted in Egypt (n = 266), South Korea (n = 212), and the United Kingdom (n = 192), using public goods games with and without punishment. While the level of antisocial punishment was higher among the Egyptian sample, compared to the South Korean and British samples, individual-level honor values and norms were not associated with antisocial punishment across all three samples. Nevertheless, individuals with stronger personal honor values exhibited heightened retaliation, particularly targeting cooperators after being punished unfairly. These findings suggest that honor is not a cultural aspiration that provokes, nor a norm that prescribes, aggression toward cooperators, but rather a cultural logic that shapes when and for whom punishment becomes a tool of harmful retaliation rather than cooperation enforcement.

articles.title: A Risk-Formulation Framework and Candidate Screening Items for Dangerous Use of Large Language Models in Clinical Psychiatry
articles.authors: Armando N. Braz; Punit Matta; Joshuah Muthee; Eren M Veziroglu; Daniel Price
articles.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) and related conversational artificial intelligence (AI) systems have moved rapidly from novelty into ordinary use across education, work, social life, and mental-health-related help seeking. Members of the public now use these systems for advice, companionship, self-disclosure, emotional support, psychoeducation, and quasi-therapeutic interactions. Existing instruments assess problematic or dependent AI use, but they do not ask whether AI has entered a pathway toward serious harm by entrenching ideation, operationalizing capability, displacing human support, or amplifying harmful conduct. To our knowledge, no brief, clinically oriented psychiatric screener has yet been developed and validated specifically for this purpose. We define dangerous AI use as generative AI use that appears to increase the likelihood, feasibility, persistence, organization, or scale of serious harm to self or others. This paper describes LLMs as interactive capability amplifiers and quasi-social systems rather than informational technologies alone, situates their risk within the technical problems of alignment and behavioral stability, and proposes a four-dimensional clinical formulation: Ideational Entrenchment, Operationalized Capability, Relational Displacement, and Broader Amplification. We then introduce two candidate instruments awaiting formal validation: the STEPS-5, a brief screen for AI involvement in acute self-harm and suicide risk, and the HEAT-4, a research-oriented framework addressing broader harmful-use amplification. These tools are intended to open clinical inquiry rather than diagnose, predict behavior, or determine disposition. Ultimately, we argue for the need to avoid both over-pathologizing ordinary AI use and ignoring when AI has become meaningfully relevant to psychiatric safety.

articles.title: Jargon as a Psychological Construct? A Multidecade Analysis of Communication Failure in Evaluation Reports
articles.authors: John Hite
articles.abstract: For seven decades, studies have asked whether the people who receive psychological evaluation reports understand what they say. Existing research has largely measured reader satisfaction rather than what readers comprehend, recall, or interpret. This narrative synthesis identified six studies, conducted between 1984 and 2025 in school psychology and, most recently, child neuropsychology, in which 253 readers were assigned to a standard-format report and had their comprehension scored directly. Comprehension ranged from 46.6% to 61.1% (weighted mean = 55.2%) and showed no detectable change across four decades. In every study that also scored an accessible version of the same report, readers understood it better, with scores from 60% to 82%. Recent evidence from pediatric neuropsychology shows the same gap: parents rated their understanding of their child's report highly, yet almost half could not state the child's diagnoses without error. Effective formats combined plain-language wording with one or more of domain-based organization, concrete behavioral examples, and elaborated recommendations. These findings suggest that jargon-related comprehension failure is a persistent, measurable, and modifiable problem spanning specialties within psychology. Implications for training, supervision, and evidence-based communication practice across school and clinical psychology are discussed.

articles.title: Formal training in a visual aesthetic domain increases shared taste in a domain-specific manner
articles.authors: Edward A. Vessel; Claire Reymond; Nancy Etcoff
articles.abstract: Although there is strong agreement for aesthetic preferences (“shared taste”) for natural kinds such as faces and landscapes, preferences for cultural artifacts such as artwork and architecture are more individual. These differences in aesthetic tastes may reflect differences in how individuals parse their perceptual world. We examined the aesthetic preferences of students enrolled in training programs for visual communication and architecture and hypothesized that formal training in an artistic domain would lead to shifts in which features individuals use to aesthetically evaluate that domain, causing changes in which images are preferred and to an increase in shared taste (convergence) across individuals. In a longitudinal study, 27 architecture and 21 visual communication students viewed images of buildings, posters, and artworks and rated them for both understanding and aesthetic appeal at 3 timepoints spread over two years. A single set of ratings were also collected from 69 online control participants. After two years of training (T3), a double-dissociation pattern emerged: architecture students agreed more on which buildings were aesthetically pleasing and understood, but visual communication students agreed more on which posters were aesthetically pleasing and understood. Average aesthetic ratings, on the other hand, were higher for the domain of study only at T1. These findings demonstrate a clear link between the development of expertise, a key form of learning, and aesthetic appeal. Rather than solely being a function of stimulus-computable features, aesthetic appeal is a function of how a person understands their visual world, reflecting personal biographies of visual experience and knowledge.

articles.title: Cerebellar contributions to social learning in autistic and nonautistic adolescents
articles.authors: Yen-Wen Chen; Shannon Cahalan; Nicole Grace Treece; Ann Clawson; Alyssa Verbalis; Christoph Korn; Gabriela Rosenblau; Allison Jack
articles.abstract:
The role of the cerebellum in social learning remains poorly understood. Although the cerebellar posterior lobe (CPL) has been implicated in social decision-making and autistic traits, its contribution to social prediction and prediction-error (PE) processing during learning is unclear. We focused on adolescence, a critical developmental period for social decision-making and learning. 71 autistic (AUT) and 75 non-autistic (N-AUT) participants completed social and non-social learning tasks during fMRI. Preregistered hypotheses predicted that the CPL would be involved in prediction and PE processing, with effects differing by diagnostic status and age.

We found no group differences in social learning. Across participants, PEs decreased more steeply during non-social than social learning; in the AUT group this difference between social and non-social learning was more pronounced. In the cerebellum, PE-related activity in the CPL (lobules Crus I/II, VI, and VIIb) showed group- and age-related differences. Contrary to our hypothesis, PE-related activity during social learning was greater in AUT than N-AUT participants in right Crus II. Across several other CPL regions, PE-related activity increased with age in N-AUT participants but showed the opposite pattern in AUT participants. Mirroring the marginally steeper behavioral PE reduction in the non-social condition in the AUT vs. the N-AUT group, PE-related brain activity was greater for non-social than social PEs in left Crus I and right lobule VI in the AUT group. Exploratory searchlight analyses showed greater PE-related connectivity between left Crus II and prefrontal cortex in AUT than N-AUT participants. 

These findings suggest that AUT adolescents may engage CPL differently during learning, particularly for social versus non-social information. Greater CPL activity and connectivity during social learning in AUT may reflect compensatory mechanisms supporting comparable behavioral performance to N-AUT youth.

articles.title: Do ‘tortured phrases’ exist in the psychology literature, and are there psychology-specific ‘tortured phrases’?
articles.authors: Patrick Nebl; Mark G McCoy; Jaime A. Teixeira da Silva
articles.abstract: Objectives: The psychology literature is occasionally quoted as being in a replication crisis due to the inability to replicate key findings caused by either integrity issues, or weak scientific protocols. This paper focuses on an unexplored topic in psychological science, ‘tortured phrases’, first to appreciate whether any psychology literature might contain such ambiguous terms, even if they are not related to psychology per se. Methods and Results: The Tortured Phrases Detector (TPD) of the Problematic Paper Screener revealed 36 journal articles (including one proceedings paper) with tortured phrases, 14 of which have been retracted to date (10 October 2025). We then induced, using a free online paraphraser, a novel methodology for detecting ‘tortured phrases’, by converting 50 standard psychological terms that started with the letter “A” into purposefully created ‘tortured phrases’. We employed Google Scholar to detect whether any of these created ‘tortured phrases’ might actually exist in published literature. The second method, with only 50 terms, was able to detect at least one potential ‘tortured phrase’ (“evaluation utensil” used to represent “assessment instrument”). Conclusions: The exploratory nature of the methodology was prone to false positives but had success. It is our hope that this study will inspire further attempts to detect tortured phrases in psychology literature in order to further increase the scientific and ethical rigor in the field of psychology.

articles.title: CortexLume: Rapid Geometry-Adaptive Cortical Feedback for Target-Informed fNIRS Design
articles.authors: Ruiyi Huang
articles.abstract: Target-informed functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) probe design requires repeated evaluation of how candidate source-detector geometries sample the cortex, but full photon-transport modeling is too costly for interactive revision. We developed CortexLume, which couples an editable target-patch-placement representation with a geometry-adaptive cortical surrogate for rapid spatial assessment. The surrogate adapts its center, orientation, and anisotropic extent to fitted source-detector geometry and local scalp-cortex relationships, and is intended to approximate normalized cortical spatial allocation rather than absolute optical sensitivity. We benchmarked the method against MCX photon transport assembled through AtlasViewer on the ICBM152 anatomical model and then evaluated the frozen formulation on the independent Colin27 model without retuning. On ICBM152, mean channel-centroid discrepancy was 2.35 mm, 90%-mass Dice was 0.746 per channel and 0.826 per patch, and Jensen-Shannon distance was 0.330; the complete formulation improved Dice in 370 of 396 channels relative to a restricted reference. On Colin27, mean channel Dice was 0.748 and patch Dice was 0.812 across 88 retained channels. Patch-field construction required a median of only 75.81 ms. These results support CortexLume as a rapid cortical surrogate for iterative probe drafting and candidate shortlisting, with subject-specific photon modeling retained for final optical refinement.

articles.title: Ready and Willing? Psychological Conditions for Demand-Side Climate Policy in a High-Income Country
articles.authors: Alaa Aldoh; Jan Michael Bauer; Joachim Peter Tilsted; Mads Ejsing; Cameron Brick; Kristian Steensen Nielsen
articles.abstract: Climate policy in high-income countries disproportionately prioritizes supply- over demand-side solutions requiring citizen behavior change. This skew partly reflects policymakers’ skepticism about citizens’ readiness and capacity for behavior change. Yet, it remains unclear whether this skepticism reflects actual conditions for demand-side engagement, how climate-relevant perceptions interrelate, and which factors predict perceived feasibility of changing high-impact behaviors. We address these questions using a nationally representative survey of 2,005 adults in Denmark—a high-income, climate-progressive country where supply-side solutions dominate despite ambitious mitigation targets. We map climate-relevant perceptions using network analysis and estimate associations with perceived behavioral plasticity across eight high-impact behaviors using Bayesian ordinal regression. The Danish public is highly concerned about climate change and expresses a strong personal responsibility for mitigation. Perceived behavioral plasticity closely tracked perceived (but not objective) climate footprints of behaviors. Carbon footprint literacy was low: participants overestimated footprints of low-impact behaviors (e.g., waste sorting) and underestimated high-impact ones (e.g., dietary change). Network analysis revealed a dense interconnected system with personal responsibility as the most central node; perceived behavioral plasticity clustered with measured psychological factors, suggesting a mutually reinforcing system. Regression models indicate that personal responsibility, climate change concern, perceived behavioral impact, and social norms consistently relate to the plasticity of eight impactful climate-relevant behaviors; higher-income households reported lower plasticity of several behaviors. Together, these findings challenge the dismissal of demand-side solutions. Psychological conditions for behavioral engagement are favorable; realizing this potential requires pairing communication strategies that strengthen norms and correct misperceptions of behavioral impact with structural policies that make high-impact change affordable and accessible.

articles.title: Understanding Medical Invalidation from the Patient Perspective: A Qualitative Interview Study Across Diseases and Healthcare Settings
articles.authors: Seraina Petra Lerch
articles.abstract:
Objective 
Research on patients feeling that their symptoms are not taken seriously (medical invalidation) has predominantly focused on individual diseases. This study explored patients' experiences across different medical conditions and healthcare contexts to identify common characteristics, contributing factors, consequences, and opportunities for prevention. 
Methods
The study was conducted in Germany between January and March 2025 using interviews undertaken remotely or in person. Data were analysed using qualitative content analysis following Kuckartz and Rädiker. Thirty-one adults (≥18 years) with self-reported experiences of not being taken seriously in healthcare were purposively recruited through patient organisations and social media to achieve maximum variation regarding symptoms and diagnoses.
Results
Participants described not being taken seriously as a cross-cutting healthcare phenomenon occurring across diverse symptoms, diagnoses, medical specialties, and healthcare settings. Experiences ranged from isolated encounters to cumulative processes that developed over repeated interactions with healthcare professionals (HCPs). Contributing factors were perceived at multiple levels, including healthcare system, HCPs, patient, disease, and interactional factors, which frequently interacted. Consequences extended beyond the initial consultation and included psychological distress, loss of trust, delayed or inappropriate diagnosis and treatment, reduced healthcare utilisation, occupational consequences, and impaired social well-being. Participants identified opportunities for prevention at different levels, highlighting structured feedback mechanisms. 
Conclusions
Medical invalidation is a multifactorial phenomenon that extends across diseases and healthcare settings. Patients emphasized that medical invalidation depends not only on clinical decision-making but on being heard, having their illness perceptions acknowledged, and receiving transparent communication. Strengthening these elements of patient-centred care may improve healthcare experiences.

articles.title: A Megastudy of Behavioral Interventions to Increase Voter Registration Ahead of the 2024 U.S. Presidential Election
articles.authors: Katherine Anne Mason; Kayley Okst; Don Green; Robb Willer; James Druckman; Jan G. Voelkel; Yash Patel; Claire Robertson; Wooyoung Choi; Jasmine Sanchez
articles.abstract: In the United States, voter registration is required for participation in most elections, yet many eligible individuals remain unregistered. Relatively little is known about how to increase the likelihood that an eligible adult registers to vote. We evaluated 10 expert-crowdsourced interventions among eligible but unregistered U.S. voters (N = 12,927) in an online survey experiment conducted before the 2024 presidential election. The study was powered to detect small attitudinal effects and effects on voter registration and turnout of roughly 3 percentage points. Nine interventions increased self-reported voting intentions, and five increased clicks on the official voter registration website. Escalating Commitment, a social pressure strategy, produced the largest absolute effect on these proximal outcomes. However, none of the interventions significantly increased voter registration or turnout. These findings highlight the challenge of translating shifts in intention into registration behavior, but also identify potentially promising messaging strategies for future large-scale field evaluation.

articles.title: The eyes have it: Perceived ocular vitality as a unifying account of eye-region dominance in social perception
articles.authors: Shiyun Zhang Isabelle
articles.abstract: The eye region has an outsized influence on first impressions of faces. Its surface features, however, have been studied one cue at a time. This narrative integrative review proposes perceived ocular vitality as a unifying construct: an observer-side inference of youthfulness, health, and alertness drawn from the eye and periocular region. Five cue domains are evaluated: periocular contrast, scleral coloration, scleral exposure, limbal ring prominence, and iris luminance and framing. Evidence ranges from strong (periocular contrast; limbal ring health effects) to contested (the direction of the pupil-size effect). Two experimentally confirmed interactions, one so far shown only with non-human primate faces, suggest that the cues work jointly. Together they also expose confounds that single-cue designs miss. Chief among them, the limbal ring health effect appears to be carried substantially by scleral brightening. Within cue-based overgeneralization theory, the construct has two channels with pre-specified routing. Photometric cues carry youth and health to the valence dimension of face evaluation. Structural cues make the eye legible, which observers read as alertness, and are predicted to reach the dominance dimension as well. The construct is specified precisely enough to be falsified, and an analysis of an existing normed corpus could decide it.

articles.title: Caregiver prosody coincides with infant sustained visual attention
articles.authors: Manash Sahoo; Valerie Bambha; Chen Yu; Linda B. Smith; Jeremy Isaac Borjon
articles.abstract: Prosodic modifications in caregiver speech are related to infant attention, word learning, and long-term language development, yet how moment-to-moment caregiver prosody relates to infant attentional dynamics during naturalistic interaction remains unclear. Here, we used unsupervised learning to categorize 12,311 caregiver utterances produced during free play across the second year of life (12-24 months) into four prosodic contour types: fall, hill, rise, and valley. Infant visual attention was measured using head-mounted eye-tracking. Proportions of contour types were stable from 12 to 24 months. Despite this stability, specific contours were temporally coordinated with the onset and offset of infant sustained visual attention (SVA). Rise contours coincided with the initiation of SVA in older infants, beginning approximately one second before onset, and valley contours coincided with the period following SVA offset in both age groups. At the dyad level, two patterns emerged. Caregivers who produced higher levels of vocalizations that coincided with the onset or offset of SVA had infants with more SVA episodes and total SVA time overall. Further, caregivers who exhibited a specific prosodic pattern in the two seconds following SVA disengagement, a fall contour in the first second and a valley contour in the following second, had infants with longer average SVA episodes.  These results dissociate two facets of dyadic temporal coordination: a broad association between caregiver prosody and the quantity of SVA episodes, and a specific post-disengagement prosodic pattern linked to the duration of SVA.

articles.title: The Association Between SES and Students’ Achievement Motivation in Secondary School: An Individual Participant Data Meta-Analysis Spanning Two Decades of PISA Data
articles.authors: Sarah Grünthal; Lena Keller; Julia Kretschmann; Hanna Dumont; Martin Brunner
articles.abstract: Major theoretical frameworks of achievement motivation link family socioeconomic status (SES) to students’ achievement motivation in school settings. However, systematic evidence on this association remains limited. This study presents the first meta-analysis on this topic, using representative individual participant data (IPD) from the Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA). The analysis included 485 student samples comprising a total of 3,576,278 15-year-old students, spanning four SES indicators, eight achievement motivation components, four academic domains, 92 countries, and eight assessment cycles across more than two decades (2000–2022). The average meta-analytic association between SES and achievement motivation was small (r = .10, 95% CI [.09, .11]), indicating slightly higher achievement motivation among students from higher-SES families. The magnitude of the association varied meaningfully across SES indicators and motivational components, but only marginally across academic domains. Educational home resources (e.g., books, educational materials) showed stronger associations with achievement motivation than parental education or occupational status, and self-efficacy exhibited the largest association among motivational components. The association increased over historical time but declined following the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic. After controlling for academic achievement, the meta-analytic average association between family SES and achievement motivation remained statistically significant, but its magnitude was attenuated. These nuanced findings highlight the complex association between family SES and students’ achievement motivation, emphasizing the multidimensionality of both constructs and providing an important empirical foundation for evaluating, refining, and advancing psychological theories that address the link between family SES and students’ achievement motivation.

articles.title: Orthographic retrieval unfolds in parallel with single-word production
articles.authors: Jens Roeser; Pablo Aros Muñoz; Markus Damian; Gary Jones; Mark Torrance
articles.abstract: Written word production is often assumed to begin after the relevant spelling has been retrieved. We challenge this pre-onset assumption by asking whether spelling-related processing can continue during output. Across four picture-word interference experiments (Ns = 60, 72, 96, 93), participants typed or spoke picture names while ignoring pronounceable non-word distractors. Distractors either preserved the target-compatible spelling pattern or introduced a phonologically plausible alternative spelling; only the latter should disrupt writing if phonology makes alternative spellings relevant during orthographic retrieval. Bayesian mixed-effects mixture models estimated the probability that response-onset latencies and post-onset intervals came from a longer-duration component. Spelling-mismatch distractors sometimes facilitated onset responses but increased long-duration probability at later timings and within typed words. These late mismatch effects disappeared for spoken responses. These time-course data challenge the classical assumption that written words are mentally prepared as complete spellings before output begins; instead, orthographic retrieval can remain vulnerable to phonologically plausible alternatives during written production.

articles.title: Item-dropping to improve in-sample Cronbach's alpha can harm true reliability: A Monte Carlo simulation
articles.authors: Ze Freeman; Ian Hussey
articles.abstract: Cronbach’s alpha is the most commonly reported metric of reliability in psychological measurement, and statistical software encourages a common post hoc revision: dropping the item whose removal most improves in-sample alpha. A Monte Carlo simulation examined what this practice does to true reliability, varying items per scale (5 to 40) and sample size (20 to 1,000), with item pools generated from a loading distribution fitted to 3,783 factor loadings from real psychological scales. Two strategies, always dropping the nominated item or dropping only when in-sample alpha improves, were evaluated against the population alpha and true reliability of the retained items. The bias in the reported alpha itself was modest, overstating true reliability only in short scales at small samples and understating it elsewhere. The decision was another matter: at the smallest scale and sample size, dropping reduced true reliability in 46.7% of the replications in which the conditional rule acted, despite requiring an apparent improvement, and almost the entire apparent gain was selection optimism. Stricter decision rules helped only in large samples: with N of 200 or more, acting only on apparent gains above .02 kept the probability of harming the scale at or below 7%, whereas at N = 20 no threshold examined made the decision safe. Because this risk depends on scale length and sample size, given loadings typical of trait scales, it is knowable before data are collected, whereas nothing inside the alpha-if-item-removed table distinguishes a genuinely weak item from a sampling artefact.

articles.title: A multidimensional normative database of experiential ratings for German nouns
articles.authors: Cristina Cara; Christian Bellebaum; Laura Bechtold; Marta Ghio
articles.abstract: Theories of semantic representation propose that concepts are grounded in multiple forms of experience, yet normative resources capturing this multidimensionality remain scarce, especially in German. We present a database of experiential ratings for 1,985 German nouns, with particularly broad coverage of abstract concepts (a 3:1 ratio of abstract to concrete nouns). In total, 354 native German speakers rated the extent to which the meaning of each word is associated with 16 experiential dimensions spanning perceptual, motor, affective, cognitive, social and magnitude-related domains, complemented by concreteness and familiarity ratings. The database additionally provides the dominant experiential dimension of each word and an exclusivity score quantifying how strongly its profile is dominated by a single dimension relative to the others. Cross-database validation against existing German norms showed strong convergence with our concreteness, valence, and arousal ratings. Longitudinal test-retest assessment of all experiential dimensions, as well as concreteness and familiarity, in a subsample of 36 participants showed moderate to high temporal stability across ratings. To characterize the multidimensional structure captured by the database, we further applied exploratory factor analysis followed by hierarchical clustering in the factor-derived semantic space. These analyses identified three broad factors interpreted as socioemotional, perceptual, and magnitude-related, and four clusters of words with distinct experiential profiles. Summary-level and participant-level data are freely available through the project website, which also provides an interactive interface for exploring the norms. The database provides a resource for research on conceptual representation in psycholinguistics, cognitive neuroscience, and computational semantics.

articles.title: Vocal Evaluation of Classical Singing in a Concert Hall: Perceptual and Acoustic Associations with Overall Scores in Male and Female Singers
articles.authors: Haruka Kondo; Sotaro Kondoh; Shinya Fujii
articles.abstract:
Introduction. In classical vocal competitions, judges reduce a performance to a single overall score, yet what that score reflects is unclear. Research has separately identified the perceptual attributes experts use and the acoustic features of trained singers. Few studies link these to expert evaluation, and those that do have used playback of sound-treated recordings and rarely tested for sex differences. Yet classical singing is judged live in halls, and male and female voices differ acoustically. We asked which attributes and acoustic features are associated with the overall score in a concert hall, and whether they differ by sex.
Methods. Twenty-two classical singers (10 males, 12 females) performed Caro mio ben a cappella in a concert hall. Five singer-instructors rated each performance on a 100-point overall score and 7-point scales for six vocal attributes. Singing power ratio (SPR), loudness units full scale (LUFS), vibrato rate (VR), and vibrato extent (VE) were computed from annotated vowel segments of close-microphone recordings. Linear mixed-effects models related the overall score to the ratings or acoustic features, with sex interactions and a random judge intercept.
Results. Higher ratings of vibrato, resonance, and expressiveness were associated with higher overall scores, whereas timbre, diction, and intonation were not. Higher SPR, greater VE, and lower VR were associated with higher overall scores, whereas LUFS was not. Sex interacted with VE and VR but not with SPR or LUFS: the VE association was stronger in females, the VR association in males.
Conclusion. Overall scores were associated with perceived vibrato, resonance, and expressiveness, and with spectral prominence at 2–4 kHz. Vibrato associations were sex-dependent: a faster rate accompanied lower scores in males, a greater extent higher scores in females. These findings give expert evaluation a measurable basis under realistic conditions and indicate that vibrato should be interpreted with reference to singer sex.

articles.title: Inhabiting digital ecologies: A qualitative approach to good digital practices
articles.authors: Esther Paniagua; Myriam Durán Vilches; Noemí Robles; Pepa Barral González; Manuel Armayones
articles.abstract:
The integration of digital technologies into everyday life has produced complex digital
ecologies in which platforms, algorithms, and social practices jointly shape experience,
identity, and emotional regulation. Although research on digital well-being has
increased significantly, little is known about how individuals reflect on their digital lives
and the practical criteria they develop to navigate these environments while preserving
well-being and autonomy.,This paper addresses these questions through qualitative
research conducted within a digital community of 100 adults residing in Spain whose
participation unfolded across four successive waves. Fieldwork combined individual
journals, thematic forums, and an open social space, generating a longitudinal corpus
on the everyday experience of inhabiting digital spaces. Results were interpreted
through discourse analysis to reconstruct shared patterns of meaning and discursive
positions.,Findings reveal an ambivalent relationship with digital environments: the
same tools that enable connection, communication, and access to information are also
described as sources of noise, overstimulation, attention fragmentation, and loss of
control. Alongside these discomforts, participants describe daily repertoires of
adjustment that crystallise into distinct discursive positions from which they inhabit
digital ecologies and develop good practices.,We propose that good digital practices
should not be understood as a universal list of self-regulatory norms, but as relational
competencies developed through reflection and experience. Methodologically, the
study shows that a digital community is a particularly suitable tool for examining
everyday, complex, largely automated phenomena, since it enables participants to
observe, compare, and transform their digital experience into practical criteria guiding
their relationship with digital ecologies.

articles.title: Questionable mediated effect of family functioning on college students’ differentiation of the self: A comment on Luo et al. (2026)
articles.authors: Kimmo Sorjonen
articles.abstract: Drawing on the covariance matrix reported by Luo et al., I reassessed the empirical basis of their mediation model linking family malfunctioning to decreased differentiation of self. I demonstrate that the observed covariance structure can be reproduced by a theoretically different latent-variable model that does not rely on the directional mechanism proposed in the original article. In this alternative account, self-reported family malfunctioning, loneliness, psychological security, and differentiation of self are conceptualized as indicators of a broader construct, core self-evaluation. The results illustrate a broader inferential problem in psychological research: multiple theoretically plausible models may provide equally adequate explanations of the same correlational pattern. Consequently, observational associations alone offer limited grounds for preferring one explanation over competing alternatives. Researchers should therefore routinely evaluate alternative models when drawing inferences about psychological mechanisms from nonexperimental data.

articles.title: Made in the Culture, Not the Voice: Lyrical Camp, Production Texture, and the Queer Anthemization of Popular Songs
articles.authors: Logan Barrett
articles.abstract: Why do some popular songs become queer anthems while others, including many by openly queer artists, do not? We tested musical affordance and historical contingency accounts in a purposive corpus of 100 songs (69 artists) designed to dissociate queer authorship, explicit queer lyrical content, and community adoption. Adoption was measured as an evidence-coded anthemization score from URL-verified documentation of Pride, drag, ballroom, club, activist, and queer-media use. Anthemization was unrelated to whether artists were publicly queer (rs = −.02) and only weakly related to explicit queer lyrics (rs = .22). Among 16 language-model-coded lyrical themes, camp potential predicted anthemization after family-wise correction and controls for era, genre, authorship, and explicit content (partial r = .40, n = 55). The association replicated with masked lyrics, among songs the coding model could not identify, with a second coding model, and with two independent outcome coders (partial r = .45–.54, n = 46), although it was not robust when the model's own anthem judgements were also partialled out. Full-mix acoustic descriptors related to formant energy and voicing predicted anthemization (|rs| = .38–.43, family-wise p < .05) but vanished when computed on Demucs-separated vocal stems (n = 80), locating the acoustic signal in production texture rather than the singer's voice; spectral brightness was confounded by genre and era. Outcome reliability was moderate (weighted κ = .57). The results support reception-centred accounts of musical queerness. They implicate lyrical camp and production as affordances for queer adoption, not a characteristic queer voice.

articles.title: One Gender Axis, Two Vocabularies: How People Conceptualize Gendered Speaking and Singing Voices
articles.authors: Logan Barrett
articles.abstract: Gender-affirming voice care is organized around speech, yet many people also want to change how they sing. Whether the two rest on one concept of vocal gender is unknown. Participants (N = 2,536) described what makes a speaking voice and a singing voice sound feminine and masculine, rated their current and ideal voices in each modality, and named people whose speaking and singing voices they would like to have. I embedded the descriptions with a sentence encoder and analyzed them, together with word frequencies, in exploratory analyses. The feminine–masculine direction in speaking descriptions was nearly identical to the direction in singing descriptions (cosine = .967), and a classifier trained on one modality separated the other with almost no loss (area under the curve = .960 and .979). The shared direction was carried by register, softness, and depth words; singing descriptions added range, notes, and power, and speaking descriptions added softness, roughness, and monotony. Individuals’ own contrasts aligned only modestly across modalities (mean cosine = .362). Wanting a more feminine speaking voice predicted choosing a female singer but not a more acoustically feminine singer within gender category. Vocal gender appears to be a shared, category-level abstraction expressed in modality-specific vocabulary.

articles.title: Using Artificial Intelligence to estimate how common alcohol references and alcohol-related brand references are among influencers on Instagram
articles.authors: Jack Delmenico; Dan Anderson-Luxford; Emmanuel Kuntsche; Jingda Du; Zhen Du; Megan Cook; Charlotte Jonhston; Paula O'Brien; Simone Pettigrew; Benjamin Riordan
articles.abstract:
Background: Young people spend hours on social media every day, where following influencers is the norm. Influencers post frequently about alcohol and alcohol brands and there has been a rise in influencer marketing. However, prevalence estimates rely on manual analyses of only a small number of posts. We used a large language model (LLM) to estimate at scale how often top Australian Instagram influencers reference alcohol and alcohol brands, and whether this varies by influencer type.
Methods: We identified 988 of the most-followed Australian Instagram influencers and retrieved all 667,531 of their posts that were visible to all users, including those under 18 (i.e., not age gated). An LLM classified whether each post referenced alcohol and these were screened manually to record brand references. Influencers were coded into 14 types (e.g., athletes, actors).
Results: Most influencers (87.45%) referenced alcohol and 47.10% referenced an alcohol brand in at least one post. Overall, 20,448 posts (3.06%) referenced alcohol and 2,869 (0.43%) a brand (14% of alcohol-related posts). Food influencers posted the most alcohol and brand-related content, while athletes posted the least alcohol-related content but had the highest proportion referencing a brand.
Conclusions: Influencer alcohol-related and alcohol-related brand content is pervasive on Instagram and reaches audiences of every age, including those under 18 who should not see alcohol advertising.
So what: Given the link between exposure and use, health promotion should aim policies and strategies at reducing alcohol-related content, particularly branded content that likely reflects influencer marketing.

articles.title: From Named Voice to Measured Sound: A Recording-to-Representation Pipeline and a Leakage-Safe Protocol for Repeated-Stimulus Designs
articles.authors: Logan Barrett
articles.abstract: People routinely name a singer they would ideally sound like. Turning that named exemplar into a measurable acoustic target, and asking whether a person’s verbal concept of a gendered voice predicts the sound they select, requires a reproducible bridge from catalog metadata to validated vocal acoustics and an evaluation protocol that cannot be satisfied by memorizing which artists appear in training. I describe both. A recording-to-representation pipeline (exemplar resolution, preview retrieval, vocal-stem isolation, eGeMAPS and singing-specific feature extraction, and artist-mean aggregation with reliability filtering) yielded acoustic profiles for 113 artists from 1,690 tracks, linked to 1,546 of 2,536 participants. In a discovery, confirmation, and hold-out design specified in a dated analysis plan, the desired direction of vocal change predicted the acoustic gender profile of the chosen singer, but its generalization to artists never seen in training did not meet the plan-specified criterion once a leakage step was corrected (retention 67.2%, 95% CI [.23, .88]), whereas participants’ specific verbal descriptions added no acoustic information beyond gender category and popularity (a bounded null). A contrastive two-tower model, retrained under a corrected protocol, also recovered no structure beyond that category. I provide the protocol in reusable form: blocking by the repeating stimulus, a retention ratio that diagnoses memorization, a chance-corrected retrieval metric, a leakage audit, and a runnable worked example.

articles.title: Does collective identification with moral convictions explain intolerance? Not just “us” versus “them”
articles.authors: Pierce D. Ekstrom; Lindsay Novak
articles.abstract: Although people often tolerate disagreement in attitude domains that concern matters of personal taste or social convention, they are much less tolerant of disagreement about moral convictions—attitudes that they construe as matters of right and wrong. The current studies test a novel theory that this ostensibly unique intolerance for moral disagreement is simply a special case of identity-based prejudice. This theory holds that moral convictions are identity-central components of the collective self, and that intolerance for moral disagreement can be explained by a tendency to use moral convictions to distinguish a moral “us” from an immoral “them.” Consistent with this theory, we found that moral conviction was associated with both self-report and reaction-time measures of identity centrality with remarkable consistency, suggesting that relatively moralized attitudes are almost always at least relatively central to the self-concept. We also found (using a recall-based task of social categorization) that participants were more likely to use their moral convictions to categorize others to the extent that participants identified with those convictions. Inconsistent with our theory, however, we found that political and social intolerance for moral disagreement were unrelated to social categorization processes; moreover, participants’ collective identification with the group of people who shared their moral convictions accounted for little if any of the link between attitude-level moral conviction and intolerance for dissimilar others. We conclude that although moral convictions are very often central to identity and invoke collectives of like-minded others, moral disagreement is not just a matter of “us” versus “them.”

articles.title: When Humor Lands or Flops: Exploring Positive and Negative Aspects of Dad Joke Experiences
articles.authors: Paul Joseph Silvia; Vi Bui
articles.abstract: What do people experience when they encounter jokes? Feelings of comic amusement—finding something funny—are the heart of effective humor, but emotional reactions to humor can be complex, as studies of sexual, disparaging, dark, and cringe humor have found. The present research explored a range of experiences to dad jokes, a joke genre marked by clean, affable content and comedic devices founded on wordplay, particularly puns and literalism. A sample of adults (n = 541) read 24 jokes from a large pool and rated each one on several dimensions (funny, interesting, irritating, boring, and confusing). Individual differences in these joke experiences formed two factors related to appeal and aversion, and stable lasso models found that people who found the jokes more appealing were distinguished by demographic features (having children and being more educated, religious, and subjectively affluent), humor self-concepts (identifying as a funny person and having a background in humor), and personality traits (being higher in agreeableness and lower in openness to experience). No stable predictors were found for joke aversiveness. The findings support the 3-WD model of humor, which proposes funniness and aversiveness as general dimensions of humor experience, and illustrate the value of studying specific joke genres instead of an abstract category of verbal humor.

articles.title: The Hierarchical Structure of Antagonism as a Predictor of Suicidal Thoughts and Behaviors
articles.authors: Timothy Allen; Michelle M. Berry; Shreya Sheth; Aliona Tsypes; Alexandre Dombrovski
articles.abstract:
Antagonism is a transdiagnostic dimension of psychopathology associated with interpersonal dysfunction, a central feature of theories of suicide risk. However, little work has evaluated how antagonism or its lower-order components relate to suicidal thoughts and behaviors (STB). We examined the hierarchical structure and external validity of antagonism in 496 adults enrolled in a longitudinal study enriched for personality pathology and suicide risk. Hierarchical factor analysis recovered five lower-order facets—dishonesty, grandiosity, callousness, aggression, and hostile distrust—closely replicating prior structural work. We tested associations of higher-order antagonism and these facets with lifetime and prospective suicide attempts, attempt lethality, and prospective suicidal ideation. Higher-order antagonism was associated with lifetime attempt history but no other outcomes. At the facet level, hostile distrust was associated with lifetime attempt history and greater likelihood and severity of prospective ideation; dishonesty predicted greater attempt lethality, whereas
callousness predicted lower lethality. Contrary to expectations, aggression was associated with lower lifetime and prospective attempt risk. Controlling for neuroticism attenuated several associations, including those of higher-order antagonism and hostile distrust with lifetime attempt history. These findings support a reproducible lower-order structure of antagonism and demonstrate that associations between the antagonism
domain and STB are modest, and in some cases, reflective of shared variance with negative emotionality.

articles.title: Accounts Balanced: The Contingent Role of Rhetoric in Who Survives Political Scandal
articles.authors: Pierce D. Ekstrom; Marti Hope Gonzales; Allison Williams; Elliot Weiner; Rafael Aguilera
articles.abstract: When accused of misconduct in their private or public lives, people choose whether to apologize or to defend their character or reputation. Previous experiments have found that when misconduct is severe or offends outgroup members, transgressors may benefit by defending themselves and denying culpability for wrongdoing. In this study, we explore whether these tendencies can successfully reduce politicians’ accountability for wrongdoing in the context of a U.S. congressional election. We constructed a novel dataset documenting Representatives’ public remarks in response the 1992 House Bank Scandal, during which Representatives from both major parties were accused of misusing funds. Contrary to predictions, conciliatory remarks were not associated with electoral failure among more severe House Bank “offenders.” Consistent with predictions, defensive remarks (refusals) lost their typical association with electoral failure when the incumbent’s party controlled the district. Results suggest that groups may allow their leaders to escape blame for wrongdoing and retain power.

articles.title: Inhabiting digital ecologies: A qualitative approach to good digital practices
articles.authors: Esther Paniagua; Myriam Durán Vilches; Noemí Robles; Pepa Barral González; Manuel Armayones

articles.title: Engaging residents in district heating retrofit:  A qualitative evaluation of a mine water heat network project in the United Kingdom
articles.authors: Michael A. Smith; Faye Doughty; Danielle Goldring; Helen Simmons
articles.abstract: The expansion of district heat networks (DHNs) is central to achieving net zero heating targets, yet social acceptance remains a major barrier to large-scale domestic retrofit. Although resident engagement is widely recognised as critical to addressing these barriers, there is little empirical evidence evaluating how engagement strategies operate during live retrofit projects. This study addresses this gap through a qualitative evaluation of the resident support and engagement approach employed during the connection of 16 existing low-rise homes to a mine water DHN in the United Kingdom. Data were collected from 18 stakeholders, including residents, local authority officers and construction contractors. The findings demonstrate that effective engagement extends beyond the provision of information. Social acceptance was strengthened through opportunities to build trusting relationships, meaningful resident involvement in decision-making, early engagement, and adaptations that responded to residents' accessibility needs. Participants also highlighted the importance of organisational coordination, accessible communication materials, clear points of contact, and the use of trusted community networks and lived experience to enhance the credibility of project information. These findings suggest that successful DHN retrofit depends not only on technical delivery but also on engagement processes that foster trust, agency and equitable participation. The present study provides the first qualitative evaluation of resident engagement during a live mine water DHN retrofit project and offers practical recommendations for engaging residents during the design and delivery of future DHN projects.

articles.title: Testing Alternative Approaches to Manipulation of Environmental Self-Identity: Behavior Recall, Anchoring, and Category-Range Manipulations
articles.authors: Jan Urban; Štěpán Bahník; Markéta Braun Kohlová
articles.abstract: Environmental self-identity, defined as the extent to which an individual sees themselves as an environmentally friendly person, has become an important concept in environmental psychology. One of the reasons for the prominence of environmental self-identity is that it has been proposed as one of the causal factors of pro-environmental behavior. Experimental studies of environmental self-identity have relied on a recall manipulation that alters the frequency scales on which people report their past pro- and anti-environmental behaviors, thus making past pro- or anti-environmental behaviors more salient. In the current study, we tested two additional alternative approaches to experimental manipulation of environmental self-identity. These rely on two powerful strategies of changing the perception of one’s past behavior, namely anchoring manipulation and category-range manipulation. We conducted a high-power web-based study (N = 4,139) to assess and compare the efficacy of the behavioral-recall manipulation and the two alternative approaches of manipulating environmental self-identity and affecting pro-environmental intention. We found substantial evidence that the three manipulations altered people's self-reports of their past pro-environmental behavior, but this did not change environmental self-identity. Evidence also favored no effect on environmental intention for the recall and anchoring manipulations, whereas evidence for the category-range manipulation was inconclusive. Other manipulations of environmental self-identity that do not rely on self-perception theory are needed for experimental research on environmental self-identity. Practical interventions are unlikely to influence pro-environmental behavior merely by highlighting or changing people's records of their past behavior.

articles.title: Cultural and Personality Predictors of Attitudes Toward AI Chatbots: A Systematic Literature  Review
articles.authors: Michelle Ming Ertl; Katherine Moore
articles.abstract:
As AI chatbots are becoming increasingly relevant in our daily life, understanding what shapes
people’s attitudes toward them is becoming more important. This systematic literature review
brings together the findings of 34 articles (from across multiple countries) to examine how
personality traits and one’s cultural background predict attitudes towards AI chatbots. The
review suggests that culture works as a primary filter that sets a person’s starting position when
they encounter AI. Western users tend to approach chatbots with more skepticism and stronger
privacy concerns, while on the other hand East Asian users show higher comfort with social AI
interaction. Within each of these cultural settings, individual personality traits fine-tune these
responses, but which trait matters most changes depending on the culture. Agreeableness
drives trust in Western samples, while Conscientiousness drives trust in Arab ones. Technology
specific variables like Personal Innovativeness in Information Technology (PIIT) and AI
configuration anxiety turned out to be stronger predictors than broad personality traits overall.
The review also identifies a persistent global gender gap in AI adaptation that operates
differently depending on cultural setting. Limitations include the overrepresentation of young
university educated participants in existing research, the Western bias present in both study
samples and AI training data, and the ongoing confusion between physical robot findings and
text-based chatbot research. The paper concludes that effective chatbot design and AI policy
require culturally adapted approaches rather than one-size-fits-all solutions.

articles.title: Caregivers’ multimodal actions scaffold word learning in the preschool years
articles.authors: Antonia Jordan-Barros; Francesco Cabiddu; Ed Donnellan; Yan Gu; Gabriella Vigliocco
articles.abstract: Children learn language in face-to-face interactions with their caregivers where they are continuously exposed to multimodal input in which verbal content is combined with non-verbal signals (e.g., caregivers looking and pointing at an object while naming it). However, little is known about how caregivers’ use of the full range of multimodal behaviours is linked to children’s word learning. Using the ECOLANG Corpus, we examined how caregivers’ multimodal behaviours predict children’s word learning during a semi-naturalistic parent-child interaction. Thirty-seven caregivers (age: 29-48, 36 female; British and American English speakers) interacted with their child (age: 3-4, 19 female) talking about 12 unknown objects for 30 minutes. Caregivers’ verbal (e.g., label repetitions, speaking rate) and non-verbal (e.g., points, gaze, gestures) behaviours were annotated and used as predictors in regression analyses of children’s learning of the novel object labels along with child vocabulary scores.
