Results showed that, in the verbal domain, caregivers’ use of high pitch and more lexically diverse speech were associated with better word learning, while caregivers’ use of representational gestures was a significant non-verbal predictor. In particular, using more representational gestures when labelling unknown objects predicted better word learning specifically for children with lower vocabulary scores, suggesting that non-verbal cues such as manual gestures can provide additional support for children with less advanced linguistic abilities. This work presents the first comprehensive investigation of the combined role of verbal and non-verbal caregivers’ behaviours and provides robust evidence that multimodal caregiver communication can shape preschool-aged children’s lexical development.

articles.title: The Impasse Model: A Clinical Formulation Framework for Understanding Psychological Impasse and Restoring Movement
articles.authors: Clare Layhe
articles.abstract:
Psychological impasse is defined here as a state in which change, resolution or 
movement is experienced as necessary or desired, yet no sufficiently viable route can currently 
be perceived, accessed or enacted. The Impasse Model arose from collaborative clinical 
formulations in which people were often highly mobilised rather than passive. They had 
explained, repaired, problem-solved, pursued reassurance, withdrawn or protected themselves, 
yet their available field of action had progressively narrowed. Relational difficulty and 
mismatches in communication or understanding were recurrent, though not universal, pathways. 
The model identifies impasse as a clinically useful warning point before higher-cost coping or 
protective responses become necessary. Formulation then proceeds in two directions: backwards, 
to understand how viable movement became restricted and forwards, to identify the smallest 
change capable of reopening it. Existing literatures on entrapment, action crisis, psychological 
inflexibility, hopelessness, decisional conflict, uncertainty and systemic constraint overlap 
substantially with this territory. The proposed contribution is therefore not a new universal 
mechanism but a clinically organised formulation framework whose distinctiveness and utility 
are open to empirical test.
Keywords: psychological impasse, formulation, entrapment, trauma, dissociation, anxiety, 
systemic formulation, EMDR, therapeutic intervention

articles.title: Affect and Words: An Instrument for the Quantitative Analysis of Emotional Vocabulary in Open-ended Responses.
articles.authors: Nigel Manchini; Óliver Jiménez; Natalia Sylvia Ramos Díaz; Daniel Trias
articles.abstract: In a context where emotions play a central role in discussions on psychology and education, the availability of various techniques and resources to assess emotional experience becomes essential. Quantitative language analysis provides a window to emotional experiences, rarely used in Spanish-speaking contexts. This study develops and cross-culturally validates an annotated dictionary of explicit emotional vocabulary, a tool for analyzing affective variables from texts and open-ended responses. A systematic protocol and expert judgment were used to select and annotate 1,041 lexical families (3,051 lemmas and 18,934 words), and pre-recorded hypotheses about the validity of the instrument were tested. Participants, adolescents from Uruguay (n = 1,208, 59% female, age M = 14.4) and Spain (n = 596, 41% female, age M = 15.7), completed Subjective Well-Being (SWB) scales and wrote about their emotional experiences in an open-ended response. The dictionary showed convergence with other instruments and acceptable inter-rater reliability. When applied to open-ended responses, it captured a substantial proportion of the words written by participants and showed significant correlations with SWB in both the Uruguayan and Spanish samples. These results suggest that quantitative analysis of open-ended responses allows the exploration of well-being, and that this freely available instrument is a valid resource for doing so, serving as a complement to quantitative and qualitative approaches for research or intervention purposes.

articles.title: Two sides of the same coin in memory: Speech and its accompanying gesture are remembered together
articles.authors: Yang Liu; Tilo Kircher; Luyao Chen; Yifei He; Benjamin Straube
articles.abstract: When a speaker gestures, speech and gesture form one multimodal event. Memory research mostly asks how gestures help people remember speech, not how the gesture is remembered or how the two relate. Participants watched videos of an actor speaking sentences with a related gesture or none (Experiment 1, N = 20), or a related or unrelated gesture (Experiment 2, N = 43). They recognized written sentences and, for each called old, judged whether a gesture had been present (Experiment 1) or related (Experiment 2), with confidence ratings. Recognition was better after related than unrelated gestures, but not better after related gestures than none. Gesture judgments were above chance and more accurate for confidently recognized sentences; for these, participants also tended to report non-matching gestures as matching (Experiment 2). Gesture reports thus appear partly retrieved with the sentence and partly inferred from it: memory for speech and gesture is closely coupled.

articles.title: Labvanced Eye Tracking 2.0: validation of webcam eye tracking with 494 unsupervised online participants
articles.authors: Caspar Goeke
articles.abstract: Webcam eye tracking has already become a powerful tool for online behavioral research, and the first generation of Labvanced's system was validated against an EyeLink 1000 in the laboratory at an accuracy of about 1.4° of visual angle (Kaduk et al., 2023). Several questions remained open. How much of that accuracy survives the uncontrolled conditions of a real online study? Why do some participants deliver far worse data than others, and can they be identified before a researcher pays for them? Can the calibration be shortened to make it more practical in ordinary online studies? And what should happen to participants who do not pass it, or otherwise do not qualify? Here we show how we improved eye-tracking accuracy, while simultaneously shortening the calibration, simplifying the setup, and optimizing the whole procedure for real online data collection with our partner Prolific. We then validated the system in seven recording batches with about 500 completed participants of a 45-target accuracy task, and publish their anonymized data so that every result can be verified. With our new standard calibration (about 2 minutes) and balanced screening, the median participant's error was 5.2 % of the screen diagonal, 1.8° of visual angle on a laptop at 60 cm. And with the 5 minute calibration and very strict screening, the median accuracy of online participants reached 4 % of the screen diagonal, which is equal to 1.4° of visual angle at a standard distance. In summary, with this release of Eye Tracking 2.0, we show that the accuracy reported in our peer-reviewed laboratory comparison can be replicated online

articles.title: Irregular Natural Environments Are Associated with Better Context-Supported Recall
articles.authors: Dylan Chau Huynh; Aja Khalid Hussein; Lars Brorson Fich; Zakaria Djebbara
articles.abstract: Natural environments are often treated as a relatively uniform category in cognitive research despite substantial variation in their spatial organization and regularity. This study examined whether episodic memory depends not only on environmental type but also on the internal structure of the environment. Sixty participants experienced four immersive virtual environments in a 2 × 2 within-subject design crossing environmental type (natural vs. urban) with structural regularity (rhythmic vs. irregular). Memory was assessed using free, cued, and delayed recall and analyzed using linear mixed-effects models controlling for presentation order. Immediate recall showed little evidence of environmental effects. In contrast, Cued Recall 1 showed a significant Environment × Regularity interaction, with the irregular natural environment producing the highest performance. Follow-up contrasts showed higher recall in irregular nature than in all three comparison conditions for Cued Recall 1 and Delayed Recall, with a more selective advantage during Cued Recall 2. Retention proportions did not differ across conditions, indicating that delayed differences reflected earlier memory advantages rather than differential forgetting. These findings suggest that episodic memory effects associated with natural environments cannot be understood through a nature–urban distinction alone. Instead, the internal organization of an environment may shape memory, with irregular natural environments potentially providing more distinctive contextual information that becomes particularly useful during context-supported retrieval.

articles.title: Understanding age-related changes in choice stepping responses using the diffusion decision model
articles.authors: Sarah Anne Kemp; Niek Stevenson; Marlee Jay Wells; Rebecca Healey; Daina L Sturnieks; Stephen R Lord; Mark R. Hinder; Andrew Heathcote; Rebecca Jane St George
articles.abstract: Stepping responses slow markedly with age, posing a significant risk for falls, yet the cognitive and motor mechanisms driving this slowing remain poorly understood. The diffusion decision model (DDM), which jointly accounts for response times and accuracy, has been used to disentangle the cognitive, sensorimotor and strategic contributors to age-related slowing in upper-limb tasks. We extended this approach to a choice reaction time task with three response conditions: finger (button press), foot (seated foot tap), and step (forward step initiation from quiet standing) to determine if the reasons for age-related slowing differ across upper- and lower-limb responses and stepping responses involving the additional complexity of postural control. Healthy older adults (n = 54) responded more slowly than younger adults (n = 28) across all response conditions. DDM analysis indicated that older adults showed slower evidence accumulation rates and longer non-decision times than younger adults, reflecting less efficient information processing and slower motor execution, respectively. Younger adults also required more evidence than older adults to trigger a decision during stepping, but not in the finger or foot responses. Together, these findings indicate that age-related slowing of choice stepping is driven primarily by reduced information-processing efficiency and prolonged non-decision processes, rather than by increased response caution during action selection. More broadly, these findings demonstrate that cognitive modelling can be extended beyond traditional upper-limb tasks and applied to postural decision making in older adults to characterise the mechanisms contributing to slowed stepping, offering a foundation for targeted therapeutic interventions.

articles.title: “Puzzling, Yet So Refreshing”: Experiencing the Value of Neurodiversity Within an Inclusive Choir
articles.authors: Nicolas Petit; Géraldine Dessertenne; Fanny Aprile; Lucie Jurek
articles.abstract: The social challenges encountered by autistic people are increasingly understood as a double empathy problem: a mutual misunderstanding between autistic and non-autistic individuals, rather than an autistic deficit. This paradigm highlights a need for inclusive spaces that foster mutual understanding, yet this remains challenging, especially in the French sociocultural context which is less familiar with the social model of disability developed in the anglophone world. As this model stresses that the majority largely shapes the social environment, finding ways to influence the general population’s attitudes toward autism is critical. Choral singing offers a promising medium to do so and facilitate cross-neurotype dynamics, as it is thought to have evolved as a biological mechanism to foster social bonding. Accordingly, this qualitative study explored how 12 general population choristers experienced a 6-month neurodiverse choir shared with 8 autistic adolescents and 3 autism specialists. We used a two-stage qualitative design, first capturing individual experiences through an open-ended online questionnaire, and subsequently deepening our analysis through a discussion with a community stakeholder panel. The findings revealed an intrinsically demanding experience, especially emotionally and cognitively, counterbalanced by important benefits, as it was also described as joyful and powerful, encouraging personal growth among the choristers and a shift in their perceptions of autism. These findings support the neurodiversity paradigm and suggest that choral singing may offer a promising double empathy solution, facilitating intergroup contact to reduce prejudice and thereby remove social barriers to the inclusion of autistic voices.

articles.title: When the brain can change: effects of neuroplasticity education on beliefs about brain-based mental disorders
articles.authors: Olha Guley; Elena Pasquinelli; Daniel Nettle
articles.abstract: Mental disorders are increasingly framed as brain-based, which can promote pessimism about recovery. We tested whether brief education about neuroplasticity, the brain’s capacity to change throughout life, can counter these beliefs. Across three preregistered vignette experiments with UK adults (Ns = 414, 411, and 418), participants viewed a brain-framed mental disorder after either a brief neuroplasticity video and text intervention or a matched control. The intervention increased the perceived possibility of recovery, but this effect was short-lived after a single exposure in Study 1 and more durable with a booster in Study 2. The effect in Study 3 was not significant, but a pooled analysis of data from Studies 2 and 3 confirmed the positive effect overall. The intervention did not affect perceived treatment efficacy, nor did it reduce desired social distance from people with mental disorders. In Study 3, higher familiarity with the disorder was associated with a higher perceived recovery and lower desired social distance. These findings suggest neuroplasticity education can increase public optimism about recovery from mental disorders, but changing treatment beliefs or social attitudes may require more targeted interventions.

articles.title: Compassion and Awe as Eco-Emotions: Experimental Inductions and their Effect on Pro-Environmental Intentions
articles.authors: Ronan Bellemin; Aurélien GRATON; Anna Tcherkassof
articles.abstract: Eco-emotions are increasingly recognized as central psychological processes shaping how individuals perceive environmental crises and engage in collective responses. While negative eco-emotions have been widely studied, positive, self-transcendent emotions may offer more psychologically sustainable pathways to pro-environmental engagement. The present research examines two such emotions—compassion for the environment and awe at nature—and investigates their emotional profiles and social-environmental implications using experimental induction. Across two pre-registered studies, participants were exposed to situations designed to elicit compassion for the environment (Study 1; N = 165) or awe at nature (Study 2; N = 117). Participants then reported their emotional experiences, intentions to engage in pro-environmental collective actions, and provided open-ended definitions of the target emotions. Results showed that compassion and awe were successfully elicited and exhibited distinct emotional patterns. Compassion for the environment was significantly associated with higher intentions to engage in pro-environmental collective actions, whereas awe at nature was not, suggesting that eco-emotions may support different forms of social and environmental engagement. Qualitative analyses revealed conceptual overlap between French participants’ spontaneous descriptions and English-language theoretical definitions. However, contrary to recent empirical categorizations, compassion was generally considered to be a negative emotion. Together, these findings highlight the value of experimentally inducing discrete self-transcendent eco-emotions to clarify their specific emotional content and their distinct roles as socially embedded drivers of environmental engagement.

articles.title: Coming of Age in Polarized Times: Affective Polarization Across Adolescence
articles.authors: Jakob Kasper; Gijs Schumacher; Lysanne te Brinke; Eveline Crone; Bert N. Bakker
articles.abstract: Concerns about affective polarization among young people have grown in political, media, and academic debate. Yet, despite adolescence being a crucial period of identity formation and young people’s central role in shaping the future of democratic societies, little is known about when affective polarization emerges, and how it varies across adolescence and political environments. Drawing on survey data from adolescents (N = 7,031; ages 11–25) and adults (N = 9,997; ages > 25) in the Netherlands, the United Kingdom, Austria, Poland, and Greece, we examine within-adolescence age differences in affective polarization, adolescent-adult differences, and temporal variation in affective polarization levels around a major political event. We find that affective polarization is already visible by early adolescence and differs remarkably little across adolescent age groups, challenging the expectation that affective polarization increases sharply around the transition to the legal voting age. Comparisons with adults in the Netherlands, the United Kingdom, and Austria show that adolescents are consistently less affectively polarized than adults. Further, our longitudinal panel evidence from the Netherlands suggests that adolescent affective polarization varies with the broader political environment, increasing around the 2023 parliamentary election and declining thereafter. This illustrates that adolescent affective polarization is not fixed but varies with political dynamics, highlighting adolescence as an important period for educational efforts that foster democratic engagement and constructive political disagreement.

articles.title: Data-Matrix-Based Overall Goodness-of-Fit Testing for Confirmatory Factor Analysis: In-Sample Prediction Error for Observed Variables
articles.authors: Young Ze Kim; Gyeongcheol Cho; Hanjoe Kim
articles.abstract:
Conventional χ²-based tests in confirmatory factor analysis assess overall fit through covariance reproduction and remain the standard inferential tools for overall goodness-of-fit testing. However, they do not directly quantify the magnitude of model misfit and may become unavailable when estimation fails to converge or produces improper solutions.
We introduce and evaluate two data-matrix-based alternatives within structured factor analysis: the in-sample prediction error for observed variables (IPEo) test for a single model and the ΔIPEo test for nested models. IPEo quantifies the proportion of variability in the observed data matrix left unexplained by the hypothesized model, while its bootstrap p value provides an inferential decision. Monte Carlo simulations showed that the IPEo-based tests controlled Type I error, gained power with increasing sample size, and remained available when conventional χ²-based tests frequently failed. An empirical illustration further showed that the IPEo value and its p value provide complementary information about the magnitude and statistical significance of model misfit. These findings support IPEo-based testing as a complementary inferential framework for evaluating CFA model fit directly at the level of the observed data matrix.

articles.title: Ostensive affective feedback and the emergence of the capacity to negotiate communicative content: the psychology of establishing agreement.
articles.authors: Wouter Wolf
articles.abstract: Inferring agreement, that is, inferring that mental content is mutually considered to be sufficiently aligned for the purposes of an interaction, is crucial for many facets of human sociality. Importantly, humans are highly skilled at facilitating such inferences through communication. Yet even within communicative interactions, agreement might fail for interpretive reasons (uncertainty or misunderstanding) or alignment reasons (disagreement). Solving either of these problems often requires iterative communicative interactions during which the content of mental states is negotiated until misunderstandings are repaired and/or disagreements are resolved through compromise. But what social cognitive mechanisms allowed humans’ successful negotiation capacities to emerge, even when conventionalized negotiation and communication systems were not available? Here, I argue that humans developed the capacity to directly negotiate the content of communication by understanding the interactive intent underlying ostension in a previously underappreciated way: To infer a lack of agreement in communicative interactions, a key piece of evidence lies in how the other reacts to one’s communicative act. However, this reaction is often ambiguous. I argue that ostension helps facilitate interpreting such reactions, not only through assumptions of mutual relevance, but in large part due to pragmatic tension that arises from ostensive non-affirmative affective feedback. This tension forces individuals to isolate content as a separate dimension of communicative acts that can be evaluated and negotiated. This facilitates the resolution of interpretive problems through boundary-setting and disagreement through compromise. As such, ostensive feedback has likely played a major role in the emergence of human sociality.

articles.title: Loneliness and Interpersonal Emotion Regulation in Everyday Life
articles.authors: Jasmin Bruna Stariolo; Anh Tran; Kristina Mei; Katharine Helen Greenaway
articles.abstract: Loneliness is a growing public health concern rooted in emotional distress and social disconnection. Interpersonal emotion regulation — managing ones’ own or others’ emotions — is a mechanism for strengthening social bonds and fostering emotional health. Their shared socio-emotional foundation raises the possibility that loneliness may be connected to how people regulate others and are regulated in turn. Accordingly, we investigated whether loneliness is associated with adaptive and maladaptive interpersonal emotion regulation strategies in the moment and over time. To address this question, we conducted a daily diary (N = 170, collected 2020; Study 1) and experience sampling study (N = 239, collected 2021; Study 2). Participants reported on global trait loneliness, then recorded momentary loneliness and use of four strategies as both regulator (regulating others extrinsically) and target of regulation (being regulated by others intrinsically) for seven days. State loneliness predicted greater invalidation as both regulator and target, and global trait loneliness predicted less physical support as regulator and target. Most consistently, the person-level average of momentary loneliness across the week predicted greater use of all strategies — responsiveness, invalidation, reappraisal, and physical support — both as regulator and target. Methodologically, our findings show the importance of assessing loneliness at different time scales. Theoretically, our findings suggest lonely individuals do actively attempt emotion regulation during interactions, yet they may be just as likely to use maladaptive strategies that undermine connection as adaptive strategies that enhance it. This work underscores the importance of interaction quality in understanding how loneliness persists and might be interrupted.

articles.title: Confirmatory Validation of the Singing Incongruence and Gender (SInG) Scale in an Independent Sample of Transgender and Gender-Diverse Singers
articles.authors: Logan Barrett
articles.abstract:
Background: Singing-related gender incongruence can be a significant source of distress for transgender and gender-diverse (TGD) individuals, yet general measures of gender dysphoria and speaking-voice instruments do not capture this domain. The Singing Incongruence and Gender (SInG) Scale was developed to address this gap, but its four-factor structure had not been confirmed in independent data.
Methods: Participants were an entirely new sample of 232 TGD individuals (141 nonbinary, 48 transgender men, 43 transgender women), with 883 cisgender respondents retained as a comparison group for known-groups validity and measurement invariance. Confirmatory factor analysis used robust weighted least squares on a polychoric correlation matrix. I also examined reliability, construct validity, a 12-item short form, and how the scale should be scored.
Results: The four-factor structure was confirmed, with all standardized loadings between .618 and .925 and better fit than a unidimensional alternative (comparative fit index .841 versus .618). Approximate fit fell below conventional thresholds, reflecting both a low ratio of cases to the 126 estimated parameters and some redundancy of item wording; a 12-item form fit better (.930), retained reliability and validity, and performed similarly in split-half cross-validation regardless of which near-equivalent items were retained. SInG scores predicted singing-voice discrepancy beyond age, identity subgroup, and general gender dysphoria (ΔR² = .192), and TGD respondents scored higher than cisgender respondents (d = 0.59; Misgendering d = 1.12).
Conclusions: The SInG Scale captures singing-related gender incongruence beyond what a general dysphoria measure explains, and is available in a brief 12-item form suited to clinical intake and choir screening. Because the subscales bear different relations to criterion outcomes, they should be reported alongside the total score.

articles.title: Made in the Culture, Not the Voice: Lyrical Camp, Production Texture, and the Queer Anthemization of Popular Songs
articles.authors: Logan Barrett
articles.abstract: Why do some popular songs become queer anthems while others, including many by openly queer artists, do not? We tested musical affordance and historical contingency accounts in a purposive corpus of 100 songs (69 artists) designed to dissociate queer authorship, explicit queer lyrical content, and community adoption. Adoption was measured as an evidence-coded anthemization score from URL-verified documentation of Pride, drag, ballroom, club, activist, and queer-media use. Anthemization was unrelated to whether artists were publicly queer (rs = −.02) and only weakly related to explicit queer lyrics (rs = .22). Among 16 language-model-coded lyrical themes, camp potential predicted anthemization after family-wise correction and controls for era, genre, authorship, and explicit content (partial r = .40, n = 55). The association replicated with masked lyrics, among songs the coding model could not identify, with a second coding model, and with two independent outcome coders (partial r = .45–.54, n = 46), although it was not robust when the model's own anthem judgements were also partialled out. Full-mix acoustic descriptors related to formant energy and voicing predicted anthemization (|rs| = .38–.43, family-wise p < .05) but vanished when computed on Demucs-separated vocal stems (n = 80), locating the acoustic signal in production texture rather than the singer's voice; spectral brightness was confounded by genre and era. Outcome reliability was moderate (weighted κ = .57). The results support reception-centred accounts of musical queerness. They implicate lyrical camp and production as affordances for queer adoption, not a characteristic queer voice.

articles.title: A Non-Parametric Approach to Modeling Accelerated Longitudinal Designs
articles.authors: Suryadyuti Baral; Jonathan Park; Emilio Ferrer
articles.abstract: Accelerated longitudinal designs (ALDs) offer an efficient means of studying large developmental periods by combining shorter longitudinal samples across overlapping cohorts. ALDs have been used to study processes that span large developmental epochs, such as cognitive development. However, traditional parametric approaches may impose structural assumptions that limit the accurate reconstruction of individual developmental trajectories. We investigate a nonparametric functional data analytic (FDA) approach for modeling latent trajectories in accelerated longitudinal data. This method allows for the recovery of smooth, continuous time trajectories that account for both shared and idiosyncratic patterns of change. We compare the FDA approach to the continuous time latent change score model with simulations that emulate nonlinear change processes often seen in developmental research. We apply both methods to two empirical datasets with individuals aged 5- to 22-years, where each person is assessed two or three times. Our results demonstrate that the FDA method captures the shape and timing of individual trajectories more accurately beyond the observed data. These findings suggest that FDA offers a robust and flexible alternative for modeling developmental change in ALDs.

articles.title: Voice Class but Not Fach: Acoustic Correlates of Operatic Voice Types in 8,681 Historical Recordings
articles.authors: Logan Barrett
articles.abstract: The German Fach system divides operatic voices into roughly 25 categories within the familiar voice classes, distinguished by tessitura, vocal weight, timbre and agility. Whether these categories are acoustically recoverable has rarely been tested on singers a model has not seen. I analysed 8,681 public-domain 78-rpm recordings by 508 singers in 27 Fächer, labelling each singer with their documented career Fach. After a design audit, 153 singers were locked aside, 12 tests were specified in advance, and the frozen pipeline was evaluated once on the held-out singers. Seven-way voice class was recovered at a balanced accuracy of .54 (chance .15), and female-range versus male-range class at .97 without explicit pitch measures. Within a voice class, the Fach label did not generalise: tenor sub-Fach classification fell from .54 on discovery singers to .38 on held-out singers (chance .34), and no single-aspect model replicated. Treated as a continuous position on the taxonomy's tessitura ordering, however, soprano Fach was predicted on held-out singers (ρ = .44). Female-range voices in electrical-era recordings showed lower singer's-formant prominence and a higher Hammarberg index than male-range voices, differences that a synthetic audit showed are not measurement artefacts of high pitch. The Fach of the role being sung was more recoverable than the singer's label. Coarse voice class is acoustically robust; within a class, the evidence favours an ordering over the discrete categories the labels draw, and points to repertoire as part of what the labels encode.

articles.title: Multi-party simulations with human participants and role-based LLM conversational agents: A design framework and validity evidence for organizational research
articles.authors: Yuki Nozaki; Naho Fujisawa; Yoshinobu Kano
articles.abstract: Dynamic organizational phenomena often unfold through ongoing communication among multiple interdependent actors, yet studying them involves trade-offs among realism, controllability, and scalability. We propose a methodological framework for using role-based conversational agents powered by large language models (LLMs) as multi-party interaction partners in organizational research. It specifies how to create standardized but contingent interaction environments through scenario design, persona prompts, interaction protocols, and iterative testing. In a preregistered illustrative study of leadership communication, we analyzed 394 employees’ text-based simulations powered by GPT-5.2, Gemini 2.5 Flash, or Claude Sonnet 4.6. Across models, participants perceived the agents as anthropomorphic and animate, and as acting consistently with their assigned backgrounds, personalities, and linguistic styles. Behavioral coding corroborated and extended these perceptions, with deviations from assigned persona prompts in 2.59% of utterances. Participants’ utterances also yielded codable indicators of theoretically relevant behavior, in this case leadership communication. These findings provide initial validity evidence that multi-party LLM-agent simulations can create plausible interaction environments, deliver persona-consistent stimuli, and elicit behaviorally analyzable responses. We also offer practical guidelines on model selection, replicability, and ethics.

articles.title: Decision as navigation
articles.authors: Sebastijan Veselic; Elena Gutierrez; Timothy Muller; Erie Boorman; Daniel Shani; Ferran Junoy-Bosch; Carl Lindersson; Sven Petersen; Janahan Selvanayagam; Steven Kennerley
articles.abstract: Understanding choice requires explaining how the brain represents decision-relevant information and uses it to guide behaviour. Research on value-based decision-making has traditionally framed choice as assigning and comparing values, yielding significant insights into its neural basis. However, it has said less about how the structure of decision problems is represented and used during deliberation, particularly when relations between options must be inferred or reused across decision problems. Here, we review evidence suggesting that, in such choices, decision-relevant attributes are assembled into a cognitive map. In this map, options are represented as locations in a metric space, and choice can be framed as navigation. This may allow the brain to compute vector-like relations between options and reuse them across decision problems to support value comparison. By linking neuroeconomics and spatial navigation research, this framework generates testable predictions about how the brain organises and uses structured knowledge for choice.

articles.title: Christian Nationalism as a Unique Predictor of Policy Attitudes and Voting Behavior: The Christian Nationalism Scale
articles.authors: Jason Michael Miller
articles.abstract: Christian Nationalism (CN) is a unique political ideology that has long been prominent in U.S. politics. Current measures of CN have poor psychometric properties (Davis, 2023). Study 1 (n=237) shows that CN predicts voting behavior and policy attitudes when controlling for established religious and political measures and provides an initial test of the Christian Nationalism Scale. Study 2 (n=603) replicates findings that CN is the best predictor of voting behavior and policy attitudes when accounting for established religious and political measures. A CFA shows excellent psychometric properties of the scale, and invariance testing shows similar factor structure across Christian denominations and racial groups. Study 3 (n=313) finds CN best predicts support for politicians who will restrict individual freedoms on topics related to traditional Christian values. These studies demonstrate that CN explains unique variance in voting (past and anticipated) and policy attitudes. This work provides a validated scale for future research.

articles.title: The Ultimate Tutorial for AI-driven Scale Development in Generative Psychometrics: Releasing AIGENIE from its Bottle
articles.authors: Lara Lee Russell-Lasalandra; Hudson Golino; Luis Eduardo Garrido; Alexander P. Christensen
articles.abstract:
Psychological scale development has traditionally required extensive expert involvement, iterative re-
vision, andlarge-scalepilottestingbeforepsychometricevaluationcanbegin. TheAIGENIE Rpackageim-
plementstheAI-GENIEframework(AutomaticItemGenerationandValidationwithNetwork-Integrated
Evaluation), which integrates large language model (LLM) text generation with network psychometric
methods to automate the early stages of this process. The package generates candidate item pools using
LLMs, transforms them into high-dimensional embeddings, and applies a multi-step reduction pipeline
— Exploratory Graph Analysis (EGA), Unique Variable Analysis (UVA), and bootstrap EGA — to
produce structurally validated item pools entirely in silico. This tutorial introduces the package across
eight parts: installation and setup, text generation, embeddings, item generation, the full AI-GENIE
pipeline, the GENIE pipeline for researcher-supplied items, advanced prompt engineering, and fully lo-
cal operation. Two running examples illustrate the package’s use: the Big Five personality model (a
well-established construct) and AI Anxiety (an emerging construct). The package supports multiple
LLM providers (OpenAI, Anthropic, Groq, HuggingFace, and local models), offers a fully offline mode
with no external API calls, and provides the GENIE() function for researchers who wish to apply the
psychometric reduction pipeline to existing item pools regardless of their origin. The AIGENIE package
is freely available on CRAN at https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=AIGENIE.

articles.title: Dyadic Theory of Mind profile shapes verbal cooperation and the trajectory of non-verbal cooperation
articles.authors: Roksana Markiewicz; Ali Mazaheri; Katrien Segaert
articles.abstract: Theory of Mind (ToM) is thought to support cooperation, yet it is studied as a property of individuals, even though cooperation is achieved by two people together. We examined whether cooperation depends on the ToM profile of a dyad: the pair's average ToM and the mismatch (absolute difference) between partners. Unacquainted pairs completed two cooperation tasks. In a verbal task, each partner held information needed to solve a shared problem, and partners had to talk to combine it. In a non-verbal task, partners synchronised button presses without communicating, adjusting their timing based on feedback. ToM was assessed using the Movie for the Assessment of Social Cognition (MASC; Dziobek et al., 2006); fluid intelligence was controlled. Across both paradigms, we found converging evidence that cooperative performance was shaped by the interaction between partners’ ToM abilities, beyond individual ToM ability in isolation. In the verbal task (N=171 pairs), larger ToM mismatches were associated with poorer cooperative performance in pairs with relatively low average ToM, whereas higher average ToM attenuated this detrimental mismatch effect. In the non-verbal task (N=175 pairs), the same pattern emerged only over time: pairs with large ToM mismatches and relatively low average ToM improved their synchrony more slowly, so that their disadvantage was most pronounced late in the task, when cooperation depends more on anticipating the partner’s adjustments. Taken together, our findings suggest that ToM operates not only as an individual socio-cognitive capacity but also as a dyadic resource that shapes how partners establish shared representations in cooperative settings.

articles.title: The cost of a violation: How children and adults determine the severity of social violations
articles.authors: Alyssa Doerksen; Alexis Sierra Smith-Flores; Madison Leigh Pesowski
articles.abstract: Social evaluations vary in severity, yet it remains unclear what determines these graded judgments. The same action can seem relatively minor in one context, but deeply objectionable in another. One possibility is that observers use a unifying utility framework to reason about costs imposed on the person affected. Across four preregistered experiments, we tested this possibility using ownership violations. Three- to 8-year-olds (N = 336) and adults (N = 336) evaluated scenarios that manipulated action severity, ownership status, resource scarcity, and subjective value while holding other aspects of the transgression constant. Across experiments, children showed adult-like patterns of evaluation, judging violations more negatively when they imposed greater objective or subjective costs on owners. These findings suggest that, even early in development, observers jointly consider whether an action violates a social norm and how it affects the person’s utility when determining the severity of social violations, in line with existing frameworks.

articles.title: Control Dilemmas Exist on Different Levels of Information Processing: Flexibility and Stability Trade off at the Task Level
articles.authors: Andrea Janker; Sebastian Musslick; Gesine Dreisbach
articles.abstract: Our cognitive system must manage two opposing demands: staying focused on one task (stability) and switching between tasks when needed (flexibility). Traditionally, a trade-off has been assumed between these two control modes. Recent studies questioned this idea. However, they do not consider that experimental manipulations can influence stability and flexibility at different levels of information processing and that a trade-off may only exist within the same level. We introduce a novel paradigm designed to investigate flexibility and stability at different levels of information processing (task vs. stimulus level). Participants switched between two categorization tasks while ignoring distractors. Distractors either came from the same (within-task) or the alternative task (between-task) and were either response-congruent or incongruent. In Experiments 1 and 2, participants categorized words superimposed on distractor images representing the generic response categories (task level interference). In Experiment 3, they categorized letters or digits flanked by distractor letters or digits (stimulus level interference). Reduced interference from between-task distractors compared to within-task distractors in Experiments 1 and 2 show shielding at the task level. At the stimulus level (Experiment 3) both distractor-types interfered to the same extent, indicating that the shielding against between-task distractors got bypassed by the automatic retrieval of learnt stimulus-response associations. Across all three experiments, shielding against between-task distractors in the previous trial improved subsequent performance, when the task repeated (i.e. it improved stability), but impaired performance, when the task switched (i.e. it impaired flexibility). This finding supports a trade-off between flexibility and stability at the task level.

articles.title: Aligning how we measure and support social media addiction with young people's lived experience
articles.authors: Lukas J. Gunschera; Jamil Adjallah; ioanna fokas; Gabriel Mackie; Jo Hickman Dunne; Alice Roe; Jade Davies; Camilla Nord; Margarita Panayiotou; Amy Orben
articles.abstract: Social media use is widely conceptualised as a potential addiction. However, the instruments used to index it are reformulations of criteria developed for established addictions, presuming pathology rather than establishing it. We inverted the direction of inference, integrating lived experience from adolescents who feel addicted to social media and experienced substantial life impairment as a consequence. We conducted eight in-person workshops with 44 adolescents (contributors) to discuss experiences constituting social media addiction, their perceived harms, and how those experiencing it could best be supported. We examined correspondence between lived experiences and features of established addictions, such as conflict (interpersonal struggles and loss of self-control), salience (preoccupation with social media), and tolerance (needing more to get the same effect). Discussions of how, by whom, and through what means adolescents could be supported were analysed using framework analysis. Correspondence between lived experience and the prevailing addiction model was partial and asymmetric. Of 121 experiences, 58.7% described conflict or salience, none described tolerance, and few described withdrawal (2.5%) or relapse (7.4%). A fifth (20.7%) fell outside the model. Effects on sleep, attention, mental health, and time displacement were ranked as most harmful, while impaired control and social comparison ranked lower. Discussions of support revealed a strong sense of individual responsibility, alongside agreement that platform redesign, provision of alternative activities, and shifts in social norms would be most effective. Clinical addiction intervention was rarely raised, despite frequent use of medical addiction language and analogies. These results raise questions about current addiction models and the assumption of pathology applied to social media use. Future work should move beyond these frameworks and ground conceptualisation and measurement in lived experience rather than predefined notions of disorder.

articles.title: Do People Think ChatGPT Is Conscious? Evidence from a Large Polish Sample
articles.authors: Hubert Plisiecki
articles.abstract:
Large language models (LLMs) like ChatGPT are increasingly treated by the public as if they
possess subjective experience, with multiple studies probing the popular opinion on the matter. The
present study provides the first large-scale measurement of this phenomenon in Poland. A
nationally distributed online survey panel (N = 1,736) rated ChatGPT’s capacity for conscious
experience on a 1–100 scale. "Most respondents (74%) attributed ChatGPT at least minimal
consciousness on the continuous rating scale, closely mirroring prior U.S. findings; because this
figure is sensitive to question format, however, we conservatively estimate that more than 10% of
respondents would affirm ChatGPT's status as an experiencer under a stricter, categorical framing.
Small exploratory associations suggested that older and more highly educated participants were
slightly more skeptical, whereas right-leaning respondents attributed slightly more consciousness.
A multivariate regression confirmed that these associations were not simply artifacts of
confounding among demographic variables, though together they explained less than 3% of the
variance in consciousness attributions. These effects, though modest, indicate theoretically relevant
variation. Interpreting these results through Epley’s three-factor anthropomorphism model, the
work argues that limited mechanistic understanding of LLMs, highly human-like behavior, and
unmet social needs likely contribute to widespread phenomenal consciousness attribution. Given
ethical concerns about over-trust, parasocial attachment, and responsibility misperception, these
beliefs matter for AI deployment and governance. Our findings highlight the need for evidence-
based educational strategies that improve public understanding of how LLMs work while allowing
beneficial use of the technology

articles.title: Can You Read Me Through the Screen? Only Extraversion Shows Distinctive Personality Accuracy in Face-to-Face and Videoconferencing Interactions
articles.authors: Valentina Andreeva; Maxim Likhanov; Elina Tsigeman
articles.abstract: Existing theories yield competing predictions regarding personality perception accuracy in face-to-face versus videoconferencing. While cue-reduction frameworks suggest videoconferencing deceases accuracy, social presence perspectives argue decreased constraints facilitate self-expression, leaving the impact of videoconferencing unresolved. This study examined personality perception accuracy following face-to-face and videoconferencing interactions. Previously unacquainted participants (N = 168; 40 videoconferencing and 44 face-to-face dyads) engaged in 40-minute interaction. Pre- and post-interaction Big Five self- and partner-ratings were analyzed via the Social Accuracy Model, partitioning accuracy into distinctive and normative components and controlling for assumed similarity. Results demonstrated that videoconferencing neither impaired nor enhanced distinctive personality accuracy relative to face-to-face. Trait-level analyses revealed only extraversion exhibited significant distinctive accuracy across both formats. These findings indicate perceptual accuracy is driven less by communication modality and more by diagnostic behavioral cues and trait observability.

articles.title: Measuring Multimodal Social Skills in the Digital Age: Development and Validation of a Questionnaire
articles.authors: Aike Horstmann
articles.abstract: As inherently social beings, humans possess specialized communicative capacities, that are essential for fostering social connection and supporting both personal and collective well-being. In an increasingly technology-driven social landscape, a psychometrically sound instrument is crucial for assessing these evolving social skills, identifying individuals experiencing interpersonal difficulties, and evaluating targeted interventions over time. This paper reports the development and validation of the Multimodal Social Skills Questionnaire (MSSQ), an instrument designed to assess social skills across diverse interaction modalities, including both online and offline environments. Multimodal social skills comprise six core dimensions: Assertiveness, Receptivity, Flexibility, Authenticity, Appreciativeness, and Resilience. Across two studies, the aim was to establish the scale’s factor structure, reliability, and construct validity. In Study One (N = 322) an initial pool of 120 items was subjected to exploratory factor analysis (EFA) and iterative item reduction, resulting in a preliminary six-factor solution. In Study Two (N = 260), confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) supported the refined six-factor structure. Construct validity was supported by expected patterns of convergent and discriminant correlations with established measures. Across both studies, the MSSQ showed strong internal consistency. Overall, the findings support the MSSQ as a reliable and valid instrument for assessing multimodal social skills in the evolving digital age.

articles.title: Constraints on kinship semantics reflect cognition over cultural practice
articles.authors: Maisy Hallam; Simon Kirby; Fiona Jordan; Kenny Smith
articles.abstract:
Languages encode similar semantic features in their kinship terminologies, the set of words denoting family members, but different languages seem to prioritise different distinctions. Is any configuration of kinship semantics possible, or are there commonalities across languages in which distinctions are encoded? We use computational methods to identify clear cross-linguistic tendencies in how six semantic features are encoded in kinship terms. Across 1242 languages, all encode information on Generation, while other features like Gender or Seniority are less consistently encoded. Importantly, the features are encoded in a predictable order of importance.  We find that this tendency mirrors participants' behaviour in a linguistic categorisation experiment, suggesting kinship semantics reflect cognitive biases active at the level of the individual. 
Additionally, despite claims that kin terms are a straightforward reflection of social practice, we find varying evidence for this; kin term semantics systematically correspond with patterns of descent, but not marriage norms.

articles.title: Slips of Action in Everyday Life: Capturing Habitual Smartphone Checking with a Decoy App Paradigm
articles.authors: Tim van Timmeren; Jonas Dano; Michael J. Moustaka; Lukas J. Gunschera; Sanne de Wit
articles.abstract: The study of habit has long faced a trade-off between experimental control and ecological validity. We translated a core laboratory test of habit to daily life: whether people continue responding despite knowing it no longer produces its outcome. For one week, participants (N = 74) replaced a frequently used social media app with a nonfunctional decoy icon. The original app was either removed (Detox) or relocated (Switch). Taps on the decoy were recorded as action slips. Nearly all participants slipped (97%), with mean daily slips dropping from 9.76 on the first day to 1.08 on the last across both groups. Slips correlated with baseline app openings (rs = .61) and self-reported automaticity (rs = .40), but not with motivation to reduce usage, problematic use, perceived control, or well-being (|rs| ≤ .09). Decoy slips thus capture a key behavioural signature of habit and reveal how strong app-checking habits can be.

articles.title: Memory precision fluctuates with theta rhythmicity in humans
articles.authors: Troy Houser; Riley Acker; Dagmar Zeithamova
articles.abstract: Rodent research indicates that the hippocampus naturally oscillates between memory encoding and retrieval phases at theta rhythm, indicating that the timing of when information reaches the hippocampus can determine encoding success. However, non-invasively probing such oscillations is challenging in humans. Here, we employed a recently developed dense sampling approach to construct a time course of memory encoding success. Using an attention-grabbing cue expected to reset theta phase, we varied the delay between the cue and to-be-remembered stimulus. Experiment 1 replicated recent finding that human associative memory performance fluctuates with theta rhythmicity, with the best fitting frequency at 8 Hz. Experiment 2 tested and confirmed a new prediction that memory precision also fluctuates with theta rhythmicity, consistent with hippocampal models postulating oscillations in the relative engagement of alternative processing pathways. Together, these findings suggest that the rapid neural fluctuations underpinning memory processes are robust enough to be observed using the dense behavioral sampling approach. Moreover, this work substantiates models of episodic memory and provides new avenues to study models of hippocampal function in humas noninvasively, providing evidence from a purely behavioral approach that human mnemonic discrimination fluctuates with theta rhythm.

articles.title: Embodied mirroring increases interpersonal synchrony of movement and social connection established in subsequent conversations
articles.authors: Yasemin Abra; Christine Falter-Wagner; Irene Sophia Plank
articles.abstract: Interpersonal synchrony, the alignment of behaviours between individuals, is thought to facilitate social connection and rapport. However, less is known about whether synchrony can be intentionally fostered and whether its effects extend beyond the context in which it is established. We examined whether participation in the Mirror Game, a fundamental exercise from theatre where two players nonverbally imitate each other’s movements, influences subsequent interactions between previously unacquainted strangers. Using recordings of facial expressions, gaze patterns, and movement, we captured multi-modal conversational dynamics during a conversation. In line with our preregistered hypothesis, dyads who played the Mirror Game before conversing exhibited greater interpersonal synchrony of movement than those who performed a non-social movement exercise, suggesting a carry-over effect of instructed to emerging interpersonal synchrony. Furthermore, playing the Mirror Game prior to the conversation also increased positive social connection and rapport. However, increased interpersonal synchrony of movement on the level of the dyad did not account for these social benefits, challenging straightforward accounts linking synchrony to social connection. By contrast, exploratory analyses further revealed that behavioural patterns capturing interpersonal adaptation at the individual level predicted participants’ positive social experiences and feelings of connection emerging in the conversation. Together, these findings demonstrate that a brief shared embodied activity can shape the quality of a subsequent interaction and provide new insight into the processes through which positive social connections emerge between strangers.

articles.title: Expertise Shapes the Multidimensional Perception of Stories
articles.authors: Qingzhi Ruby Zeng; Derek Lilienthal; Coraline Rinn Iordan; Aaron Steven White; Elise A. Piazza
articles.abstract: Storytelling is a primary means of human connection and creative expression, but it is unclear how mechanisms of story perception may vary across people with differing expertise. Here, we examined how expertise in creative storytelling shapes ratings of five dimensions of story quality (creativity, imagination, novelty, complexity, cohesiveness), as well as how these ratings are influenced by four linguistic feature categories (language productivity, lexical predictability, semantic similarity, and lexical composition). Online storytellers (N=18) improvised six spoken stories each (for a total of 108 stories). The transcript of each story was rated by both novices (N=10-31) and creative writing/storytelling experts (N=15) on the five story dimensions and analyzed using the four linguistic feature categories above. Overall, experts and novices provided similar average ratings, and their rating spaces both showed two distinct underlying principal components–essentially, creativity and cohesiveness–which were, in turn, predicted by distinct linguistic features. However, experts perceived the five dimensions as more differentiated, and their ratings were less driven by linguistic features than novices’. These findings indicate that experts’ judgments are more nuanced but also may rely less on fine-grained structural features of narratives, highlighting the importance of capturing individual differences and multidimensionality in story perception.

articles.title: Everyday use of AI for emotion regulation depends on the person and the situation
articles.authors: Simon M. Li; Junkang Averi Lin; Shufang Sun; Shanshan Xu; Bin Yu; Mark S. Chen
articles.abstract: Young adults increasingly use AI to seek support and manage their feelings. Understanding when and where they use AI for emotion regulation (ER) and its effectiveness can provide evidence needed for research, practice, and policy. In a 13-day ecological momentary assessment study, 3,048 Chinese university students reported emotional situations, ER strategies, and affect four times daily. AI use for confiding, advice, or emotional support was reported on 2.0% of 134,275 prompts and by 17.3% of participants at least once. In person-level logistic regression, use was concentrated among students with greater lifetime AI use (OR up to 3.12); in multilevel logistic regression, it was more likely during digital, academic, and interpersonal situations (OR 1.22-2.56). AI use did not predict next-prompt affect overall, but was followed by lower positive affect when neither stressors nor positive events had occurred, weakening as more events co-occurred. AI has entered everyday ER as a context-dependent resource.

articles.title: Inhabiting digital ecologies: A qualitative approach to good digital practices
articles.authors: Esther Paniagua; Myriam Durán Vilches; Noemí Robles; Pepa Barral González; Manuel Armayones
articles.abstract:
The integration of digital technologies into everyday life has produced complex digital
ecologies in which platforms, algorithms, and social practices jointly shape experience,
identity, and emotional regulation. Although research on digital well-being has
increased significantly, little is known about how individuals reflect on their digital lives
and the practical criteria they develop to navigate these environments while preserving
well-being and autonomy.,This paper addresses these questions through qualitative
research conducted within a digital community of 100 adults residing in Spain whose
participation unfolded across four successive waves. Fieldwork combined individual
journals, thematic forums, and an open social space, generating a longitudinal corpus
on the everyday experience of inhabiting digital spaces. Results were interpreted
through discourse analysis to reconstruct shared patterns of meaning and discursive
positions.,Findings reveal an ambivalent relationship with digital environments: the
same tools that enable connection, communication, and access to information are also
described as sources of noise, overstimulation, attention fragmentation, and loss of
control. Alongside these discomforts, participants describe daily repertoires of
adjustment that crystallise into distinct discursive positions from which they inhabit
digital ecologies and develop good practices.,We propose that good digital practices
should not be understood as a universal list of self-regulatory norms, but as relational
competencies developed through reflection and experience. Methodologically, the
study shows that a digital community is a particularly suitable tool for examining
everyday, complex, largely automated phenomena, since it enables participants to
observe, compare, and transform their digital experience into practical criteria guiding
their relationship with digital ecologies.

articles.title: Digital Reflections of Social (Dis)connectedness: A Snapchat Data Donations Study
articles.authors: J. Loes Pouwels; Milou Tilstra; Lara Vreeswijk; Nienke Prot; Michelle Alexandra Pingel
articles.abstract: By linking self-reported psychosocial experiences to actual Snapchat interactions, the present study aims to provide a nuanced understanding of how social experiences are reflected in digital contexts. Specifically, the study investigates how adolescents’ experiences of friendship closeness, peer belongingness, loneliness, and social exclusion are related to adolescents’ online interactions with friends by combining real-time experience sampling methodology (ESM) with objective social media data from Snapchat. Participants were 123 adolescents (M age = 13.33 years; SD = 1.10; 58.50% girls). Adolescents with higher disconnectedness (i.e., greater loneliness and social inclusion) had more unanswered friendship requests and spent relatively more time on messaging. After controlling for multiple testing, social (dis)connectedness was not associated with the actual number of sent or viewed messages in the past two months, the number of friendships, Snapscore, or Snapchat AI usage. These findings do not provide clear evidence for either the social enhancement hypothesis or compensation hypothesis.

articles.title: Displacement and Compensation: How Online and In-Person Interactions Relate to Adolescents’ Social and Emotional Connectedness
articles.authors: J. Loes Pouwels; Marlies Maes; Daan Hulsmans; Maaike Verhagen
articles.abstract: By proposing that superficial online interactions displace deeper, in-person connections, displacement theory has given rise to widespread societal concerns about adolescents' use of social media. However, previous research only showed limited evidence for the displacement theory. Therefore, this study aims to provide a more nuanced understanding of how both online and in-person interactions shape adolescents' sense of connectedness. A total of 335 adolescents in Grades 7-9 participated in a 4-week Experience Sampling Methodology study. Three times a day, they reported on their in person and online interactions with friends and peer groups, as well as the quantity and quality of these interactions and their perceived connectedness to their friends and peer groups. Multilevel analyses will be used to examine how the occurrence of in-person and online contact, as well as the quantity and quality of these interactions, are related to adolescents’ social and emotional connectedness.

articles.title: The Not So Illusory Truth Effect: Source Credibility and the Effect of Repetition on Belief
articles.authors: Reed Orchinik; David Gertler Rand; Rahul Bhui
articles.abstract: The illusory truth effect, in which repetition increases belief, is often seen as a cognitive bias. Here, we argue that it may reflect a rational adaptation to generally high-quality information environments. A formal model shows that increasing belief in repeated statements improves accuracy when a source usually tells the truth but sometimes errs. The model captures previous findings and, unlike existing accounts, predicts that repetition should do little to increase belief when the source is not credible. In a large (N = 4,947) preregistered experiment with a quota-matched U.S. sample, the effect was substantially smaller when headlines appeared in a mostly false rather than mostly true newsfeed. In a second preregistered experiment (N = 2,484), repetition increased partisans' belief only in claims from the 2024 U.S. presidential candidate they trusted. Repeated misinformation may therefore be most persuasive when it comes from sources people trust.

articles.title: Cross-Lagged Panel Analysis Using Structural Equation Modeling: Trends and Suggestions Based on a Literature Review of 111 Studies
articles.authors: Asuka Nishida; Satoshi Usami
articles.abstract:
Cross-lagged panel analysis based on structural equation modeling (SEM) has been widely used in the behavioral sciences. The present study provides a literature review based on 111 studies published in major psychology journals that conducted cross-lagged panel analysis. Through this review, we offer an overview of current trends in study design, analytical methods (e.g., estimation method, missing data handling), and model selection, and discuss practical challenges and implications for future applications. A major finding is that the use of the random intercept cross-lagged panel model (RI-CLPM) has increased substantially (41% of the studies) over the past few years. At the same time, most studies rely on longitudinal data with a small number of measurement occasions (e.g., T = 3 − 4). Studies that employed the RI-CLPM on the grounds that it enables inference about within-person relations tended to conduct only limited comparisons with potential alternative models, and only 3% of the studies evaluated model fit from the perspective of local fit (i.e., residual correlations). Although many studies using psychological scales relied on sum scores, only 40% of the studies examined longitudinal measurement invariance, suggesting that there is
still room for improvement.

articles.title: Attachment-Informed Leadership (AIL):  A New Leadership Framework based on Attachment Theory and Social Neuroscience
articles.authors: Pascal Vrticka; Jonathan Wolf-Phillips
articles.abstract: Leadership research has catalogued many styles, among them transformational, authentic and servant leadership, but has offered few accounts of the regulatory mechanisms through which leader-follower relationships operate. We propose that attachment, understood through social neuroscience, supplies one such mechanism. Humans regulate environmental demands relationally, and attachment organises this social regulation of a finite bioenergetic budget under challenge. When followers face threat, dependence or uncertainty, this relationship can come to serve attachment functions, and the leader's reliability as a security provider bears on how much of followers' regulatory resources remains available for work. Building on the Social Neuroscience of Human Attachment (SoNeAt), we develop an attachment-informed leadership (AIL) framework spanning social allostasis, attachment and caregiving, predictive regulation and biobehavioural synchrony. We position AIL relative to evolutionary accounts of leadership and derive nine propositions that distinguish attachment processes from exchange, trust and identification, measurable from self-report to physiology and brain activity.

articles.title: Questionable mediated effect of adolescent neuroticism on short-form video overuse: A comment on Liu and Wu (2026)
articles.authors: Kimmo Sorjonen; Bo Melin; Marika Melin
articles.abstract: Drawing on the covariance matrix reported by Liu and Wu, we reassessed the empirical basis of their mediation model linking adolescent neuroticism to short-form video overuse (SVO). We demonstrate that the observed covariance structure can be reproduced by a theoretically different latent-variable model that does not rely on the directional mechanism proposed in the original article. In this alternative account, self-reported neuroticism, depression, anxiety, and SVO are conceptualized as indicators of a broader construct, core self-evaluation. The results illustrate a broader inferential problem in psychological research: multiple theoretically plausible models may provide equally adequate explanations of the same correlational pattern. Consequently, observational associations alone offer limited grounds for preferring one explanation over competing alternatives. Researchers should therefore routinely evaluate alternative models when drawing inferences about psychological mechanisms from nonexperimental data.

articles.title: Stability, Asymmetric Recovery, and Sociodemographic Heterogeneity in Social Health Trajectories Across Social Disruption: A Four-Wave Hidden Markov Model
articles.authors: Karoline Huth; Lisanne Catharina Johanna Steijvers; Senne Maria Catharina Elisabeth Wijnen; Olga Schiepers; Matty Crone; Rik Crutzen; Nicole Dukers-Muijrers
articles.abstract: Social health is a key pillar of overall health, yet knowledge of distinct social health states, how these change during long-term social disruption, who is at risk of social ill-health, and how social health states affect mental and physical illness remains limited. We used Hidden Markov models to analyse prospective data from 954 adults aged 40 and over who were assessed before, during, and after the onset of the 2019–2025 pandemic. This enabled us to identify latent social health states based on network size, density, loneliness, and emotional support, and to estimate transition probabilities between states over time.  We examined the impact of sex, education, and age on state membership and trajectories, as well as the association between states and depressive symptoms and physical health. Three states were identified: socially isolated (15.9%), moderately connected (55.5%), and socially thriving (28.6%). Most participants (72.5%) remained in one state throughout the observation period; 14.4% deteriorated, 6.5% recovered, and the rest fluctuated.  Being male and having completed a practical education were associated with the socially isolated state, while being female was associated with the thriving state, as well as state deterioration. Worse states showed a graded association with depressive symptoms. Social health is characterised by three relatively stable states, even in the face of persistent social disruption. Nevertheless, many individuals exhibited persistent deterioration even after social restrictions were lifted. The differing risk across sociodemographic groups highlights the need for targeted strategies to promote resilient social health.

articles.title: Development and Accuracy Evaluation of an LLM-Assisted Workflow for Screening and Data Extraction in Large-Scale Syntheses
articles.authors: Vsevolod Scherrer; Franzis Preckel; Moritz Breit
articles.abstract:
Large-scale research syntheses are labor-intensive and prone to human error, and large language models (LLMs) could support their screening and data extraction. Building on current recommendations, we developed an integrated workflow for title and abstract screening (Step 1), full-text screening (Step 2), and data extraction (Step 3), and evaluated it in a preregistered proof-of-concept study.
The study updated a meta-analysis on the rank-order stability of cognitive abilities, in which records may report several nested coefficients. Every step used ensembles of five LLM-instances, and we evaluated 2,960 workflow configurations against a human gold standard of 892 records, of which 692 records with 102 coded effect sizes formed the evaluation set. Without human review, Steps 1 and 2 retained 96.72% and 100.00% of eligible records. At Step 3, the LLMs missed 35.05% of gold effect sizes in rule-based extracted text but none in text from machine-learning-based parsing, which also lowered their coding error from 10.16% to 2.61%. In the recommended configuration, human review was confined to Step 3, where checking effect sizes of 5 of 40 records and 16.43% of the cells raised specificity to 100.00% and coding accuracy from 97.39% to 99.24%.
We derive five recommendations: (1) refine criterion-specific prompts on a calibration set, (2) use machine-learning-based PDF parsing for data extraction, (3) aggregate ensemble ratings leniently at screening and strictly at data extraction, (4) focus human review on data extraction, targeted via flags and ensemble disagreement, and (5) identify nested effect sizes in a separate stage with unique identifiers.

articles.title: The Meta-Awareness – Equanimity Framework of Self for Psychiatry: Phenomenological Insights from Psychosis and Mindfulness
articles.authors: Saampras Ganesan; Antoine Lutz; Andrew Zalesky; Vanessa Cropley; Barnaby Nelson
articles.abstract: Psychiatric disorders remain a major global health challenge, yet research does not adequately incorporate first-person lived experience. A central component of lived experience is the sense of self, which is often profoundly altered in psychiatric conditions and can serve as a prognostic phenomenological marker, particularly in psychosis. In psychiatry, the most minimal form of self, i.e., the basic-self, is conventionally conceptualized as an enduring, individuated subjectivity defined by perspectival ownership and a clear boundary between self and world. Conversely, some contemplative frameworks, including mindfulness and certain non-dual perspectives, view the basic-self as a dynamic, conditioned process, such that experience need not be fundamentally structured by a self–world distinction or a fixed perspective. Drawing on phenomenological evidence from published first-person reports, we argue that the contemplative view can illuminate previously unexplored mechanisms underlying basic-self disturbances in psychosis-spectrum disorders. We formalize this view in a testable meta-awareness - equanimity (MA–E) framework of self that maps key phenomenological overlaps and distinctions across mindfulness, psychosis, and psychedelic experiences. Finally, we outline future research directions for validating and operationalizing the MA–E framework with implications for intervention design in psychosis.

articles.title: Day-to-day fluctuations in craving and the value of drugs and food in daily life
articles.authors: Sergej Grunevski; Emmanuel E. Alvarez; Emma M. Schweitzer; Julia Kong; Sahar Hafezi; Anna B. Konova
articles.abstract: Craving is a powerful urge for a specific target (e.g., food, drugs) that prompts decisions directed at satisfying craving. While prior laboratory studies suggest craving biases behavior by amplifying target-specific value, the real-world generalizability of this mechanism remains unknown. We validate and extend these findings in a 28-day naturalistic smartphone-enabled study in patients with opioid use disorder (N=67) and community controls (N=49) who reported on their food (savory, sweet) and drug (opioid) urges and willingness-to-pay values. Despite person-level (mean) covariation, food and drug urges fluctuated largely independently within individuals while maintaining target-specific relationships with value. Using dynamics in drug urge and value and computational modeling, we isolated a distinct, ecologically relevant craving “state” tied to drug cue exposure and drug use in daily life. This research shows craving acts on normative valuation processes in real-world decision making and offers a novel approach to infer clinically vulnerable moments for behavior change.

articles.title: The Climate Stance Inventory: Development and validation in a large longitudinal sample of UK adults
articles.authors: Leo Johnson; Orestis Zavlis; Laurence Wainwright; Omid V. Ebrahimi
articles.abstract: The climate attitude–behaviour gap persists, with individual variables explaining limited behavioural variance. To address this problem, we develop and validate the Climate Stance Inventory (CSI), a continuous measure of 15 recurring orientations towards climate change and climate action derived from the Norm Activation Model. In a three-wave longitudinal study, 1,503 adults from the United Kingdom completed the CSI and measures of climate appraisals and environmental behaviour over approximately 10 weeks. Across waves, exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses identified a 15-factor solution that exhibited good fit (CFI = .979, RMSEA = .034), high internal consistency (α/ω = .69–.88) and test-retest correlations (r = .58–.89) and full longitudinal measurement invariance. Climate stances showed theoretically coherent associations with threat certainty, responsibility-related appraisals, efficacy, institutional trust and pro-environmental behaviour. In hierarchical regressions, they explained substantial additional variance beyond demographic characteristics and climate change anxiety in pro-environmental voting (14.2%), workplace behaviour (19.5%) and behaviour outside work (22.4%). The Bystander stance also explained unique variance beyond a conceptually adjacent established barrier measure. These findings support the CSI as a reliable, temporally stable and substantively valid measure that can distinguish different psychological routes to climate (in)action and support the development and evaluation of more targeted climate-belief interventions.

articles.title: Left Out for Too Long? Chronicity of Social Exclusion as a Key Factor in Explaining the Exclusion-Radicalism Link
articles.authors: Linda Dörr; Andrew Hales; Kipling D. Williams; Christiane Marie Büttner; Michaela Pfundmair
articles.abstract:
Chronic social exclusion has been linked to radicalization processes in real-world terrorism
cases. However, experimental research regarding this link has focused on situational
experiences of exclusion, not accounting for chronicity of exclusion. Given the differences in
the psychological consequences of chronic and short-term exclusion, across three studies, we
investigated the association between chronic social exclusion and radicalism (i.e., readiness
to engage in violent and illegal political action) as well as activism (i.e., readiness to engage
in non-violent and legal political action). We hypothesized that chronicity might act as a key
condition for the effect of social exclusion on radicalism. In a survey study (N = 370), the
frequency of different types of exclusion experiences positively predicted radical intentions.
In a quasi-experimental survey study (N = 324), participants who reported chronic exclusion
(vs. no exclusion) in their everyday lives reported higher radical intentions. Participants who
reported only short-term exclusion did not differ in radical intentions from those reporting no
exclusion. In a five-month longitudinal study with weekly assessments (N = 343, k = 5,319
assessments), average exclusion experiences across the five-month period (i.e., a chronic
assessment of exclusion) positively predicted radical intentions and behaviors. Across
studies, chronic exclusion was associated with radicalism, but not activism. Thus, chronic
experiences of social exclusion might drive radical intentions and behaviors, highlighting
chronicity as a relevant yet understudied factor of the exclusion-radicalism link. In light of
these findings, reducing chronic experiences of exclusion might represent a particularly
promising avenue for the prevention of radicalism.

articles.title: Employing ventilation and mobile air cleaning in classrooms and elderly care homes for infectious disease reduction: multi-stakeholder perspectives on acceptability, feasibility and perceived effects
