If it is the case that morphology interacts with phonetics, such morphological effects should also be observed in languages other than English. We also hypothesise that effects should also occur in articulatory realisations such as tongue movements. In the present study, we compared acoustic duration and tongue movements between two German suffixes -er [ɐ] and -t [-t]. We found that the suffixal -er [ɐ] was significantly longer in duration and significantly lower in tongue positions than its segmentally identical non-suffixal counterpart, and the lower tongue position could not be simply attributed to longer duration. Importantly, however, no effect of morphological status was found for -t [-t] for either duration or articulatory trajectory. These findings show that morpho-phonetic adaptation manifests in multiple cues and may depend on segment identity, with implications for models of speech production.

articles_hidden.title: The Global Measure of Masturbation Satisfaction (GMMAST): Scale Development and Preliminary Validation
articles_hidden.authors: David Cornelius de Jong; Nantje Fischer; Maximiliane Uhlich
articles_hidden.abstract:
Solo masturbation is a common sexual behavior, but its role in well-being is poorly understood.
One reason is that the extant literature has generally focused on how engagement in masturbation
(e.g., in the past 4 weeks) relates to well-being while neglecting how the subjective experience of
masturbation (e.g., as valuable and positive, or not) might impact well-being. This report
describes the development of the brief, five-item Global Measure of Masturbation Satisfaction
(GMMAST). The measure was developed using a sample of 2,486 adults who had masturbated
in the past month, drawn from the Masturbation and Sexual Health Survey, a U.S. national
survey. Exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses, and tests of measurement invariance,
suggested the scale has strong psychometric properties. Associations with related constructs
(e.g., positive and negative masturbation attitudes, masturbation motives, receipt of sexual
education) provide preliminary evidence of validity.

articles_hidden.title: The limits of ensemble perception: Hierarchical grouping and object-based encoding
articles_hidden.authors: Sabrina Hansmann-Roth; Bilge Sayim
articles_hidden.abstract:
The visual system can efficiently summarize information by extracting ensemble statistics such
as the average of visual features. However, it remains unclear how ensemble perception
operates when individual features are grouped into meaningful objects. In the present study,
we investigated whether ensemble statistics of local features can still be extracted when
oriented line segments form letters. Across two experiments, observers estimated the average
orientation of line elements either as unconnected lines in a typical ensemble display, arranged
into intact letters, or transformed into pseudo-letters. Although the number and orientation of
line elements were identical across conditions, grouping into meaningful letters systematically
impaired performance. Grouping interfered with observers’ ability to estimate average
orientation when intact letters did not provide a useful global orientation cue, leading to larger
errors and greater response variability than pseudo-letters or ungrouped lines. However, when
the average orientation coincided with the mirror-symmetry axis of a letter, observers could
rely on this global structure, resulting in improved performance. Crucially, these effects
replicated in peripheral vision, indicating that ensemble extraction is constrained by perceptual
organization even when access to local feature information is limited. Together, these results
show that ensemble perception is modulated by object-based grouping and perceptual
organization.

articles_hidden.title: Perceived parents’ relationship quality and young adults’ dating experiences
articles_hidden.authors: Le Hoai Linh Vu; Aida Fernandez-Jimenez; Savannah M. Bodden; Simran Rooprai; Nicholas Daniel Ramcharran; Michael Petrovski; Aldo Spina; Sintayehu Daba Wami; Joseph FX DeSouza
articles_hidden.abstract: Based on the combination of attachment theory, social learning theory and family system theory, the purpose of this survey study is to examine the influence of the quality of interparental relationships on the early dating experiences of young adults, as well as to investigate the mediating role of parent-child bonds in this association. Data was collected from 122 York University undergraduate students (mean age 19.4 years) through an online survey portal (QuestionPro). Perceived parents’ levels of conflict and affection were measured with adapted Children’s Perception of Interparental Conflict Scale (CPIC) and Dyadic Adjustment Scale (DAS). Parental Bonding Instrument (PBI) was used to measure parent-child bond, while dating experiences were evaluated using Relationship Assessment Scale (RAS) and modified Conflict Tactics Scale (CTS2-Short). Correlational analysis and structural equation modelling (SEM) were conducted to analyze the data. It was found that higher perceived parental conflict predicted worse mother-child and father-child bonds. Neither parental relationship quality nor parent-child bonds significantly predicted relationship satisfaction or constructive conflict behaviours. Mediation effects were not supported. In conclusion, the findings indicate that the early perceptions of parents' relationship quality may not influence young adults’ early dating experiences; however, it may predict the bond between parents and child.

articles_hidden.title: Assessing psychological, neural and AI-based representational geometries across multiple similarity properties
articles_hidden.authors: Johan Alejandro Gamba; Megan A. K. Peters; Vincent Taschereau-Dumouchel; Brian Odegaard
articles_hidden.abstract: Assessing similarity between objects is a fundamental cognitive process, and similarity judgments can assess many different attributes, including objective properties (color, shape) or subjective appraisals (preference, scariness). Here, we investigated how psychological similarity across eight different properties relates to neural representational geometries and artificial models. We first collected large-scale pairwise similarity ratings for 280 objects. Using representational similarity analysis (RSA) and multidimensional scaling, we identified three mental representational spaces: one defined by multiple object features and general similarity, a second by affective evaluations, and a third by color. Combining fMRI and RSA in 80 participants, we found that object feature ratings significantly correlated with representational structures in visual and prefrontal cortices. Unexpectedly, affective ratings also correlated with patterns in visual cortices. Crucially, regional variability strongly shaped these correspondences: visual cortices exhibited high noise ceilings and consistent alignment with behavior, whereas associative regions showed greater across-subjects variability and weaker correlations. Finally, algorithms and neural networks with high classification performance on specific properties strongly correlated with behavioral and fMRI RSA matrices. Together, these results demonstrate that similarity is a multidimensional construct that comprises multiple representational spaces whose neural correspondence is shaped by representational content, regional variability, and modeling methodology.

articles_hidden.title: Vision and body representation: Insights from blindness
articles_hidden.authors: Dominika Radziun; Luke E. Miller
articles_hidden.abstract: Body representations arise from the integration of multiple sensory signals that provide information about the body’s size, posture, and internal states. Vision often plays a dominant role, calibrating and aligning signals from touch, proprioception, and interoception. Yet, individuals born without sight still construct coherent and functional body representations, suggesting that the role of vision in building these representations may be more flexible than previously thought. Here, we synthesize recent behavioral and neuroimaging findings on body representations in blind individuals. We argue that blindness offers a powerful case study in how body representations can emerge through non-visual pathways, revealing the brain’s capacity to flexibly reorganize the sensory inputs supporting its internal models of the body. In doing so, we highlight the broader relevance of visual loss for understanding the plastic and multisensory nature of body representation.

articles_hidden.title: Feasibility and acceptability of smartwatch-delivered micro-ecological momentary assessment (µEMA) during in situ exercise among breast cancer survivors
articles_hidden.authors: Elizabeth Webb Lampe; Aislinn E. Mitcham; Paget E. Chung; Carly Bobak; Hannah C. Edmonds; Sivakumar P. Kandasamy; Calie S. Sorenson; Hollin R. Hakimian; Kathleen Doyle Lyons; Amanda J. Emerson
articles_hidden.abstract:
Objectives. Micro-ecological momentary assessment (µEMA) facilitates in-real-time data capture using succinct prompts delivered to a smartwatch. µEMA overcomes limitations of smartphone-based EMA for activities where carrying a smartphone would be burdensome/impractical. To date, µEMA during exercise has only been conducted with younger, non-clinical samples. We evaluate the feasibility and acceptability of µEMA during in situ, self-directed exercise among breast cancer survivors within 5-years of completing cancer treatment.

Method. A µEMA app was installed on Fitbit Versa 3 smartwatches. N = 27 stage 0-III breast cancer survivors enrolled and 22 (81.5%) submitted ratings of affective response (via modified Feeling Scale) and physical effort (via modified Rating of Perceived Exertion Scale) during exercise sessions completed over 10 consecutive days. Feasibility was assessed as µEMA app response rates. Acceptability was assessed via User-Friendliness Scale ratings from daily dairy surveys as well as System Usability Scale (SUS) scores and exit interviews collected at end-of-study.

Results. Participants (Mage = 60.8 years, SD = 11.5) completed M = 4.7 (SD = 2.4) exercise sessions (walking most common) while responding to µEMA. The overall µEMA response rate across all exercise sessions was 77.7% (SD = 19.5). SUS scores (M = 82.9, SD = 15.5) exceeded the threshold for adequate usability (i.e., ≥ 68) and overall average person-weighted user-friendliness was ‘satisfactory’—‘good,’ M = 4.7 (SD = 1.1). Interviews revealed preference for µEMA over smartphone-based EMA during exercise. Notably, some technical issues were common. 

Conclusions. Results support the feasibility and acceptability of µEMA during in situ exercise among breast cancer survivors.

articles_hidden.title: Synthometricon: A search engine to identify conceptual overlap in measures in the behavioral sciences
articles_hidden.authors: Björn Erik Hommel; Annika Iris Külpmann; Ruben C. Arslan
articles_hidden.abstract: Every month, scores of new measures and constructs enter the behavioral science literature. Researchers struggle to keep an overview of their subfields, let alone the wider field, with an estimated number of allegedly different constructs now exceeding 30,000. Proposing constructs is easy, finding redundancies and overlaps is not. The effort of finding redundancies using participant responses grows quadratically with the number of measures. This cost motivates the use of language models, which can simplify and speed up the process without requiring new data collection. Earlier work employed latent semantic analysis (LSA) to make use of the textual nature of questionnaires in the social and behavioral sciences. However, LSA treats sentences as bags of words and ignores word order, syntax, and negation, all of which shape how respondents interpret items. Recent advances demonstrate that transformer-based sentence embedding models offer a more viable solution for predicting empirical relatedness between survey items. In the presented work, we use a fine-tuned language model, the SurveyBot3000, to introduce the Synthometricon, an open-access web application for systematic detection of conceptual overlap. The application indexes over 570,000 items across more than 97,000 scales from approximately 28,000 instruments in the APA PsycTests database and other sources.

articles_hidden.title: Congenital visual impairment does not impede the development of infants’ ability to reach to the self
articles_hidden.authors: GIULIA CAPPAGLI; Matej Hoffmann; Lisa K Chinn; Jason A.M. Khoury; Jeffrey J. Lockman; Sabrina Signorini; gori monica
articles_hidden.abstract: While early visual deprivation can hinder some spatial skills, it can also lead to sensory enhancements. Evidence from visually impaired infants is sparse but suggests preserved unisensory orienting and greater reliance on touch alongside reduced multisensory spatial integration and delayed spatially guided action.1,2 Reaching to touch on the body is a spatial task requiring touch to be remapped relative to body posture. Visual impairment could therefore delay this ability if vision calibrates spatial representations, or preserve or enhance it if attention to somatosensory input supports compensation. We tested sighted, low-vision, and blind infants (6–24 months) reaching to vibrotactile targets. Reaching success was comparable across groups and increased with age. Low-vision infants reached more slowly than sighted infants, whereas blind infants did not differ from sighted infants. Thus, body-centered tactile localization can develop without typical visual experience, although degraded visual input may selectively slow somatosensory guidance of action.

articles_hidden.title: More Than a Keypress: Continuous Key-Actuation Dynamics for Decomposing Speeded Responses
articles_hidden.authors: David Levi Tekampe; Philip Samuel Santangelo
articles_hidden.abstract: Conventional keypress measurement reduces a continuous motor action to a discrete event, typically represented by reaction time (RT) and accuracy. The present study evaluated continuous analogue key-actuation as a method for characterising the unfolding response while retaining a conventional two-choice keypress format. Seventy-seven adults completed the Attention Network Test-Revised (ANT-R) while response-key depth was recorded continuously. We derived target- and press-locked waveforms together with pre-specified measures of response timing, morphology, variability, preparation, and bilateral coor-dination. Established ANT-R manipulations served as experimentally controlled tests of measurement sensitivity. Target-locked waveforms differentiated six of the seven planned ANT-R contrasts after Holm adjustment; location conflict was not significant, and the alerting effect was less robust in sensitivity analyses. No exploratory press-locked contrast survived mul-tiplicity correction. Initiation time and peak-actuation time showed reliable effects across multiple attentional contrasts, whereas ramp time (the initiation-to-peak interval) showed no reliable modulation. Effects in the morphology, coordination, and preparation/control families were more selective and were confined to flanker conflict. Exploratory models further showed that ramp, rise-to-maximum, and return durations and hold jitter predicted trial-level accuracy after controlling for RT, whereas initiation time did not. These findings show that continuous key-actuation can decompose when a speeded re-sponse begins and how it unfolds, while selected key-actuation measures provide response-quality information beyond con-ventional RT. Continuous key-actuation therefore provides an experimentally sensitive measurement approach for extending standard keypress responses, although reliability and cross-device generalisation remain to be established.

articles_hidden.title: Validating the Chinese Version of the Manifestation Scale (CVMS): Translation, Cultural Adaptation and Psychometric Extension
articles_hidden.authors: Jiaqi Guo; Lucas J Dixon; Kehan Mei; Mei Shi
articles_hidden.abstract: The Manifestation Scale assesses belief in metaphysically attracting success through positive self-talk, visualization, and symbolic actions. We translated and validated a Chinese version (CVMS) in 1,901 Chinese-speaking adults and compared it with data from 1,023 English-speaking participants. Analyses supported correlated Personal Power and Cosmic Collaboration dimensions within a broader general manifestation construct. Cosmic Collaboration was more distinct in the CVMS, and one item contributed more clearly to the general factor than to specific factors. Findings supported an 11-item Total scale, a six-item Personal Power subscale, and a four-item Cosmic Collaboration subscale, with high internal consistency and three-month stability. Partial scalar invariance supported cross-language latent comparisons. Associations with positive thought-action fusion, hope, perceived success, risk propensity, and get-rich-quick beliefs broadly replicated validity, alongside some cross-language differences in how the scale dimensions were related to metaphysical belief. The CVMS provides the first evidence that manifestation belief can be measured beyond Western contexts.

articles_hidden.title: Calling Development: A Systematic Review of Longitudinal Evidence
articles_hidden.authors: Sophie Gerdel; Anna Dalla Rosa; Bryan Dik; Michelangelo Vianello
articles_hidden.abstract: Although career calling is linked to many beneficial outcomes for both individuals and organizations, knowledge on how a sense of calling develops is limited and, in some ways, controversial. To clarify this issue, we conducted a systematic review of longitudinal studies that analyzed the temporal relation between calling and other variables in its nomological network. Across 14 studies, the strongest longitudinal evidence suggests that calling is more often an outcome of career development processes rather than an initiating cause. Specifically, vocational self-definition, agency, and career feedback and appraisal appear to precede calling, whereas personal resources more often follow calling, and life meaning and values appears reciprocally linked with calling. On this basis, we propose a preliminary integrative developmental framework of calling in which calling emerges through recursive cycles of career clarification, agentic engagement, contextual feedback and appraisal, and life meaning- and value-based integration.

articles_hidden.title: La Pirámide del Sueño: desarrollo y difusión nacional de una herramienta de comunicación basada en hábitos para promover un sueño saludable
articles_hidden.authors: Manuel Armayones; Sílvia Gismera; Laura Armayones-Carranza
articles_hidden.abstract: La Pirámide del Sueño es una herramienta de educación para la salud que ordena las recomendaciones de higiene del sueño en cuatro niveles: ritmos y horarios; hábitos y rutinas que ayudan a desconectar; ambiente óptimo para el sueño, y estrategias en la cama. Se desarrolló en la Alianza por el Sueño combinando el formato, ya familiar, de las pirámides alimentarias con el enfoque de diseño de conducta y formación de hábitos de Fogg, que convierte cada recomendación en un pequeño hábito asociado a una rutina. Se presentó en mayo de 2025 con 26 organizaciones colaboradoras y, según el seguimiento de medios, generó 210 impactos informativos y 26 entrevistas, con una audiencia acumulada de 69,9 millones, además de 260 menciones en redes sociales. Unir una metáfora visual conocida y un modelo sencillo de formación de hábitos es una estrategia viable y de bajo coste para promover el sueño saludable; su efecto sobre la conducta está por evaluar.

articles_hidden.title: Questionable mediated effect of artificial intelligence anxiety on academic burnout: A comment on Long et al. (2026)
articles_hidden.authors: Kimmo Sorjonen
articles_hidden.abstract: Drawing on the covariance matrix reported by Long et al., I reassessed the empirical basis of their mediation model linking artificial intelligence anxiety to academic burnout. I demonstrate that the observed covariance structure can be reproduced by a theoretically different latent-variable model that does not rely on the directional mechanism proposed in the original article. In this alternative account, self-reported artificial intelligence anxiety, perceived stress, rumination, and academic burnout are conceptualized as negative indicators of a broader construct, core self-evaluation. The results illustrate a broader inferential problem in psychological research: multiple theoretically plausible models may provide equally adequate explanations of the same correlational pattern. Consequently, observational associations alone offer limited grounds for preferring one explanation over competing alternatives. Researchers should therefore routinely evaluate alternative models when drawing inferences about psychological mechanisms from nonexperimental data.

articles_hidden.title: Spatial Aspects of Felt Presence and the Phenomenon of Childhood Imaginary Companions: Peripersonal Space, Embodied Perspective, and Continuity of Agent Propensity
articles_hidden.authors: Burak; Bigna Lenggenhager
articles_hidden.abstract:
Felt presence (FP) refers to the experience of sensing another agent nearby despite the
absence of corresponding sensory evidence, and has been reported across neurological,
psychiatric, and non-clinical populations. However, its potential phenomenological similarity and
continuity with the common childhood experience of imaginary companions (ICs) have received
little attention. The present study characterizes the spatial and perspectival features of
retrospectively reported childhood IC experiences, evaluates their parallels with the
phenomenology of FP, and interprets these convergences within the theoretical framework of
bodily self-consciousness (BSC) and peripersonal space (PPS). Three theory-driven predictions
were tested using retrospective self-reports from a healthy adult sample (N = 185; IC+ = 45; IC−
= 140) excluding participants with psychiatric or neurological diagnoses. First, we examined
whether IC representations were spatially anchored within PPS (Peripersonal Anchoring). Second,
we assessed whether IC experiences were predominantly reported from an embodied, first-person
or third-person perspective. Third, we tested whether individuals reporting childhood ICs show a
greater adult propensity for presence-related experiences (Continuity of Agent Propensity).
Results supported all three predictions. Most spatial distance reports (76.1%) fell within 70 cm of
the body, with an overall median distance of 12 cm, consistent with PPS anchoring. IC experiences
were primarily reported from a first-person perspective (55.6%) and referenced to the body
(88.9%). Furthermore, individuals with childhood ICs reported higher scores on the Sensed
Presence Questionnaire (SenPQ; 15 items, excluding Item 7 due to cross-loading) during
adulthood, whereas dissociative tendencies did not differ between groups. Exploratory logistic
regression identified perceived presence proneness as the only significant predictor of IC history.
Together, these findings suggest that both adult FP and childhood IC experiences may be grounded
in the spatial organization of the bodily action field and reflect a stable disposition for internally
generated social-agent representations.

articles_hidden.title: Cognitive reserve differently impacts cognition and metacognition across domains
articles_hidden.authors: Audrey Mazancieux; Lucile Meunier-Duperray; Coline Grégoire; Christine Bastin; Céline Souchay; Chris Moulin; Lucie Angel
articles_hidden.abstract: Preservative effects of cognitive reserve on age-related decline have been widely studied in episodic memory, however less is known about how cognitive reserve influences other domains such as semantic memory or visual perception. Similarly, recent studies suggest that the decline of metacognition observed with age might be reduced by cognitive reserve in the memory domain, but the domain-generality of such effect remains unexplored. This study is part of a published study investigating the effect of age on cognition and metacognition in episodic memory, semantic memory, executive functioning, and visual perception (Meunier-Duperray et al., 2025). Here, we focused on cognitive reserve measured by the CRIq on cognition (i.e., task performance) and metacognition in a subsample of 319 participants (aged from 18 to 79). We expected an effect of cognitive reserve only on tasks sensitive to age-related decline: episodic memory, executive functioning, and visual perception for task performance and episodic and semantic tasks for metacognition. Overall, these results suggest evidence for the null hypothesis for the effect of cognitive reserve on the age-related decline in cognition and metacognition. Only anecdotal to small evidence was found for an effect of cognitive reserve on episodic memory performance across the lifespan suggesting that reserve reflects earlier individual differences rather than differences in the rate of decline. However, the low variability of our high-reserve sample may have masked some effects.

articles_hidden.title: When attention turns inward: Mind wandering reduces perceptual sensitivity across visual fields
articles_hidden.authors: Bianca de Haan
articles_hidden.abstract: We all mind wander from time to time, where instead of being focussed on our task, we start thinking about task-unrelated personal events or concerns. In daily life, however, mind wandering is often associated with reduced processing of external information. This is commonly explained by the decoupling hypothesis, which posits that processing of external sensory information is attenuated when attention turns inward. However, it remains unclear whether perceptual decoupling reflects a global, uniform attenuation of sensory processing, or a spatially-specific reduction linked to lateralised attentional mechanisms. In the current, pre-registered study, we used an online signal detection task to assess the impact of mind wandering on perceptual performance in the left and right visual fields. While performing the task, participants periodically reported whether they were mind wandering or on task. Consistent with the decoupling hypothesis, perceptual sensitivity (d′) was significantly reduced on trials during which participants reported mind wandering compared to on-task trials. However, this reduction in sensitivity did not differ between stimuli presented in the left and right visual field. These findings suggest that perceptual decoupling during mind wandering reflects a global attenuation of sensory processing, and that attentional systems involved during mind wandering may be distinct from those associated with slower fluctuations of attentional resources such as reductions in alertness.

articles_hidden.title: Exploring the Role of Physical Effort in the Rewarding Value of Sedentary Behavior
articles_hidden.authors: Silvio Maltagliati; Pam ten Broeke; Philippe Sarrazin; Ryan Rhodes; Erik Bijleveld; Genevieve Fridlund Dunton; Cedrick Bonnet; Benjamin Gardner; David A. Raichlen; Matthew W Miller
articles_hidden.abstract: Objective: Sedentary behavior is commonly studied based on the value of the higher-order task being performed, such as watching TV, using a phone, or playing video games. However, it is possible that the low physical effort associated with these behaviors also contributes to their appeal. That is, individuals may be drawn not just to the task but to the low effort it is paired with. This study aims to test this possibility by manipulating body position (sitting vs. standing) while participants engage in a familiar sedentary task (i.e., playing Tetris). Methods: To test this hypothesis, we manipulated body position during a smartphone video game task to examine how sitting versus standing affected the rewarding value assigned to the game. Results: Our results (two independent studies, N = 228 and N = 129) show that the rewarding value of this sedentary behavior also stems from the low effort cost associated with sitting. Conclusions: These findings suggest that the perception of effort may contribute to influencing sedentary preferences and provide valuable insights for interventions aimed at reducing excessive sedentary behavior, such as targeted strategies to increase the valuation of physical effort.

articles_hidden.title: Sampling Thoughts During Music Listening: A Systematic Comparison of Probe-caught, Self-caught and Retrospective Thought Reporting Methods
articles_hidden.authors: Nao Toyama; Kelly Jakubowski
articles_hidden.abstract: Music listening experiences dynamically unfold over time. However, as previous research has relied predominantly on short music excerpts and retrospective post-listening self-reports, how qualitative thought content unfolds during extended listening remains underexplored. Crucially, addressing this requires effective real-time sampling, yet direct empirical comparisons of such methods––i.e., experimenter-led versus participant-led approaches––and their impact on data quality and listener experience are remain lacking. To address these gaps, the present study systematically compared three experience-sampling methodologies (probe-caught, self-caught, and a retrospective control) using participants’ own smartphones during an 18-minute video of a classical music performance. While the control group yielded significantly fewer thoughts, both experimental groups (probe- and self-caught) reported a comparable total number of thoughts. The probe-caught method exhibited greater inter-participant stability and generated significantly more detailed qualitative descriptions. Importantly, participants’ subjective perceived interference on their listening experience was low and did not differ across groups, confirming that real-time thought reporting did not disrupt the natural listening experience compared with traditional retrospective reporting. By validating the efficiency, stability, and minimal invasiveness of the probe-caught method, this study provides an empirical foundation for future research investigating real-time subjective experiences across diverse listening environments.

articles_hidden.title: Iconicity and Age Make Distinct Contributions to Symbolic Correspondence in Early Childhood
articles_hidden.authors: Keyi Yang; Ruoxi Chen; Suizi Xue; Jiajia Zhou; anonymous; Juan Wang; Jingmei Wang; Jinliang Qin
articles_hidden.abstract: Iconicity has been proposed to support children’s symbolic understanding, yet it remains unclear when iconicity contributes to symbolic correspondence and how this contribution varies across early childhood. The present study examined semantic judgments in 204 Chinese preschool children (Mage = 5.36 years, SD = 0.78; 102 boys) across three representational formats: line drawings, Oracle Bone script, and simplified Chinese characters. Children judged whether sequentially presented picture–symbol pairs referred to the same objects or actions, allowing broad format differences to be distinguished from graded item-level iconicity within each format. Children were consistently more accurate when rejecting mismatches than when confirming matches. Iconicity was especially informative when children had to confirm that different forms shared a meaning. Diffusion decision modeling further showed that this advantage was expressed in the accumulation of decision-relevant evidence during confirmation. Older age was associated with more efficient evidence accumulation for establishing semantic correspondence across representational formats, but age did not systematically strengthen or weaken the iconicity-drift relation. These findings suggest that iconicity and age make distinct contributions to symbolic correspondence: iconicity functions as a task-dependent source of information, whereas age-related differences are characterized by broader gains in the efficiency of establishing correspondence across symbolic forms.

articles_hidden.title: Sentiment Analysis of Clinical Interviews Identifies Language Markers of Identity Diffusion in Adolescents with Personality Disorder
articles_hidden.authors: Katarina Lodrant; Filip Melinscak; Ayse Nur Beris; Valentin Schneider; Klara Czernin; Anselm Bründlmayer; Paul Plener; Frank Scharnowski; David Steyrl; Clarissa Laczkovics
articles_hidden.abstract:
Identity diffusion – a fragmented sense of self and others maintained by splitting-based defenses – is a core feature of impaired personality functioning, theorized to involve heightened negative affectivity and affective instability. Evidence from other psychopathologies suggests that markers of affective disturbances can be automatically extracted from spontaneous speech, yet the linguistic correlates of identity diffusion have rarely been examined – particularly in adolescents, the age group in which personality pathology assessment is most challenging but also most consequential for early intervention.
Transcripts of the Structured Interview of Personality Organization (STIPO) for adolescents were analyzed in a sample of 72 German-speaking participants (50 patients, 22 healthy controls) spanning the full spectrum from consolidated identity to severe identity diffusion. An interpretable lexicon-based sentiment analysis framework combined word frequency measures (LIWC) with continuous word-level valence indices (VADER), capturing both the prevalence and the dynamics of emotional tone.
Greater identity diffusion was associated with higher affective variability (r = .48–.55), a more negative overall affective orientation (strongest effect: r = −.62), more frequent negative affective language, and more extreme negative expression, with weaker evidence for reduced positive language. Measures of positive extremes, affective expressiveness, and verbosity showed no significant associations.
Identity diffusion in adolescents is thus associated with a distinctive affective language profile, detectable from clinical interview transcripts using sentiment analysis. The results are consistent with psychodynamic accounts of splitting and affective dysregulation, and support the potential of automated language analysis as a reproducible, scalable complement to clinical assessment.

articles_hidden.title: NICE’s 2026 Consultation Draft Guideline for OCD and BDD (GID-NG10435): A Critical Appraisal with Secondary Analysis of NICE’s Published Data
articles_hidden.authors: Himanshu Tyagi; Mark Paramlall
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background. In September 2026 the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) opened consultation on the first batch of its update to the 2005 guideline for obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) and body dysmorphic disorder (BDD) (GID-NG10435). The draft replaces stepped care with matched care and reviews first-line treatment.

Methods. We appraised the draft and its supporting documents against six questions informed by selected AGREE II domains, analysing NICE’s published effect estimates, sample sizes, sensitivity analyses and economic results descriptively; every value was checked against its source document. Comparison guidelines were identified by a documented search.

Results. The adult OCD review included 82 randomised controlled trials and the BDD review 13 studies. The committee cited small samples and wide credible intervals when it did not recommend metacognitive therapy (52 participants) or eye movement desensitisation and reprocessing (EMDR; 59 participants). Self-administered cognitive behavioural therapy with therapist support, the second adult option, rests on 61 participants, with a wider credible interval than EMDR’s, and was recommended on other documented grounds. The top-ranked adult option had a probability of 0.17 of being the most cost-effective. The first-listed BDD option ranked fifth of nine in the network meta-analysis. The draft gives no drug-specific dose targets, no consolidated definition of an adequate trial and no primary severity measure for allocation or response. Treatment after non-response to an adequate trial is outside the scope of Batch 1; on the assumptions in NHS England’s 2013 specification, a cascade beginning with 48 million adults in England and Wales yields approximately 48,000 people not responding to a serotonin reuptake inhibitor followed by local graduated exposure. All six selected multimodal OCD comparison guidelines address augmentation; none provides a treatment pathway for BDD.

Conclusions. The draft rests on a substantial evidence synthesis. The published rationale does not fully explain why small samples and imprecision precluded recommendations for some treatments but not others; several operational parameters are not specified; and further-line treatment is outside the first batch.

articles_hidden.title: First Frequency, then Transitional Probability: Insights from primate statistical learning
articles_hidden.authors: Andreas Lazartigues; Thomas Chartier; Frédéric Lavigne; Joel Fagot; Arnaud Rey
articles_hidden.abstract: Statistical learning is a fundamental cognitive capacity, whereby humans and other species extract the structure of sequences based on statistical cues. Among these cues, Transitional Probability (TP) quantifies the probability of the next stimulus given the preceding one(s), while Frequency quantifies the relative occurrence of local sequences. Mechanistic explanations have generally considered TP the prevalent cues, but a role of Frequency cannot be ignored. Yet, the specific contributions of each, and their interaction, are not well understood. Here, we report a simple serial reaction time experiment that 1) provides online, trial-by-trial learning data, 2) allows a clear dissociation of Frequency and TP, 3) excludes the involvement of internal verbalized rules by testing non-human primates (Guinea baboons, Papio papio). Our results show that, contrary to the traditional view, Frequency can be the main cue influencing statistical learning. Indeed, we found learning to be primarily determined by Frequency in the first 2,000 trials of the learning phase, while the usual prevalence of TP emerged only later on. These data provide a better understanding of the interactions between statistical factors involved in sequence processing. They also constitute new constraints for computational models of statistical learning and challenge existing results.

articles_hidden.title: Dissociable neural oscillations track subjective value under risk and ambiguity
articles_hidden.authors: Shuting Mei; Leyou Deng; Gökhan Aydogan; Christian Carl Ruff; Ya Zheng
articles_hidden.abstract: How the brain values uncertain prospects and translates them into choices is a central question in decision neuroscience. Current accounts propose that decisions under risk and ambiguity share a valuation process that integrates outcome with probability information, with ambiguity additionally requiring evaluation of the uncertainty about the probabilities themselves. Here we used computational modeling to estimate trial-wise subjective value and tested whether it was tracked by shared or distinct neural dynamics under risk and ambiguity. Participants accepted or rejected risky and ambiguous monetary gambles while we recorded neural activity using electroencephalography (Experiment 1) and magnetoencephalography (Experiment 2). Across both experiments, alpha-band (9–14 Hz) activity localized to the precuneus and superior parietal cortex tracked subjective value under both risk and ambiguity. By contrast, delta-band (1–3 Hz) activity localized to the ventromedial prefrontal and anterior cingulate cortices tracked subjective value only under ambiguity. These findings reveal dissociable neural signatures for the two forms of uncertainty and suggest that the brain resolves ambiguity by combining a shared valuation process indexed by alpha activity with an additional process indexed by delta activity that may reflect the motivational salience of options with ambiguous outcome probabilities.

articles_hidden.title: Consistency: A Critical but Often Overlooked Requirement for Causal Inference in Psychological Research
articles_hidden.authors: Lukas Junker; Michael P. Grosz
articles_hidden.abstract: Psychologists are often interested in specific causal quantities (“What is the effect of reducing social-media scrolling by 20 minutes on well-being?”) but tend to focus on vague questions (“Does ‘time spent on social media’ predict well-being?”). There is a mismatch between the causal effects researchers care about and the associations and correlations they compute. In this article, we highlight consistency as a foundational requirement for causal inference that can bridge this mismatch and make statistical estimates causally interpretable. Consistency shows how causal quantities are interpretable only when (a) the causal quantity of interest—the causal estimand—is described precisely enough that it does not bundle different versions of the treatment (e.g., passive scrolling, reading distressing news, or chatting with friends on social media) that have different effects, and (b) the way that the treatment variable changes in the data matches this causal estimand of interest. We clarify these requirements and illustrate how to state and assess them in settings common in psychological research, with a focus on indirect experimental manipulations and multidimensional constructs. Making this step explicit helps researchers articulate their estimands more transparently and is a prerequisite for other concerns such as confounding and model specification.

articles_hidden.title: Questionable mediated effect of police work stress on life satisfaction: A comment on Qiu et al. (2026)
articles_hidden.authors: Kimmo Sorjonen
articles_hidden.abstract: Drawing on the covariance matrix reported by Qiu et al., I reassessed the empirical basis of their mediation model linking police work stress to decreased life satisfaction. I demonstrate that the observed covariance structure can be reproduced by a theoretically different latent-variable model that does not rely on the directional mechanism proposed in the original article. In this alternative account, self-reported police work stress, perceived social support, sleep disturbance, and life satisfaction are conceptualized as indicators of a broader construct, core self-evaluation. The results illustrate a broader inferential problem in psychological research: multiple theoretically plausible models may provide equally adequate explanations of the same correlational pattern. Consequently, observational associations alone offer limited grounds for preferring one explanation over competing alternatives. Researchers should therefore routinely evaluate alternative models when drawing inferences about psychological mechanisms from nonexperimental data.

articles_hidden.title: Health care practitioners’ knowledge, attitudes and perceptions of psychedelic treatments for mental disorders: A scoping review
articles_hidden.authors: Jacqueline Samantha Womersley; Gabriela Iacovou; Yumna Kathrada; Marnus Janse van Vuuren; Hannah Lukic; Soraya Seedat
articles_hidden.abstract: Interest in psychedelic treatments for mental health conditions is growing. Health care professionals will be key in the implementation, recommendation, and administration of psychedelic-assisted therapy (PAT) if and when it is approved for clinical use, making their knowledge, attitudes, and perceptions (KAPs) central to successful translation into practice. We conducted a scoping review of health care professionals’ KAPs toward the psychedelic treatment of mental health conditions. Thirty-nine studies, comprising both quantitative and qualitative investigations, were included. The number of studies, and range of health care professionals surveyed, increased over time, though research remained concentrated in North America, Europe, and Australia. Participants mostly performed well on objective knowledge assessments, but this did not necessarily align with subjective knowledge, which indicated lower self-reported confidence in PAT theory and practice. Attitudes toward psychedelics’ therapeutic potential, safety, and legalisation were generally favourable, although concerns included potential misuse, risk of precipitating subsequent psychiatric disorders, and cognitive impairment. Participants generally perceived psychiatrists and specialised facilities as most suitable for PAT administration, and the need for further research was strongly supported. A lack of trained personnel and resources, and cost, side effect, and misuse concerns, were the most frequently endorsed barriers to implementation. Research into health care professionals' KAPs regarding psychedelic treatment is maturing, but important gaps remain: granular insight into KAPs toward specific compound-disorder combinations is lacking, and geographic coverage does not reflect the global burden of mental illness. Addressing these gaps will be important as PAT moves closer to clinical implementation.

articles_hidden.title: Intentions to Help Friends Across Cultural Groups: The Role of Emotional Connectedness
articles_hidden.authors: Arzu Karakulak; Michael Bender
articles_hidden.abstract: Across five studies (N = 1,859), we examined cross-cultural variation in emotional connectedness and intentions to help a family member, a friend, and a stranger. Samples included a nationally representative Dutch panel (Study 1), Turkish and Dutch students (Study 2), Turkish and German working adults (Study 3), culturally primed Turkish-German biculturals (Study 4), and bilingual Turkish students (Study 5). Contrary to the traditional view that collectivists prioritize in-group ties more strongly than individualists, we hypothesized greater intentions to help friends among participants from relatively individualistic contexts or primed with an individualistic cultural frame. Results consistently supported the hypothesized differences for intentions to help friends, while differences in intentions to help a family member and a stranger were less consistent and generally not reliable. Study 1 further suggested that emotional connectedness statistically accounted for group differences in intentions to help friends, and Study 5 provided tentative converging evidence that an English-language prime was associated with greater connectedness with friends than a Turkish-language prime. Together, these findings suggest that considering the role of particular relational targets within their cultural context may provide a more differentiated account of cross-cultural variation in helping than broad individualism–collectivism or in-group–out-group classifications alone.

articles_hidden.title: Divided attention during encoding constrains the benefits of interim testing for subsequent learning
articles_hidden.authors: Bernhard Pastötter; Karl-Heinz Bäuml
articles_hidden.abstract: Retrieval practice can enhance learning of subsequently studied target information, a phenomenon known as the forward testing effect or test-potentiated new learning. The present study examined whether this effect depends on attentional engagement during encoding. In two experiments, participants studied three lists of unrelated words (Experiment 1) or three educationally relevant prose passages (Experiment 2). After the first two learning blocks, they either restudied the material or were tested on it. Attention during encoding of the final target material was manipulated by a concurrent secondary task. Under full attention, interim testing enhanced recall of the final target material in both experiments and improved performance on a final knowledge transfer test in Experiment 2. Under divided attention, these effects were reduced in Experiment 1 and eliminated in Experiment 2. The findings indicate that the beneficial effect of interim testing depends critically on attention during encoding of the latter studied information.

articles_hidden.title: Music as Emotional Regulation in the Climate Crisis: Relationships with Eco-Anxiety, Eco-Guilt, and Eco-Grief
articles_hidden.authors: Friederike Koehler; Dana Swarbrick; Suvi Saarikallio
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Climate change increasingly evokes complex emotional responses, yet little is known about how everyday practices, such as music listening, relate to these emotions. Given that music is one of the most common tools people use to manage affect in daily life, examining its role in the climate context offers huge potential for insights into eco-emotional experiences. 
Methods: 312 adults completed an online survey on music‑based mood regulation and eco‑anxiety, eco‑grief, and eco‑guilt. Associations were examined using structural equation modelling.
Results: Zero-order bivariate correlations indicated positive correlations between eco-emotions and all music-based mood regulation strategies except for entertainment. Structural equation models further revealed two distinct patterns: using music for mental work, discharge, solace, and strong sensation were associated with higher levels of eco‑distress, whereas entertainment, revival, and diversion were linked to lower distress. This suggests that when distressing climate emotions arise, individuals who experience them more intensely may immerse themselves more deeply in their emotional processing through music, while those who experience less distress may use music in lighter, recreational ways. Qualitative responses showed that individuals use music in diverse ways to navigate climate emotions, including calming listening, engaging with climate‑themed lyrics, creative expression, community, and nature‑evoking soundscapes, while others reported no connection. 
Conclusions: Findings highlight music as a meaningful yet heterogeneous context in which people relate to climate emotions, offering new insight into the emotional dimensions of the climate crisis. Through integrating music psychology and climate-emotion research, the study underlines the value of everyday cultural practices as part of individual and collective adaptation.

articles_hidden.title: Choosing Stimuli Wisely by Using Individual Differences: A Step-by-Step Tutorial for the One-Stimulus-Per-Factor Principle in Vision Science and Optometric Assessment
articles_hidden.authors: David Henry Peterzell
articles_hidden.abstract: Given that data collection time in vision research and clinical assessment is limited, investigators and clinicians must select stimuli that maximize diagnostic information with minimum redundancy. This article proposes that analyzing individual differences—through factor analysis (FA), principal component analysis (PCA), and multidimensional scaling (MDS)—offers a principled approach. The covariance structure of individual variation reveals the minimum number of independent factors underlying a visual function, and therefore the minimum number of stimuli needed for efficient, non-redundant characterization. I term this the One-Stimulus-Per-Factor Principle: one well-chosen stimulus per factor is both necessary and sufficient. A complementary rule governs discovery: at least two to three stimuli per expected factor are needed to establish the factor structure. Converging evidence from luminance and chromatic contrast sensitivity, stereoscopic disparity, motion, hue scaling, face recognition, perceptual organization, and other domains shows that the dimensionality of individual variation is often lower than dense sampling suggests—and sometimes higher than sparse clinical testing captures. The approach also tests construct validity, revealing whether behavioral measures index the mechanisms investigators assume. These findings carry implications for clinical instruments across contrast sensitivity, color vision, stereopsis, and visual field assessment, many of which either oversample a single factor or undersample the full factor space. The same framework clarifies psychiatric applications—including contrast-sensitivity changes in depression, schizophrenia, and ADHD—by separating retinal-neural deficits from optical contributions such as higher-order aberrations and from attentional lapses, and it extends to oculomotor biomarkers. The article develops the Principle as a step-by-step tutorial, with a worked example.

articles_hidden.title: Musical Groove as Stabilization of Coordinated Movement: A Dynamical and Embodied Approach to Musical Rhythm
articles_hidden.authors: Ji Chul Kim
articles_hidden.abstract: Research has shown that the bodily experience of pleasurable urge to move to music, called groove, is the strongest for rhythms with an intermediate level of syncopation. Current theories explain groove in terms of predictive processes in the brain, as an active inference which resolves prediction errors caused by syncopation. Here we present an alternative explanation of groove from a new dynamical and embodied approach to music perception and action. The new theory, called embodied dynamics of music (EDM), describes musical rhythm as a dynamic pattern of coordinated movement distributed in the brain and the body and governed by the principles and constraints of coordination dynamics. Specifically, beat-based rhythm is described as a coordinative structure in which beat-carrying oscillatory movements provide anchor points for coordinating discrete movements corresponding to individual rhythmic events. In this view, syncopation is a potentially destabilizing force in the coordinative structure, and groove is an active engagement that stabilizes the coordinative structure by reinforcing beat-carrying oscillation with body movement. We support this theory with an analysis of coordination dynamics and a minimal dynamical model of groove which stabilizes syncopated coordination with a metronome by amplifying its self-sustained oscillation.

articles_hidden.title: Identity Centrality and Trauma- and Stressor-related Psychopathology: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
articles_hidden.authors: Kari Ellen James; Blake M McKimmie; Fiona Maccallum
articles_hidden.abstract: Over the past two decades there has been growing interest in how events, roles, or relationships that are central to an individual’s identity relate to trauma- and stressor-related psychopathology. However, the field lacks a systematic review to synthesize current knowledge across various facets of identity centrality and guide future research in meaningful ways. This systematic review and meta-analysis of the relationship between identity centrality and trauma- and stressor-related psychopathology identified 154 studies (96.1% traumatic stress, 9.7% prolonged grief) representing 66,371 individual participants. Three constructs were identified: event centrality (96% of studies), role centrality (1.9% of studies), and relationship centrality (2.6% of studies). Meta-analysis of 124 studies examining event centrality (k = 249) revealed a medium to large positive association between measures of centrality and severity of traumatic stress and prolonged grief symptoms (mean effect size of r = .446). However, heterogeneity was high. Moderators of outcomes included event type and cultural background. Notably, most studies were cross-sectional (86.4%), precluding causal conclusions. However, emerging evidence indicates that identity centrality and symptom severity may follow independent trajectories over time, raising questions about whether centrality represents a cause or consequence of distress, or a distinct process, and about the role of associated appraisals. Further, the literature is dominated by studies from WEIRD countries. The field would benefit from systematic reporting of key study characteristics such as time since index event, and studies designed to examine causal relationships. Further, most attention has been paid to event centrality, yet this is only one form of identity centrality. Constructs such as role centrality and relationship centrality should be further investigated where theoretically indicated.

articles_hidden.title: Where, Not How Far: Gender-Diverse Pronoun Use and the Ideal Singing Voice
articles_hidden.authors: Logan Barrett
articles_hidden.abstract: Many transgender and gender-diverse (TGD) people want their voices to change, but how pronoun use, a public expression of gender that only partly overlaps with identity labels, relates to the voice people want is unknown. In an online survey (N = 2,536), participants placed their current and ideal singing voices on a 5-point masculine–feminine scale. In exploratory analyses, participants who used they/them pronouns, alone or with she or he (n = 130), wanted larger changes than binary-pronoun users (n = 2,272; d = 0.84, 95% CI [0.66, 1.02]). The difference was robust to age and sex assigned at birth and was attenuated but still present after adjustment for gender identity and recruitment cohort. Among TGD participants, however, the two pronoun groups wanted changes of similar size (d = 0.11 [−0.16, 0.37]), so the full-sample contrast largely reflected comparison with cisgender binary-pronoun users. Pronoun use instead distinguished the destination of change: among TGD participants, 48.1% of gender-diverse pronoun users placed their ideal at the gender-neutral midpoint, compared with 18.3% of binary-pronoun users, whose ideals more often lay at a masculine or feminine pole. A moderation pattern in which singing-related gender incongruence strengthened the link between desired change and the acoustics of a chosen model singer did not replicate in a held-out test set and is not supported. Pronoun use appears to index where, more than how far, people want their singing voices to go; vocal goals and the scales that measure them should accommodate gender-neutral targets.

articles_hidden.title: Willpower or Choice? A Within-Country, Cross-Linguistic Comparison of Free Will Judgments
articles_hidden.authors: Alison Oliver; Paulius Rimkevičius; Renato Cesar Cardoso; Marcel Brass; Uri Maoz
articles_hidden.abstract: Does the language we speak influence how we think about free will? Previous work has often compared free will judgments across linguistic and cultural groups without isolating language from broader cultural differences. More recent work has found cross-cultural variation, but these designs could not determine whether language itself contributed to that variation. Here we report two exploratory studies in which language was varied while culture was held relatively constant. In Study 1, monolingual English- and French-speaking Canadians rated comics depicting choice and willpower on whether they represent free will. The English phrase free will makes will, and so willpower, salient; the French phrase libre arbitre makes choice salient (as in “to arbitrate”). If language shapes the concept, English-speakers should associate free will relatively more with willpower, and French-speakers relatively more with choice. They did not: the two groups showed almost exactly the same preference for choice, and equivalence testing rules out anythingbeyond a small difference. Study 2 asked why choice comics were favored. Participants rated thesame comics on choice, willpower, doing what one wants, and absence of constraints. Across thenine comics, free will judgments closely tracked ratings of doing what one wants and of choice, but tracked absence of constraints less closely. Free will might therefore be associated most closely with choice and doing what one wants.

articles_hidden.title: Wrong Note, Wrong Time: Age and Musicianship-Related Influences on Rhythmic and Melodic Timing
articles_hidden.authors: Logan Barrett; Sarah Anne Sauvé; Andrea Rita Halpern; Benjamin Zendel
articles_hidden.abstract: Musical expectancy theory posits that listeners anticipate both the pitch that will occur and when it will occur; however, the interaction between these dimensions across age and expertise is less understood. In this study, 175 adults (ages 18–82; musicians and non-musicians) rated the final note of short monophonic melodies on its melodic and temporal fit. Endings were systematically manipulated in terms of pitch (tonal, chromatic, or atonal) and timing deviations. Results showed a strong effect of melodic expectancy: pitch deviations substantially reduced goodness-of-fit ratings, whereas timing shifts had comparatively weak effects. Musicians gave lower ratings overall, indicating heightened sensitivity to expectancy violations, whereas non-musicians were more lenient. Although age alone did not predict ratings, an age × musician interaction emerged: older musicians diverged most strongly from older non-musician peers, suggesting that expertise sharpens expectancy sensitivity across the lifespan. These findings demonstrate that pitch dominates expectancy judgments, while also revealing how aging and musicianship jointly influence the perception of musical errors—an area that remains underexplored in music cognition.

articles_hidden.title: Color cues, developmental coupling, and the limits of the late-sighted model: A commentary on Vogelsang et al. (2024)
articles_hidden.authors: David Henry Peterzell
articles_hidden.abstract:
Vogelsang et al. (2024) report in Science that congenitally blind individuals who gain sight late in life rely disproportionately on color cues for object recognition, unlike normally sighted controls. They propose that this pattern reflects the adaptive value of neonatal color immaturity: because typical infants experience a period of degraded chromatic input, they develop object representations grounded in luminance rather than color.
The theoretical account, however, rests on an incomplete engagement with the developmental literature. Decades of research indicate that color and luminance sensitivity are developmentally coupled through shared photoreceptor immaturity: the same front-end bottleneck that degrades chromatic input in neonates simultaneously degrades luminance and spatial processing. If this coupling is real, there is no luminance-first window, because the bottleneck lifts for both dimensions together. The account's central premise is therefore undermined not by arguing independence, but by showing that color and luminance do not develop in the sequence the account requires.
I further identify methodological concerns: a small and unusual sample, a fixed order confound in the primary behavioral task, a computational model implementing a binary switch rather than the gradual chromatic cascade of normal development, and a color sensitivity test using non-equiluminant stimuli, leaving open the possibility that luminance rather than chromatic contrast sensitivity drove performance.
Together, these issues require qualification of the conclusions of Vogelsang et al. and reconciliation of the proposed account with classical findings in infant visual development. This broader question remains important, but the answer is unlikely to hinge on color alone.

articles_hidden.title: Evaluating Large Language Models on Clinical Risk Judgement: An Example from Alcohol Use Disorder
articles_hidden.authors: Charles M. Bolton; Kiwon Song; Katelyn A Wasson; Clintin P Davis-Stober; Konstantina Sokratous
articles_hidden.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are being explored for medical risk assessment, yet performance on standardized benchmarks does not necessarily establish clinical competency. The present study evaluated whether LLM-generated Alcohol Use Disorder (AUD) risk judgments aligned with epidemiological evidence and remained consistent as clinical and demographic context changed. Three LLMs—GPT-5.5, LLaMA-2-70B, and MEDITRON-70B—completed four pairwise-comparison experiments involving DSM-5 AUD criteria, demographic characteristics, criteria paired with demographic characteristics, and narrative clinical vignettes. LLM-implied rankings were compared with epidemiological benchmarks derived from the National Epidemiological Survey on Alcohol and Related Conditions, Wave Three (NESARC-III). Our results show that none of the LLMs reproduced the implied severity ordering of the AUD criteria. Demographic cues consistently influenced AUD risk judgments, although the direction and magnitude of these effects varied across LLMs, demographic attributes, and clinical contexts. Demographic rankings also showed only partial stability as contextual information changed. LLMs differed substantially in decisiveness, with GPT-5.5 assigning substantially higher probability to selected responses than LLaMA-2-70B or MEDITRON-70B. These findings demonstrate a gap in current LLM risk-assessment capabilities and highlight the importance of evaluating the direction, magnitude, stability, and certainty of LLM judgments alongside accuracy.

articles_hidden.title: Subjective and Behavioral Difficulties in Social Contexts: Unique and Interacting Effects on Social Dysfunction Transdiagnostically
articles_hidden.authors: Kathryn Kemp; Carly A Lasagna; Scott D. Blain; Cynthia Z. Burton; Costanza Colombi; Aubrey M Moe; Ivy Fei Tso
articles_hidden.abstract: Prior research indicates that social functioning is impacted by both social engagement and subjective experience regarding social interactions. The goal of this study was to examine the extent to which each component, as well as their interaction, contributes to social dysfunction in a combined nonclinical and transdiagnostic psychiatric sample. A sample of young adults (n=193) spanning the social dysfunction spectrum completed measures that capture different forms of psychopathology relevant to social dysfunction, from which two dimensions – Subjective Psychosocial Difficulties (SPD) and Observed Social Difficulties (OSD) – were extracted using Principal Components Analysis. Participants additionally completed a variety of clinician-rated and self-reported social functioning measures that were aggregated into one overall social functioning score. Hierarchical regression was used to examine the unique contribution of SPD and OSD and their interaction on overall social functioning. SPD and OSD explained unique variance (Δr2=61.0%), indicating that elevated SPD and OSD levels predicted worse social functioning. The SPD-by-OSD interaction was positive and explained significant additional amounts of variance (Δr2=1.9%), indicating a less-than-additive effect on social dysfunction. The findings suggest that examining observable social behaviors and subjective psychosocial experience simultaneously is important for understanding social functional outcomes in clinical populations.

articles_hidden.title: Interval-Dependent Effects of Action and Choice Availability on Temporal Binding
articles_hidden.authors: Lauren Claire Fong; Silvia Seghezzi; Paul Michael Garrett; Mia Nightingale; Philip L. Smith; Robert Hester; Daniel Feuerriegel
articles_hidden.abstract: Temporal binding research proposes that voluntary actions compress perceived time between actions and their outcomes, reflecting an implicit sense of agency. However, it remains unclear whether such effects are stable across action--outcome interval durations and whether they depend on the degree of decisional freedom, such as the availability of choice options. Here, we investigated whether action generation (action vs. no action) and choice availability (one vs. two options) influence interval estimation across multiple action-outcome intervals using a yoked action-baseline design. Across two experiments, action-baseline differences consistent with temporal binding were observed only at the shortest interval (300 ms), where action trials produced relatively shorter interval estimates than matched baseline trials. However, these differences did not generalise to longer intervals and reversed in direction at longer intervals in one experiment. Across the full interval range, baseline estimates shifted more steeply with interval duration than action estimates, producing a crossover pattern in which shorter intervals were overestimated and longer intervals underestimated across conditions. We did not find evidence that choice availability, operationalised as one versus two options, modulated interval estimates in either experiment. These findings suggest that action-related differences in interval estimation are temporally constrained and may arise from an interaction between action-related processes and general perceptual biases in temporal estimation, including regression toward the mean. More broadly, the results show that apparent temporal binding effects in interval-estimation tasks can depend strongly on where tested intervals fall within the broader interval range, highlighting the importance of accounting for interval-dependent estimation biases when interpreting temporal binding effects in interval estimation tasks as proxy measure of the sense of agency.

articles_hidden.title: In need of adaptation:  The intersecting role of adaptive capacity and demands during the Menopausal Transition on psycho-cognitive wellbeing.
articles_hidden.authors: Laetitia Bruno; Guillaume T. Vallet; Annie Duchesne
articles_hidden.abstract: The menopause transition involves physiological changes that may intersect with changes in identity, social roles, and relationships, as well as pressures related to ageism and sexism. These interacting demands provide a basis for considering cognitive and emotional experiences through the relationship between adaptive demands and available resources. We propose adaptive capacity as an organizing framework encompassing the physiological, psychological, interpersonal, and contextual resources that individuals may mobilize or access during this transition. This framework recognizes diverse menopausal experiences and considers how accumulating or persistent demands may give rise to different adaptive needs. It also draws attention to the resources required to engage with existing treatments and health-related behaviors. We discuss two complementary candidate processes: vagal regulation, relevant to physiological regulation and recovery, and future time perspective, relevant to perceived future opportunities, motivation, and goal-directed action. Breathing-based approaches and interventions supporting future opportunities and planning may offer ways to strengthen resources alongside existing care. Longitudinal and intervention studies are needed to establish their contribution to adaptation during the menopause transition. This framework supports integrated, person-centered, and empowerment-oriented care that combines individualized support with attention to the social and structural conditions shaping access to adaptive resources.

articles_hidden.title: Toward process-level decoding of cognition with cross-domain transfer
articles_hidden.authors: Soroush Mirjalili; Dobromir Rahnev; Audrey Duarte
articles_hidden.abstract: Higher-order cognition emerges from the interaction of multiple cognitive processes (e.g., perception, attention, inhibition). Yet, these processes remain difficult to measure during ongoing task performance. Traditionally, researchers have studied each cognitive domain in isolation. In contrast, emerging studies have used multiple-task designs from multiple cognitive domains to better understand the relationship between different cognitive processes. These studies, spanning across humans, non-human animals, and artificial neural networks, suggest that cognition is compositional — built from abstract neural representations that generalize across tasks to support flexible behavior. These findings suggest that, with appropriate experimental design, neural signatures associated with a specific cognitive process can be decoded in one task and tested for transfer to another.  We term this approach ‘cross-domain transfer.’ Here, we explore the possibility that cognition's compositional architecture, instantiated through abstract neural representations, provides a basis for understanding how reusable cognitive processes can flexibly combine across tasks and contexts. We place cross-domain transfer within the broader evolution of cognitive decoding methods, discuss its theoretical foundations, and synthesize emerging evidence across cognitive domains. Through systematic task selection and validation, this framework provides a way to test competing theories of cognition and develop more interpretable, process-level approaches to measuring and predicting behavior.

articles_hidden.title: How Adults in Spain Perceive Love:  Individual Differences in Cultural Attunement and Evaluative Style
articles_hidden.authors: Saida Heshmati; Lindy Williams; Dana Hussein; Jaymes Paolo Rombaoa; Royce Anders; Zita Oravecz
articles_hidden.abstract: Love is culturally universal in presence, yet highly variable in how people perceive it. The present study examined individual differences in cultural attunement and judgment styles related to love. Adults (N = 502) living in Spain rated 61 everyday scenarios according to how likely each would make most people feel loved. Using the Continuous Response Model within Cultural Consensus Theory, we captured individuals’ alignment with the shared understanding of love (i.e., their cultural attunement) in Spanish culture. Greater attunement was observed among women, individuals with higher perceived support from a significant other, those with lower anxiety, and those who valued benevolence. Weaker attunement, on the other hand, was associated with endorsement of power and traditional values. In addition, individuals differed in how they expressed their judgments: older adults and men used a narrower range of responses, whereas those higher in extraversion and conscientiousness showed greater differentiation across scenarios. More educated individuals were less likely to judge situations as loving overall, whereas those higher in agreeableness were more likely to do so. These findings highlight that judgments of love experiences reflect not only shared cultural knowledge but also systematic individual differences in how that knowledge is applied.

articles_hidden.title: Stress and Work Performance among Doctors in Clinical Settings: A Cross-Sectional Study
articles_hidden.authors: Tuba Kalam
articles_hidden.abstract:
The present study examined the relationship between perceived stress and work performance among doctors working in clinical settings across India, including government hospitals, private hospitals, and clinics. Doctors frequently operate under demanding conditions involving heavy workloads, long working hours, emotional pressure, and continuous responsibility for patient care, which may affect psychological well-being and professional functioning. A quantitative correlational research design was employed with a sample of 50 doctors selected through convenience sampling. Data were collected using offline and online methods and assessed using the Perceived Stress Scale (PSS-10) and an adapted version of the Individual Work Performance Questionnaire (IWPQ). Descriptive statistics and Pearson’s product-moment correlation were used for data analysis. Most participants reported moderate levels of perceived stress and moderate-to-high levels of work performance. Pearson’s correlation revealed a statistically significant negative relationship between perceived stress and work performance (r = -0.599, p < 0.01), indicating that higher perceived stress was associated with lower work performance in the present sample. These findings highlight the importance of addressing occupational stress and promoting physician well-being through supportive workplace practices and appropriate stress-management interventions.
Keywords: Perceived Stress, Work Performance, Doctors, Occupational Stress, Clinical Settings

articles_hidden.title: Exploring Equivalence Testing with the Updated TOSTER R Package
articles_hidden.authors: Aaron R Caldwell
articles_hidden.abstract: Despite decades of methodological guidance, researchers continue to misinterpret non-significant results as evidence for the absence of an effect. Equivalence testing via two one-sided tests (TOST) provides a principled alternative, but adoption remains limited by software accessibility and lack of training. The TOSTER R package, originally developed by Lakens (2017), made TOST accessible to experimental psychologists. This paper describes a major update to the package that expands its scope with (1) a unified t-test interface supporting both equivalence and minimal effect testing, (2) a simplified hypothesis testing interface returning standard R objects, (3) tools for computing and testing standardized effect sizes and correlations, (4) robust and resampling-based alternatives including bootstrap and permutation tests, (5) equivalence testing for ANOVAs, and (6) power analysis and sample size planning. Each capability is demonstrated with worked examples. TOSTER is also available as a jamovi module for researchers who prefer a graphical interface.

articles_hidden.title: The Semantic Shift in Autobiographical Memory and Aging: Do Retrieval Goals Contribute to Age-Related Memory Differences?
articles_hidden.authors: Daniel Eric Cohen; Vannia Alexandra Puig Rivera; Jessica R. Andrews-Hanna; Matthew D. Grilli
articles_hidden.abstract: Relative to young adults, cognitively healthy older adults typically include more semantic details when narrating remembered, personal events. This age difference in autobiographical memory is mostly interpreted in the literature as a sign of cognitive and brain decline, and the consequences are largely assumed to be negative. Complementing decline-based accounts, the current perspective builds on a recent proposal that developmental changes in memory-guiding motives may help shape how and why older adults reflect on their personal past (Grilli & Sheldon, 2022). We identify theoretical support and accumulating empirical evidence suggesting that young and older adults may pursue distinct goals when retrieving autobiographical memories. A closer examination of these goals raises the possibility that young adults’ goals may be especially well served by episodically specific memories, whereas older adults’ goals may be better aligned with semantic autobiographical knowledge. Although experimentally causal evidence remains limited and an important direction for future research, the reviewed literature identifies age-related changes in retrieval goals as a plausible contributor to the semantic shift and yields testable predictions for distinguishing this account from decline-based explanations.

articles_hidden.title: Macrostructural Determinants and Social Oppression Forces in Latin American Youth Alcoholism: A Three-Level Model Third-Order Secondary Analysis
articles_hidden.authors: Carlos Fernando Pantoja-Muñoz
articles_hidden.abstract:
Objective: to execute a meta-synthesis grounded in third-order interpretations to critically deconstruct the distal determinants and social oppression forces driving problematic youth alcohol consumption in Latin America. This study analyzes a curated documentary corpus of 18 studies encompassing 21 countries indexed between 2015 and 2020, aiming to transcend dominant individualistic and Eurocentric reductionism in contemporary literature.
Methods: a critical secondary analysis was developed using a third-order interpretive framework. The secondary corpus was derived from a prior systematic review conducted under the PRISMA statement.
