From an initial screening of n = 16,921 records (Google Scholar, Redalyc, SciELO), a strict analytical sample of 18 empirical investigations was selected (aggregate sample of N = 5,253 adolescents). Qualitative data were processed using structured thematic content analysis and axial coding within a personal, familial, and macrostructural relational model.
Result: epistemological re-analysis identified five latent macrostructural dimensions operating asymmetrically across geographical regions: (1) socioeconomic inequality, (2) traditional consumption norms, (3) public health infrastructure deficiencies, (4) localized historical traumas, and (5) systemic violence. Furthermore, findings demonstrate that conventional scientific literature systematically omits these macrostructural determinants within direct empirical research designs.
Conclusions: the findings elucidate a mechanism of social determination wherein economic macrostructures exert top-down oppressive violence, severely constraining micro-familial systems. These forces generate unsustainable pressure driving alcohol consumption and subsequent molecular damage as an adaptive somatic response that modulates gene expression in reaction to biopolitical traps. For social health research, these outcomes underscore the urgent need for an epistemic paradigm shift toward public policies targeting structural environmental interventions.

Keywords: biopolitics, youth alcoholism, third-order secondary analysis, social determinants of health, macrostructural approach, epistemic violence.

articles_hidden.title: Non-commitment in mental imagery is distinct from perceptual inattention, and supports hierarchical scene construction
articles_hidden.authors: Yichen Li; Veronika Hammond; Tomer David Ullman
articles_hidden.abstract: When calling an image before the mind's eye, people often do not include basic properties of the mental scene. For example, when imagining a person knocking a ball off a table, people may neglect to consider the color of the ball. This "non-commitment" in imagery has been part of ongoing debates on the nature of mental imagery in philosophy and cognitive science, but the central question of its origin remains open. It is possible that this lack of detail in the imagination reflects actual non-commitment, as one constructs a hierarchical mental scene. But it is also possible that people do form highly detailed mental images, but fail to notice, encode, or recall properties of the image, for the same reasons that they do not notice, encode, or recall details of real scenes in direct perception. We tested these contrasting hypotheses across three experiments (N=3,895 total). First, we compared non-commitment patterns in mental imagery with the details that participants failed to notice in briefly presented real images. We found no correlation between properties that were non-committed to in the imagination, and those missed under rapid perception, indicating that non-commitment does not simply arise from perceptual noise. Next, we examined the temporal unfolding of mental imagery, and found consistent evidence of a hierarchical pattern: core entities and spatial relations, then physical properties, then surface details like color and texture. Attempts to interrupt or constrain scene construction did not change the hierarchical ordering. We suggest the results support a hierarchical partial-scene construction account of mental imagery.

articles_hidden.title: A Transcultural, Digital, and Global Perspective: Beyond Family Risk Environments in Adolescent Alcohol Use Disorders
articles_hidden.authors: Carlos Fernando Pantoja-Muñoz
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background and Aims: high-resource Western models restrict adolescent alcohol use disorders (AUD) to static micro-environmental or behavioral variables. This study aims to refute conventional linear predictive frameworks and validate the Global Multidimensional Paradigm against contemporary restrictive models.
Design and Setting: A systematic methodology based on the PRISMA statement was employed to contrast transnational linear parameters against structural evidence derived from an epidemiological screening across 21 Latin American countries.
Participants and Measurements: a pre-pandemic (2015–2020) screening of 16,921 epidemiological records was conducted, extracting data from 18 included studies to consolidate a total aggregated sample of 5,253 adolescents. Transnational profiles from the World Bank and WHO (cellular toxicity, acute intoxication, and immunosuppression) were analyzed alongside macro-structural variables.
Findings: comparative analysis demonstrates that traditional Anglo-Saxon models fail by omitting global macro-structural forces highlighted by the Lancet Commission. The proposed paradigm reveals that alcohol use disorders are determined by a three-dimensional interaction intersecting the micro-family environment with 21st-century digital dynamics (algorithmic marketing on TikTok and Instagram, e-commerce, and systemic violence), validating Krieger’s eco-social theory of embodiment (2024).
Conclusions: by displacing linear biomedical approaches, this study establishes that adolescent alcohol use disorders constitute the literal biological embodiment of macro-structural inequalities, offering an indispensable new conceptual standard for international epidemiology. 

Keywords: adolescence, alcohol use disorders, multidimensional model, biological embodiment, digital networks.

articles_hidden.title: A modality-general bias towards meaning, not enhanced prior knowledge, is linked to hallucination-proneness in the general population
articles_hidden.authors: Freya Hammers; Xiaoran Wu; Ben Alderson-Day; Chelsi Clarke; Eamon Blake; Samuel Evans
articles_hidden.abstract: Predictive processing theories propose that hallucinations arise from excessive influence of prior expectations on perception. Although these theories implicitly generalise across modalities, previous findings suggest potentially different mechanisms in vision and audition. In this study, we tested predictive processing accounts in the visual and auditory modalities in 177 healthy adults using well-matched prior knowledge tasks. Participants discriminated degraded meaningful targets from control stimuli before and after exposure to clear template stimuli, providing explicit prior knowledge. Signal detection analyses quantified pre-exposure response bias (criterion, C) and improvements in discrimination sensitivity (d′) following exposure. Hallucination-proneness was measured using the Cardiff Anomalous Perceptions Scale (CAPS). Prior knowledge improved discrimination equally across modalities, but individual differences in this benefit were unrelated to hallucination-proneness, with Bayesian analyses supporting the null hypothesis. Instead, hallucination-proneness was associated with a more liberal pre-exposure response bias in both modalities. When entered together in regression models, response bias was a stronger predictor of hallucination-proneness than prior knowledge benefit in both modalities. These findings suggest that hallucination-proneness is characterised by a modality-general bias towards meaningful interpretations of ambiguous sensory input, rather than enhanced directed use of prior knowledge.

articles_hidden.title: Event segmentation aligns emotional learning and episodic memory
articles_hidden.authors: Patrick Laing; Josh Cisler; Joseph E. Dunsmoor
articles_hidden.abstract: Emotion prioritizes not only what was significant, but when it was significant. When temporal structure is insufficient to bind emotional relevance to distinct episodes, emotional experiences can lead to overgeneralization and source confusion. Here, we tested whether event boundaries serve as a control mechanism that allows emotional prioritization in memory to reset and re-bind as relevance changes over time. Participants completed a preregistered two-day Pavlovian category-conditioning in which category-shock associations reversed across multiple learning phases. In one group, each reversal phase was preceded by a brief but explicit event boundary signaling an associative transition; in the other group, reversals occurred continuously without an explicit boundary. Episodic recognition memory for trial-unique conditioned stimuli, tested 24-hours later, showed selective enhancement for threat-predictive items in the segmentation group—most prominently during early and final learning epochs—whereas continuous encoding produced flatter, less selective memory profiles that failed to fully track changing emotional contingencies. Individual differences in learning dynamics during encoding predicted selective episodic memory at 24hrs, with event segmentation shifting this learning-memory coupling to the most recent threat reversal rather than the earliest one. Overall, event boundaries promoted tighter alignment between episodic memory and emotional relevance at the time of experience. These findings suggest that event segmentation supports adaptive memory prioritization by binding emotional significance to what is most relevant in the moment.

articles_hidden.title: Estimand or estimator? Comparing vowel overlap measures against a known ground truth
articles_hidden.authors: Grant M Berry
articles_hidden.abstract: Deciding how much two vowel categories overlap is a core problem in laboratory phonology and sociophonetics, and the field has proposed several metrics to quantify overlap: the Pillai trace, Bhattacharyya distance, and Euclidean distance, among others. Researchers rarely compute multiple metrics on the same data, and what look like distinct overlap definitions are sometimes different estimates of the same quantity. I introduce Phontrast, an open-source R toolkit that computes multiple overlap metrics on the same tokens, and I simulate distributions with known overlap to disentangle each measure's estimator from its estimand. Two public vowel corpora show how measures behave on real data, in F1 × F2 space and thirteen-dimensional MFCC space. Mean- or Gaussian-based measures are precise but unresponsive to separation in higher moments. Kernel estimates are biased and bandwidth-dependent, but within the simulation's operating region they recover the ordering on average, whatever the mechanism. Pillai is the most precise for small samples and whenever separation is driven by means. Since this is rarely known a priori, I foreground Jensen–Shannon distance, a distribution-free distance between the two vowels' probability distributions that registers separation however it arises, for ordering speakers and contrasts—with Pillai beside it to show movement in category means.

articles_hidden.title: Unconscious Archetypal Selection Bias in Professional Ice Hockey: A Multivariate Positional Analysis of Astrological Ephemeris Data and the Relative Age Effect
articles_hidden.authors: David R. Juillet; Jorge M. Rodrigues; Joanne V. Longtin
articles_hidden.abstract: This study investigates whether unconscious scouting bias exists in National Hockey League (NHL) talent acquisition, driven by psychological and behavioral archetypes. Analyzing a dataset of 777 players across all 32 NHL rosters, the research quantifies standard physical maturity biases, such as the Relative Age Effect (RAE), against independent lunar variables (Sign, Element, Modality) mapped to emotional typologies. Utilizing exact binomial tests, Cohen’s h effect sizes, and Savage-Dickey Bayes Factors (B10), 4,864 distinct positional configurations were evaluated. Results indicate no archetypal solar advantage capable of overcoming the RAE physical penalty. However, when evaluating independent lunar placements across specific positional subgroups (e.g., Centers, Left Wings, Right Wings, Defensemen), extreme localized scouting biases emerge. Front offices consistently filter players through highly distinct, positional psychological profiles, with 13 franchises exhibiting three or more concurrent statistical anomalies, indicating that human evaluation networks unconsciously draft for specific behavioral mechanics.

articles_hidden.title: Domain-Specific or Domain-General? An Examination of Patterns of Mathematics Performance Across Achievement Groups
articles_hidden.authors: Hillary Mastarciyan; Michael Slipenkyj; Lien Peters; Alyssa Counsell; H Moriah Sokolowski
articles_hidden.abstract: Many children experience persistent difficulties in mathematics throughout elementary school. However, relatively little is known about whether patterns of mathematical performance differ in children whose low achievement is specific to mathematics compared to those whose low achievement extends across academic domains and to typically achieving children. Curriculum-based educational assessments, which evaluate multiple aspects of mathematics achievement, provide a unique opportunity to compare patterns of performance across mathematics domains in population-based samples. The present study examined whether children with low mathematics achievement, low general achievement and typical achievement exhibit distinct patterns of performance across five mathematics curriculum strands in Grades 3 and 6. Data were drawn from three cohorts of children who completed a province-wide math assessment in Canada, yielding a population-based sample of 2,968 elementary school students who were identified as belonging to one of three achievement groups. Analyses compared patterns of strand-level mathematics performance across the three achievement groups in Grades 3 and 6. Children with low math and low general achievement demonstrated strikingly similar patterns of performance across strands, which differed from those of typically achieving children. These findings provide new evidence that children with low mathematics achievement and low general achievement share similar patterns of curriculum-based mathematics performance, informing theories of domain-specific and domain-general academic achievement.

articles_hidden.title: The samplr package: A tool for modeling human cognition with sampling algorithms
articles_hidden.authors: Lucas Castillo; Yun-Xiao Li; Adam N Sanborn
articles_hidden.abstract:
Many models of cognition have sampling as a central component. These have been used to explain human performance across a wide range of tasks, involving perception, probability reasoning, and choice. 
One family of these models takes inspiration from sampling approaches developed in statistics, either by adjusting samples with prior beliefs or by implementing a sampling algorithm that overcomes the difficulty of independent samples at the expense of autocorrelation. 
While these models have been successful in modeling human behavior, their adoption has been slowed by the technical difficulties in applying them. 
Here, we introduce the samplr package, which includes a variety of these algorithms and cognitive models built upon them. We show how models in this package can match qualitative patterns found in human data, and walk readers through an example of how to compare these models quantitatively to human data. This tool aims to make these methods accessible to many more researchers.

articles_hidden.title: Dissociable neural oscillations track subjective value under risk and ambiguity
articles_hidden.authors: Shuting Mei; Leyou Deng; Gökhan Aydogan; Christian Carl Ruff; Ya Zheng
articles_hidden.abstract: How the brain values uncertain prospects and translates them into choices is a central question in decision neuroscience. Current accounts propose that decisions under risk and ambiguity share a valuation process that integrates outcome with probability information, with ambiguity additionally requiring evaluation of the uncertainty about the probabilities themselves. Here we used computational modeling to estimate trial-wise subjective value and tested whether it was tracked by shared or distinct neural dynamics under risk and ambiguity. Participants accepted or rejected risky and ambiguous monetary gambles while we recorded neural activity using electroencephalography (Experiment 1) and magnetoencephalography (Experiment 2). Across both experiments, alpha-band (9–14 Hz) activity localized to the precuneus and superior parietal cortex tracked subjective value under both risk and ambiguity. By contrast, delta-band (1–3 Hz) activity localized to the ventromedial prefrontal and anterior cingulate cortices tracked subjective value only under ambiguity. These findings reveal dissociable neural signatures for the two forms of uncertainty and suggest that the brain resolves ambiguity by combining a shared valuation process indexed by alpha activity with an additional process indexed by delta activity that may reflect the motivational salience of options with ambiguous outcome probabilities.

articles_hidden.title: ‘The difference between us is that I am an optimist and you are a pessimist.’ An autoethnographic study on suppression of critical scholarship
articles_hidden.authors: P. Matthijs Bal; Mehmet A. Orhan; Yvonne van Rossenberg
articles_hidden.abstract: Critical scholarship constitutes an important part of business and management research, including related fields such as work psychology. However, critical work is also often met with resistance from colleagues and gatekeepers within the discipline. Yet, there is little insight into how this resistance manifests in daily academic practice. This autoethnographic study by multiple critical scholars in work and organizational psychology analyzed 34 events whereby their critical work was suppressed and silenced. Thematic analysis of the events revealed ten different mechanisms through which critical work is suppressed, which could be ordered within four sequential stages of suppression: closing space, discrediting work, discrediting research(-ers), and disciplinary control. Jointly, these stages represent an escalating process of how alternative perspectives, including critical work, are suppressed and silenced in hegemonic fields. The paper contributes to existing critical scholarship by being the first to empirically elucidate how and through which strategies critical work is silenced. The study has important implications not only for the development of critical perspectives within scientific fields, but also for academia more widely, as political and societal forces that undermine academic freedom call for a better understanding of how critical work is suppressed, and how it could be nurtured for a more dignified, equal, and democratic society.

articles_hidden.title: Charting the ontogeny of mnemonic processes in childhood: the COMIC dataset
articles_hidden.authors: Tydings M. McClary; Elisa Buchberger; Ann-Kathrin Joechner; Ulman Lindenberger; Chi T. Ngo; Markus Werkle-Bergner
articles_hidden.abstract: The human memory system balances two complementary functions: generalization, which involves extracting regularities across experiences, and specificity, which involves retaining the unique details of individual events. Understanding how this balance develops can benefit from a neurocomputational perspective in which three core computations, pattern categorization, pattern separation, and pattern completion, differentially support generalization and memory specificity. Guided by this framework, we present a dataset from 180 children aged 4–8 years who completed four age-appropriate memory tasks that provide behavioral indices of these computations. Children additionally completed three standardized intelligence subtests. Alongside the dataset, we describe a semi-automated data-cleaning pipeline designed for developmental behavioral data, which can serve as a template for identifying and resolving common data-quality issues in studies with young children. In sum, this dataset provides a resource for investigating the development of memory computations supporting adaptive functioning across early and middle childhood.

articles_hidden.title: From Mortality Salience to Existential Reflection: A Four-Level Model of Reflecting Upon Personal, Human, Biotic, and Cosmic Finitude
articles_hidden.authors: JianHui Zhang; Yixin He; Michel Ferrari; Chao S. Hu
articles_hidden.abstract: Death-related thought can shape emotional responses, meaning-making, health decisions, and social responses to loss. Mortality-salience research has made death-related cognition experimentally testable. Yet a mortality-salience induction does not establish that a person has reflected on death in a sustained or personally consequential way. We propose a Four-Level Model of Existential Reflection. The model distinguishes reflecting upon personal finitude, shared human finitude, the finitude of living beings, and cosmic finitude. These levels identify different objects of thought, not a universal developmental sequence. People may engage with one or more levels in different orders. Culture, spirituality, scientific worldviews, relationships, and life circumstances shape the felt significance of these forms of reflection. The model generates hypotheses about long-term-perspective activities, death-thought accessibility (DTA), movement among levels, and their psychological consequences. It links laboratory mortality-salience research with lived experiences of death, care, meaning, and growth.

articles_hidden.title: Induced sad mood biases responses to sad and neutral faces under low visibility: behavioral and ERP evidence
articles_hidden.authors: Xueqiao Li; Elisa Vuoriainen; Elina Kangas; Piia Astikainen
articles_hidden.abstract: Facial expression recognition is shaped by both stimulus properties and the perceiver’s affective state. Research on emotional face processing under backward masking has largely focused on threatening expressions, and few studies have examined how an observer's mood influences recognition of non-threatening facial expressions under limited visibility. The present study investigated how experimentally induced sad versus neutral mood modulates behavioral and neural responses to sad and neutral facial expressions under low (10 ms) and high visibility (200 ms) backward masking conditions. Participants underwent sad and neutral mood induction on separate days and performed a facial expression categorization task while electroencephalography was recorded. Behavioral and event-related potential (ERP) analyses included 25 and 20 participants, respectively. Behaviorally, a mood effect on response criterion was observed in the low visibility condition: the criterion was lower in sad than neutral mood, reflecting a reduced tendency to categorize faces as neutral. Discrimination sensitivity was higher under high than low visibility but was not significantly affected by mood. Facial expressions modulated N170, P2, and P3 amplitudes under high visibility, and N170 and P2 under low visibility. P2 amplitude in the low visibility condition showed an interaction effect between mood and facial expression. In neutral mood, sad faces elicited larger P2 amplitudes than neutral faces, whereas in sad mood, the relation was the opposite. These findings highlight the influence of the observer’s affective state on behavioral and neural responses to facial expressions under limited visibility, extending previous findings beyond threat-related expressions to sadness.

articles_hidden.title: Noradrenergic influences on human thought
articles_hidden.authors: Claire O'Callaghan
articles_hidden.abstract: Neuromodulators help balance the trade-off between flexibility and stability that is needed for adaptive cognition and behaviour. Among the neuromodulators, the noradrenergic system plays a key role in balancing this trade-off: it helps shape whether we pursue a given behaviour or task, versus shifting our behaviour to pursue an alternate strategy. Put differently, the noradrenergic system drives the balance between a stable versus flexible engagement with the world around us. How might this capacity relate to human thought? In this chapter, we review the functional and organisational principles of the locus coeruleus–noradrenergic system, and consider how it might modulate different aspects of human thought. Highlighting examples from attention, belief-updating, spontaneous thought and stress. Together, revealing how the locus coeruleus–noradrenergic system helps shape the balance of flexibility and stability in human thought.

articles_hidden.title: Playing at scale: a long-term population perspective on the relationship between play and innovation
articles_hidden.authors: Elena Miu; Marc; Iulia Badescu; Cedric Boeckx; Camilla Cenni; Jean Baptiste Leca; Sheina Lew-Levy; Elodie Lepauldier; Luseadra Joy McKerracher; Mathilde Vestergaard Meyer
articles_hidden.abstract: The multifaceted relationship between play and innovation has long fascinated scholars across disciplines. Yet, we lack robust empirical evidence regarding the causal pathways that may connect these two behavioural concepts. While much work has revolved around how play might drive innovation in childhood, there has been little focus on how play might contribute to transformative societal innovation. Studies investigating play and innovation have taken a short-term synchronic perspective to innovation and have focused mainly on invention (i.e. the first instance of a novel behaviour), interested in how play might increase behavioural flexibility and problem-solving skills. Although these approaches cannot speak to population-level innovation (i.e. novel information that spreads across groups), evidence from such studies is often marshalled to support claims about the role of play for societal innovation dynamics over time. Here we propose that the link between play and population innovation has not been robustly demonstrated because of 1. a lack of precise specification of the causal pathways linking the two and 2. a mismatch between the scale on which play is measured and the scale on which population-level innovation operates. We narrow in on a specific kind of play (object play), a specific life history period (childhood), and a specific kind of innovation (population-level), and introduce a causal framework highlighting long-term processes to understand the state-of-the-art knowledge landscape and to guide future work. We synthesise three mechanistic pathways linking the children’s play and population-level innovation: exploration, development, and cultural evolution. We design formal causal diagrams that link children’s play and population-level innovation via the three mechanisms we identified, and consider potential confounds relevant to each. Our explicit long-term populational perspective on the link between play and innovation sheds light on productive means to move the field forward.

articles_hidden.title: CARTE: An LLM-based automated tool for semantic clustering and switching identification in associative verbal fluency
articles_hidden.authors: Lucie Vigreux; Victor Altmayer; Mathias Benedek; Thomas Hills; Yoed Kenett; Emmanuelle Volle
articles_hidden.abstract:
Semantic Verbal fluency is a core component of neuropsychological assessment,
valued for its clinical sensitivity and ease of administration. Yet, its full potential is rarely
fully exploited: performance is typically reduced to a total word count, overlooking the rich
dynamics of semantic foraging, such as clustering (exploitation within a semantic category)
and switching (exploration across categories). Although these dynamics are central to models
of memory search, they require laborious manual coding, limiting their large-scale analysis
and use for scoring. Automated alternatives exist, but none can identify which specific
category each response belongs to, and their agreement with manual scoring remains only
moderate.
Here, we introduce CARTE (Category Attribution and Response Transitions
Evaluation), an automated scoring method that identifies semantic categories and detects
clustering/switching transitions in responses to the Polysemous Fluency Task (PolyFT).
Because PolyFT is an associative verbal fluency task relying on polysemous cue-words,
semantic categories map naturally onto distinct cue-meanings, making them easier to identify
- a process we automate in CARTE by means of a large language model. Analyzing responses
from 90 French-speaking participants across 35 polysemous cues, we show that CARTE
outperforms existing automated methods in matching human raters. Crucially, CARTE’s
performance is independent of sample size: once classified, a word is permanently indexed in
a cumulative semantic database, ensuring computational efficiency, reproducibility, and
scalability across studies. By bridging cognitive richness and methodological feasibility, this
work offers a simple yet robust tool for studying the dynamics of semantic memory search.

articles_hidden.title: Visuospatial features influencing the evaluation of two-body interactions
articles_hidden.authors: Andrea Orlandi; Mohammad Soleyman Nejad; Matteo Candidi
articles_hidden.abstract: Visual evaluation of aesthetic, semantic, and emotional aspects of two-body interactions is fundamental for social cognition, yet the contribution of objective stimulus features to these evaluations remains largely unexplored. This study investigated how different visuospatial features of two-body implied interactions influence their evaluations in terms of aesthetic pleasure, symmetry, emotional valence, meaning, and interest. Across four studies involving 200 participants, we found that visually ‘entangled’ two-body interactions, defined by the extent of shared interpersonal space, were rated as more aesthetically pleasing, interesting, and meaningful than their disentangled versions. Using Representational Similarity Analysis and hierarchical multiple regressions, we identified the contribution of each stimulus feature to these evaluations. These findings suggest that two-body entanglement enhances the perceived dyads’ aesthetic and semantic value, possibly facilitating their configural processing. The study expands prior literature and highlights a dissociation between visuospatial features and mechanisms underlying pleasure and interest in dancing bodies.

articles_hidden.title: Measuring musicality at home: Preliminary validation of the Music@Home questionnaires in a Greek population
articles_hidden.authors: Katerina Drakoulaki; Christina Anagnostopoulou; Angeliki Triantafyllaki; Orianna Bairaktari; Aikaterini Nina Polytimou
articles_hidden.abstract: Music@Home was developed in the United Kingdom as a systematic instrument for the assessment of informal musical interactions in the home environments of children under the age of 5. It has been successfully adapted and validated in German, and widely used in research with typically developing children, children with neurodevelopmental disabilities, and adults reporting their early music exposure retrospectively. In the present study, we adapted and conducted a preliminary validation of the Music@Home Infant and Preschool questionnaires for a Greek-speaking population. A total of 238 Greek-speaking primary caregivers completed either version, along with measures of cognitive stimulation at home and child language and communication development. Both Greek questionnaires demonstrated acceptable to good confirmatory fit, strong internal reliability, and evidence for divergent validity, with test-retest reliability established for the Preschool version, indicating that musical engagement represents a distinct aspect of the home environment rather than general cognitive stimulation. Exploratory analyses revealed modest positive associations between Infant scores and parent-reported language outcomes, consistent with previous research linking early musical experiences and language development. These findings provide initial evidence that the Greek Music@Home is a psychometrically sound tool for assessing the home musical environment in Greek-speaking populations and highlight the value of cross-cultural adaptations for research on music cognition, language, and broader developmental outcomes.

articles_hidden.title: Eat your vegetables: Exploring food learning cues in 12-month-old infants
articles_hidden.authors: Camille Rioux; Karola Schlegelmilch; Annie E. Wertz
articles_hidden.abstract: Food learning in early life largely relies on social learning. Previous research has shown that infants learn something is edible when they directly observe someone else eating it. However, the role of other forms of food-related social information remains largely unknown. Food processing actions (e.g., chopping, mashing) are essential components of human food behaviors and a ubiquitous part of infants’ everyday lives. Here we examined whether infants (i) differentially attend to eating and food processing actions compared to control actions and (ii) learn that novel foods are edible after observing eating and food processing actions performed with them. We tested 12-month-olds’ responses to three different actions: eating, food processing, and a control action (touch). First, we showed infants side-by-side videos of an adult performing two different actions with novel foods across three between-subjects conditions and measured their gaze and pupil dilation with an eye-tracker. Then, we offered infants the novel foods shown in the videos and measured their choices and eating behaviors. Our eye-tracking results indicate that infants differentially attend to eating and food processing actions relative to the control action, and show increased pupil dilation for the control action relative to the two actions that may indicate edibility (eating and cutting). When asked to choose which novel food they could eat, infants chose the novel food they saw an actor eat, but only when that eating action was paired with the control action. These findings help identify important mechanisms that increase acceptance of healthy foods early in life.

articles_hidden.title: Same Effect, Different Magnitude: How the Choice of Pre- or Post-Treatment Standard Deviation Shapes Standardized Effect Sizes in Psychological Clinical Trials
articles_hidden.authors: Matthias Pillny; Anika Buchholz; Anna Suling; Antonia Zapf; Tania Marie Lincoln
articles_hidden.abstract: Standardized mean differences (SMDs) are used to express treatment effects on a common metric, yet there is no consensus on whether mean differences should be standardized using the outcome standard deviation (SD) at baseline or follow-up. This study examined whether this choice systematically affects effect-size magnitude in a reproducible sample of 100 randomized psychological clinical trials. For each trial, SMDs were calculated using either the pooled baseline SD (SMDpre) or the pooled follow-up SD (SMDpost). The unweighted paired mean difference showed that |SMDpre| was, 0.11 SMD units larger than |SMDpost|, 95% CI [0.07, 0.14]. In a multilevel meta-regression |SMDpre| was 0.082 SMD units larger than |SMDpost|, equalling a 13% increase, 95% CI [0.042, 0.123]. Bland–Altman analysis indicated substantial between-study variation, 95% limits of agreement [−0.25, 0.46]. Secondary analyses including 2,228 effect sizes across all follow-ups mirrored this pattern, indicating a 7% increase of SMD magnitude associated to |SMDpre|, 95% CI [0.021, 0.044]. Moderator analyses suggested that discrepancies were larger in studies applying symptom-threshold eligibility criteria, and in secondary analyses, using the same measure both to determine eligibility and to assess the outcome and with longer follow-up. Importantly, 70% of included studies did not report how SMDs were operationalized. These findings demonstrate that the choice of standardizing SD systematically affects estimated treatment-effect magnitudes and that the discrepancy can become more pronounced under specific design conditions. Researchers should therefore carefully consider the choice of standardizer and explicitly report the time point and method used to derive the SD.

articles_hidden.title: The impact of professional development programs on K–12 teachers’ AI literacy: A systematic review and meta-analysis
articles_hidden.authors: YING MA; Chloe Gordon; Tingting Li; Ziwen Teuber; Theresa Dicke; Taren Sanders; Michael Noetel; Rebecca J Collie; Kewen Liao; Chengliang Wang
articles_hidden.abstract: Teachers' artificial intelligence (AI) literacy is an increasingly important focus of professional development (PD). This systematic review synthesized evidence from 62 empirical studies (61 records), including 36 studies eligible for effect-size estimation, involving pre-service and in-service teachers. Most programs emphasized AI-related knowledge and skills, with less systematic attention to attitudinal and ethical dimensions. Common design features included temporal flexibility (e.g., synchronous and asynchronous learning), role diversification (e.g., co-designers and collaborators), and contextual orientation (e.g., task- and project-based learning). The primary combined-design multilevel meta-analysis after influence diagnostics, based on 212 effect sizes from 34 studies, indicated a significant positive average effect across knowledge, skills, and attitudes/values (g = 0.76, 95% CI [0.50, 1.02], p < .001). Substantial heterogeneity indicated considerable variation across programs and contexts. Although possible small-study effects and publication selection may have inflated the magnitude of the primary pooled estimate, Bayesian selection-model analyses continued to support a positive average effect. No statistically significant moderation was detected by career stage, school level, intervention-duration category, research design, outcome measurement type, or gender composition. These findings provide an important quantitative benchmark for the emerging evidence base and indicate that AI literacy PD can support multiple dimensions of teachers' AI literacy.

articles_hidden.title: Cultural Differences in Emotion Regulation May Not Be Unique to Expressive Suppression
articles_hidden.authors: Sooyeon Kim; Katharine Helen Greenaway; Peter Koval
articles_hidden.abstract: Controlling emotion expression is theorized to be more valued and thus more frequently used and beneficial among Easterners than Westerners. However, existing evidence relies on global self-reports capturing culturally informed beliefs about suppression rather than moment-to-moment suppression. Moreover, whether cultural differences are specific to suppression or reflect broader emotion-regulation patterns remains unclear. Using three experience-sampling datasets, we tested cultural differences in suppression across global and momentary self-reports and their specificity. Easterners reported greater suppression at both global and momentary self-reports. Cultural differences were specific to suppression at global levels but generalized to reappraisal and rumination at momentary levels. We found less support for cultural differences in the affective correlates of emotion regulation. However, there was moderate evidence that momentary suppression, reappraisal, and rumination were less strongly associated with negative affect among Easterners than Westerners. We provide the first comprehensive test of cultural differences in suppression and suggest they may reflect broader emotion-regulation patterns.

articles_hidden.title: Unsupervised transfer in relational category learning
articles_hidden.authors: Hilary Don; Micah Goldwater; Kit S Double; Evan James Livesey
articles_hidden.abstract: Abstraction of relational structures beyond surface features is essential for transfer of learning across contexts. However, learners often fail to apply relational knowledge outside the original learning setting. Our prior work shows that inference-learning can promote relational abstraction and supervised far transfer, but it remains unclear whether such learning supports spontaneous transfer without feedback. This study tested whether inference learning improves unsupervised far transfer across tasks with distinct surface characteristics. Participants learned to categorise stimuli based on monotonic versus non-monotonic relations among line lengths, under classification or inference-learning conditions. Transfer was assessed for luminance-based dot arrays and digit sequences, presented in counterbalanced order. Inference-learning led to stronger relational responding during training and significantly improved far transfer performance overall, even in the absence of feedback. Transfer accuracy was higher for digit sequences than dot arrays, particularly among participants who demonstrated strong relational learning. Moreover, an unexpected finding was that completing the digit task first selectively improved subsequent transfer to the dot task, suggesting that symbolic representations may scaffold relational alignment. These findings provide evidence that inference-learning fosters abstract relational representations that support far transfer, while also highlighting the role of representational format and task sequencing in enabling effective generalization.

articles_hidden.title: Empirically derived phenotypes can reduce diagnostic heterogeneity
articles_hidden.authors: Miriam K. Forbes; John F. Buss; Daniel P. Moriarity; Eiko I Fried; Holly Frances Levin-Aspenson; Lorenzo Lorenzo-Luaces; Kasey Stanton; Ashley L. Watts; Gregory W. Forbes
articles_hidden.abstract: Diagnostic heterogeneity is a longstanding challenge for the classification of mental illness because people who receive the same diagnosis can differ markedly in their symptom presentations as well as in the mechanisms underlying those symptoms. High heterogeneity undermines both the clinical utility of diagnostic labels and what we can learn from research that treats disorders as coherent constructs. In this study, we examined heterogeneity across six internalizing disorders (specific phobia, social anxiety disorder, agoraphobia, generalized anxiety disorder [GAD], major depressive disorder [MDD], and posttraumatic stress disorder [PTSD]) using three complementary approaches to quantifying heterogeneity: 1) descriptive heterogeneity (how many symptom profiles can theoretically satisfy the diagnostic criteria, and how many are observed in practice), 2) person-focused heterogeneity (whether diagnostic labels capture people with similar symptom presentations), and 3) construct-focused heterogeneity (whether diagnostic labels group symptoms with similar patterns of association with external validators). Analyses drew on subsamples from a large convenience sample with elevated psychopathology, predominantly from Australia and the USA (n = 14,762, mean [SD] age = 38.0 [18.0]; 55% women). Results showed that specific phobia was consistently the least heterogeneous; social anxiety disorder, agoraphobia, and GAD had mixed results; and MDD and PTSD were highly heterogeneous across all metrics. Notably, empirically derived phenotypes nested within each disorder substantively reduced heterogeneity relative to the DSM diagnoses. The study provides both a systematic multi-method approach to characterising different types of diagnostic heterogeneity, and a practical path toward more precise and informative constructs that can be implemented by rescoring existing data.

articles_hidden.title: Moral Goodness is Feminine
articles_hidden.authors: Jordan Wylie; Ana Gantman; Peter Mende-Siedlecki; Tianyi Xiong; Heleni Singer; Liane Young; Paul Bloom
articles_hidden.abstract: Care and communality are crucial features of morality. Given that women are consistently judged to be more caring and communal than men, we investigated whether the concept of moral goodness itself is seen as feminine. Indeed, at the representational level of faces, behaviors, impressions, and possibilities (N = 5,758), we find that moral goodness is feminized. Using reverse-correlation methods, we show that mental representations of the face of “a morally good person” is a woman’s face. Across 1,864 previously normed behaviors, we find that actions associated with moral goodness are stereotyped as feminine. In a novel impression updating task, we find that equivalent moral transgressions led to larger negative character updating for women than for men, suggesting that women face harsher penalties than men for deviating from everyday moral expectations. Finally, when asked to spontaneously generate possible responses to a moral dilemma, people produce fewer morally acceptable courses of action for men to engage in to solve the dilemma than they do for women, which is not moderated by benevolent sexism. In sum, moral goodness is gendered: people associate moral goodness with femininity.

articles_hidden.title: Assessing the Impact of Language on Visual Threat Detection:  cTBS over the anterior temporal lobe impairs semantic processing but not visual threat detection
articles_hidden.authors: Adam Fahmi; Nicola Thibault; Roxane Hoyer; Philippe ALBOUY; Isabelle Blanchette
articles_hidden.abstract: Constructionist models of emotion propose that conceptual knowledge is integral to emotion perception, but whether the rapid detection of threat depends on conceptual knowledge remains causally untested. The ventrolateral anterior temporal lobe (vATL), a core hub of the semantic system, offers a site for testing this dependence with neuromodulation. In a within-subject, sham-controlled design, 20 healthy adults received continuous theta-burst stimulation (cTBS) over the left vATL and a sham stimulation in separate sessions. Before and after stimulation, participants completed three reaction-time tasks: a category membership task indexing semantic processing, a pattern matching task serving as a non-semantic control, and a visual search task measuring the threat superiority effect (faster detection of threatening than neutral targets). Relative to sham, cTBS slowed semantic categorization but not pattern matching, indicating that the stimulation disrupted semantic processing. In contrast, the threat superiority effect was present before and after both stimulations, and its magnitude did not differ significantly between conditions. Rapid visual threat detection therefore showed no detectable reliance on the conceptual knowledge supported by the left vATL. Constructionist accounts may need to distinguish the rapid prioritization of danger from the categorization and experience of threat, where conceptual knowledge may still play a role.

articles_hidden.title: Echoes of Thought: Task Complexity, Inner Speech Analogs, and Prompt Design Shape LLMs' Response
articles_hidden.authors: Franziska Usée; Daniel Schad
articles_hidden.abstract:
Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown impressive performance across a wide range of tasks, yet
the mechanisms behind theirresponse behaviorremain poorlyunderstood. Drawing on insights from
cognitive science and the computational framework of model-free and model-based reinforcement
learning (RL), we examined conditions under which GPT-3.5 and four open-weight LLMs can exhibit
behavioral signatures of model-based RL in the two-step task, a well-established paradigm for
studying human learning and decision-making. Across nine simulation studies, we varied the task
complexity and prompt design to examine conditions under which previously reported model-based
RL signatures could be replicated. We found that GPT-3.5 showed model-based RL signatures in
simplifiedtasksettings,butthattheseeffectsdisappearedunderde-simplifiedtaskversions.Crucially,
model-based reasoning signatures could be re-established when incorporating an inner speech-
analog prompt, requiring the LLM agent to reflect on previous trials and anticipate consequences of
future actions. For the open-weight LLMs tested, diminished signatures of model-based reasoning
evolved under both de-simplified and facilitative task conditions. Our fine-grained analyses of
behavioral learning dynamics highlight the role of structured reflective and anticipatory linguistic
processes in enabling complex response patterns in LLMs and reveal both similarities and differences
to human decision-making patterns.

articles_hidden.title: Work-focused cognitive behavioural therapy for common mental disorders: a systematic review and meta-analysis
articles_hidden.authors: Anna Finnes; Magnus Johansson; Robin Bernhardtz; Lars-Göran Öst
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background
Common mental disorders (CMDs) are a major cause of sickness absence and work disability. Although cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) effectively reduces symptoms, effects on return-to-work (RTW) outcomes are limited. Work-focused CBT (W-CBT) integrates RTW processes into treatment, but the evidence base remains heterogeneous with unresolved methodological challenges. This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated the effectiveness of W-CBT on psychiatric and work-related outcomes, examined moderators of treatment effects, assessed methodological rigor, and identified common intervention components, with particular attention to how RTW outcomes are analyzed.
Methods
Systematic searches were conducted in Medline, PsycINFO, and Web of Science from inception to December 2025. Randomized and non-randomized studies evaluating CBT with an integrated work focus among working-age adults on sickness absence due to CMDs were included. Random-effects meta-analyses were performed using multilevel models with cluster-robust standard errors to address outcome dependency. Moderator analyses examined treatment content, number of sessions, and study characteristics. RTW outcomes were evaluated regarding their statistical properties, summary measures, and analytic methods used in primary studies. Risk-of-bias was assessed using Cochrane Risk of Bias toos version 2 and ROBINS-I. 
Results
Twenty-four studies comprising 26 W-CBT treatment conditions (n = 3,279 participants) were included. Large within-group improvements in psychiatric symptoms were observed and maintained at follow-up, while between-group effects were statistically significant but small. At post-treatment, 56% of participants had returned to work, increasing to 87% at follow-up, with a higher likelihood of full RTW in W-CBT compared with controls. Greater CBT content, stronger work focus, and higher treatment dose were associated with larger symptom improvements. However, RTW outcomes showed substantial heterogeneity. Many studies used analytic approaches assuming normally distributed data for outcomes that were bounded, skewed, or zero-inflated, or reported hazard ratios with limited comparability, constraining valid synthesis.
Conclusions
W-CBT is associated with meaningful symptom improvement and increased likelihood of RTW. However, misalignment between RTW outcome properties and analytic methods represents a major threat to validity. Future research requires improved outcome definitions, appropriate statistical modeling, and greater methodological consistency.

articles_hidden.title: Identifying attentional control mechanisms related to the performance of high- and low-skilled First-Person Shooter game players: With exploratory data on expert older-adult esports players
articles_hidden.authors: Inhyeok Jeong; Akinori Takeda; Daisuke Shimane; Masaki Takeda
articles_hidden.abstract: High-skilled First-Person Shooter (FPS) game players are known to have superior attentional control—the ability to select information relevant to a task (selective attention) and maintain an appropriate response (sustained attention). However, it is unclear whether the attentional control strategies between high- and low-skilled FPS players differ, and whether these differences are related to FPS performance. Therefore, we investigated differences in attentional control between low- and high-skilled FPS players using electroencephalography, as well as correlations between gaming performance and attentional control. In addition, as an exploratory aim, we examined the characteristics of older FPS players. We recruited 11 high- and 11 low-skilled FPS players (under 25 years) and five older FPS players (over 65 years). Participants completed a task responding to colors regardless of the semantic meaning (Stroop task), clicked on targets quickly and accurately (aiming task), and played an FPS (esports task), respectively. We measured event-related potentials (ERPs) during the Stroop task to evaluate attentional control. In addition, we examined the relationship between ERP components and performance on the aiming and esports tasks. As a result, high-skilled players showed significantly smaller ERP amplitude in the 150-250 ms time window and greater ERP amplitude in the 280-380 ms time window (parietal region) during the Stroop task. These results suggest that high-skilled FPS players allocated attentional resources to relatively later stages of stimulus evaluation and processing. Furthermore, ERP amplitude showed a significant correlation with performance on aiming and esports tasks. Notably, older adults performed comparably to highly skilled young players on the FPS task, despite exhibiting smaller ERP amplitudes than young adults. These results suggest that attentional control is related to FPS performance and may be different with age.

articles_hidden.title: Adaptive Memory and Metacognition in Older Adulthood: A Path Towards Successful Aging
articles_hidden.authors: Ashley Chen; Kara Hoover; Emma Kandel; Alan Castel
articles_hidden.abstract: Aging is characterized by normative changes in memory and a continued capacity for goal-directed learning and adaptation. Consequently, the maintenance and preservation of cognitive abilities that enable responsible remembering (e.g., selectivity, schematic support) and build resilience may equip older adults with the skills needed to navigate memory challenges in a technologically-advanced world. Research demonstrates that older adults can effectively monitor and self-regulate their behaviors under high task demands, modify encoding strategies to compensate for memory declines, and draw upon prior knowledge and expertise to reinforce learning. Regularly engaging in leisure activities (e.g., creative hobbies, curiosity-driven exploration, educational classes about aging and cognition) may also enhance neuroplasticity, lower dementia risk, and promote positive self-perceptions of aging. Overall, leveraging older adults’ metacognitive abilities and enhanced motivation through targeted interventions may offer a promising approach to promoting successful aging among an increasingly growing aging population.

articles_hidden.title: Attention in model-based cognitive neuroscience: Mechanisms for optimization under constraint
articles_hidden.authors: Emily Ruth Weichart; Ryan Pierce Kirkpatrick; Jared Vance
articles_hidden.abstract: Two major criticisms of attention research are: 1) verbal theories lack the specificity to make falsifiable predictions about how the various mechanisms of attention operate; and 2) the term ``attention’’ is frequently ascribed to conceptually similar phenomena despite dissociable neural underpinnings. The field of model-based cognitive neuroscience is well-positioned to address (1) through mathematical formalization of hypothesized processes, but may perpetuate (2) insofar as similar algorithms and parameters may recur across modeling traditions without necessarily drawing upon a shared neuro-mechanistic basis. This review provides a function-first organization of the algorithms that have been hypothesized to implement or give rise to ``attention'' at various levels of processing: perception, decision-making, and learning. We ground mathematically-formalized processes in the performance-relevant objectives they serve and the processing constraints that limit them. In doing so, we provide a road map of the broader computational-level solutions that ``attention'' mechanisms have been invoked to provide.

articles_hidden.title: Yes, ChatGPT (and other models) need a psychiatrist: parallels between experimental neuropsychiatry and AI alignment science
articles_hidden.authors: Karthik V Sarma
articles_hidden.abstract: AI chatbots (such as ChatGPT or Claude) sometimes state false information with confidence, a behavior popularly termed “hallucination.” In their recent perspective, de Boer et al. [1] compared these errors to confabulation in patients with memory disorders, and asked whether ChatGPT needs a psychiatrist. I argue that it does, but for different reasons. False statements from chatbots may be better explained by how they are trained: first to produce contextually consistent text rather than true text, and later by being rewarded to produce answers. The more meaningful parallel lies elsewhere: because these systems learn to simulate human characters, they may also reproduce human personality traits and patterns resembling the symptoms of mental illness. Understanding them may require the methods of experimental psychiatry and psychology, and could advance our understanding of the human mind.

articles_hidden.title: mlstats: An R package for multilevel descriptive statistics and data preparation
articles_hidden.authors: Felix Dietrich
articles_hidden.abstract: Mobile research methods such as experience sampling, smartphone logging, and daily diary designs produce nested data, in which within-level fluctuations must be distinguished from between-level differences. Yet, there is no established convention for preparing and descriptively reporting such multilevel data. This paper introduces mlstats, an open-source R package that computes multilevel descriptive statistics — including intraclass correlation coefficients and within- and between-group correlations — in a single call, exports publication-ready tables, and decomposes variables for random effects within-between (REWB) modeling. Supporting both frequentist and Bayesian estimation, mlstats is freely available on CRAN with extensive online documentation at https://felixdidi.github.io/mlstats/.

articles_hidden.title: Why Testing Structural Theories Requires the Unconscious Condition
articles_hidden.authors: Zefan Zheng; João Pedro Parreira Rodrigues; Lukas Kob; Karla Matić
articles_hidden.abstract: Consciousness science has traditionally proceeded by contrasting neural activity when a stimulus is consciously perceived against activity when the same stimulus is not perceived. This contrastive approach is well suited to locating neural correlates of consciousness, but it says little about why an experience has the particular character it does. A recent structural turn addresses this gap by comparing the relational structure of qualia with the relational structure of a candidate physical substrate. We review the main structure-matching programmes and what they offer beyond the contrastive approach. We then argue that all of them rest on an assumption that has never been tested directly, which we call the structural exclusivity assumption: That a neural structure matching the qualia structure reflects the neural substrate of consciousness itself, rather than merely the processing of information that can occur without conscious experience. The assumption is empirical rather than philosophical, and the standard structure-matching design cannot test it, because qualia and physical structures are estimated while the content is consciously perceived. We set out the design that would test it, and review the psychophysical and neural evidence currently bearing on it. That evidence consistently suggests that relational structure survives absence of awareness, though no existing study settles the question. We argue that structure-matching and contrastive designs must be combined, and consider what follows for the selection of candidate structures and for the promise of the dissolution of the hard problem of consciousness.

articles_hidden.title: The Male Evaluator Penalty: How Participant Sex and Relationship Context Shape the Perceived Credibility of Male Sexual Violence Victims
articles_hidden.authors: Martina Giorgio; Robyn Mooney
articles_hidden.abstract: Male victims of female-perpetrated “forced-to-penetrate” sexual violence experience significant psychological harm and stigma shaped by traditional gender scripts. However, research is scant regarding how such victims are perceived by others. This study investigated how participant sex (male vs. female), perpetrator-victim relationship context (intimate partners vs. strangers), and male rape myth acceptance affect the perceived credibility of male sexual violence victims. Using an experimental vignette design, 300 participants (50.3% male, aged 18-35) living in the Netherlands were asked to read a description of a female-perpetrated sexual assault and complete self-report measures of perceived victim credibility and male rape myth acceptance. Results of a moderated multiple regression analysis indicated that higher myth acceptance universally predicted lower credibility ratings for the male victim. Furthermore, male evaluators displayed significantly higher myth acceptance and rated the victim as less credible overall than female evaluators. Crucially, male victims assaulted by an intimate partner were perceived as significantly less credible than those assaulted by a stranger, but this penalty was applied exclusively by male evaluators. These results highlight the urgent need for targeted education for legal professionals and gender-inclusive legal reforms to ensure equitable justice for male victims of female-perpetrated sexual violence.

articles_hidden.title: So much variety, so much to eat : The neuro-cognitive bases of visual food categorization in infancy
articles_hidden.authors: Camille Rioux; Pia Rämä; Elodie Farineaux; Lionel Granjon; Olivier Mascaro; Stefanie Peykarjou
articles_hidden.abstract: Food is fundamental to life. Yet, detecting members of the food category raises a substantial cognitive challenge as different foods do not have any apparent common visual features. Moreover, what is deemed edible and appropriate to eat also varies greatly across social groups. While the neuro-cognitive bases of visual food category representations are well documented in adults, their early ontogenetic origins remain unknown. The current study investigated the emergence of visual food categorization abilities in infants’ brains, using the fast periodic visual stimulation paradigm (FPVS) coupled with electroencephalography (EEG). In FPVS paradigms, images from a target category are periodically inserted into a rapid stream of base images from other categories. If the brain treats the target images as a distinct category relative to the base images, a distinct EEG response appears at the frequency of presentation of the target images. In our study, French-speaking adults, 12- and 6-month-old infants (n = 25 per age group) were presented with target food stimuli inserted into sequences of base stimuli from various non-food categories (e.g., man-made objects, plants). Results show that, similarly to adults, 12-month-old infants distinguished images of food from those of other categories. In contrast, 6-month-old infants showed no detectable categorization response for food images. The current study is the first to investigate the developmental course of visual food categorization in the human brain and showed that, by their first birthday, infants already group perceptually diverse foods into a single category.

articles_hidden.title: When attention turns inward: Mind wandering reduces perceptual sensitivity across visual fields
articles_hidden.authors: Bianca de Haan
articles_hidden.abstract: We all mind wander from time to time, where instead of being focussed on our task, we start thinking about task-unrelated personal events or concerns. In daily life, however, mind wandering is often associated with reduced processing of external information. This is commonly explained by the decoupling hypothesis, which posits that processing of external sensory information is attenuated when attention turns inward. However, it remains unclear whether perceptual decoupling reflects a global, uniform attenuation of sensory processing, or a spatially-specific reduction linked to lateralised attentional mechanisms. In the current, pre-registered study, we used an online signal detection task to assess the impact of mind wandering on perceptual performance in the left and right visual fields. While performing the task, participants periodically reported whether they were mind wandering or on task. Consistent with the decoupling hypothesis, perceptual sensitivity (d′) was significantly reduced on trials during which participants reported mind wandering compared to on-task trials. However, this reduction in sensitivity did not differ between stimuli presented in the left and right visual field. These findings suggest that perceptual decoupling during mind wandering reflects a global attenuation of sensory processing, and that attentional systems involved during mind wandering may be distinct from those associated with slower fluctuations of attentional resources such as reductions in alertness.

articles_hidden.title: Playing at scale: a long-term population perspective on the relationship between play and innovation
articles_hidden.authors: Elena Miu; Marc; Iulia Badescu; Cedric Boeckx; Camilla Cenni; Jean Baptiste Leca; Sheina Lew-Levy; Elodie Lepauldier; Luseadra Joy McKerracher; Mathilde Vestergaard Meyer
articles_hidden.abstract: The multifaceted relationship between play and innovation has long fascinated scholars across disciplines. Yet, we lack robust empirical evidence regarding the causal pathways that may connect these two behavioural concepts. While much work has revolved around how play might drive innovation in childhood, there has been little focus on how play might contribute to transformative societal innovation. Studies investigating play and innovation have taken a short-term synchronic perspective to innovation and have focused mainly on invention (i.e. the first instance of a novel behaviour), interested in how play might increase behavioural flexibility and problem-solving skills. Although these approaches cannot speak to population-level innovation (i.e. novel information that spreads across groups), evidence from such studies is often marshalled to support claims about the role of play for societal innovation dynamics over time. Here we propose that the link between play and population innovation has not been robustly demonstrated because of 1. a lack of precise specification of the causal pathways linking the two and 2. a mismatch between the scale on which play is measured and the scale on which population-level innovation operates. We narrow in on a specific kind of play (object play), a specific life history period (childhood), and a specific kind of innovation (population-level), and introduce a causal framework highlighting long-term processes to understand the state-of-the-art knowledge landscape and to guide future work. We synthesise three mechanistic pathways linking the children’s play and population-level innovation: exploration, development, and cultural evolution. We design formal causal diagrams that link children’s play and population-level innovation via the three mechanisms we identified, and consider potential confounds relevant to each. Our explicit long-term populational perspective on the link between play and innovation sheds light on productive means to move the field forward.

articles_hidden.title: Memory precision fluctuates with theta rhythmicity in humans
articles_hidden.authors: Troy Houser; Riley Acker; Dagmar Zeithamova
articles_hidden.abstract: Rodent research indicates that the hippocampus naturally oscillates between memory encoding and retrieval phases at theta rhythm, indicating that the timing of when information reaches the hippocampus can determine encoding success. However, non-invasively probing such oscillations is challenging in humans. Here, we employed a recently developed dense sampling approach to construct a time course of memory encoding success. Using an attention-grabbing cue expected to reset theta phase, we varied the delay between the cue and to-be-remembered stimulus. Experiment 1 replicated recent finding that human associative memory performance fluctuates with theta rhythmicity, with the best fitting frequency at 8 Hz. Experiment 2 tested and confirmed a new prediction that memory precision also fluctuates with theta rhythmicity, consistent with hippocampal models postulating oscillations in the relative engagement of alternative processing pathways. Together, these findings suggest that the rapid neural fluctuations underpinning memory processes are robust enough to be observed using the dense behavioral sampling approach. Moreover, this work substantiates models of episodic memory and provides new avenues to study models of hippocampal function in humas noninvasively, providing evidence from a purely behavioral approach that human mnemonic discrimination fluctuates with theta rhythm.

articles_hidden.title: Eye-Tracking Data Quality Across Human Infants, Adults, and Chimpanzees: Challenges and Solutions for Developmental and Comparative Psychology
articles_hidden.authors: Daniela Schmidt; Ingmar Visser; Luke Maurits; Maleen Thiele
articles_hidden.abstract: Originally developed for adult humans, modern corneal-reflection eye-tracking has become applicable to diverse populations. This has driven its popularity in developmental studies with preverbal infants and comparative research with other animals, including nonhuman primates. However, these novel applications introduce unique methodological challenges, raising critical questions about data quality and the validity of cross-group comparisons. Here, we systematically investigated eye-tracking data quality (accuracy, precision, robustness) in 4-, 6-, 9-, and 18-month-old infants, adults, and zoo-housed chimpanzees. In Experiment 1, most strikingly, chimpanzees showed markedly lower accuracy compared to all human groups, including even 4-month-olds, who showed poorer accuracy than older infants and adults. Furthermore, some data quality metrics co-varied with key eye-tracking measures (e.g., number and duration of fixations, relative looking times), underscoring how data quality shapes inferences about psychological processes. Experiments 2 and 3 explored whether calibration adjustments can optimize data quality. In Experiment 2, modifying the conventional calibration procedure for chimpanzees yielded significant improvements. Compared to using an individual’s own 2-point calibration, another conspecific’s 5-point or a human 9-point calibration substantially enhanced accuracy. Conversely, in Experiment 3, a conceptually similar approach for human infants (using a peer’s or adult’s 9-point calibration) did not improve data quality compared to infants’ standard baseline (own 5-point calibration). Together, these findings offer profound implications and practical recommendations for navigating data quality challenges in comparative and developmental eye-tracking. Moving forward, we emphasize the necessity of species-specific method development and call for closer interdisciplinary collaboration to establish shared standards across application fields.

articles_hidden.title: Selective reductions amid global increases in neural information dynamics jointly track self-dissolution in meditation
articles_hidden.authors: Daniel Andrew Atad; Pedro A. Mediano; Fynn-Mathis Trautwein; ‪Yair Dor-Ziderman‬‏; Henrik Röhr; Yoav Schweitzer; Ohad Nave; Stephen Fulder; Aviva Berkovich-Ohana
articles_hidden.abstract: The sense of self is fundamental to experience, yet its neural basis remains unresolved. Contemplative traditions and empirical evidence suggest it can be voluntarily dissolved while retaining awareness, offering a window onto this question. We combined magnetoencephalography with in-depth phenomenology in long-term meditators (N=45, mean 3,832 practice hours) who reliably modulated self-boundaries across rest, self-maintenance and self-dissolution. Meditation broadly increased entropy and information transfer, yet selective reductions characterized self-dissolution. Reduced posterior-medial high-beta entropy and within-cingulate information transfer differentiated dissolution from maintenance. Information transfer reductions from occipital, cingulate, limbic, and subcortical regions, alongside orbitofrontal entropy stabilization, correlated with dissolution phenomenology. Combined with posterior-medial high-beta power reductions, these correlates explained 52% of dissolution depth variance, yet only information transfer predicted held-out participants. We propose selfhood relies on distributed processes that can be reconfigured in meditation through relaxed priors, gated bottom-up evidence, and stabilized evaluative dynamics, distinct from global disruption during psychedelic ego-dissolution.

articles_hidden.title: Morphological analysis when morphemes are hard to detect: evidence from infixation and reduplication
articles_hidden.authors: Dave Kenneth Tayao Cayado; Kathleen Rastle
articles_hidden.abstract: There is substantial psycholinguistic evidence that skilled reading involves morphological analysis, whereby morphologically complex words like teacher are recognised via constituent morphemes {teach}+{-er}. The ability to recognise morphemes is vital as it allows readers to interpret both familiar and unfamiliar words. However, over 50% of the evidence for this claim comes from studies of suffixation in English, where morphemes typically have a relatively consistent surface form across exemplars (clean in cleaner, cleanliness; -ed in walked, jumped). It remains unclear whether morphological analysis is also robust when morphemes lack a consistent surface form. Using the morpheme interference paradigm in Tagalog, we test whether infixes and reduplicants are detected during prelexical processing. Infixes are inserted within a stem and therefore reduce the consistency of its surface realisation (e.g., tawag → t-in-awag ‘called’), while reduplicants involve partial or full copying of a stem and therefore lack a consistent surface realisation (e.g., tawag and lundag become tatawag ‘will call’ and lulundag ‘will jump’, where ta- and lu- are instances of the same reduplicant morpheme). We found robust morpheme interference effects in both accuracy and RTs. Specifically, nonwords with morphological structure induced significantly lower accuracy and longer RTs than nonwords without. Our findings show skilled readers’ acquired sensitivity to these sophisticated morphological structures and motivate refinements to theories of morpheme learning.

articles_hidden.title: Retro-cue Characteristics and Visual Masking Differentially Influence Voluntary and Involuntary Attention
articles_hidden.authors: Germán A. Cipriani; Carlos González-García; Elisa Martín-Arévalo; Juan Lupiáñez; Fabiano Botta
articles_hidden.abstract: This study examined whether voluntary and involuntary retrospective attention prioritize competing working memory (WM) representations involving low-level perceptual features and high-level semantic categories. In external attention, interactions between attentional voluntariness and representational level have been reported, with voluntary and involuntary attention differentially modulating high- and low-level content. In contrast, previous WM studies using either central or peripheral retro-cues found no such interaction. We therefore tested whether increasing retro-cue predictivity and using fully non-predictive cues would reveal this dissociation. We also investigated whether late visual masking promotes retrospective attention by protecting WM representations from visual interference. Across four experiments (n=140), retro-cue reliability (Experiments 1a–1b) and late visual masking (Experiments 2a–2b) were manipulated using peripheral and central retro-cues. Reaction times and accuracy were modeled using hierarchical drift-diffusion modeling. Voluntariness did not differentially modulate competing perceptual and semantic WM contents. Furthermore, four novel findings emerged: (1) voluntary attentional benefits on WM representational quality were enabled by increasing the reliability of central retro-cues and operated through protection from visual interference; (2) reducing retro-cue predictivity from low to non-predictive had little effect on involuntary attention elicited by peripheral retro-cues, whereas evidence for central retro-cues remained ambiguous; (3) eliminating late visual masking generally did not reduce voluntary attentional deployment; and (4) for peripheral retro-cues, masking selectively altered involuntary attentional benefits across representational quality and retrieval processes in opposite directions, while increasing the difference between voluntary and involuntary attentional deployment. Together, these findings indicate that retro-cue type, reliability, and visual masking differentially influence voluntary and involuntary selection in WM without altering their relative effects on competing perceptual and semantic representations.

articles_hidden.title: Isolating domain-specific and domain-general contributions to global confidence
articles_hidden.authors: Sophie Bavard; Andrew McWilliams; Flora Chartier; Karim N'DIAYE; Stephen M Fleming; Marion Rouault
articles_hidden.abstract: While metacognition - our ability to evaluate our own cognitive processes - has been extensively studied by measuring trial-by-trial self-assessments of task performance (local confidence), real-world decisions often require a broader perspective, drawing on evaluations of performance over wider timespans (global confidence). Despite its pervasive influence on decision-making and mental health, it remains unknown whether global confidence is formed through similar or distinct processes across cognitive domains. Here we employ a novel gamified approach to compare how global confidence is formed in the domains of memory and perception. In memory, we found that both local accuracy and confidence contributed to global confidence, whereas in perception, global confidence was predicted by local confidence alone. By comparing the formation of global confidence across domains, our study provides new insights into the mechanisms underpinning self-evaluation, paving the way for the development of metacognitive interventions in education and psychiatry.

articles_hidden.title: Toward a Sequencing Framework for Teaching and Using Self- Enactable Behavior Change Techniques: A Conceptual Review and Proposed Approach
articles_hidden.authors: Alexandre Mazéas; Nikos Ntoumanis
articles_hidden.abstract:
Objective: Self-enactable behavior change techniques (BCTs) may help individuals initiate and sustain health behavior change. However, existing taxonomies provide limited guidance on how such techniques should be selected, taught, combined, and sequenced over time. This perspective aimed to review previous approaches and to develop a conceptual framework for organizing and sequencing self-enactable BCTs for intervention design and participant learning.
Methods: A critical conceptual review was conducted to identify published approaches to BCT grouping, temporal organization, prerequisites, and stage-specific sequencing. Literature identified through four databases was synthesized alongside the compendium of self-enactable BCTs to inform a five-step framework-development process.
