Results: The review showed that existing taxonomies and sequencing approaches provide useful classifications but limited guidance for progressive teaching and self-enactment. To address this gap, we proposed a framework comprising 108 self-enactable BCTs organized into nine clusters and 27 groups. We mapped prerequisite relations, classified techniques by their predominant prospective or reactive function, and sequenced their groups across the Model of Action Phases. 
Conclusion: Our framework provides a theory-informed structure for teaching and applying self-enactable BCTs. It is intended to guide intervention design and generate testable hypotheses about technique sequencing that need to be empirically explored in future studies.

articles_hidden.title: Validácia veľkých jazykových modelov pri kvantifikácii obsahového prekryvu psychodiagnostických škál
articles_hidden.authors: Viktória Gajdošová; Matus Adamkovic
articles_hidden.abstract: Krízu replikovateľnosti v psychológii prehlbuje aj netransparentný výber psychodiagnostických škál. Výskumníci často predpokladajú zameniteľnosť škál deklarujúcich meranie rovnakého konštruktu bez toho, aby overili ich skutočný obsahový prekryv, ktorého manuálna kvantifikácia expertmi je subjektívna, časovo náročná a neškálovateľná. Overovali sme, či veľké jazykové modely (GPT-5.1) a sémantické vektorovanie (text-embedding-3-large) dokážu posúdiť obsahovú podobnosť škál. Automatizovane sme replikovali tri expertné štúdie z domén depresie, mánie a traumy a porovnali štyri prístupy: sémantické vektorovanie, hybridnú metódu (extrakcia symptómov pomocou LLM a vektorovanie), zero-shot a chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting. Výsledky naznačujú, že LLM sa dokážu priblížiť expertnému úsudku, no ich úspešnosť nerastie so zložitosťou prístupu. Sémantické vektorovanie fungovalo najlepšie pri položkách s jednotným formátom; pri komplexných položkách extrakcia symptómov zlepšila poradie dvojíc škál, no prekryv nadhodnocovala. Najvýkonnejší bol zero-shot prompting, ktorý bez ohľadu na zložitosť textu dosiahol strednú až dobrú konzistenciu s expertným hodnotením (ICC: trauma 0.86, depresia 0.64, mánia 0.54). CoT prompting paradoxne zhodu znížil, možno v dôsledku „over-reasoningu“. Voľbu metódy odporúčame prispôsobiť dátam a zdrojom: sémantické vektorovanie je rýchle a lacné pri jednoduchých položkách, kým zero-shot prompting je univerzálny. Využitie vidíme ako podporný nástroj pri výbere a porovnávaní dotazníkov z hľadiska obsahovej validity.

articles_hidden.title: Naar een nieuwe generatie gedragsinzichten voor beleid: Denk na over hoe mensen kunnen en willen meedoen in de samenleving
articles_hidden.authors: Denise De Ridder; Lotte Frederike van Dillen; Marleen Gillebaart; Inge Merkelbach; Lars Tummers; Beate Volker; John de Wit
articles_hidden.abstract: In de afgelopen jaren zijn grote stappen gezet om beleid effectiever te maken door beter rekening te houden met wanneer en waarom mensen bereid en in staat zijn om hun gedrag te veranderen. Nu is het tijd om te bedenken wat belangrijke opgaves zijn voor de toekomst van gedragsinzichten voor beleid. Wij zien vier belangrijke kwesties: (1) Baseer beleid op het inzicht dat mensen in beginsel zonder hulp van buitenaf in staat zijn om verstandige keuze te maken; (2) Integreer interventies gericht op individuen in structurele of systemische maatregelen die mensen helpen hun gedrag te veranderen; (3) Richt interventies op intermediaire actoren en sociale netwerken die een rol spelen bij de implementatie van gedragsinterventies; en (4) Gebruik falende interventies als diagnostisch instrument om beleidsmaatregelen aan te passen. Mede op basis van een opiniepeiling onder Nederlandse beleidsmakers/gedragskundigen, gaan we in deze sessie in debat met de deelnemers over innovatie in gedrag en beleid met als doel hen te inspireren. We bespreken de relevantie van deze speerpunten, en hoe de wetenschap de praktijk hierin het beste kan ondersteunen.

articles_hidden.title: The locus coeruleus – norepinephrine system as a regulator of social perception
articles_hidden.authors: Maryam Ziaei; Camilla Bay Panduro Jensen; Hazim Hussein; Claire O'Callaghan; Valerio Zerbi; Heidi I. L. Jacobs
articles_hidden.abstract: Social perception allows us to rapidly interpret others' emotions, intentions, and actions, yet the underlying neural mechanisms remain incompletely understood. Here, we propose a framework linking neuromodulatory function to large-scale networks involved in social perception. The framework centers on the locus coeruleus-norepinephrine (LC–NE) system as an orchestrator of cortical networks. We argue that social perception is optimized when moderate tonic LC activity is paired with strong phasic responses to social-emotional cues, enabling selective attention, flexible updating of expectations, and accurate interpretation of social information. By contrast, both reduced and excessive LC activity are predicted to impair social perception. LC hypoactivity limits engagement with socially relevant cues, whereas hyperactivity produces diffuse arousal, distractibility, and hypervigilance, reducing discrimination of relevant from irrelevant social signals. We further propose that social perception emerges through modulation of local cortical gain, large-scale brain networks, and perceptual evidence accumulation, providing a mechanistic bridge between cellular processes and social behavior. Finally, we outline testable predictions and consider how disrupted LC function may contribute to social cognitive deficits in aging, neurodegenerative diseases, and neuropsychiatric disorders. By placing the LC–NE system as orchestrator of adaptive social perception, this framework offers a unifying account of how neuromodulation shapes social behavior.

articles_hidden.title: Does Singing Together Foster Learning, Well-being, and Prosociality in Children? Evaluation of the EVE Project in French Priority Education.
articles_hidden.authors: Romain di Stasi; Carla Aimé-Jubin; Camille Basile; Dalila Bovet; Rana Esseily
articles_hidden.abstract: Research has highlighted the effects of musical engagement on children’s social, academic, and personal development. However, most studies have focused on instrumental training, while the few studies on choral singing have reported effects on self-esteem in children and adolescents and social inclusion in adults. This study examines the impact of choral singing on academic achievement, social interaction, and well-being in children. This research was conducted within the “EVE project,” a three-year choral singing program organized by the Philharmonie de Paris in two socioeconomically disadvantaged schools in Paris and its suburbs. Using a longitudinal design, the study evaluated 133 children in the first year (94 EVE, 39 control), 123 in the second year (86 EVE, 37 control), and 112 in the third year (81 EVE, 31 control). At each yearly assessment, children completed three social interaction tasks (sharing, cooperation, and helping), measures of school learning abilities using the BMT-i test, and well-being questionnaires. Our results showed that regular participation in choir singing was associated with improvements in verbal memory, but no evidence of improvement was observed for working memory, dictation performance, or mathematics achievement. Choir participation was also associated with higher well-being and greater social interaction during cooperative tasks, as reflected by increased smiling and gaze toward peers. Overall, these findings suggest that choral practice may be associated with selective near-transfer benefits, particularly for verbal memory, and underscore the social nature of musical engagement and its potential to support children’s well-being and social bonding.

articles_hidden.title: Towards Natural Behaviour Processing for Representation and Prediction of Digital Human Behaviour
articles_hidden.authors: Clemens Stachl; Brittany I Davidson; Gabriella M. Harari
articles_hidden.abstract:
Studying how people behave and understanding why their actions unfold differently are
major goals of psychological science. However, most research relies on nomothetic
approaches that aggregate behavioural data into summary statistics, obscuring
person-specific patterns that afford person-specific understanding. The progressing
proliferation of digital technologies such as smartphones, wearables, and computermediated
systems now generates fine-grained, temporally ordered records of everyday
behaviour, creating unprecedented opportunities to study both systematic interindividual
differences and patterns of intra-individual variation. Here, we propose
Natural Behaviour Processing (NBP) as a framework for analysing digital behavioural
data using sequence modelling approaches adapted from natural language
processing. We argue that behaviour shares critical structural properties with
language: both involve a repository of possible actions (vocabulary), systematic
patterns governing how elements typically combine (grammar), and context-dependent
meaning (semantics). These structural parallels motivate applying sequence-based
models that have revolutionised language processing to the study of behaviour more
broadly. We review pioneering studies on diverse topics of research, including life
outcomes, decision-making, social media use, consumer behaviour, online education,
and health, demonstrating that sequential approaches capture person-specific patterns
that are typically lost in aggregation. We discuss the challenges facing NBP adoption,
including the tension between predictive modelling and theoretical understanding, the
need for large-scale curated behaviour datasets, and methodological training
requirements. The adoption of NBP could transform the way psychology
operationalises, conceptualises, and ultimately understands human behaviour by
simultaneously accounting for person-specificity in real-world complexity while
maintaining predictive performance at population levels.

articles_hidden.title: Loneliness is reflected in the sub-second temporal dynamics of the resting brain: an EEG microstate study
articles_hidden.authors: Kentaro Ono
articles_hidden.abstract: Loneliness, a subjective state of perceived social isolation characterized by chronic social hypervigilance, is a profound risk factor for physical and mental health conditions. While functional neuroimaging studies link loneliness to altered salience network connectivity, the sub-second temporal dynamics of the resting lonely brain remain unexplored. We investigated the relationship between trait loneliness and resting-state electroencephalography (EEG) microstates. Sixty-one healthy young adults completed the UCLA Loneliness Scale and Beck Depression Inventory-II (BDI-II) and underwent 3-minute resting-state EEG recording. A criterion-based five-class microstate solution identified a topography corresponding to the canonical Class C/E, associated with both self-referential and salience-related processing. Higher loneliness scores were significantly associated with reduced Class C/E occurrence, which remained significant after controlling for depressive symptoms, age, and sex. Exploratory source localization revealed that lonelier individuals showed reduced current density in the middle cingulate cortex (MCC). These findings suggest that chronic social hypervigilance suppresses the spontaneous mobilization of the salience network at rest, with reduced MCC engagement reflecting a dispositional attenuation consistent with chronic relational threat.

articles_hidden.title: Seeing good and bad for what they are: Preverbal infants discern valence in geometric-agent interactions
articles_hidden.authors: Yaying (Tiffany) Bai; Hiromichi Hagihara; Yasuhiro Kanakogi
articles_hidden.abstract: Animated shapes have informed much of what is known about early sociomoral cognition, but concerns have been raised about this approach and the interpretations based on it. In particular, whether infants perceive interactions between geometric agents as socially and affectively meaningful has received little direct attention, despite being a prerequisite for moral evaluations. Two preregistered experiments conducted between 2025 and 2026 addressed this gap in infants aged 6.5 to 10.5 months (N = 92; 43 girls), recruited from middle-socioeconomic-status families living in urban and suburban areas of [city name], Japan (all Japanese or other East Asian). In Experiment 1 (n = 28; 13 girls), infants preferentially attended to agent-directed, relative to perceptually matched object-directed, caressing (prosocial) and hitting (antisocial), which indicates sensitivity to social structure. In Experiment 2 (n = 64; 30 girls), infants attended more when caressing and hitting were preceded by affectively congruent rather than incongruent music (i.e., prosocial-positive, antisocial-negative), suggesting that they attributed corresponding valence to these interactions. The results substantiate the use of geometric-agent paradigms and provide evidence that foundational evaluations of good and bad emerge within the first year of life, extending prior findings beyond simple approach-avoidance responses to prosociality and antisociality.

articles_hidden.title: Moment-to-Moment Affect During Film-Induced Somatic Anxiety
articles_hidden.authors: Micah G. Allen
articles_hidden.abstract: Studying sustained anxiety requires tracing how unpleasant arousal develops, persists and subsides over an unfolding experience. We characterised a 13.5-min first-person film of people undertaking dangerous activities at height as an induction for this purpose. Using an open-source browser-based platform developed for this study, online participants continuously rated their own valence and arousal and completed the somatic subscale of the State-Trait Inventory for Cognitive and Somatic Anxiety before and after viewing. In the confirmatory sample (N = 124), arousal was elevated during the film's rising and sustained phases and declined towards the end, while valence was more unpleasant during the sustained phase than during the opening. Group-mean trajectories closely reproduced the temporal shape observed in an exploratory sample (n = 21; arousal r = .99; valence r = .94). Somatic anxiety increased after viewing (dz = 1.03). Participants reporting larger increases rated the film as more arousing (ρ = .24) and more unpleasant (ρ = −.38). The open-source platform and reference trajectories provide a reusable resource for studying the temporal course of affect during a sustained anxiety induction.

articles_hidden.title: Reimagining Psychotherapy: Toward an Integrative Afrocentric-Decolonial Framework for Relational Healing and Practice
articles_hidden.authors: Ohiro Oni-Eseleh
articles_hidden.abstract: Western models of psychotherapy practice are often inadequate to address issues related to African identity, which is rooted in communal existence, cultural histories and systems that shape perceptions of illness and healing. In African cultural contexts, psychotherapy plays out against the background of relational patterns grounded in African tradition and enduring histories of colonialism. Grounded in individualism and intrapsychic causation, this article draws from African philosophy and decolonial literature as it conceptualizes the adaptation and practice of psychotherapy in African settings. What is proposed is a relational model of psychotherapy practice that is informed by the importance of decoloniality, rooted in consciousness of culture and history, and an intellectual and practical embrace of epistemic and community-embedded care. Such an approach strengthens clinical practice while challenging global mental health to review its epistemological assumptions and determinations of what expertise means. Specifically, this article highlights the need to incorporate African cultural perspectives into psychotherapy to enhance the efficacy of treatment in that culture.

articles_hidden.title: iTemplate2: An Open-Source Python Toolbox for Automatic Eye-Movement Analysis of Dynamic Facial Stimuli
articles_hidden.authors: Naiqi G Xiao; Rafael Román-Caballero; Wei Fang; Sara Ripley; Danyang Han; Laurel Trainor
articles_hidden.abstract: Template-based gaze-to-face registration enables standardized analysis of eye movements by mapping gaze coordinates onto a canonical facial template, reducing variability introduced by manual area-of-interest (AOI) definition across heterogeneous stimuli. However, existing implementations are largely restricted to static images, rely on semi-manual landmark annotation, and depend on proprietary software, limiting scalability and reproducibility. These constraints become increasingly problematic as research shifts toward dynamic stimuli, wearable eye-tracking, and open-source workflows. We present iTemplate2, a fully open-source Python-based redesign of the original system. The framework introduces four key advances: (1) support for dynamic stimuli via frame-wise coordinate transformation, including a normalization module for wearable and scene-based eye-tracking data; (2) integration of MediaPipe’s Face Landmarker for automated detection of 478 facial landmarks per frame, with multi-face tracking and identity persistence mechanisms that reduce manual annotation requirements; (3) a complete Python reimplementation using NumPy, pandas, OpenCV, PyQt6, and Apache Parquet, providing a cross-platform graphical interface without commercial dependencies; and (4) expanded visualization and analysis tools, including interactive heatmaps, snap-to-landmark AOI definition, and extraction of facial blendshape parameters for concurrent expression analysis. The system is applicable across diverse domains, including infant face scanning, cross-cultural gaze research, clinical screening, and naturalistic social interaction paradigms using wearable eye-tracking. It robustly processes complex multi-face video datasets that are difficult to analyze using conventional template-based methods. iTemplate2 modernizes the template-based registration framework for contemporary behavioral research, converting idiosyncratic visual data into a unified, reproducible analytical space. The software is freely available as an open-source tool at https://osf.io/54v9e/overview?view_only=5ac289558a3d4897a02336124ae409a1.

articles_hidden.title: Biased processing of multiple outcomes in human reinforcement learning: evidence from computational modeling and eye-tracking
articles_hidden.authors: Henri Vandendriessche; Gruson Charlotte; Antonios Nasioulas; Camille Straboni; Maël Lebreton; Stefano Palminteri
articles_hidden.abstract: In many circumstances, choices result in multiple simultaneous outcomes, all of which should be integrated to optimally update reward expectation. Yet, to date, empirical investigations of reinforcement learning have mostly focused on situations where choices deliver only one outcome at a time. To understand how humans learn from multiple outcomes, we designed a new reinforcement learning task, where the selection of an option resulted in two outcomes drawn from the same underlying distribution over potential gains and losses, even if ultimately only one of the two counted for the final payoff. Behavioral results show that the two - equally informative- outcomes are considered, yet asymmetrically as function of their valence. This behavioral observation is backed up by computational analyses showing that, on top of previously documented asymmetric update, multiple outcome integration is biased, such as it overweighs rewards over punishments. Behavioral and computational results were paralleled by eye-tracking analysis showing that attention deployment is biased by outcome valence and relevance. The main results were confirmed in a second experiment featuring complete feedback information. Overall, our findings suggest that, when options deliver multiple discordant outcomes, losses tend to be neglected compared to gains.

articles_hidden.title: Learning to Enumerate Reorganizes Magnitude Representations
articles_hidden.authors: Lauren S Aulet
articles_hidden.abstract: Human adults show a number bias in magnitude perception, weighting numerical information more heavily than continuous magnitudes like area. However, developmental research suggests this bias is not innate: young children show an area bias that reverses to a number bias only later in development. What drives this shift? Here we use deep neural networks as a tool for testing computational sufficiency, asking whether learning to estimate number is by itself enough to reorganize how a visual system weights magnitude. We trained ResNeXt-50 networks on an enumeration task (labeling the number of dots in an image, an operationalization of a functional outcome of counting) and measured representational bias by linearly decoding number versus cumulative area from penultimate-layer features, with the two dimensions decorrelated by design. Untrained networks showed a robust area bias, with area more decodable than number. Critically, networks trained to estimate number showed a reversal, with number becoming substantially more decodable than area, and this shift emerged after a single epoch of training. The effect was not a trivial consequence of training on a dimension: a matched control trained to estimate area did not produce the mirror-image effect, because enumeration training actively suppressed area information rather than merely amplifying number. Principal component analysis confirmed a reorganization of representational geometry, with numerosity becoming the dominant axis of variation (r² = 0.95) and area variance strongly reduced. These findings provide a computational proof-of-concept that learning to enumerate can restructure magnitude representations, suggesting that the perceptual primacy of number in adults may be partly a consequence, rather than a precondition, of symbolic number acquisition.

articles_hidden.title: The psychology of cringe
articles_hidden.authors: Paul Deutchman; Shaon Lahiri
articles_hidden.abstract: While cringe is an increasingly common term in social discourse and popular media—often used to describe a situation perceived as awkward or uncomfortable—we currently understand little about its underlying psychology and function in human social life. Across five studies (N = 1416; three preregistered), we examined the social cognition of cringe as a stable individual difference trait and as a fleeting affective state, investigating whether it is the same as, or functionally distinct from, vicarious embarrassment. We propose that cringe is a specific variety of vicarious embarrassment elicited by intentional, reputationally damaging social norm violations, that functions as a signal of normative competency—communicating recognition and alignment with group norms—and motivates norm compliance and enforcement. We first developed and validated the novel 20-item Cringe Scale to measure individual differences in trait cringe which we found positively predicted state cringe perceptions, incentivized donations, and behavioral intentions. Additionally, we found that cringe, as compared to vicarious embarrassment, was elicited more intensely by intentional and public norm violations, and was associated with heightened moral wrongness and punishment judgements as well as reduced empathy and prosocial motivation toward the transgressor. Path analyses revealed that perceptions of transgressor intent and norm violation severity mediated these differences. Together, our results establish cringe as a functionally distinct variety of vicarious embarrassment characterized by psychological distancing rather than empathic concern. The findings inform our understanding of an increasingly important self-conscious emotion and illuminate the adaptive social functions of cringe in social cognition.

articles_hidden.title: The Genesis of Grievance: Examining the Formation of Grievances and their Impact Upon Violent Extremist Outcomes
articles_hidden.authors: Bettina Rottweiler; Paul Gill
articles_hidden.abstract: The causal role of grievances, personal and political, is commonly attributed to the development of violent extremist outcomes. However, our conceptual and empirical understandings of how grievances develop and why only a minority with grievances go on to become radicalised remain underdeveloped. This paper uses structural equation modelling to examine the effects of perceived victimhood, personal grievances, and anger rumination on attitudes and intentions to engage in violent extremism via revenge motivation and reduced self-control capacity. We further analyse the protective effects of trait forgiveness on anger rumination and revenge motivation as well as self-control. The findings demonstrate that the experience of personal grievances mediates the effects of individuals’ tendency for interpersonal victimhood on anger rumination. The findings further highlight the mediating effects of revenge motivation and low-self-control on individuals’ attitudes and intentions to engage in extremist violence. We also demonstrate the indirect protective effects of trait forgiveness on support for and intentions to engage in extremist violence via its negative relationship with anger rumination, revenge motivation and low self-control. Our findings have important practical implications. Anger rumination may serve as a warning sign that an individuals’ perceived victimhood and personal grievances are translating into an increased vulnerability and potential escalation towards engagement in violent extremism, and thus may be a crucial point of intervention. During this rumination phase, there may be opportunities to intervene in the case by sign-posting critical information or warning signs about the consequences of going further than simply ruminating. Collectively, this suggests ways to inform programmatic approaches to prevent and counter violent extremism, while suggesting future avenues for joint risk assessment and management efforts tackling violent extremism.

articles_hidden.title: Bounding Causal Effects in Pretest-Posttest Designs with a Control Group
articles_hidden.authors: Muwon Kwon; Peter M. Steiner
articles_hidden.abstract: With data from a pretest-posttest design with a nonequivalent control group, researchers have two main options for identifying the causal impact of a treatment: covariate adjustment (CA) or difference-in-differences (DID). Each strategy rests on strong assumptions: the adjustment criterion (unconfoundedness) for CA and the common trend assumption for DID. In practice, neither of these assumptions is typically fully satisfied, resulting in biased effect estimates. To address uncertainty about potential assumption violations, we propose reliability-based bounds for the average treatment effect (ATE) that rely on a linear structural causal model and the reliability of the outcome's pretest measure with respect to an unobserved confounder. Unlike existing bracketing approaches, the reliability-based bounds do not require the stationarity assumption and remain valid even when the pretest and posttest measures are on different scales. Using simulated data, we demonstrate that the proposed bounds outperform existing methods by covering the true ATE even when stationarity is violated, while often producing narrower bounds when stationarity holds. The bounds also remain informative under moderate violations of linearity and the single-unobserved-confounder assumption. An empirical example illustrates how the bounds are established based on subject-matter knowledge and that they tend to cover the benchmark effect estimate from a corresponding randomized experiment.

articles_hidden.title: Latent visual mechanisms as computational phenotypes: Toward a precision science of vision
articles_hidden.authors: David Henry Peterzell
articles_hidden.abstract: Vision science has traditionally sought mechanisms shared across observers, treating individual differences as noise. Yet factor-analytic and latent-variable studies show that variation among observers is highly structured, recovering reproducible dimensions in contrast sensitivity, color, stereopsis, motion, and face recognition, among others. What are these latent dimensions? I propose they be treated as candidate computational phenotypes: a term borrowed from computational psychiatry and re-operationalized for vision as a stable, measurable pattern of visual information processing recovered from the covariance structure of individual differences. A computational phenotype is not a latent factor, mechanism, endophenotype, or biomarker; it occupies Marr's algorithmic level, between behavior and biology, and earns the name only by meeting stringent criteria of reliability, replication, convergent validity, and mechanistic relevance. I review candidate phenotypes drawn from many laboratories, recast development, aging, and disease as perturbations of phenotypic structure, and turn the strongest objection (that vision has no common factor) into support, since the relevant phenotypes are narrow and mechanism-specific. The payoff spans audiences: diagnostic profiles for clinicians, a non-invasive way to count and test visual mechanisms for basic scientists, and performance-predicting traits for human-factors work. The framework moves vision science from the average observer toward a precision science of visual computation.

articles_hidden.title: Does Parent-Rated Neurocognitive Functioning of Children with ADHD Moderate the Effects of Different Behavioral Parent Training Techniques?  A Randomized Controlled Microtrial
articles_hidden.authors: Dominique Petra Amadee Doffer; Barbara van den Hoofdakker; Tycho Dekkers; Rianne Hornstra; Marjolein Luman; Saskia van der Oord
articles_hidden.abstract: The effectiveness of behavioral parent training (BPT) techniques for children with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) may vary across individuals. Using a microtrial, we studied whether parent-ratings of child “hot” and “cool” executive functions moderated effects of stimulus-control (antecedent-based) versus contingency-management (consequent-based) techniques on child behavioral difficulties. Parents of 92 children with ADHD were randomly assigned to antecedent-based training, consequent-based training or waitlist. Results indicated that consequent-based techniques were particularly effective for children with lower arousal regulation and higher reward responsivity, while antecedent-based techniques were most effective for children with lower sensitivity to aversive stimuli. Possible explanations for these findings are discussed.

articles_hidden.title: The other side of social dance for mental health: What needs to be addressed before it can be offered to vulnerable populations?
articles_hidden.authors: Brennan Delattre
articles_hidden.abstract: A growing body of research suggests that social dance can be good for mental health, especially for individuals with depression, anxiety, and loneliness. However, less work has been conducted investigating for whom and in what circumstances social dance is beneficial, what safety considerations should be in place, and who might not yet be included in social dance spaces. In light of ongoing research investigating whether salsa dancing should be offered as an option to patients seeking care for depression and anxiety through the United Kingdom’s National Health Service (NHS) Talking Therapies as a social prescribing initiative and on a larger scale, and given the growing interest in social dance as a mental health solution more broadly, this Perspective piece highlights key issues that need to be addressed in community-based social dance spaces before social dance can be offered safely and equitably for vulnerable populations through public healthcare prescribing channels.

articles_hidden.title: Canine-Assisted Interventions and Symptoms Associated with Borderline Personality Disorder: A Scoping Review
articles_hidden.authors: Emma Pestell; Richard Gorman
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background:
Borderline personality disorder (BPD) is associated with symptoms including self-harm, suicidality, impulsivity, anger, and mood disturbance. Although psychotherapeutic approaches are commonly used in treatment, there remains interest in alternative and complementary approaches for managing BPD-related symptoms. Canine-assisted interventions (CAI) have been investigated across a range of mental health settings, though their relevance to BPD-related symptoms has not previously been described.

Aims:
This scoping review aimed to map the available research on CAI addressing symptoms associated with BPD, describing study populations, intervention characteristics, outcome measures, and gaps in the evidence.

Methods:
A systematic search was conducted across 5 databases. Studies were considered eligible if they examined the effects of CAI on predefined BPD-related symptoms, involved CAI interventions, and reported primary empirical data. Study populations, intervention characteristics, outcome measures, and reported findings were tabulated and summarised descriptively.

Results:
Eleven studies met the inclusion criteria. Studies varied in their populations, intervention formats and outcome measures, and coverage of the selected symptoms was uneven. Most studies reported reductions in at least some BPD-related symptoms following CAI. However, several studies demonstrated important methodological limitations, including small sample sizes, non-randomised designs, and limited control for confounding. Most included studies did not recruit participants with a formal diagnosis of BPD specifically.

Conclusion:
Existing research on CAI does address several symptoms associated with BPD, but spans diverse populations, interventions and outcome measures. There are, however, gaps in symptom coverage and research involving populations specifically diagnosed with BPD, providing priorities for future investigation.

articles_hidden.title: Beyond Standardized Affirmation: Transgender and Nonbinary Youths’ Experiences and Recommendations for Flexible Crisis Care
articles_hidden.authors: Juan Pablo Zapata; Alyssa N Gorkin; Aileen Kangavary; Amanda Smock
articles_hidden.abstract: Suicide rates are particularly high among transgender and gender-diverse (TGD) youth. Although gender-affirming care is increasingly incorporated into crisis services, little is known about how its delivery across crisis-care touchpoints may support or undermine safety and affirmation. This study used a youth-centered, iterative, qualitative design to examine practices shaping TGD youths’ experiences of gender-affirming care across crisis encounters. The study included 12 TGD youth aged 13–17 years (M = 16.3), all of whom reported suicidal-related thoughts and behaviors within the past month. Participants completed 22 semi-structured interviews across two iterative waves. Wave 1 explored experiences across crisis-care touchpoints and informed prototypes of gender-affirming practices, which participants reviewed and refined in Wave 2. Data underwent two-phase inductive-deductive analysis, with Wave 1 interviews coded to identify themes, and Wave 2 interviews coded to examine responses to emerging findings and practices. Across in-person acute care and virtual touchpoints, three themes described a mismatch between crisis response and gender affirmation: (1) standardized gender-affirming practiced could feel scripted; (2) agency and control over disclosure and decisions about care, shaped whether encounters felt affirming; and (3) direct and indirect experiences shaped trust and future use of crisis-care resources. A fourth theme focused on proposed improvements to gender-affirming care; across waves, participants favored approaches that adapted affirmation to individual identities, knowledge, and preferences rather than applying standardized practices uniformly. Findings highlight the need for crisis care that addresses immediate safety while tailoring gender-affirming practices to youths’ identities, knowledge, preferences, and disclosure control.

articles_hidden.title: Not “born that way”: Homophobic social preferences and non-essentialism of sexual orientation in childhood
articles_hidden.authors: Rebecca Peretz-Lange
articles_hidden.abstract: Although prejudice begins early in development, very few studies examine the developmental roots of homophobia. We explored the onset and developmental timecourse of homophobic social preferences as well as the cognitive and environmental factors predicting these preferences. We were particularly interested in whether children would essentialize orientation (e.g., consider it inborn and uncontrollable), since essentialism often positively correlates with prejudice but negatively correlates with adolescents’ and adults’ homophobia. As environmental predictors, we explored parents’ anti-prejudiced values and children’s LGBTQ contact. A diverse sample of participants from across the United States (n = 128 six- to nine-year-olds, 60 girls & 68 boys, 42% White & 58% of color) selected between heteroparental and homoparental peers in a Playmate Preference Task and then completed an essentialism assessment. Parents reported their anti-prejudiced values and children’s LGBTQ contact. Homophobic social preferences were present by age seven and increased across childhood. Moreover, despite children’s pervasive essentialist tendencies, participants overwhelmingly rejected the idea that being in a same-gender vs. other-gender marriage reflects any internal uncontrollable characteristic. Instead, children viewed this as a matter of choice. Essentialism was very low overall and did not predict social preferences. Instead, parents’ values and children’s LGBTQ contact predicted these preferences. In sum, children view orientation as reflecting a choice rather than an intrinsic nature, and then rely on the adults in their lives to determine how to feel toward that choice. Homophobic social preferences therefore emerge early and in the context of behavioral views of orientation. Social, cognitive, and developmental implications are discussed.

articles_hidden.title: Forging ahead, pulling back, and acting strategically: Climate activists’ responses to criminalisation and repression in the UK
articles_hidden.authors: Peter Gardner; Sunniva Davies-Rommetveit; Jenny Douch; Anna Aretha Sach
articles_hidden.abstract: In response to the post-2018 rise in climate protest, many liberal democratic countries have witnessed the criminalisation and repression of environmental activists. Instead of assessing macro-level effects of repression on activism, this paper explores the micro-level responses to surveillance, arrest, fines, and imprisonment. Drawing on socio-legal scholarship that understands the law as socially constructed rather than objective and external, this paper delves into the black box of political repression, offering an examination of how climate activists respond to state sanctions. Analysing a survey of 1,375 Extinction Rebellion UK activists through thematic analysis and quantitative coding, we demonstrate that individual biography and narrativisations of the law lead activists to forge ahead, pull back, or act strategically in response to repression.

articles_hidden.title: Felt but Not Detected:  Salience Versus Detectability of Affective Change in Ambulatory Assessment
articles_hidden.authors: Aleksandra Kaurin; Mario Wenzel; Paula Philippi; Jonas Dora
articles_hidden.abstract: Ambulatory assessment (AA) captures within-person fluctuations in daily life, yet not all observed change exceeds measurement error, and not all reliable change is subjectively experienced. We propose a preregistered dual-threshold framework distinguishing statistical detectability (smallest detectable change, SDC) from experiential salience (minimal important change, MIC). Adults (N = 250) completed a 14-day AA protocol with twice-daily and event-contingent assessments (5,982 observations), rating momentary stress, positive affect, and negative affect (0–4) and perceived change since the previous assessment. SDC₉₅ estimates ranged from 1.56 to 1.92 scale points, so roughly three-quarters of consecutive changes fell below reliable detection. Anchor-based MICs, in contrast, were 1 point for all constructs. Correspondence between detectable and perceived change was asymmetric: sensitivity was high (.77–.87), but specificity (.46–.56) and positive predictive values (.24–.31) were low, as participants frequently reported change without reliable change; directional reversals were rare. Reliable change strongly predicted perceived change (ORs 4.6–12.5). Event-contingent assessments, higher prior states, and person-level characteristics (e.g., impulsivity, emotion regulation) increased the general propensity to report change but did not moderate this link. Felt change thus precedes measurable change: detectability and salience are distinct thresholds that intensive longitudinal research must evaluate separately.

articles_hidden.title: Increased monetary incentives enhance goal-directed reinforcement learning but fail to suppress automatic learning processes
articles_hidden.authors: Ido Ben-Artzi; Noham Wolpe; Nitzan Shahar
articles_hidden.abstract: Adaptive reinforcement learning requires assigning outcomes to the features of actions that causally determine them. Yet humans also learn reward associations with action features that are explicitly known to be outcome-irrelevant, and these associations can bias subsequent choices. Whether such maladaptive learning is regulated by motivational incentives remains unclear. Here, we tested whether increasing monetary stakes differentially modulates the influence of outcome-relevant and outcome-irrelevant learned values on choice. Participants (N = 287) completed a multi-armed bandit task in low- and high-stakes conditions while explicitly instructed that card identity predicted reward whereas card location did not. Computational modelling revealed that higher stakes increased the influence of outcome-relevant values on choice, but did not change the influence of outcome-irrelevant values. Critically, outcome-irrelevant value influences persisted even though they produced substantially greater monetary losses under high stakes. These findings show that monetary incentives selectively enhance the use of outcome-relevant learned values without improving the selectivity of credit assignment. More broadly, they suggest that only some components of reinforcement learning are sensitive to motivational control.

articles_hidden.title: Is GenAI Helpful for Writing? A Re-Analysis Using Robust Bayesian Meta-Analysis (RoBMA)
articles_hidden.authors: Shawn Hemelstrand
articles_hidden.abstract: A recent meta-analysis showed that genAI has a strong impact on writing. The current analysis instead shows that the effects are negligible after correcting for heterogeneity and publication bias.

articles_hidden.title: To replicate or not to replicate? My nine failures to publish a successful replication
articles_hidden.authors: Sharon Gilaie-Dotan
articles_hidden.abstract: Simmons, Nelson, and Simonsohn (2011) proposed disclosure-based practices — a priori power analyses, full reporting of conditions and exclusions, results reported with and without exclusions applied — as a remedy for the replication crisis. Following these practices explicitly, our lab attempted to publish an online replication and extension of our earlier PNAS findings on image size and memory, expecting that doing so would make publication straightforward. It did not. The manuscript was rejected nine times over 2.5 years, largely on the grounds that a transparent, successful replication lacked sufficient theoretical novelty to warrant publication on its own; it was accepted only after this framing was substantially minimized in favor of additional analyses and an alternative theoretical framework. Here, I reflect on this experience and raise open questions about whether the field's evaluation of replications has kept pace with its stated commitment to them.

articles_hidden.title: Assessing resurgence as persistence in the Valproic Acid rat model of Autism Spectrum Disorder
articles_hidden.authors: Ana J O Cerveira; Eldereis de Paula; Andréia Schmidt; Fernando Eduardo Padovan-Neto
articles_hidden.abstract: Behavioral persistence poses a clinical challenge in patients with Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD), as targeted problematic behaviors resist elimination and reemerge upon treatment discontinuation (resurgence). Prenatal exposure to valproic acid (VPA) has been proposed as a rat model of ASD that would increase behavioral persistence, but findings in this model have been inconsistent. This study investigated whether prenatal VPA exposure increases persistence by assessing the persistence of target responding on a three-phase resurgence procedure: Training (target response reinforced), Elimination (target response placed on extinction while an alternative response is reinforced), and Testing (alternative response also placed on extinction, producing resurgence of target responding). Male and female Sprague-Dawley rats prenatally exposed to saline (SAL) or VPA were compared. Target and alternative response rates did not differ between SAL and VPA animals in either sex at any phase, nor did the proportional change from target to alternative responding during Elimination or the magnitude of resurgence at Testing. Males did, however, display higher resurgence magnitudes than females in both prenatal conditions. Together, these findings indicate that VPA-exposed rats do not behave more persistently, but contribute to the investigations of potentially ASD-related traits in this animal model in a behavioral analytic perspective.

articles_hidden.title: Regardless of Task Demands, Delayed Goal-Directed Processing Persists in Adult ADHD
articles_hidden.authors: Jahla Osborne; Jacob Sellers; Han Zhang; Su Wang; Sarah Liberatore; Chandra Sripada; Priti Shah; John Jonides
articles_hidden.abstract: Inhibitory control challenges have long been theorized to underlie deficits in ADHD, but the precise mechanism(s) have remained unclear. Recent research using “forced-response” conflict tasks and computational modeling, capable of distinguishing the time-dependent contributions of habitual and goal-directed response preparation, has provided evidence that supports the idea that delayed goal-directed processing underlies inhibitory control challenges in adult ADHD. Still, it remains unclear how habitual and goal-directed responding adjust with increased (or decreased) interference that requires more (or less) inhibitory control, which matters because daily life involves varying levels of interference. To address this gap, we recruited adults meeting criteria for ADHD to complete a forced-response version of the arrow flanker task. We created circumstances of increased and decreased interference by manipulating the size of target and non-target (distractor) stimuli relative to each other. We utilized a crossover design, in which participants completed the arrow-flanker once while medicated and once while unmedicated (counterbalanced). Results showed that goal-directed responses were prepared more slowly for participants when unmedicated, regardless of interference circumstance. We directly tested the interaction between medication and interference, and the presence of medication did not especially help in one interference circumstance over the other. These findings add to a growing body of literature working toward better understanding the nature of inhibitory control within adult-ADHD.

articles_hidden.title: The role of pragmatic context in children’s quantification of parts and wholes
articles_hidden.authors: David Barner; Hannah Bryer; Miguel Mejia; Mahesh Srinivasan
articles_hidden.abstract: Why do children sometimes include the pieces of broken things when asked to count (e.g., “Count the forks”)? In five experiments, we test two ideas: (1) that adults, but not children, exclude parts from counts by reasoning that speakers must only be interested in whole objects with functions that fulfill desired goals, and (2) that only adults exclude parts on the basis of a Gricean inference, on which it is assumed that if a speaker wanted parts to be counted, they would say so. In Experiments 1-3, we find that although children and adults are somewhat less likely to count pieces of objects when speaker goals are explicitly mentioned, large developmental differences remain unexplained. In Experiments 4-5, we provide evidence that children differ most from adults when pieces are presented in the presence of complementary parts (with which they together would form a whole), and that these pieces are significantly more likely to be conceptualized and labeled as “parts”, especially by adults. Together, these findings suggest that adults – but not children – are more likely to exclude broken parts from their counts in response to requests like “Count the forks!” when they are also able to understand that more informative requests could have been made (e.g., “Count the pieces of fork!”).

articles_hidden.title: Rethinking Spaced Practice Under Limited Instructional Time: The Benefits of Repetition Depend on Spacing
articles_hidden.authors: Meng Cao; Paulo F. Carvalho
articles_hidden.abstract: Spacing and repetition are two fundamental principles of learning, yet under limited instructional time, increasing repetitions necessarily shortens the intervals between encounters. Prior research found that more repetitions with shorter spacing produced better learning than fewer repetitions with longer spacing, but the respective contributions of spacing and repetition remained unclear. The present study sought to disentangle these contributions and replicate prior findings. Data were collected in 2026 from 120 English-speaking U.S. adults. Participants learned Indonesian-English word pairs three or six times under both massed and spaced schedules within a fixed instructional time. Retention was assessed immediately, one day, and three days later, and forgetting curves were used to estimate initial memory strength and forgetting rate. We replicated the advantage of more repetitions with shorter spacing. Spaced practice produced greater initial memory strength and slower forgetting than massed practice, whereas additional repetitions increased initial memory strength only when practice was spaced. These findings suggest that, under time constraints, additional repetitions benefit learning primarily when spaced, indicating that the advantage of repeated practice depends on the accumulation of learning across spaced encounters.

articles_hidden.title: Artificial observers and real individual differences: A roadmap for a computational psychometrics of vision
articles_hidden.authors: David Henry Peterzell
articles_hidden.abstract: Deep neural networks are increasingly used as models of vision, yet they are evaluated against the average observer: average performance, average neural response, average representational geometry. This discards one of the richest constraints on theory: stable individual differences. Fitting the average is necessary but not sufficient. I argue that future models should be judged not only by their fit to mean human performance, but by whether populations of artificial observers reproduce the covariance structure and latent factors found across human observers. Two mature but disconnected literatures motivate this. Decades of factor-analytic psychophysics and electrophysiology show that interindividual variation is signal, not noise: the pattern of correlations among observers reveals the number and tuning of underlying mechanisms, and fractionates vision into many narrow factors rather than one general ability. Meanwhile, neural networks differing only in random initialization develop measurably different internal representations, so any single trained network is one sample from a distribution of possible observers. Joining these yields a computational psychometrics of vision: construct a designed population of artificial observers (varying in architecture, initialization, training diet, and front-end sampling), submit them to the same latent-variable analyses used on humans, and test whether the recovered factor structure matches. Recent work showing that seed-varied networks align with specific individuals is an existence proof. This article generalizes it into a framework, a staged roadmap, and a benchmark, together with the safeguards that keep such a benchmark from becoming an optimization target, for testing hypotheses about human visual variation with artificial observer populations.

articles_hidden.title: On Color and Emotion: What Can Vision Science Learn from the Rorschach?
articles_hidden.authors: David Henry Peterzell
articles_hidden.abstract: For a century, clinicians have recorded how people use color when they interpret inkblots, rank colored cards, or draw. They believed that how a person handles color reveals how that person handles feeling. Vision science has rarely read this literature, and the most complete modern review of color and emotion research excluded it. This paper introduces the projective color literature to vision scientists in plain language. Three conclusions follow. First, the tradition’s central belief, that chromatic color stirs emotion directly, was tested from the 1940s onward and largely failed. Second, narrower findings survived. The degree to which a person lets color lead over form in an ambiguous image is modestly related to several independently assessed clinical, behavioral, and biological outcomes. Some indices that set color in balance with other responses, such as coping versus overload, are also supported. What these scores measure is disputed. Third, the findings concern how color is weighted against form, which vision science already studies, yet only one study has linked that weighting to an object-recognition task, and none has used calibrated stimuli. I then read both literatures through a constructivist model of color in which the percept and the wider event it belongs to determine each other reciprocally. On this reading, the question is not only whether color influences emotion but also whether emotion influences color. The projective tradition raised the second question. Modern color-emotion science has mostly set it aside. Five studies are proposed that would join the two fields.

articles_hidden.title: Theories of Symbolic Number Learning
articles_hidden.authors: Hillary Mastarciyan; H Moriah Sokolowski
articles_hidden.abstract: Understanding numerical symbols (e.g., the verbal number word ‘six’ or the Arabic digit ‘6’) is fundamental to the development of mathematical knowledge, yet how humans acquire meaningful representations of numerical symbols remains an ongoing theoretical question. In this review, we examine major theoretical accounts of symbolic number learning and consider how these perspectives explain the emergence and development of symbolic numerical knowledge. We focus particularly on the processes through which children establish meaningful connections between numerical symbols and their referents, addressing the longstanding symbol-grounding problem in numerical cognition. By synthesizing perspectives across developmental psychology and cognitive neuroscience, we identify areas of convergence and divergence among existing theoretical accounts and highlight key unresolved questions. Building on this synthesis, we propose the Grounded-to-Abstraction Theory, in which symbolic number knowledge emerges through a reciprocal process whereby small number words are initially grounded in exact quantity representations, and learning these symbols simultaneously scaffolds attention to numerical information. As this system develops, attentional control and approximate magnitude representations support the extension of numerical meaning beyond small quantities, while the emerging verbal number system scaffolds the acquisition of Arabic digits, yielding increasingly abstract and interconnected numerical representations. This framework integrates and extends existing theoretical perspectives and generates testable predictions regarding the behavioural and neural mechanisms underlying symbolic number learning in children. Overall, this review positions symbolic number learning as a dynamic developmental process involving multiple interacting representational systems and provides an integrative theoretical framework for understanding how children develop increasingly sophisticated representations of numerical symbols.

articles_hidden.title: Form Theory: The Conceptual Architecture of Human Thought
articles_hidden.authors: Paul Haward
articles_hidden.abstract: Human thought takes place in a world that is uncertain and constantly changing. Yet the character of human thought is often quite different. People routinely simplify complex realities and hold their beliefs with a certainty and rigidity the world itself rarely warrants. The present paper develops Form Theory, a theory of conceptual structure according to which these recurring tendencies are surface signatures of a common underlying format. Form Theory proposes that each concept contains a central form: a default structure that encodes a compressed subset of the concept’s information, gives that information default influence within cognition, and activates strong default beliefs about the encoded information. On Form Theory, distortion is one natural consequence of this structure. Yet the same structure also yields benefits for cognition. By encoding selected information in a stable, certainty-generating, domain-neutral format, the central form makes rapid, complex thought possible, supports conceptual and linguistic creativity, helps establish an internal sense of identity, and provides stable conceptual structure for the frameworks through which people organize their mental worlds. Form Theory therefore characterizes the conceptual architecture of human thought as a default conceptual structure whose signatures recur throughout cognition, with both benefits and costs for cognition and for human life.

articles_hidden.title: A curriculum for neural networks to process two-digit arithmetic like humans
articles_hidden.authors: Samuel Lozano; Markus Spitzer; Korbinian Moeller; Miguel Ruiz-Garcia
articles_hidden.abstract: Understanding and operating on multi-digit numbers is a critical step in the development of mathematical skills and concepts. Empirical and computational modeling evidence suggest that multi-digit number magnitude is processed in a componential manner, decomposed into units, tens, hundreds, etc. However, computational models evaluating whether such componential processing generalizes to multi-digit \textit{arithmetic} have so far relied on discrete symbolic inputs rather than on noisy magnitude representations. Accordingly, we developed a hierarchical neural network model of multi-digit addition based on componential processing of noisy single-digit magnitude representations. To evaluate model performance we implemented two training curricula: (i) an all-at-once curriculum and (ii) a step-by-step curriculum, where single-digit addition is trained before progressing to multi-digit problems (following school curricula). Under the training conditions tested, only the step-by-step curriculum allowed the model to learn multi-digit addition. Once trained this way, the model reproduced the carry-over and problem-size effects observed in reaction times of children and adults, both across problem categories and across individual items. These findings generalize the idea of decomposed processing of multi-digit number magnitude to arithmetic and highlight the importance of structured, incremental learning in both cognitive modeling and education.

articles_hidden.title: The multidimensional structure of perceptual and aesthetic evaluation: Independent features, interacting feature values, and perceptual unity
articles_hidden.authors: Eline Van Geert; Nori Jacoby
articles_hidden.abstract: Subjective appearance and aesthetic appreciation are inherently multidimensional, arising from the combined influence of a variety of visual features such as color, shape, and size. Yet, how multiple feature dimensions jointly shape perceptual and aesthetic evaluations remains poorly understood. Most previous studies either employ multidimensional stimuli without precise parametric control or use parametrically controlled stimuli that vary along only one dimension, limiting our understanding of the multidimensional structure underlying subjective evaluations. To address this challenge, we combined two methodological advances: the Order & Complexity Toolbox for Aesthetics (Van Geert et al., 2023), which enables the generation of parametrically controlled multidimensional stimuli, and Gibbs Sampling with People (Harrison et al., 2020), which efficiently characterizes subjective evaluations in high-dimensional stimulus spaces. Our stimuli consisted of visual displays containing multiple elements that varied in color, shape, and size and were arranged according to different organizational structures. Across nine experiments involving more than 1,000 participants and over 125,000 evaluations, we estimated multidimensional probability distributions underlying perceptual evaluations of order and complexity and aesthetic evaluations of pleasure and interest. Three main findings emerged. First, evaluations depended on both absolute feature values and relative differences between elements for each feature dimension, indicating that observers are sensitive not only to the characteristics of individual elements but also to the relations among them. Second, the influence of these relative differences depended on the overall perceptual organization of the display. Preferences for simplicity — operationalized as small differences in feature values between elements — varied systematically across evaluation criteria and with the degree of perceptual unity within the display. Third, despite these contextual effects, different visual features (color, shape, and size) conributed largely independently to the evaluations, suggesting that their influences on subjective evaluations are relatively separable. Together, these findings provide a multidimensional account of how visual features and their relations jointly shape perceptual and aesthetic evaluations.

articles_hidden.title: Changes in Single People’s Attachment Models and Co-Development with Life Satisfaction
articles_hidden.authors: Michael Dominik Krämer; R. Chris Fraley; Laura Buchinger; Julia Stern; Omri Gillath; William J. Chopik; Geoff MacDonald; Wiebke Bleidorn
articles_hidden.abstract: Attachment security (i.e., low levels of attachment anxiety and avoidance) is important for both partnered and long-term single people’s well-being. However, research gaps limit knowledge to what extent attachment processes generalize to single people. Research has often not distinguished global and relationship-specific attachment; most studies of single people were cross-sectional; and little is known about attachment change and its co-development with well-being. The present study examined selection into long-term singlehood, change in relationship-specific attachment, and co-development with life satisfaction. We used longitudinal data spanning 30 months (N = 3,542; 39,492 assessments; 82% women; M_age = 34.54) and compared consistently single, consistently partnered, and intermittently partnered people. Baseline global, romantic, and friend-specific avoidance, but not anxiety, prospectively predicted remaining single. Compared to consistently partnered people, consistently single people showed higher global and romantic attachment insecurity, and both groups decreased mostly in parallel. However, single people increased slightly more adaptively in some of the non-romantic attachment models. Intermittently partnered people were similar in romantic attachment at baseline to single people but became more secure over time. Across most attachment models, people who increased in attachment security also increased in life satisfaction. This co-development was similar between groups, except that decreasing romantic avoidance was less closely tied to increasing life satisfaction among single people. Together, persistent differences in global and romantic attachment may reflect selection into relationship status rather than distinct development. In addition, similar attachment–well-being links across groups indicate that attachment operates in similar ways in both partnered and long-term single people.

articles_hidden.title: “Puzzling, Yet So Refreshing”: Experiencing the Value of Neurodiversity Within an Inclusive Choir
articles_hidden.authors: Nicolas Petit; Géraldine Dessertenne; Fanny Aprile; Lucie Jurek
articles_hidden.abstract: The social challenges encountered by autistic people are increasingly understood as a double empathy problem: a mutual misunderstanding between autistic and non-autistic individuals, rather than an autistic deficit. This paradigm highlights a need for inclusive spaces that foster mutual understanding, yet this remains challenging. Choral singing offers a promising medium to facilitate cross-neurotype dynamics, as it is thought to have evolved as a biological mechanism to foster social bonding. Accordingly, this qualitative study explored how 12 general population choristers experienced a 6-month neurodiverse choir shared with 8 autistic adolescents and 3 autism specialists. We used a two-stage qualitative design, first capturing individual experience through an open-ended online questionnaire, and subsequently deepening our analysis through a discussion with a community stakeholder panel. The findings revealed an intrinsically demanding experience, especially emotionally and cognitively, counterbalanced by important benefits, as it was also described as joyful and powerful, encouraging personal growth among the choristers and a shift in their perceptions of autism. These findings support the neurodiversity paradigm and suggest that choral singing may be a powerful double empathy solution, facilitating intergroup contact to reduce prejudice and thereby enhance the participation of autistic voices.

articles_hidden.title: The Other-Race Effect in Implicit Memory for Face Combinations
articles_hidden.authors: Yoko Higuchi; Kiwako Shimada
articles_hidden.abstract: Other-race faces are remembered less accurately than own-race faces, a robust phenomenon known as the other-race effect or cross-race effect. However, most evidence for the other-race effect comes from tasks that require explicit encoding or recognition of individual face identities, leaving unclear whether the effect is confined to explicit memory demands. Here, we report evidence for an other-race effect not only in explicit memory, but also in implicit memory for repeated face combinations. In Experiment 1, Japanese participants intentionally encoded Asian and Caucasian faces and later performed an explicit recognition task; recognition sensitivity was higher for own-race Asian faces than for other-race Caucasian faces. In Experiment 2, Japanese participants performed an implicit memory task in which repeated face combinations were presented without awareness of the repetitions; implicit memory for repeated face combinations developed more reliably for own-race Asian faces than for other-race Caucasian faces. Taken together, these results suggest that the cognitive difficulties associated with other-race faces should be understood not only as a problem of explicit face memory, but also as a problem of implicit memory formed through repeated face exposure in everyday life.

articles_hidden.title: Facial evidence matters less for stereotype-consistent judgments: Weaker formidability-aggression associations in Black vs. White faces
articles_hidden.authors: Kirstan Brodie; Brandon Cohen; Youngki Hong
articles_hidden.abstract: Facial characteristics are reliably associated with social judgments, but these relationships may depend on whether a judgment is consistent with stereotypes of the target’s social group. Across four studies with adult participants, we tested this possibility using perceived aggression and threat in Black and White faces. Perceived dominance (Study 1, N=117) and physical strength (Study 2, N=626) predicted aggression judgments less strongly for Black than White faces. Dominance also predicted perceived threat less strongly for Black than White faces after controlling for several threat-related covariates (Study 3, N=380). Furthermore, machine learning analyses found less overlap in dominance- and threat-predictive facial information for Black faces. Finally, face morphing that matched featural variation across race while manipulating apparent race showed a weaker dominance-aggression relationship for Black-appearing faces (Study 4, N=467). Together, these findings are consistent with the possibility that facial evidence has reduced influence on judgments of stereotype-consistent traits.

articles.title: Sobre el Estado de Naturaleza como un uso meta teórico en el derecho y la política: excesos y tensiones
articles.authors: Ángel Gutiérrez Escobedo
articles.abstract: La relación entre Derecho y Política se disuelve cuando, desde la teoría de la primera, se confunden sus respectivas autonomías operativas con las descripciones propias de una distinción que se excluye a sí misma de lo observado. Durante la presente investigación, se argumentará en contra del principio teórico que sustenta dicha confusión, porque la separación entre Estado de Naturaleza, Sociedad o Legalidad/violencia, son puntos de apoyo insostenibles para sustentar teóricamente el problema de la nomo-génesis. Identificamos el origen de dicha paradoja, a saber, ¿por qué existen las leyes?, en la traducción contemporánea de distintas tesis contractualistas pues el planteamiento original encontraba fortaleza en concepciones sustancialistas ya contradictorias para el presente. Sugerimos, reconfigurar dicho punto de partida para propiciar nuevas perspectivas del derecho que no aseguren su preferencia o necesidad desde la amenaza del Sin-Derecho.

articles.title: Manufactured Desire： How Social Media and Influencer Agencies Sexualise and Monetise Pregnant Influencers
articles.authors: Yuting Qin
articles.abstract: This article examines how pregnant influencers on Douyin, the Chinese version of TikTok, are sexualised and monetised through the interlocking practices of the platform, influencer agencies and influencers themselves. Taking the 2024 controversy around the appearance influencer YīLìXiǎoShāZi and the # 孕妇摇 (Pregnancy Swing Dance) challenge as its point of departure, the study combines visual analysis of top-ranked Douyin posts, in-depth interviews with an influencer, an influencer agency employee and a platform employee, and sentiment analysis of 4,874 user comments. This article interprets platform monetisation structures and influencer agency production routines as organising influencers’ embodied labour into standardised production roles and measurable commercial attributes. It proposes the “factory of desire” as a framework for understanding how platforms, influencer agencies and influencers mutually enable and constrain the commodification of pregnant bodies. Interviewees described unwritten rules through which sexualised content can remain visible under mainland China's restrictions on pornography: perceived emphasis on skin exposure in automated moderation, a grey zone known as 擦边 (cābiān, "skirting the boundary"), and appeals framed around "pregnancy beauty". The analysis suggests that these commercial and regulatory conditions can encourage pregnant influencers to reproduce porn chic conventions, while constraining their subsequent commercial options. Within the sampled comments on videos criticising the sexualisation of pregnancy, disgust had the highest average model score; these findings describe this selected discussion rather than public opinion as a whole.

articles.title: Buying Books, Buying Diversity? Public Procurement Theory and the Brazilian State as Book Buyer
articles.authors: Marcel Felipe Machado Lopes; Paula Roméro Cajaty Lopes
articles.abstract:
Governments are among the largest single buyers of books, yet public procurement research rarely asks what state purchasing does to the diversity of the market it buys from. This article examines federal book procurement in Brazil using item-level electronic invoice (NF-e) data published by the Office of the Comptroller General (CGU). The data cover 60 months between October 2021 and September 2026 and R$21.9 billion in purchases, 96.7% of which were made by a single buyer, the National Fund for Education Development (FNDE). Drawing on Stirling's variety–balance–disparity framework, we build five indicators of bibliodiversity: supplier concentration (Herfindahl–Hirschman index), the share of the four and eight largest suppliers, supplier evenness, title evenness, and territorial inequality among suppliers.
The results describe a market with high variety but low balance. A median of 280 suppliers invoice the federal government each month, yet the four largest take a median 68% of value, and two publishers, FTD and Moderna, account for 45% of the whole series. Concentration is episodic rather than trending: 13 of 60 months exceed the HHI threshold of 2,500, with no significant monotonic trend. Territorial inequality is extreme and stable (median Gini 0.93), with São Paulo-based emitters taking 93% of value. Title diversity falls when supplier concentration rises (Spearman ρ = −0.61) and has declined sharply since mid-2025.
We read these patterns against transaction cost, principal–agent, competition, strategic-procurement and institutional theories. We argue that, in markets for unique cultural goods purchased without price competition, the locus of competition moves from the tender to the pre-selection stage, so programme design rather than tendering rules becomes the main lever for diversity. We derive five propositions and discuss the data-quality limits of invoice-based procurement analytics.

articles.title: Compensatory Input Versus Unequal Gains: Why Schooling Does Not Necessarily Equalize Socioeconomic Achievement Gaps
articles.authors: Jan Skopek
articles.abstract: Recent research has failed to provide clear-cut evidence that schooling equalizes social gaps in achievement. This stands at odds with the dominant view of compensatory input, which holds that even unequal schooling equalizes learning because it compensates for the even more unequal learning inputs children would receive in its absence. I test the previously neglected mechanism of unequal gains from schooling, which could counteract compensatory input and thus explain why studies often fail to find equalization. The unequal gains hypothesis posits a Matthew effect whereby learning gains from schooling depend on children’s prior skills, so that students from higher (lower) socioeconomic backgrounds benefit more (less) from schooling because of their, on average, higher (lower) skills at school entry. Because both mechanisms can operate simultaneously, assessing the equalizing power of schooling requires accounting for achievement prior to schooling. Using data from the newborn cohort of the German National Educational Panel Study (NEPS), I first replicated earlier findings from Germany on the beneficial but non-equalizing effects of school exposure on student achievement—scientific literacy and vocabulary—in Grade 1. Second, after accounting for children’s achievement before schooling, I found evidence of unequal gains counteracting equalization; net of these unequal gains, school exposure did level out learning gaps by social background, although only in the domain of scientific literacy. The findings underline the importance of incorporating prior achievement into studies of school equalization.

articles.title: Accountability Gap Behind Predatory Publishing in Philippine Academia
articles.authors: Jeconiah Dreisbach
articles.abstract: The mandate of the Philippines’ Commission on Higher Education ties faculty promotion in state universities and colleges to research publications. This commentary argues that the policy's emphasis on publication volume, unmatched by a corresponding verification mechanism, has created conditions in which predatory journals, conferences, and award bodies can thrive. Rising demand for indexed journal publications has already produced unsolicited offers to acquire legitimate, non-profit university journals, commercializing a system meant to signal quality. The threat extends beyond obviously fraudulent venues: recent evidence of paper mines (Barnett & Byrne, 2026), in which openly available datasets are mass-mined into formulaic, artificial-intelligence-assisted manuscripts that pass peer review in ostensibly legitimate journals, shows that volume-based incentives corrupt the research record even when every formal quality marker is present. Reading the Philippine case alongside this global pattern suggests that whitelisting indexed venues is necessary but insufficient. Accountability requires Philippine authorities to complement indexing criteria with a national research integrity framework, institutional verification of authorship, conference, and data provenance, and financial support that does not make ethical publishing contingent on personal wealth.

articles.title: Similar disruptions, different reactions? Refugee crises and the politicization of immigration in Sweden and Switzerland
articles.authors: Marco Bitschnau; Didier Ruedin; Anders Hellström; Marie Sundström
articles.abstract: We investigate how major refugee crises affected the immigration debate in Sweden and Switzerland, two countries that have long been among the most popular European destinations for immigrants in general and refugees in particular. Analysing claims from newspapers during two crises, the Balkans refugee crisis of the 1990s and the European refugee crisis of 2015–16 (N=3,593), we find (1) fairly diverse patterns of politicization, with slightly greater polarization in Switzerland but higher salience peaks in Sweden; (2) no significant differences in how actors position themselves in relation to the status quo; and (3) substantial differences in how they use certain frames. We conclude that despite their proximity to immigration matters, refugee crises do not always lead to more politicized debates. There may be some crisis impact—but certainly no reason for crisis determinism. Instead, factors such as the domestic context and the relative shock value of each crisis appear to be relevant and should be given more consideration.

articles.title: What QCA Cannot See: Identification Bounds for Configurational Solutions with Missing Set Memberships
articles.authors: Maikel Yelandi Leyva Vázquez
articles.abstract: Qualitative comparative analysis (QCA) needs a membership score for every case in every set, and applied studies commonly remove cases whose scores are missing. In a truth table, removal can turn a configuration that exists but was not scored into a logical remainder available as a simplifying assumption. We propose partial-identification QCA (PI-QCA).
