Each missing score is represented by an interval, every completion is considered, and the analysis reports exact bounds for the consistency and coverage of any term, the sure solution (the terms present in the solution of every completion), the possible region, bracketed by an inner bound from sampled completions and an outer bound from enumeration, and the identification gap. A solution outside the outer bound is produced by no completion. By construction, the sure solution cannot contain a term absent from the complete-data solution. In 900 simulated data sets its sampled approximation also satisfied this in every replicate, whereas case deletion and mean imputation returned false terms about as often as the complete-data analysis on average but up to 22 percentage points more often under some missingness mechanisms. The price is an empty sure solution in 71–95% of replicates when a fifth of the scores were missing. In an illustration with 131 economies, deletion returns a solution that no completion produces when the outcome is kept at its recorded values. Reanalyses of two published studies find a certified empty sure solution for one outcome and, for another, published solutions attained by none of 208 sampled completions.

articles.title: Group Affect and the Electoral Protection of Transgender Rights
articles.authors: Sophie Mainz; Michal Grahn
articles.abstract: When does positive affect for a minority group translate into electoral protection for its rights? We examine this question for trans rights, which are being rolled back in many democracies. We ran a pre-registered experiment with 1,500 British adults in May 2025, weeks after the UK Supreme Court restricted the legal definition of `woman' to biological sex. Respondents chose between candidates from their preferred party who either endorsed or opposed the Supreme Court ruling, alongside other traits. We find a preference for candidates who endorse trans rights retrenchment that transcends much of the left-right divide. Crucially, although warm feelings toward trans people are twice as common as cold ones, cold affect translates more readily and more strongly into candidate choice. This asymmetry produces an overall electoral advantage for candidates endorsing trans rights retrenchment, with only those holding the warmest feelings toward trans people preferring candidates who oppose the ruling.

articles.title: Solidarity at War: The Quest for the Decolonial Subject in Russian Feminism
articles.authors: Leandra Bias
articles.abstract:
Since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine a new debate in transnational feminism
and feminist security studies has framed decolonisation as a precondition for solidarity.
This discussion has primarily focused on relations between Western and Ukrainian and
Central and Eastern European feminists, leaving Russian feminism largely unexamined.
This article thus asks whether and to what extent these decolonial debates have
travelled to Russia by analysing the Feminist Anti-War Resistance (FAR). Drawing on a
content analysis of FAR’s Telegram channel and its self-published newspaper the article
shows that while FAR has an awareness of decolonial critiques, the engagement remains
limited in breadth and direction. References to decolonisation and imperialism are
marginal, concentrated in the early months of the full-scale invasion, and inwardlooking,
focusing on internal hierarchies within the Russian Federation while eclipsing
Ukraine. The article concludes with an assessment of the implications for future crossborder
solidarity between Russian and Ukrainian feminists.

articles.title: Following the Feedback: Audience Engagement and Politicians’ Issue Attention on Social Media
articles.authors: August Lohse; Tobias Priesholm Gårdhus; Snorre Ralund; Hjalmar Bang Carlsen
articles.abstract: Political representatives increasingly communicate in social media environments where every message generates immediate and quantified audience feedback. Although likes are not a representative measure of public opinion, they provide information about which issues attract attention from politicians' online audiences. We examine whether politicians devote more attention to issues that generate high engagement. Our analysis draws on 128,204 Facebook posts published by 123 Facebook-active Danish Members of Parliament between 2011 and 2018. We find that issues receiving relatively more audience feedback are consistently more likely to appear in politicians' subsequent posts. This pattern is present across political topics and different forms of engagement, but weakens during election campaigns, when heightened electoral incentives and institutional constraints coincide. The findings show that quantified platform feedback is systematically linked to the allocation of political attention, but that this alignment varies with the context in which politicians communicate.

articles.title: My (22m) Girlfriend (23f) Comes Home and Does Nothing”– Gendered Perceptions of Paid and Unpaid Work in Reddit Relationship Discussions over Time
articles.authors: Birgit Zeyer-Gliozzo; Johanna Hölzl; Gundula Zoch; Philipp Doebler
articles.abstract: The COVID-19 pandemic reignited longstanding debates around gender inequalities in paid and unpaid work. While survey research has advanced our understanding of these disparities, it typically relies on predefined categories and is susceptible to social desirability and recall bias. Online postings, by contrast, capture intimate experiences in real time but rarely include demographic attributes. We leverage a unique dataset of discussions in Reddit relationship communities that combines rich descriptions of conflicts around (un)paid work with demographic information to examine: Which topics do men and women discuss in relationship conflicts around paid and unpaid work? We use Large Language Models (LLMs) and systematically vary GPT-family models and prompting strategies to classify manifest (demographic information) and latent variables (whether posts discuss romantic relationships, paid, and unpaid work) in Reddit posts. Using classifications from the best-performing approach, we apply Structural Topic Models to explore which topics partners discuss and how discussions evolve over time. We find temporary pandemic shifts in topics, and women more often discuss mental health in paid work-related conflicts, while men more frequently emphasize career objectives. In conflicts related to unpaid work, men more frequently express concerns about sexual intimacy. Our analysis offers new insights into topics driving relationship conflicts around (un)paid work. We also contribute to the growing literature on LLMs’ capabilities and limitations in classifying social-science constructs. By combining demographic information with sensitive narratives, our dataset captures forms of relational conflict rarely accessible in survey or social-media research, opening promising avenues for future research.

articles.title: In Silico Advertising Tests
articles.authors: Marta Trales; Guillaume Hochard; Christophe Benavent
articles.abstract:
This research examines whether large language model agents can produce analytically useful evidence for advertising testing when treated as synthetic respondents rather than as substitutes for human consumers. We report an in-silico comparative post-test of two television advertisements in the French telecommunications market, conducted on a panel of 800 profile-conditioned consumer agents. The study evaluates the synthetic corpus through internal validity criteria: whether the questionnaire covers the main dimensions of advertising response, whether evaluative dimensions form coherent relations, whether the two stimuli are discriminated across preference labels, scores, lexical patterns and semantic embeddings, and whether responses vary intelligibly across social profiles.
The results indicate that the synthetic panel produces structured and interpretable evidence. The contribution is not that the analysis discovers a contrast invisible in the advertisements themselves: Bouygues and Orange are clearly built around different persuasive registers. Rather, the contribution is methodological. The synthetic-interview pipeline consistently recovers and differentiates these registers across preference labels, scores, lexical patterns and semantic comparisons. Bouygues is associated mainly with creative, humorous and memorable qualities,
while Orange is associated with reliability, informativeness, purchase orientation and overall preference. This structure is visible quantitatively in the main six dimensional coding scheme. Among all 800 synthetic agents, Bouygues leads on creativity (83.6% versus 14.8% for Orange), whereas Orange leads on informationseeking or consideration (76.8% versus 14.8% for Bouygues) and overall preference (54.8% versus 20.6% for Bouygues), with the remaining responses classified as mixed or neutral. The analysis remains deliberately limited to synthetic respondents.
Claims about similarity to human preferences or market behaviour would require external comparison with representative human data or market-level indicators.

articles.title: Polity Size and Women's Representation: Evidence from Two Large-scale Boundary Reforms
articles.authors: Moa Frödin-Gruneau; Jan Teorell; Kåre Vernby
articles.abstract: Do larger polities hinder gender parity in elected office? We theorize that when populations grow faster than elected assemblies, a “seat congestion” effect intensifies competition for nominations, enabling men candidates to crowd out women. We test this argument using two nationwide natural experiments: Swedish municipal amalgamations in 1952 and 1973 that abruptly increased electorates. We track the effects in newly digitized historical panel data. Where electorate-per-seat ratios rose, growth in women's representation slowed. Decomposition analyses show that expanding councils only partially offsets congestion. By identifying polity size as a systematic brake on descriptive representation, the study adds a demographic dimension to debates on institutional design and points to an overlooked cost of increasing jurisdictional size.

articles.title: Why We Cling to Flawed Influencers: Psychological Mechanisms Behind Loyalty to Deceptive Social Media Figures
articles.authors: Asma Alolyan
articles.abstract:
Abstract  
Existing studies on loyalty to social media influencers have mainly focused on cognitive  dissonance, parasocial bonding, halo effect, social identity, and just world belief, each in  isolation. This paper advances another argument: that these five mechanisms occur not  independently but in a predictable sequence, each reducing psychological resistance to the next,  producing loyalties more resistant than any single mechanism alone. We call this the  compounding loyalty model. Cognitive dissonance is the initial motivation causing a follower to  realise something is wrong; parasocial bonding makes rationalisation a requirement, not an  option; the halo effect provides a surface level base for maintaining trust despite misbehaviours;  social identity makes loyalty costly to lose; and just world belief provides a final, motivated  argument that deception did not happen at all. We draw this model from cases including James  Charles (2021) and Ramon Abbas, convicted of fraud in 2022. Media literacy, ethical marketing  and platform policy are discussed. 

Keywords: Influencers, social media, Cognitive dissonance, Para-social relationships, Halo  effect, social identity theory, just world hypothesis, Compounding loyalty model.

articles.title: Larger, younger, faster, harder: expansion, transformation, and inequality in YouTube’s creator economy (2019–2026)
articles.authors: Bernhard Rieder; Adrian Padilla; Ariadna Matamoros-Fernández; Òscar Coromina
articles.abstract: The growth of YouTube's creator economy raises a question that accounts of individual success and precarity cannot settle: how are the conditions of participation changing across the platform? Comparing two population-scale crawls from 2019 and 2026, we examine expansion, changes in production, and the distribution of attention across millions of channels. The population above the 1,000-subscriber threshold for advertising monetization grew from 4.4 million to 24.5 million, while its video catalogues grew ninefold. Expansion was strongest in South, Southeast, and East Asia, with India's share of channels declaring a country rising from 10 to 27 percent. This growth accompanied substantial turnover: most channels recorded in 2019 had no recent upload in 2026, and continued participation differed sharply by prior standing. Production also changed fundamentally. Median video duration fell from 247 to 60 seconds, with shortening across every content category and channel size. Among channels above 100,000 subscribers, new entrants accounted for most of the shift toward short form, while most continuing incumbents also shortened their output. Attention became more concentrated even among the same channels observed at both dates, and advertising revenue grew more slowly than the population meeting the subscriber threshold. These findings show how the output imperative extends from producing more to adapting what is produced, while sustained participation remains sharply unequal. They also place the increasingly Asian geography of the creator economy at the center of questions about platform labor, opportunity, and precarity.

articles.title: Perceived Manipulation, Fairness, and Trust in Competitive Mobile Gaming: A Cross-Cultural Analysis of Player Discourse
articles.authors: Hanieh Hatefi Yousefi
articles.abstract:
Perceptions of fairness play a central role in player experience within competitive mobile games, yet the processes through which players develop and sustain beliefs about manipulation remain insufficiently understood. This study investigates fairness-related discourse across two cultural and platform contexts through a five-year longitudinal qualitative analysis (2022–2026) of player-generated content from competitive mobile backgammon games.
The primary corpus consists of more than 52,000 Persian-language player reviews collected from Iranian app distribution platforms, supplemented by anonymised customer support transcripts. The comparative corpus comprises a stratified random sample of 750 negative reviews drawn from 4,116 reviews posted on an anglophone app-store listing over the same period. Using Inductive Thematic Analysis (ITA), the study identified seven recurring themes: dice manipulation, pay-to-win mechanics, bot opponents, connectivity sabotage, predetermined outcomes, statistical anomaly reporting, and support dismissal. These themes were subsequently organised into three higher-order meta-themes: Perceived Agency Erosion, Trust Erosion, and Statistical Misinterpretation.
The findings reveal both convergent and culturally distinct patterns. Beliefs that game outcomes are manipulated through unfair dice behaviour emerged as the dominant theme in both datasets, suggesting common cognitive mechanisms underlying fairness perceptions in stochastic competitive environments. At the same time, the two contexts differed in their developmental trajectories, complaint framing, and institutional response structures. Fairness-related complaints increased substantially across the Persian-language corpus over the study period, whereas comparable concerns remained relatively stable within the anglophone sample. Players in both contexts employed statistical reasoning to support manipulation claims, although the rhetorical and cultural framing of these arguments differed. Institutional responses to complaints also varied structurally, yet both contexts exhibited patterns that players frequently interpreted as dismissive or insufficiently responsive.
These findings contribute to research on player psychology, digital trust, and cross-cultural user experience by demonstrating how perceptions of unfairness emerge through the interaction of cognitive biases, community discourse, and platform communication practices. The study further highlights the importance of transparency design and context-sensitive trust-building mechanisms in competitive free-to-play games.

articles.title: Beyond the Joke: A Thematic Content Analysis of Russian-Linked Meme Pages Targeting Azerbaijan
articles.authors: Gudrat Guluyev
articles.abstract: As internet memes evolved from mere entertainment into a tool of digital propaganda, their role in modern warfare has become increasingly significant. This study examines their role in the case of Russian-linked information operations targeting the Azerbaijani audience on Facebook.  While the existing literature on meme-based Russian propaganda focuses heavily on the United States and Ukraine, the South Caucasus, one of the important regions of Russia’s “near abroad” policy, remains overlooked. The research addresses this critical gap by analyzing how these strategies are adapted to Azerbaijan's specific cultural and political context. The study relies on qualitative, multimodal analysis and emergent coding of 78 memes from nine Russian-linked Facebook pages targeting Azerbaijan between January 2023 and December 2024. The analysis identifies four consistent themes (the negative othering of the West, the discrediting of Western leaders, the reframing of the Nagorno-Karabakh Conflict, and the promotion of Azerbaijani sovereignty) and various propaganda techniques that have already been revealed in existing studies. The research paper concludes that these pages conduct a systematic influence campaign that sophisticatedly blends pro-Russian narratives with culturally conservative and patriotic domestic sentiments to resonate with the local audience.

articles.title: Research on Han Nationalism in China in the 2020s (VIII): Five Ideological Tendencies within Han Nationalism and Their Real-World Demands
articles.authors: ZY Liu
articles.abstract: This article is an exploratory study in the series “Research on Han Nationalism in China in the 2020s.” It examines different ideological tendencies within Han nationalist discourse on the Chinese Internet. Unlike approaches that treat Han nationalism as a single political position, this article argues that contemporary Han nationalism on the Chinese Internet is not a unified movement with a common political program, but a collection of ideological tendencies formed around different real-world problems. Based on long-term observation of relevant online discourse, historical narratives, cultural phenomena, and public discussions, the article identifies five ideal types: establishment Han nationalism, renunciation-oriented Han nationalism, left-wing Han nationalism, cultural Han nationalism, and right-wing Han nationalism. These five tendencies primarily focus, respectively, on policy correction; central–local relations and fiscal responsibility; ethnic and class inequality; Han cultural identity; and population decline and the long-term demographic continuity of the Han. Although they share dissatisfaction with some differentiated ethnic policies and particular historical narratives, they differ substantially in their explanations of the causes of these problems and in their proposed solutions. Some of their demands also overlap with left-wing politics, liberalism, or regional autonomy. Han nationalism therefore cannot simply be equated with nationalism in the conventional right-wing sense. Its internal political demands in fact reflect real tensions in Chinese society concerning employment, working conditions, fiscal pressure, regional governance, population decline, marriage and fertility, and cultural identity. This article does not attempt to estimate the actual social size of these tendencies. Instead, it treats the five categories as analytical ideal types for understanding internal differences within Chinese Internet Han nationalism in the 2020s.

articles.title: Did local authorities lose revenue following banning unhealthy food advertising?
articles.authors: Mark Alan Green; Emma Boyland
articles.abstract: UK local authorities are increasingly exploring restrictions for the advertising of unhealthy foods on their estates to promote healthier food environments. Concerns about effects on revenue can be a barrier to progress. In this study, we provide preliminary evidence that these policies did not negatively affect total advertising revenue across four local authorities in North West England. In some cases, we found that revenue increased post-implementation.

articles.title: Organisational Knowledge Brokerage in Science Diplomacy: The Making of AI Governance at UNESCO and the European Union
articles.authors: Adam McCarthy; Alice Naisbitt; Pedro Dos Santos Maia; Barbara Riberio; Kieron Flanagan; Philip Shapira
articles.abstract: We examine how expertise, evidence and authority are organised in the international governance of Artificial Intelligence (AI), and what this reveals about the practice of science diplomacy. Science-diplomacy scholarship has become increasingly attentive to the political character of expertise and to the ways knowledge is mobilised within international governance. Yet less attention has been paid to the organisational practices through which such knowledge is brokered within governance processes. Drawing on documentary analysis and 23 semi-structured interviews, we compare UNESCO’s Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence and the EU AI Act. Through an abductive analysis, we develop Organisational Knowledge Brokerage (OKB) to explain how a contested object such as AI is made workable for governance. We identify four connected practices through which this occurs: stabilising the governance object, legitimising expertise, building authority and operationalising governance. These practices took different forms under contrasting institutional mandates and governing capacities. UNESCO worked through global intergovernmental standard-setting and implementation support, while the EU combined supranational regulation with expert advice and Member State coordination. Across both cases, OKB also produced a cross-cutting process that we term normative translation, through which contested values acquired practical meaning in definitions, assessments and procedures. We show how this brokerage allowed each organisation to establish workable and revisable settlements around AI under conditions of technological uncertainty and dispersed authority. The article therefore develops a practice-oriented account of science diplomacy as organisational work through which knowledge, values and institutional authority are assembled for collective action in international technology governance.

articles.title: Product Market Reform and Enterprise Software Diffusion: Evidence from European Industries
articles.authors: Frenki Shatku
articles.abstract: This paper examines whether product-market reforms in upstream network sectors are associated with faster diffusion of enterprise software in downstream European industries. The analysis combines Eurostat data on Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) and Customer Relationship Management (CRM) adoption with OECD ETCR and REGIMPACT indicators for 24 economies and 13 industries over 2010–2021. Reform exposure is constructed using major annual regulatory declines and fixed 2010 US input-output weights, while the empirical specification includes country-by-interval, industry-by-interval and country-industry fixed effects. Industries more exposed to major reforms experience faster growth in the combined ERP-CRM adoption index. At the median nonzero reform exposure, the estimate corresponds to approximately 1.5 percentage points of additional adoption growth. The response is stronger for CRM, while ERP is smaller and less precisely estimated. Minor and moderate regulatory changes show no comparable relationship. The results remain similar across alternative samples, reform thresholds and controls for the initial stage of software diffusion. The findings connect upstream product-market reform to downstream diffusion of organizational technologies.

articles.title: Conceptualizing Political Consumerism in the Attention Economy
articles.authors: Christopher Starke; Claes de Vreese; Natali Helberger
articles.abstract: Social media platforms increasingly become targets of politically and ethically motivated user protest, yet existing approaches do not sufficiently explain how deliberate platform use can operate as political participation. This conceptual paper extends the established concept of political consumerism to the attention economy, defining it as individuals’ market-oriented behaviors to punish or reward social media platforms on political or ethical grounds. It argues that three main factors constrain political consumerism on social media platforms: opaque value extraction, limited ethical alternatives, and high switching costs. Because political consumerism can take many forms, the paper suggests distinguishing user actions by their economic impact and whether they signal user preferences to the platform company. It further explains how social media literacy and regulation can improve the legibility and actionability of these practices. Finally, it outlines methodological implications for studying political consumerism through mixed-method designs that combine user motivations with behavioral data.

articles.title: Utility Function and Labor Supply -- The case of ces functions: an elementary approach
articles.authors: Françoise Larbre
articles.abstract:
In this note, we revisit the consumption-leisure (or equivalently, consumption-labor) trade-off and show that models relying on a Cobb-Douglas utility function (characterized  by a unit substitution elasticity between leisure and consumption) obscure important elements of labor supply behavior. To this end, we explore the possibilities offered by the family of CES functions to represent the preferences of the consumer-worker agent. This choice enables us to generate a variety of labor supply functions, not necessarily monotonically increasing with respect to the real wage. Throughout the note, we explicitly highlight the dependence of the reservation wage on the substitution elasticity  as well as a threshold of non-wage income crucial for 
its evolution. We find ourselves back in a debate that remains relevant questioning a possible disincentive effect of unemployment benefits. We begin by reviewing the definitions of key concepts and analytical tools, and the examples provided are constructed to allow for clear graphical representations.

articles.title: Resilience in a Discordant Security Culture: Georgia between Institutional Continuity and Political Realignment
articles.authors: Mariam Bibilashvili
articles.abstract: Challenging the common understanding in the relevant literature, this study reconceptualizes resilience to hybrid threats as a politically mediated process rather than purely a matter of institutional capacity-building. To examine how policy frameworks and political rhetoric interact to shape resilience, it traces Georgia’s security culture in the aftermath of the Russo-Georgian war. Through intertextual discourse analysis, the article cross-examines the institutional architecture of digital resilience, encompassing cybersecurity (systemic), media regulation (protective) and media literacy (empowerment) measures, with the government’s shifting rhetoric (2023–2025), while interview data provide contextual insights. The analysis reveals a discordant security culture manifested in fragmented governance and discursive struggle over resilience. Although formal policy frameworks normatively align with the West and consistently identify Russia as the principal security threat, governmental rhetoric portrays the same Western actors as sources of foreign interference and prioritizes political autonomy over cooperation while still invoking commitments to the constitutionally enshrined Euro-Atlantic trajectory. This dichotomy between institutional design and political discourse results in strategic ambiguity. It suggests that in hybrid regimes formal frameworks may function symbolically to signal external alignment, while practice is determined by short-term political calculations and discretionary authority, leaving institutions and societies vulnerable to evolving forms of foreign interference.

articles.title: Speed-Quality Tradeoffs Shape the Structure of Decision-Making Collectives
articles.authors: Chanuwas Aswamenakul; Tyler Marghetis; Paul E. Smaldino
articles.abstract: Many human groups employ hierarchical decision-making, in which only a few individuals hold the power to make decisions for the collective. A common explanation for the prevalence of hierarchical decision-making is that it provides group-level benefits by speeding up the decision-making process. However, groups can often do better by taking more time to explore a problem space or generate ideas. These contrasting accounts suggest that hierarchical or egalitarian decision structures may emerge under different circumstances. To more clearly distinguish between these circumstances, we studied an evolutionary model of group decision-making that includes both intra-group and inter-group dynamics. We show that the emergent social structure depends critically on the trade-off between speed and decision quality: scenarios that demand rapid decisions favor the evolution of skewed, hierarchical structures, while scenarios that reward extended deliberation favor the evolution of flat, egalitarian structures. Our results suggest that, instead of inevitably becoming centralized and hierarchical, groups and organizations are likely to evolve social structures that reflect the relationship between the speed and the quality of decisions they collectively make.

articles.title: “AI” as gaslighting – Considering the affordances of stochastic generative systems in relation to anthropo-centered epistemic operations
articles.authors: Daniel Cardoso
articles.abstract:
This paper mobilizes the notion of ‘AI’ as a carcinogen, as developed by Berman, to then inquire and analyze what is the possible human impact that results from the democratization of the use of Large Language Models and Generative Pretrained Transformers, from the perspective of how epistemic frameworks are mobilized as a core component of sociability.
It then advances the proposal that we understand ‘AI’ as a case of the ‘Thomas Theorem’, and that, as such, LLMs and GPTs can effectively operate as systems of non-targeted, non-intentional, gaslighting.
From that approach, the paper follows up with a materially-grounded analysis of how the operations performed on data for the creation and usage of LLMs and GPTs mean that these technologies have the affordance of being episteme-fixative, and that such an affordance (as defined here) is specific to these technologies, in a way that allows for non-essentialist and non-deterministic analysis that considers both changes and continuities in both media systems and our everyday engagement with them.
It concludes by suggesting venues of inquiry that are made easier by the previous conclusions, and returns to capitalism’s uptake of technology, rather than to any immanent aspect of technology, as a central aspect to consider in evaluating the epistemic harms that might come out of these affordances.

articles.title: “Safe for now?” Boundary work and tensions of AI Adoption in Sign Language Interpreting and Speech-to-Text Reporting in Belgium and the Netherlands
articles.authors: Maartje De Meulder; Karolien Gebruers; Deborah Giustini
articles.abstract:
Abstract
This article examines how sign language interpreters (SLIs) and speech-to-text reporters (STTRs) in Belgium (Flanders) and the Netherlands understand and navigate artificial intelligence (AI)-driven language technologies in their professional lives. While speech-to-text reporting already faces displacement by automated transcription, sign language interpreting remains partly sheltered by the limited AI training data for Flemish and Dutch Sign Language. Drawing on an online survey (N = 134) conducted in 2025, and theorized through  boundary work, we identify three tensions structuring practitioners' accounts: a temporality tension, in which anticipated disruption coexists with present stability; an access tension, in which AI expands available options while enabling institutions to narrow the definition of "sufficient access"; and a professional identity tension, in which the technology threatening practitioners' livelihoods may simultaneously advance the profession's own emancipatory ideal. Respondents describe AI as a new third actor in interpreted interaction, shifting some practitioners toward editing and quality-control roles that lack institutional recognition. We argue that AI in language access is actively produced through practitioners’ ongoing boundary work and calls for recognizing them — alongside deaf consumers — as epistemic actors in governing just technological transitions.

articles.title: Associations between content and engagement vary across social media communities
articles.authors: Alberto Acerbi
articles.abstract: Research on social media engagement often seeks general content features that are associated with online success. However, social media platforms contain communities with different audiences, topics, and norms, and the same features may have different associations with engagement within different communities. This research considers 1,078,044 items from 587 communities in five corpora spanning Reddit, Stack Exchange, X, and YouTube. For each corpus, negativity, moralization, arousal, and in-group versus out-group language were measured. Their relationships with engagement were compared using multilevel models imposing one within-community slope per feature with models allowing slopes to vary across communities. Varying-slope models fit the data better in all five corpora. The estimated community slopes varied substantially in magnitude and, frequently, direction. Nevertheless, the average slopes from the varying-slope models remained small. The improved fit therefore reflects heterogeneity across communities rather than stronger average associations. These findings show that a weak average association can conceal stronger but opposing associations across communities. General claims about the content associated with social media engagement need to account for the specific communities in which that content appears.

articles.title: BirthClim_IT: A Harmonized Municipality-Level Dataset on Fertility,  Environment, and Territorial Contexts in Italy, 2003–2022
articles.authors: Chiara Baldan; Anna Giraldo
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND
Environmental conditions and climate change, alongside spatial heterogeneity in fertility, have received increasing attention in fertility research. However, research combining these perspectives remains limited, partly due to the lack of data linking fine spatial resolution with detailed demographic, environmental, and socioeconomic information. This is particularly relevant in Italy, where substantial spatial variation in fertility coexists with heterogeneous environmental conditions.
OBJECTIVE
This paper introduces BirthClim_IT, a harmonized longitudinal dataset designed to support research on fertility and its environmental and territorial contexts across Italian municipalities. The dataset description is accompanied by two empirical applications illustrating its use.
METHODS
The BirthClim_IT dataset combines monthly demographic information with environmental, climatic, geographic, and socioeconomic indicators for 7,896 Italian municipalities from January 2003 to December 2022. The dataset contains 126 variables, harmonized to the administrative boundaries in force on January 1, 2024. To address sparsity in monthly birth counts, we also provide a spatially aggregated version comprising 4,936 spatial units and a customizable aggregation procedure. 
RESULTS
The dataset provides both municipality-level and aggregated data, allowing fertility patterns to be examined jointly across space and time. The two descriptive applications illustrate its use in identifying distinct environmental profiles across Italian municipalities and in examining seasonal variation in fertility and environmental conditions.
CONTRIBUTION
Given the growing interest in environmental dimensions of fertility and increasing attention to the spatial dimension of demographic processes, BirthClim_IT provides a new and flexible resource combining fine spatial and temporal resolution with information spanning multiple dimensions of the demographic, environmental, and socioeconomic context.

articles.title: Scrutiny, sanctions, and attacks on scholars: Public acceptance and perceived deservingness in Switzerland
articles.authors: Niels G. Mede; Julia Metag; Mike S. Schäfer
articles.abstract: Different forms of critical and hostile public engagement with science have been documented worldwide. They range from valuable scrutiny to public protests, support for funding cuts, and attacks. Whether people accept such engagement, and whether they consider it deserved, has rarely been studied with representative data. Using a preregistered, nationally representative survey from Switzerland (n = 698), we examine acceptance of public scrutiny, support for sanctions, and attacks on scholars and their perceived deservingness when scholars speak out politically. We find that acceptance follows a graded hierarchy: Most respondents accept scrutiny, fewer accept sanctions, and hardly anyone accepts attacks. Two thirds consider criticism of politically outspoken scholars deserved, whereas attacks are largely rejected, although noteworthy minorities consider them deserved. Acceptance of attacks is associated with science-related populist attitudes, right-leaning views, younger age, lower income, and active online engagement. Moreover, perceived political distance from scholars is associated with acceptance of scrutiny.

articles.title: How Model Choice Obscures Forecast Uncertainty: The Rashomon Effect and the 2026 Senate
articles.authors: Jack T. Rametta; Christopher Hare
articles.abstract: Election forecasts report ostensibly precise predictions that depend on modeling choices. These include the size of the incumbency advantage, the weight on state partisan lean, and how strongly national conditions move individual races. We show that the record of Senate elections between 2010 and 2024 is insufficient to adjudicate such choices. While hundreds of Senate races provide information about race-level relationships, the role of shared national conditions must be learned primarily from comparisons across only eight election cycles. Indeed, of 120 plausible models varying these weights, 117 predict past elections similarly well. This “Rashomon set” illustrates how different assumptions can produce comparable predictive performance but distinct substantive findings. Our reference model predicts a 50.6% chance of Democratic control of the 120th Senate with 50.5 expected seats (90% interval 45–56). The 117-model Rashomon set, however, puts the chances of Democratic control anywhere between 43.2% and 57.6%. We recommend reporting this range alongside conventional predictive intervals from a single model.

articles.title: Social media and the prevention or reduction of harmful gambling: a rapid evidence review with integrated lived experience
articles.authors: Jenny Sweetman; Liz Littlewood; Patricia Darcy; Greg Forshaw; Amanda Perry; su golder
articles.abstract:
Background and aims: Research has established a clear link between social media use and harmful gambling. Existing systematic reviews highlight how social media platforms enable and normalise gambling. This rapid evidence review aimed to identify interventions using social media to prevent or reduce harmful gambling. 

Methods: Searches were conducted (January 2026) in MEDLINE, Embase and PsycINFO. Searches of grey literature searches, and backward and forward citations from included references, were also completed. Independent screening, data extraction and quality assessment was undertaken by two independent reviewers. Data were analysed using narrative synthesis methods. An expert by experience group directly informed each stage of the review process.

Results: From 1138 unique records, 10 studies met our inclusion criteria (2 randomised controlled trials, 2 cohort studies, 2 mixed methods studies and 4 qualitative studies). Included studies focused on brief messages, the impact of a social media platform outage, and the use of gambling support forums. Findings highlighted the benefits and potential risks of implementing gambling harm reduction strategies on social media, the role of interaction with others, and opportunities to use social media to better understand the process of recovery from problem gambling.

Discussion and Conclusions: There is some evidence that social media platforms could usefully support the reduction or prevention of harmful gambling. Further research is required, co-designed by those with lived experience to optimise engagement and impact, to better understand how online interventions can support different people and to assess the effectiveness through large high-quality randomised controlled trials.

articles.title: Tricky Trade-Offs on a Transparency Spectrum: How the Financial Times Approaches Transparency about AI Use in News
articles.authors: Liz Lohn; Felix M. Simon
articles.abstract: As news organisations adopt artificial intelligence (AI), they face growing pressure to be transparent about when and how it is used – yet practical approaches remain uneven. This paper examines AI transparency through an in-depth case study of the Financial Times (FT). Drawing on 13 semi-structured interviews with 12 senior managers across editorial, product, data science, and communications, together with internal documents, we show that the FT approaches transparency as a hybrid of policy, process, and practice, framed by a desire to safeguard both internal and external trust. Transparency is calibrated to context: internally, AI use is signposted in tools and reinforced through training and personal accountability; externally, the prominence of disclosure scales with system autonomy and editorial oversight, with stronger labelling for no-human-in-the-loop features than for AI-assisted, journalist-edited outputs. We identify nine factors that shape audience-facing disclosure – legal/provider requirements, industry benchmarking, nature of the task, human oversight, system novelty, audience expectations, perceived risk, commercial sensitivities, and design constraints – and five crosscutting challenges, including site-wide consistency (especially on mobile) and potential “transparency backfire.” Conceptually, our analysis links AI transparency to isomorphic pressures and to intersecting institutional logics. We argue that AI transparency in news is best understood as a spectrum, evolving with technological advancements, commercial, professional and ethical considerations and shifting audience attitudes.

articles.title: Doubly Preferential: The Treatment of Contested Experts in News Media
articles.authors: François Claveau; Jacob Hamel-Mottiez; Léon Gatien; Olivier Santerre
articles.abstract: This article contributes to the characterization of media bias by analyzing how Canadian news media select and contextualize messages originating from think tanks, an influential yet ideologically marked form of expertise. Drawing on a large media corpus (2017–2021), this article shows that Canadian journalists make relatively limited use of textual indicators of credibility, but that these indicators systematically reflect the ideological preferences already evident in their source selection. Think tanks that are more frequently solicited thus benefit from more favorable contextualization, corroborating the hypothesis of a doubly preferential treatment. The study concludes by discussing the normative implications of these practices for journalistic standards, such as impartiality, in the face of contested expertise.

articles.title: Commercial video games improve species-related knowledge, perceptions, and action
articles.authors: Katie Blake; Paul J Johnson; Diogo Veríssimo
articles.abstract: Digital media often mediates human-wildlife interactions. It is feared that overexposure to virtual animals will distort public awareness and valuation of real-world species. This is alarming given the current rate of extinction. Commercial video games have attracted much attention for their capacity to engage players with biodiversity and conservation. Yet their impact for this is unclear. We use an online experiment to explore whether this medium can improve species-related knowledge, perceptions, and actions, as well as test assumptions that digitised wildlife are favoured by players over real-world counterparts. Our findings are based on a sample of 272 players and 273 non-players of Planet Zoo, using species that feature in this title. We found that both gameplay hours and recency of playing Planet Zoo are positively linked to: more accurately identifying species’ names and conservation status; how much the species are liked; threat appraisals about the likelihood and impact of species loss; and increased donations. Players donated nearly twice as much to species protection as non-players on average (£7.16 versus £4.68), and they allocated the maximum possible donation value of £20 three times as often. Furthermore, we did not observe any detrimental outcomes for digitised wildlife on responses compared to real versions, and we found that any positive effects from experience with Planet Zoo tended to be greater for reptiles than mammals. Our findings do not support concerns that digital media necessarily has harmful implications for public engagement with biodiversity and conservation. Rather, we show that commercial video games might provide an avenue for players to better understand the natural world and take action to protect it, and they might even be particularly beneficial for less desirable taxa. We challenge more game studios to bridge the gap between virtual and real nature where appropriate, joining efforts to ensure that wildlife can also persist beyond digital spaces. We encourage more researchers to pursue this line of inquiry. Given the rapid loss of biodiversity, we cannot continue to overlook how these platforms with global reach might be leveraged to drive conservation action.

articles.title: Evidence from China: A quantitative examination of China's new competition regime for the digital economy
articles.authors: Leonard Baum; Joanna J. Bryson
articles.abstract: Growing global concern about the problems associated with concentrated market power in the digital economy is leading to a renewed interest in competition policy. Since the late 2010s, China’s government has squarely confronted the problems of its own ‘Big Tech’ with a new competition regime for digital markets. The ensuing ‘tech crackdown’ of late 2020 provides a rare quasi-natural experiment to study the impact of antitrust regulation. Here we deploy a novel market capitalization approach that builds on the informativeness of China’s financial markets. Harnessing Bloomberg data of 1142 publicly listed firms for the period 2019 to 2022, we find that across China's digital economy, this unprecedented intervention is associated with both reduced market concentration and reduced market-capitalization growth, but no harms to revenue. Employing a difference-in-differences and event-study design, we identify a causal link between China’s new competition regime and a reduction in concentration in the primary markets of China's three most dominant digital platforms — Baidu, Alibaba and Tencent (BATs). Other empirical findings include a negative association between market concentration and the openness of digital markets and a non-relationship between market concentration and profits. Our results indicate that neither profit- nor revenue-based metrics are entirely appropriate for measuring digital market power effectively. We conclude by discussing the relative success of China’s digital competition policy as well as the relevance of these insights for global, including Western regulatory strategies.

articles.title: University-affiliated sustainability badges: Shared identity, tourist perceptions, and hotel manager receptivity
articles.authors: Peter Lewin; Danyelle; Anna Kristina Zinn; Sarah MacInnes; Sara Dolnicar
articles.abstract: Hotel sustainability research shows that pro-environmental behaviour‑change interventions are often effective in field experiments, but widespread adoption by hotels remains limited. One possible explanation is that hotels lack external recognition that would make adopting these measures visible to guests and rewarding to managers. This study investigates whether university-affiliated sustainability badges could serve as a recognition mechanism, testing their effectiveness across two studies drawing on Signalling Theory and Social Identity Theory. In an online experiment (N=975), prospective hotel guests viewed simulated hotel booking pages featuring one of the four badge options, or no badge, across budget, mid-range, and luxury hotel pricing segments. All badge variations increased perceived hotel sustainability and guests’ sense of belonging to a community of environmentally conscious travellers (group identification). Badges did not trigger negative emotions, but the university affiliated logo did not perform better than a generic environmental logo on almost all measures, suggesting these effects are based on the presence of any badge, rather than the university partnership specifically. Semi-structured interviews with ten hotel managers found conditional receptivity to university-affiliated badges, primarily through a sense of shared values and community orientation with the partnering institution (collective values) rather than the badge’s function as a credibility signal. These findings suggest that collective values and shared identities, rather than signalling, may be the more promising mechanism for engaging hotels and guests around sustainability initiatives, and offer an encouraging direction for potential university-hotel partnerships that may translate into the future implementation of pro-environmental behaviour change interventions.

articles.title: Do Chatbots Sound Equally Sure in French and in Arabic? A Pilot Audit of Expressed Certainty in ChatGPT and Gemini
articles.authors: Houda Es-sqalli
articles.abstract: People increasingly ask chatbots about health and public services and pass the answers on to others. Whether they check first may depend on how sure an answer sounds. This pilot audit asks whether the certainty cues that chatbots give change with the language of the question. Ten questions on public health and public services in Morocco were asked once in French and once in Modern Standard Arabic to ChatGPT and Gemini (40 answers). Answers were scored with a bilingual lexicon of hedges and boosters. Both chatbots hedged less in Arabic than in French, and the pattern held under two alternative versions of the lexicon. A model-assisted second coding of 10 answers showed that the lexicon captured boosters well but missed about a third of hedges. With 10 questions and one run each, these results are a first look, not a finding. They motivate a larger audit with repeated runs and human validation.

articles.title: Social Origin and the Baccalauréat: Curriculum, Sex, Teachers and Sector in French Upper-Secondary Schools, 2017–2023
articles.authors: Adrien Dufour
articles.abstract:
2022–23, an index of the social composition of each school’s pupils. We use these sources, combined into a panel of 2,394 general and technological lycées observed over the seven sessions from 2017 to 2023, to ask how far social origin still determines what pupils obtain at the end of secondary school, and through which parts of the system that determination passes.
At national level, passing the baccalauréat has become close to universal, but the gap between the children of senior managers and the children of manual workers has not narrowed since 1998. Between schools, social composition orders results with considerable force: a ten-point difference in the social index corresponds to about eight percentage points in the share of candidates passing with distinction, and this single relationship accounts for more than half of the variation between establishments. The two pandemic sessions of 2020 and 2021, awarded largely on continuous assessment, temporarily compressed this relationship; it returned to its earlier level after the 2021 reform of the examination.
We then examine four further lines of division. Curricular choice is the strongest: the technological streams are offered where the pupils served are least advantaged, and since the reform replaced the general-track streams with a menu of specialisms, mathematics has become the clearest social marker in the system. Sex produces a second, largely independent segregation that is greater in curricular terms than the social one. Teaching staff are distributed unequally in a way that closely follows pupils’ social origin, but this inequality accounts for little of the outcome gap once pupils’ social origin is held constant. The gap between the public and the subsidised private sector is about half a matter of the pupils each sector serves; the remainder resists every adjustment we can make.
We conclude that the published indicators describe social sorting more than institutional quality, and that the additions needed to change this are known and modest.

articles.title: Do polls underestimate support for right-wing parties? Assessing variation in polling error by party family
articles.authors: Stuart Perrett; Will Jennings; Jonathan Mellon; Christopher Prosser; Christopher Wlezien
articles.abstract: Pollsters have underestimated support for notable right-wing electoral outcomes, including Donald Trump’s vote share in 2016, 2020, and 2024, the UK Conservative Party in 2015 and 2024, and Leave in the 2016 EU referendum. Do these outcomes reflect isolated polling failures, or a persistent partisan asymmetry in polling error across democracies? We provide the first comparative analysis of partisan polling error. Drawing on over 38,500 election-poll-party observations across 32 countries and 372 elections between 1945 and 2025, we use a Bayesian hierarchical modeling framework to estimate latent election-party polling error. We find that, on average, support for parties on the left is overestimated, while support for parties on the right is underestimated. This pattern is evident across countries, party classifications, and vote intention polling dating to the 1940s. In spotlighting persistent partisan asymmetries, our findings contribute to understanding institutional and contextual correlates of pre-election polling accuracy.

articles.title: Answering without disclosing: How officials under scrutiny compress what they say
articles.authors: Nasrul Ismail; William S. Harvey
articles.abstract: How do organisational actors withhold information while continuing to answer under scrutiny? Research on organisational silence has largely treated withholding as a question of whether actors speak. This article examines variation within speech through 1 781 question-and-answer exchanges from 102 recorded interview encounters with senior officials in prison health governance across three studies conducted between 2016 and 2023. Narrative absence was coded across six features and response timing was derived from audio and validated against blinded listener judgements. Higher narrative absence was associated with substantially shorter answers within encounters, and this association held across all robustness checks. Changes in response onset were much smaller, while pausing supported no independent association, and the automated measure of fillers and repairs failed validation. The findings identify controlled compression as a response form through which disclosure contracts while interactional responsiveness continues. Separating responsiveness from disclosure matters because organisational accountability is routinely assessed through visible responsiveness even though meaningful accountability depends on disclosure. An actor may therefore satisfy every observable requirement of cooperation while narrowing what is made available. The article shows that where speaking is expected, withholding does not cease but relocates into the answers themselves.

articles.title: Fairness Perception and Trust Erosion in Competitive Mobile Gaming: A Five-Year Longitudinal Study of a Persian-Language Backgammon Platform
articles.authors: Hanieh Hatefi Yousefi
articles.abstract:
Fairness perception is a critical yet understudied dimension of player experience in competitive mobile games. This paper presents findings from a five-year longitudinal qualitative study (2022–2026) examining how players construct, reinforce, and communicate beliefs about unfairness in a competitive mobile gaming environment. Using Inductive Thematic Analysis (ITA), we analysed a corpus of more than 52,000 player reviews collected across multiple mobile app marketplaces, supplemented by anonymised customer support interaction transcripts obtained through a research collaboration agreement.
Data were collected using a longitudinal sampling design that examined the same calendar month across five consecutive years, enabling the identification of long-term trends while reducing seasonal effects. Analysis identified seven operational themes describing players’ fairness-related beliefs and behaviours, which were subsequently consolidated into three higher-order meta-themes: Perceived Agency (the belief that game systems determine outcomes independently of player skill), Trust Erosion (the progressive reinforcement of manipulation beliefs through negative experiences and platform interactions), and Statistical Misinterpretation (the attribution of probabilistic outcomes to intentional system design). The proportion of 1-star reviews citing fairness-related concerns increased from 3% in 2022 to 18% in 2026, indicating a substantial decline in player trust over the study period.
The study further proposes a ten-stage Player Journey of Distrust, mapping the cognitive and emotional progression from initial doubt to entrenched beliefs about manipulation. Findings suggest that fairness complaints are often better understood as expressions of deteriorating trust rather than perceptions of technical malfunction. The paper discusses implications for transparency design, player communication strategies, support systems, and the broader study of trust in digital gaming environments.
Keywords: fairness perception; player experience; trust erosion; mobile gaming; thematic analysis; player psychology; app store reviews; cognitive bias; longitudinal qualitative research; trust in digital systems

articles.title: Assaults, Self-Harm, and the Allocation of State Resources in English and Welsh Prisons, 2009-2010 to 2024-2025
articles.authors: Nasrul Ismail
articles.abstract: Routine prison allocation in England and Wales is based on staffing, occupancy and regime, but does not incorporate assaults or self-harm. Using 1,727 public-sector establishment-years of Ministry of Justice expenditure and safety data from 2009-2010 to 2024-2025, this article examines whether deteriorating conditions were followed by changes in expenditure. Real expenditure per place fell 28.7 per cent by 2016-2017 before recovering, while prisons retained their relative positions. Higher assault rates were associated with increased expenditure in the following year before 2019-2020, but not thereafter; the interaction test did not establish a change between periods. Self-harm showed no statistically detectable association with subsequent expenditure in either period. Routine allocation continued throughout, but did not consistently respond to deteriorating safety conditions.

articles.title: Reference Observability and Journal Universe Choice in Open Reconstructions of Recursive Journal Metrics
articles.authors: Utz Weitzel
articles.abstract: Open reconstructions of recursive journal indicators can differ from a benchmark along two dimensions: reference observability, which determines which citation records enter the calculation, and the recursive journal universe, over which prestige circulates. We analyze the two dimensions separately in a factorial design. First, we reconstruct Clarivate’s 2024 Article Influence Score (AIS) with OpenAlex data as the Article Network Score (ANS) for a JCR-derived universe (J), the Norwegian Register (N), and the OpenAlex journal universe (A), with ANS defined for 21,706, 22,577, and 107,268 journals, respectively. Then, using a common sample of 15,951 journals, we cross the three universes with two treatments: RAW includes all cited-window articles and reviews, whereas REF retains only those for which OpenAlex records at least one reference. REF improves agreement with AIS in every universe: mean error falls and rank agreement rises. An additional component experiment shows that this improvement does not come from changing the ANS denominator alone, but from its joint change with citation-edge eligibility. Across universes, J and N yield similar results, whereas A has consistently higher errors and lower rank agreement. Robustness checks support the main results on larger journal sets, in the Leiden/CWTS core universe, and in 2023.

articles.title: Doubly Preferential: The Treatment of Contested Experts in News Media
articles.authors: François Claveau; Jacob Hamel-Mottiez; Léon Gatien; Olivier Santerre
articles.abstract: This article contributes to the characterization of media bias by analyzing how Canadian news media select and contextualize messages originating from think tanks, an influential yet ideologically marked form of expertise. Drawing on a large media corpus (2017–2021), this article shows that Canadian journalists make relatively limited use of textual indicators of credibility, but that these indicators systematically reflect the ideological preferences already evident in their source selection. Think tanks that are more frequently solicited thus benefit from more favorable contextualization, corroborating the hypothesis of a doubly preferential treatment. The study concludes by discussing the normative implications of these practices for journalistic standards, such as impartiality, in the face of contested expertise.

articles.title: Self-Constructed Recovery from Cognitive Collapse: An analytic autoethnography
articles.authors: Xin Sun
articles.abstract: Severe childhood maltreatment is known to impair brain development. However, this retrospective single-case autoethnography illustrates that an individual with extreme developmental trauma can achieve functional recovery without formal intervention. This study covers the participant’s life from birth to age 28, and the core recovery period begins with cognitive collapse at age 14 and ends with high functional recovery at age 28. This recovery is marked by the participant‑researcher’s ability to produce this manuscript. Consequently, this case shapes a distinct recovery trajectory that existing models do not capture.

articles.title: Hate speech against scientists can backfire – but so can counterspeech: Evidence from a four-country experiment
articles.authors: Niels G. Mede; Lena Frischlich
articles.abstract: Hate speech against scientists can harm their well-being and undermine knowledge-based societies, and counterspeech by bystanders is often proposed as a remedy. But comparative evidence on how bystanders perceive hate speech targeting scientists and on whether counterspeech helps is lacking. In a preregistered experiment with quota samples weighted to national population margins from Denmark, Germany, the United Kingdom, and the United States (N = 2,769), participants saw a fictitious social media post by a scientist either alone, with a hateful comment, or with a hateful comment plus a counterspeech reply. Hate speech backfired: Participants rated the scientist’s post more positively in both comment conditions. Counterspeech had mixed effects: It increased participants’ intentions to speak up themselves, but in Germany and the United Kingdom it made the hateful comment appear more acceptable. Our findings advance research on attacks against epistemic authorities and demonstrate the value of comparative, multi-outcome designs.

articles.title: AI Systems for Filmmaking: A Survey of HCI Research from a Labor-Centered Perspective
articles.authors: YUYING TANG; Lin Gao; Haotian Li; Baiqiao Zhang; Rebecca Fiebrink; Sebastian Deterding; Xiaojuan Ma; Huamin Qu
articles.abstract: Artificial intelligence is integrated into filmmaking and has attracted attention in human-computer interaction (HCI). Existing studies have primarily characterized AI systems for filmmaking by their capabilities and supported tasks, with limited attention to the organisation of filmmaking labor during system use. We review 31 HCI system papers and develop a three-layer taxonomy of labor sites, labor types, and human-AI allocation, examining where AI systems are positioned, what types of labor are involved during system use, and how those labor types are allocated between humans and AI. Our analysis reveals a concentration on individual below-the-line contexts, increasing attention to structural and meaning-making labor beyond execution, comparatively limited relational labor, and substantial variation in human-AI allocation across labor types. We further identify opportunities for the design and evaluation of AI systems that account for the broader organization of filmmaking labor. This review provides a labor-centered taxonomy for synthesizing AI systems for filmmaking and a basis for examining how AI may become involved in broader organizations of creative labor.

articles.title: Cruelty Across Substrates: From Animal Cruelty to Embodied AI and the Coming Detection Gap
articles.authors: Travis Gilly
articles.abstract:
Childhood cruelty to animals is among the most durable behavioral warning signs of later interpersonal
violence in the forensic and clinical literature. The predictive mechanism does not rest on any settled
answer about the moral status of the target. It rests on what the perpetrator practices, rehearses, and
trains in themselves: desensitization, dominance affect, and the social learning of cruelty as pleasure.
This paper offers a conceptual continuity argument and research agenda. We argue that the substrate
of the target is incidental to that training, with one critical qualification: the configuration of the target
matters. Routine digital destruction in static media (the static video game target, the scripted non player
character) is a categorically different case from the closed loop, contingent emotional response systems
on which the argument turns. As world models, embodied robotics, and closed loop emotional voice
systems converge toward agents that perform distress in ways a user cannot reliably distinguish from a
being in pain, we argue that the dispositional consequences of practiced cruelty against those agents are
likely to recruit sufficiently similar mechanisms to warrant clinical and forensic attention. The paper does
not claim that synthetic agents are moral patients. It claims that the warning signal forensic and clinical
fields have relied upon for fifty years risks migrating to a venue with substantially diminished detection
infrastructure. Existing human robot interaction research already shows that users do not need to believe
a synthetic agent is conscious to respond to it through social, emotional, or dominance based scripts. The
Kantian observation that cruelty corrupts the cruel is sufficient to ground the argument. Conduct disorder
assessment, character evidence frameworks, school counseling protocols, and pre employment screening
for sensitive roles will need to adapt or lose one of the more durable early behavioral indicators available
to forensic and clinical assessment. The paper is offered as agenda setting; the operational protocols it
identifies as necessary are deliberately scoped to a planned companion paper.

articles.title: Platform visibility and protest recirculation in the Cockroach Janta Party movement
articles.authors: No authors listed
articles.abstract:
This paper examines how the Cockroach Janta Party connected digital communication and street
protest in India between May and July 2026. I draw on nineteen public documentary records and a
separate retrospective account of my participation. I follow calls to attend demonstrations, a
request to share protest photographs and videos, Sonam Wangchuk's involvement, and disputes
over platform access. In my early visits, I remember small gatherings, people who stayed only
briefly, and volunteers who hoped the protest would grow but were unsure how far it would spread.
These observations make it difficult to assume that online popularity leads to sustained
participation. I use a visibility-action-recirculation framework to examine how gatherings produce
material that returns to digital circulation. A limited comparison with Nepal's September 2025
protests considers how people maintain communication when services are restricted. The evidence
documents deliberate organizing and reported interruptions. It does not establish how
recommendation systems, emotional appeals or recirculated material affected attendance.

Keywords: Cockroach Janta Party; platform visibility; digital protest; recirculation; platform governance;
India; Nepal

articles_hidden.title: Policy, Procedure, and Public Trust in the Bureaucracy
articles_hidden.authors: Alexander Love; Alexander Sahn
articles_hidden.abstract: Bureaucracies derive their legitimacy from a perception of impartiality, but in polarized societies preferences over outcomes may trump faith in procedure. We study citizens’ evaluations of the policymaking process as a joint function of individual beliefs that bureaucratic procedure was followed and preferences over outcomes. We recontacted and surveyed individuals who recently commented on rules proposed by American federal agencies; in the survey, we embedded two experiments in which individually tailored treatments successfully manipulated beliefs about procedural thoroughness and knowledge of policy outcomes. We find no effects of procedural knowledge but a strong polarizing effect of outcome knowledge: commenters whose preferred outcome was congruent (incongruent) with the agency's action symmetrically increased (decreased) their perceptions of rule legitimacy, attitudes toward notice-and-comment, and agency trust. These findings cast doubt on a major purported benefit of an otherwise costly administrative practice.

articles_hidden.title: Social Prescribing and community activities for people living with chronic pain: A Realist Synthesis
articles_hidden.authors: Leila Heelas; Daisy Fancourt; Karen Barker; Alexandra Bradbury; Ann Livingstone; Alexandra Burton
articles_hidden.abstract:
Chronic pain is associated with significant physical and mental health burden to individuals and society. Social determinants of health are associated with an increased prevalence of chronic pain and disability. Social prescribing is an intervention designed to address social determinants of health; however, little is known about how social prescribing can support people living with chronic pain (PECP).
To investigate the mechanisms and contexts by which participation in social prescribing and/or community activities lead to health and wellbeing outcomes in PECP.
A realist synthesis was conducted in November 2024 and updated in March 2026. Context-mechanism-outcome configurations (CMOCs) were produced and mapped to the Multi-Level Mechanisms of Leisure Framework to identify potential psychological, biological, social and behavioural mechanisms.  A programme theory was developed to illustrate how and why social prescribing interventions lead to health and wellbeing outcomes in PECP. 
Of 9761 studies, 35 were included. Four sources explored social prescribing link worker models and thirty-one investigated individual community activities. 15 overarching CMOCs were identified including seven psychological, three biological, three social and two behavioural mechanisms. The CMOCs highlight how creative, cultural and leisure activities, social prescribing pathways and volunteering, lead to intended and unintended outcomes (such as pain resulting in reduced participation in volunteering). This synthesis provides evidence for how social prescribing interventions lead to improved health and wellbeing in PECP and can be used to inform non-clinical service provision, especially where access to pain services is limited.

articles_hidden.title: Unionization in Higher Education: An Industry-Level View
articles_hidden.authors: Joseph van der Naald
articles_hidden.abstract: This research note presents estimates of union membership and collective bargaining coverage in the higher education industry using data from the Current Population Survey. The paper analyzes the extent of union membership and collective bargaining coverage from 1983-2025, both in the industry and among faculty specifically, and estimates of the variation in union membership by employment sector, race and gender for 2024. Using a 10-year span of data, the paper also estimates union wage premiums in the industry and among faculty. This note finds union membership and bargaining coverage has remained stable over the past four decades, but documents notable gendered and ethnoracial disparities in both measures in 2024. Faculty and industry collective bargaining results in earnings premiums ranging between 4% and 5%. The findings present quantitative estimates of unionism and its material effects for higher education workers that complement recent research published by the National Center for the Study of Collective Bargaining in Higher Education and the Professions.

articles_hidden.title: Flourishing and Health in Kenya. Philosophical Perspectives and Empirical Insights.
articles_hidden.authors: Maike Ritzer; Steffen Flessa
articles_hidden.abstract: Numerous studies have demonstrated positive associations between broader dimensions of wellbeing and health. However, evidence from Kenya on this association is scarce and mostly focused on broad evaluative measures of wellbeing, such as life satisfaction. This study draws on conceptualizations of wellbeing from Sub-Saharan African philosophical literature as motivation for examining various specific dimensions of wellbeing in the Global Flourishing Study and analyzing their association with subsequent health in Kenya as a case study, using a longitudinal panel design. Data were drawn from waves 1 (2023; n=11389 individuals) and 2 (2024; n= 7698 individuals) of the Global Flourishing Study. The data are representative of the general population in Kenya. Linear regression models with a lagged dependent variable are used to test the association of wave 1 wellbeing indicators with subsequent physical and mental health at wave 2. The findings indicate that several dimensions of wellbeing - including livelihood security, satisfaction with personal relationships, meaning and purpose, agency and freedom to pursue what is most important in life - are positively associated with subsequent self-rated physical and mental health in Kenya.

articles_hidden.title: The Impact of U.S. Tariffs on European Public Opinion: Evidence From a Natural Experiment
articles_hidden.authors: Joseph Noonan
articles_hidden.abstract: How do tariff escalations shape public attitudes in targeted countries? This registered report examines how the second Trump Administration's April 2025 tariff escalation affected European public opinion. Leveraging the announcement's timing during the fieldwork of Standard Eurobarometer 103.3 as an unexpected event, I compare respondents interviewed before and after. Drawing on theories of external threat, in-group identity, and cooperative reciprocity, I test whether the escalation strengthened pro-EU sentiment, worsened views of the United States, and shifted cooperation preferences. I find that it reduced favorable views of the United States, while effects on EU attachment and cooperation preferences were small and non-significant. The decline in favorable views of the United States is concentrated in the most negative response category, indicating that negative views intensified. These results suggest that economic threats from an ally can sharpen antagonism toward the threatening actor without producing broad in-group consolidation or shifts in trade cooperation preferences.

articles_hidden.title: Rails, Risks, and Resilience: A Dynamic Spatial Equilibrium Analysis with Catastrophic Natural Disaster Risk
articles_hidden.authors: Daisuke Adachi
articles_hidden.abstract: We develop a dynamic stochastic spatial model in which catastrophic disasters temporarily reduce regional productivity and disrupt the transportation network, applied to Japan's Tokai Trough Earthquake (TTE) risk and the Chuo Shinkansen (CS) maglev train project. Productivity-recovery and network-disruption are estimated on the 2011 Tohoku Earthquake, and the model qualitatively reproduces the observed slow population decline and wage overshoot in the affected regions. The population-weighted welfare cost of TTE risk is 4.96\% of permanent consumption, of which 97\% flows through the migration option-value channel, representing a spatial-spillover mechanism where even far-epicenter zones lose welfare because their fallback destinations also become riskier. As the CS plays a role as insurance against transport-network disruption, it delivers welfare gains of 0.83\% under TTE risk versus 0.63\% in the risk-free benchmark, resulting in a 0.19 percentage-point redundancy premium. Overall, our framework extends dynamic spatial analysis beyond perfect-foresight counterfactuals to reveal spatial welfare spillovers and a redundancy value of infrastructure under catastrophic risk.

articles_hidden.title: Unequal Geographic Coverage of Air-Quality Monitoring across Wealth Groups in Delhi
articles_hidden.authors: Saishha Vikram Agarwal
articles_hidden.abstract: Air-quality monitoring networks are the basis for measuring and reporting urban pollution, but their value depends in part on how well they represent the populations they are intended to serve. The study examines whether Delhi's air-quality monitoring network provides equal geographic coverage across wealth groups. It combines the locations of current air-quality monitoring stations with the Relative Wealth Index (RWI), which provides estimates of relative wealth for small geographic areas. Delhi's population is divided into five population-weighted wealth groups, and the distance from each location to the nearest monitor is calculated. Residents in the poorest wealth quintile live, on average, 7.58 km from the nearest monitor, compared with 4.69 km for the richest quintile.
