The difference of 2.89 km is positive even after accounting for spatial clustering (95% spatial-block bootstrap interval: 1.60 to 4.28 km). Monitoring coverage is also higher among the highest-wealth residents: 45.7% of the poorest quintile lives within 5 km of a monitor compared with 67.3% of the richest quintile. The results show that Delhi's monitoring network provides unequal geographic coverage across wealth groups. The study contributes theoretically by framing monitoring-network representativeness as an equity question. Practically, it contributes by suggesting that future network expansion consider population-weighted accessibility and coverage of lower-wealth populations along with conventional technical siting criteria. The results do not, however, show that monitors were deliberately placed to favor wealthier areas, nor do they establish that greater distance necessarily causes less accurate pollution measurement.

articles_hidden.title: An Overview of Public Administration Research: Insights From Publications in Leading Journals (2000–2024)
articles_hidden.authors: Vener Garayev
articles_hidden.abstract: This study examines paradigmatic changes, thematic developments and authorship patterns in public administration research by analyzing 4,317 articles published in Public Administration Review, Public Management Review, and Journal of Public Administration Research and Theory between 2000 and 2024. Using natural language processing (NLP) techniques through Python software to analyze content of titles, abstracts, and metadata, the article identifies key thematic clusters and paradigmatic shifts across the period, shaped by global events, contextual challenges, and technological advancements. The findings reveal a transition from bureaucratic efficiency to participatory governance, from reform to resilience, and from administrative theory to data-driven governance. Additionally, analysis of authorship patterns reveals increasing collaboration and concentration of scholarly output among top prolific contributors. This study contributes to a growing body of literature on bibliometric and content analytical studies in public administration, offering a comprehensive, data-driven perspective on the field’s intellectual evolution over the past quarter-century.

articles_hidden.title: Partial Exit and Bargaining Power: How Exit Menus Shape Institutional Design
articles_hidden.authors: Chendi Wang
articles_hidden.abstract: A government can often refuse a collective undertaking in more than one way. It may leave the organization, stay out of one initiative, withhold a contribution or block one legal route. I extend exit, voice and loyalty to such exit menus. The refusal a government would actually choose fixes both its own fallback and the others' cost of disagreement. A narrower exit can therefore activate leverage or displace a threat that had secured accommodation. Others who still want the government inside can pay it, restrict common uses or change the scale of provision, and relative marginal costs shape which margin adjusts. Accommodation need not benefit its recipient. When what refusal yields depends on the capacity on offer, an improved alternative can lead the others to build less and leave a retained government worse off despite larger payments. Euro-area rescue finance documents decision-specific refusal rules, rejected protections and reciprocal conditions.

articles_hidden.title: Silicon Ethics: Comparing the Dynamics of Human and LLM Responses to Ethical Dilemmas
articles_hidden.authors: W. Russell Neuman
articles_hidden.abstract: A key element in alignment research is commonly captured by the phrase “alignment with human values.” Human ethical judgment, however, is plural, unstable, affectively charged, socially embedded, and often justified after the fact. This article proposes a systematic comparative methodology emphasizing the potential complementarity of how human and silicon ethics may differ.   Drawing on literature of moral psychology, it identifies five dynamics of human ethical judgment systematically comparing them with their functional analogues in generative models. The goal is not to anthropomorphize LLMs or treat human judgment as a gold standard, but to compare the latent structures of the dynamics in vivo and in silico. The article argues that such comparison can extend alignment research beyond mimetic reproduction of human preferences toward compensatory intelligence: AI systems that help humans notice neglected consequences, test consistency, consider alternative moral frames, and deliberate more responsibly about their own commitments.

articles_hidden.title: Apuestas en Chile: regulación y peso económico de un mercado en expansión
articles_hidden.authors: Andrés Araya; Fabian Belmar; Xiomara Kuwae; Sebastián Aliaga
articles_hidden.abstract: El mercado de apuestas ya no puede entenderse solo como una actividad presencial. La expansión de internet, los teléfonos inteligentes, los medios de pago digitales y la publicidad deportiva trasladó parte relevante del juego de azar hacia plataformas online. Chile reguló históricamente el juego mediante autorizaciones parciales: hípica, loterías, casinos municipales y casinos bajo la Ley N.º 19.995. Ese diseño permitió ordenar segmentos específicos, pero quedó tensionado frente a un mercado digital transnacional. El juego de azar es un problema de política pública, no solo una actividad recreativa. Involucra recaudación fiscal, competencia entre operadores, protección al consumidor, prevención de lavado de activos, integridad deportiva y riesgos asociados al juego problemático. El mercado online no autorizado se ubica en una zona compleja: no forma parte del mercado autorizado, pero tampoco ha sido desplazado de manera efectiva. La Corte Suprema ha declarado ilegales las apuestas online no autorizadas, mientras persisten dificultades prácticas de fiscalización, persecución penal y control de dominios. En 2025, el mercado regulado registró ingresos brutos del juego por $787.281 millones (0,23% del PIB) y generó $148.712 millones en recaudación específica asociada al juego de azar, sin considerar IVA ni impuesto a la renta. Cerca del 70% del mercado regulado corresponde a casinos físicos. Este informe estima el mercado online no autorizado como la brecha entre la tendencia contrafactual del mercado regulado y sus ingresos efectivamente observados. En 2025, esa brecha alcanzó $431.489 millones (0,13% del PIB), es decir, poco más de un tercio de la industria. Bajo una tasa específica de 20% sobre ingresos brutos del juego, la pérdida potencial de recaudación sectorial asociada al mercado online no autorizado se aproxima a $86.298 millones en 2025.

articles_hidden.title: Crecer en campamentos. El drama de un doble vínculo
articles_hidden.authors: Rosario Palacios; Fabian Belmar; Aldo Mascareño
articles_hidden.abstract: En la última década, los campamentos en Chile se han vuelto, nuevamente, una alternativa de habitación permanente para familias de bajos ingresos, sin capacidad de ahorro o inmigrantes. Su número ha pasado de cerca de 700 campamentos en 2011 a alrededor de 1.400 en 2025, en los que viven cerca de 120.000 familias y 84.000 niños. Por medio de análisis estadísticos de tres bases de datos construidas a partir de cuestionarios a cuidadores de niños en campamentos de cinco regiones del país, en este artículo argumentamos que la vida en campamentos produce para los niños un doble vínculo: por un lado, los expone a altos riesgos de entorno, seguridad y económicos, pero la permanencia en el campamento estabiliza su inclusión educativa y de salud, además de hacerlos visibles para beneficios sociales. Los resultados confirman este patrón dual en variables relevantes y, a la vez, abren una posibilidad de superación de esta condición a través de los llamados barrios transitorios, unidades reguladas factualmente (territorio cercado, en márgenes de campamento), socialmente (reglamento comunitario, selección) y temporalmente (orientación a vivienda definitiva). Estos barrios erigen barreras de inmunidad que mantienen la inclusión institucional de los niños (educación, salud, beneficios) y, a la vez, reducen significativamente sus riesgos de entorno, de seguridad y económicos. El artículo concluye que el modelo de barrios transitorios tiene potencial para convertirse en una política público-privada de salida de campamentos hacia soluciones de vivienda definitivas, aunque con limitaciones en cuanto a tiempos y envergadura.

articles_hidden.title: El mundo según Polymarket: control del futuro en mercados de eventos
articles_hidden.authors: Aldo Mascareño; Fabian Belmar; Juan Rozas
articles_hidden.abstract: Los mercados de eventos o mercados de predicción como Polymarket han irrumpido en la escena global bajo la estructura de contratos derivativos de mercados financieros digitales; más allá del dinero, han expandido la lógica financiera hacia eventos principalmente geopolíticos sobre cuya realización cualquier ciudadano puede adquirir acciones y algún nivel de supervisión. Por medio de una amplia investigación bibliográfica y de fuentes primarias, en este artículo argumentamos que la frontera de aceptabilidad de las apuestas se ha desplazado en décadas recientes desde el casino online a apuestas deportivas y eventos geopolíticos socialmente generalizadas. Este desplazamiento cumple la función específica de aportar a los participantes un control de incertidumbre mediante la reducción de un futuro indeterminado a un presente observable a través de las trayectorias de las apuestas y su dinámica en vivo. El futuro se convierte en un presente proyectable de corto plazo. Los análisis muestran que este control de futuro resulta particularmente atractivo para nuevas comunidades especulativas compuestas mayoritariamente por jóvenes. Ellas combinan sociabilidad online y offline, expresan opiniones sobre el mundo a través de sus apuestas y movilizan acciones simbólicas y materiales en plataformas algorítmicas. Los riesgos asociados son múltiples; van desde el clásico insider trading hasta el insider agency, esto es, actores que apuestan sobre eventos en los que ellos mismos intervienen. El artículo concluye que el escenario general es el de una frontera aún difusa entre ilegalidad y operación regular. En ello, la legislación chilena sobre casas de apuestas deportivas, una vez que sea aprobada por el Congreso, quedará obsoleta en relación con la frontera que ya han movido los mercados de eventos.

articles_hidden.title: El lado B de la megarreforma: señales de alerta temprana sobre problemas futuros
articles_hidden.authors: Aldo Mascareño; Fabian Belmar; Pablo A. Henríquez; Juan Rozas
articles_hidden.abstract: Desde el anuncio del Proyecto de Reconstrucción la discusión pública ha girado en torno a temáticas económicas organizadas por la diferencia entre crecimiento y estabilidad fiscal. El predominio de estos temas tiene el efecto de eclipsar otros problemas sociales —emergentes o derivados del proyecto de reconstrucción— que se incuban en las capas subyacentes de esta discusión. Por medio de un análisis computacional de datos de redes sociales, en este artículo argumentamos que tales problemas incuban situaciones críticas futuras que pueden transformarse en conflictos mayores en el mediano plazo. Para ello extraemos las weak signals (señales débiles de alerta temprana) que anuncian procesos de incubación de problemas complejos. Los resultados muestran que estas situaciones críticas se forman en diversos ámbitos que van desde la seguridad hasta la cultura, pasando por problemas sociales clásicos, medioambientales, de género y tecnológicos. El artículo concluye que el análisis de señales débiles, o señales de alerta temprana, ofrece oportunidades de intervención antes de que los problemas se hagan ingobernables, por lo que muestra su utilidad cuando el interventor tiene capacidad de acción y decisión para desactivar constelaciones críticas emergentes.

articles_hidden.title: La cuenta pública del presidente Kast: una cuestión doctrinaria
articles_hidden.authors: Aldo Mascareño; Juan Rozas; Pablo A. Henríquez; Fabian Belmar
articles_hidden.abstract: Las primeras cuentas públicas de cada presidente reflejan su diagnóstico de la situación del país y el sentido programático que le quieren imprimir a su gobierno. Las capacidades de articulación entre los problemas de las personas y una visión de sociedad de largo plazo anclada en principios doctrinarios que orientan la acción política son clave en este tipo de discursos. Por medio de distintos procedimientos algorítmicos de análisis de texto, en este artículo argumentamos que la primera cuenta pública del presidente José Antonio Kast muestra selecciones temáticas y lingüísticas que evidencian un sentido doctrinario distinto al expresado por otros gobiernos chilenos desde el retorno a la democracia en 1990. Los resultados muestran que hay varias condiciones de continuidad en los pesos programáticos del discurso del presidente Kast en comparación con la primera cuenta de los presidentes anteriores, por ejemplo, en temas políticos y económicos. Sin embargo, una diferencia radical está en el posicionamiento inédito, en el primer lugar, del tema de seguridad, lo que anticipa un conjunto de reformas institucionales y discursivas profundas. Los resultados también muestran que la construcción doctrinaria de este primer discurso se articula sobre los conceptos de familia, patria y esfuerzo, los que funcionan como nodos de legitimación y justificación de las acciones políticas propuestas. El artículo concluye que el discurso inaugura un nuevo escenario político que se alinea no solo con la eficacia de las políticas, sino con el tipo de sociedad que impulsan.

articles_hidden.title: Demographer Views about U.S. Fertility: Results from a Survey
articles_hidden.authors: Philip N. Cohen
articles_hidden.abstract: The view that birth rates in the U.S. (where the total fertility rate is now 1.57) is a crisis – even an existential crisis – is increasingly common, but academic demography has not adopted this frame. Demographers should not expect unquestioning acceptance of our views on population issues, but it is useful to make our perspective known, individually as well as collectively. To that end, I report on a new survey of 190 self-identified U.S. demographic researchers (either U.S. nationals or based in the U.S.) on birth rates and population trends. The sample was drawn from demography journal authors, with a response rate of 27.7%. Results show that only 3% agreed the U.S. is in a “demographic crisis.” A majority agreed that government should take measures in order to increase fertility if the total fertility rate were to fall to 0.8 – while 43% believe governments should “never intervene” to raise birth rates. On the other hand, with “the right policies,” 84% agreed the U.S. would benefit from substantially increased immigration. Asked to rank global population issues for the coming years, respondents ranked climate change, aging, and inequality most important, with low birth rates rating eighth out of 12 issues.

articles_hidden.title: Digital capacity in Brazilian municipalities: fiscal autonomy, bureaucratic structure and heterogeneity
articles_hidden.authors: Yago Paiva; Lizandro Lui
articles_hidden.abstract: Over the past decades, digital transformation has become a central aspect of state modernization. In this article, we treat this process as a form of state capacity building — specifically, of the digital capacity of the state. Our aim is to assess whether, at the municipal level, fiscal capacity and bureaucratic quality account for higher levels of digital capacity. To this end, we adapt to the municipal context a concept originally formulated for national states and construct the Municipal Digital Capacity Index (ICDM), a novel and comprehensive measure built from the seven waves of the Brazilian Survey of Basic Municipal Information (MUNIC) that include an information and communication technology module between 2004 and 2024, covering virtually all Brazilian municipalities in each wave. Using the ICDM as the dependent variable, we estimate panel models designed to recover between-municipality effects. Fiscal autonomy is the strongest determinant of digital capacity, with a magnitude far exceeding that of bureaucratic attributes, whose effects are positive but modest. None of these effects, however, operates uniformly: own-source revenue yields more in low-income municipalities, staff qualification pays off only where there is organizational structure to absorb it, and the share of politically appointed staff, whose average effect is null, is positive in poorer municipalities and negative in wealthier ones.

articles_hidden.title: Unmade Ground: Displacement, Dispossession, and the Erosion of Spatial Memory Among Kurdish Forced Migrants
articles_hidden.authors: Ramazan BOZTEPE
articles_hidden.abstract: Forced displacement does not merely relocate people; it dismantles the material infrastructure through which place becomes memory. Drawing on 80 semi-structured interviews conducted across three settings of the Kurdish experience of internal displacement and diaspora resettlement in Turkey (Bölge, n=25; Central Anatolia, n=25) and Western Europe (Diaspora, n=30), this article examines how the destruction, abandonment, and transformation of inhabited space unmakes collective and intergenerational memory. Transcripts were coded thematically against an eleven-category framework, independently verified through a two-coder reliability process (Cohen's κ=0.838 overall; κ=0.667 for the spatial-memory category, which was coded positive in 45 of the 80 interviews). Using Cernea's (1997) Impoverishment Risks and Reconstruction model alongside Malkki's (1992) critique of sedentarist assumptions about place, the analysis identifies four interlinked processes: urban redevelopment, rural demographic hollowing, diaspora gentrification, and the institutional foreclosure of access to common and sacred land. Participants describe memory as materially anchored — carried in streets, soil, and threshold spaces — such that narrative transmission alone cannot repair its loss. The article argues that spatial memory loss constitutes a distinct impoverishment risk inadequately addressed by existing frameworks, extends Cernea's model by specifying the memorial — and not only economic — stakes of lost access to common property, and proposes the concept of inherited spatial memory: attachment to places the second generation has never physically inhabited.

articles_hidden.title: A Representation-Theoretic Method for Analyzing Order Dependence in Decomposition Analysis: An Application to Fertility Change in Korea
articles_hidden.authors: Changin Jeon
articles_hidden.abstract: Decomposition analysis is widely used to attribute changes in an aggregate outcome to changes in its underlying components. When several factors change simultaneously, however, sequential replacement generally yields different contributions depending on the order in which factors are replaced. The Shapley value resolves this problem by averaging marginal contributions over all possible orders, but the variation across those orders is itself potentially informative. This study proposes a decomposition method that analyzes this order dependence rather than averaging it away. For each factor, its contribution over all decomposition paths is treated as a function on the symmetric group. Harsanyi dividends are used to express path dependence in terms of interaction components, and irreducible representations of the symmetric group are then used to decompose the variance of path-specific contributions into interpretable spectral components. This framework distinguishes three properties of a decomposition result: average contribution, order instability, and the interaction complexity underlying that instability. For a decomposition with six factors, the method generates 64 counterfactual states and 720 replacement paths. Synthetic experiments confirm the predicted relationship between interaction order and admissible representation components and verify the numerical decomposition of order variance to machine precision. The empirical application examines fertility change among Korean women aged 20–49 using population size, age structure, marital composition, parity composition among married women, nonmarital fertility, and parity-specific marital fertility. Between 2000 and 2024, marital composition and parity-specific marital fertility contributed strongly to the decline in births, while changes in parity composition substantially offset that decline. The results also show that path-specific contributions can vary substantially around their Shapley means: for marital composition, parity composition and parity-specific marital fertility, the path standard deviation amounts to roughly 31–42% of the total change between 2000 and 2024. Cross-period differences in spectral structure, however, are strongly shaped by the magnitude of change over each interval. The proposed method extends decomposition analysis from the allocation of average contributions to the analysis of the full distribution and structure of path-specific contributions. It therefore provides an additional diagnostic layer for studying interaction, robustness, and structural dependence in multi-factor decomposition.

articles_hidden.title: Mistrust the State, Trust the Market  Mass Investing Culture with Postsocialist Flavour
articles_hidden.authors: Karel Němeček
articles_hidden.abstract: In this paper, I aim to make sense of the meanings surrounding the recent surge in popularity of non-professional investing in the Czech and Slovak postsocialist context. The research is based on interviews with individual retail investors and fieldwork conducted at various investor events, meet-ups, and conferences. My Czech and Slovak research partners view investing as a means to ensure the long-term continuation of their household’s wealth and security. Being invested then represents a certain hedge against the growing inaccessibility of housing and the cost-of-living crisis. My interviewees entrust what Giddens calls ontological security to institutions of global capitalism rather than to local state systems. The shift in trust remains embedded in distinctly postsocialist moral framing, proclaiming a more ethical, self-responsible, and rational type of household financial management, which aligns with the core moral imperative of mass investment culture – everybody should invest. Conversely, welfare-state-based alternatives face generalized distrust as unreliable.

articles_hidden.title: Building better parenting leave survey data: A repository of survey questions for comparative policy analysis
articles_hidden.authors: Cassandra Engeman; Marie Valentova; Laurène Thil; Anna Stastna; Anne Hartung; Alzbeta Bartova; Ivana Dobrotic; Ásdís A. Arnalds; Stephan Köppe; Elitsa Dimitrova
articles_hidden.abstract: This document presents a repository of questions that can be used in cross-national comparative surveys to collect data on parenting leave. With our collated and proposed questions, we aim to assist researchers and data collection agencies build better parenting leave data to understand when and how parents use such provisions. In the following sections, we present questions related to measuring (1) formal and perceived eligibility for leave provisions, (2) leave use and non-use, (3) reasons for non-use, and (4) views about parenting leave. While questions in the first three sections primarily measure behaviour, we include questions about parents’ views, because they can inform behaviour. Each of these four main sections includes our research- and theory-based motivations for the phrasing, inclusion and design of the questions as well as their shortcomings.

articles_hidden.title: Ecological responsibility, wellbeing, and transformative reach: a three-dimensional framework for assessing ecovillages as social innovations toward sustainability
articles_hidden.authors: Alexandre Zénon
articles_hidden.abstract: Ecovillages are collective experiments in maintaining wellbeing within planetary limits, testing whether human flourishing can be maintained while material throughput is reduced. Drawing on a critical narrative review of intentional communities, ecological economics, commons governance, and self-determination theory, we propose a three- dimension, two-layer framework joining ecological limits, wellbeing, and the propagation dynamics of social innovations. The outcome layer includes five elements across three dimensions: critical natural capital and biophysical flows (ecological), material sufficiency and eudaimonic wellbeing (wellbeing), and transformative effect (transformative), an outward axis specific to social innovations. The lever layer includes three transversal levers: a sufficiency economy that drives throughput reduction, a commons governance built on Ostrom's design principles, and a propagation infrastructure that carries practices beyond the host site. Empirically, ecovillages deliver 35 to 80% footprint reductions and achieve partial closure of nutrient cycles. They meet a decent material floor through commons-based provisioning while sustaining or improving wellbeing. They propagate practices via transmission, replication, partnerships, and political influence. Four structural challenges constrain systemic contribution: limited actual impact on ecological, host- territory, and cultural dimensions; dependence on the mainstream provisioning system; barriers to scale (demanding resident profiles, high attrition); and social selection. We argue that ecovillages are best understood as generative laboratories of transposable knowledge and living alternatives that act as vectors of cultural changes. We propose an agenda for a wider community-based transition, associating multi-scale architectures with supportive economic models, facilitative institutions, and a deliberate research program. We situate this Northern articulation within a wider pluriverse of place-based sustainability projects, of which ecovillages are one strand among many.

articles_hidden.title: Given and Chosen Ties: Status, Personal Networks, and Political Behaviour in Britain
articles_hidden.authors: Giacomo Melli
articles_hidden.abstract: Political participation in Britain is stratified not only by where people stand but by who stands with them. Bringing social network analysis to the study of social stratification, this article draws on ego-networks from the British Household Panel Survey, which link respondents to their closest friends and to partners and relatives who are themselves panel members. It examines how the status of these networks relates to turnout, political interest, and party choice across four general elections, and whether given ties, such as parents and siblings, differ from chosen ties, such as partners and friends. Status homophily is strongest among friends. The status of partners, friends, and the family of origin is associated with each outcome. The family of origin is as closely associated as chosen ties, and more closely with interest, whereas adult children stand largely apart. Status also reaches further than behaviour: two steps from ego, alters' status is still associated with ego's turnout, while their turnout is not. These associations reflect stable differences between people, pointing to durable status milieux. Between 1992 and 2005, these milieux came to separate voters from abstainers more, and Labour from Conservative voters less.

articles_hidden.title: The Evolutionary Hearth: An Environment-Dependent Game-Theoretic Framework for Javanese Maternal Domestic Pedagogy
articles_hidden.authors: Muhammad Sukri Bin Ramli
articles_hidden.abstract: This study introduces the Principle of Conditional Cultural Adaptiveness, establishing that the evolutionary performance of cultural strategies depends strictly on environmental state variables and shifts through equilibrium migration as those macro-conditions change. Modernity is formally conceptualized not as cultural erosion, but as equilibrium migration between state-dependent optima. Existing scholarly interpretations of Javanese maternal domesticity and the construct of kanca wingking frequently emphasize patriarchal gender hierarchies, symbolic cosmology, or moral norms without formally modeling how domestic practices dynamically adjust to resource volatility, environmental hazards, and shifting household bargaining power. We develop an environment-dependent game-theoretic frame work linking selected maternal instructions to material resource allocation, homeostatic regulation, risk management, health capital investment, cultural information transmission, and costly signaling. By integrating ethnographic philology with evolutionary game theory, bargaining theory, dynamic optimization, and eco-evolutionary feedback modeling, this research provides a formal computational social science framework for representing cultural persistence and transformation while explicitly differentiating stable household equilibria from equitable distributions of welfare.

articles_hidden.title: Organicity And Structural Coincidence. Intellectual Activity Across Fields
articles_hidden.authors: Matteo Puoti; Antoine Roger
articles_hidden.abstract:
Intellectual activity is examined as a crucial component in the formation of dominant principles of perception, classification, and action. Drawing on Bourdieu’s field theory, the analysis focuses on the structural coincidence of struggles across relatively autonomous fields, showing how concordant principles may emerge without central coordination and contribute to naturalising the established order. Gramsci’s concepts of organicity, intellectual function, civil society, and common sense broaden this perspective by extending the range of agents, practices, and institutions implicated in hegemonic processes. This also foregrounds their relational and pedagogical dimensions and the need for an empirical inventory of the sites and symbolic forms through which common sense takes shape. Hegemony is thus treated as the contingent outcome of differentiated struggles whose effects become aligned across fields. A case study of agricultural capitalism in Romania illustrates the empirical operationalisation of this framework.

For a fuller discussion and further developments of these themes:
https://www.routledge.com/On-Gramsci-and-Bourdieu-Hegemony-Fields-and-Tools-for-Social-Research/Puoti-Roger/p/book/9781041299523

articles_hidden.title: Cooperation as Routing: A Network-Layer Formalization of How Help Propagates Through Social Networks
articles_hidden.authors: kazutaka hayashi
articles_hidden.abstract:
Most models of how things spread on social networks are broadcast models: a state
reaches whoever is reachable, and the analysis asks how far it spread. Cooperation often
does not spread this way. A request for help has no xed recipient; a person who receives
it either helps or, unable to help, passes it toward someone who can. Repeated, this for-
warding carries the request across the network hop by hop, much as a packet is routed
toward a host it has never met. Classical work on decentralized search established that
such address-free messages can reach a target through local decisions, and that chains die
mainly because intermediaries stop. We formalize the decision layer of this process: help-
requests are packets, participants are nodes, and each node facing a request acknowledges
it, forwards it, does both, or drops it. We dene an eective forward as one whose next
hop itself acts, and show that crediting only eective forwards, to the immediate previous
hop only, rewards every intermediary on a successful path without backward propagation,
rewards routing quality rather than volume, and gives no reward for acting in isolation. We
specify the provenance records needed to measure these quantities and illustrate, on the
log of an operating mutual-aid platform, how chains that reached four hops could not be
reconstructed because provenance was missing at the second hop. We discuss implications
for cooperative multi-agent systems and for instrumenting platforms that route help.

articles_hidden.title: Research and Impact of Prompt Engineering Nexus on Programming and Routine Tasks: Exploring Future Possible Directions
articles_hidden.authors: Felix Reichel
articles_hidden.abstract:
Prompt engineering has developed as a transformative subfield in artificial intelligence
(AI), enabling humans to enhance AI systems through structured (PROLOG-like) instructions
to perform specific tasks. This paper shines a light on its multi-dimensional impact on
programming, routine tasks and broader AI applications, drawing on insights from recent
studies. By using techniques such as parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT), zero-shot
learning, multi-shot learning and linguistic feature analysis, prompt engineering often is used
to tackle remaining issues in software engineering (SE), language processing (NLP) and AI
safety. The body of literature highlights its role in optimizing AI performance, reducing
computational overhead and reducing biases. Additionally, it highlights critical gaps in 
current methodologies, such as the comparative energy intensity of state-of-art large language
models (LLMs) and the requirements for adaptive and scalable prompt crafting strategies.
Finally, the paper suggests future directions for research, highlighting the importance of
human-centered design and collaboration to advance the field.

articles_hidden.title: Unexpected heat suppresses emigration from the world's poorest countries
articles_hidden.authors: Ashley Vicary
articles_hidden.abstract: Whether climate stress displaces people or traps them in place is unresolved. The common intuition is displacement: crops fail, heat becomes unliveable and people leave. Other work predicts the opposite for poor countries, where migration abroad is expensive and the shock that sharpens the wish to leave can destroy the means to go. Estimates disagree, partly because realized temperature mixes warming that households anticipated with warming they did not. I isolate the unanticipated part with temperature forecast errors, the warmth or cold a forecast missed, and estimate their effect on monthly international migration from countries holding most of the world’s population. Here I show that unexpected warmth does not detectably move migration on average, but that in low-income countries an unexpectedly hot month lowers departures over the following year. No richer income group shows a detectable response. The migration suppression is strongest where incomes depend on agriculture, also appears outside the growing season and leaves in-migration flat, consistent with heat removing the means to move. For the poorest countries, unexpected heat may hold people back rather than push them abroad. Projections and policies built around displacement may overstate departures from these countries and overlook those who cannot afford to leave.

articles_hidden.title: Defaulting to Decarbonization?  Financial Insolvency and the Energy Transition in India’s States
articles_hidden.authors: Johnathan Guy
articles_hidden.abstract:
How do financial constraints shape the energy transition in developing countries? I study this question in India, where electricity procurement is governed at the subnational level. Electoral politics motivates state governments to subsidize electricity consumption, resulting in financial stress for electricity distribution utilities (DISCOMs). Using multiple sources of original data on utility and plant operations, I investigate the relationship between financial distress and decarbonization. I theorize that the effect of utility insolvency depends on the margin considered—dispatch vs. capacity investment—and on institutions. Counterintuitively, but consistent with my theory, I find that financial stress is associated in the short run with greater relative procurement of renewable energy and less procurement of fossil fuels. Mechanism tests suggest that coal dispatch is more sensitive to liquidity constraints, as distressed DISCOMs cut back on coal deliveries while renewable energy remains protected by “must-run” dispatch regulations. In contrast, I find at most weak evidence that insolvency raises challenges for decarbonizing electricity in the long run: insolvency shows no relationship with renewable-energy tendering, only suggestive evidence that it slows renewable capacity investment, and similarly weak evidence that it curtails expansion of transmission lines that renewables need to scale. The results qualify the conventional wisdom that electricity utility
insolvency is a binding constraint on the energy transition.

articles_hidden.title: Explaining historical persistence in Germany's electoral geography across 130 years: a cleavage-perspective on continuity in spatial patterns of party support
articles_hidden.authors: Leon Gawenda
articles_hidden.abstract: This article studies the long-run persistence of electoral geographies. Drawing on cleavage theory, I argue that spatial patterns of party support persist where cleavages remain politically salient and the social groups they mobilise stay in place. I evidence this argument for Germany, combining electoral and census data from the German Empire (1890–1912) and reunified Germany (2002–2021) at the municipality, county and electoral-district level. The spatial analyses reveal substantial continuity in the electoral geographies of the mainstream left and right. The analysis traces both to one source, the persistent spatial distribution of Catholics. Christian democrats continued historical strongholds of the Center Party where Catholics stayed concentrated, while the SPD persists as its mirror image in the non-Catholic space. Persistence therefore rests on the stability of the religious geography and cleavage, not on the class cleavage and the economic geography, which has changed markedly. The findings position cleavage-based persistence as a complement to cultural-transmission accounts of historical legacies, locating continuity in the ongoing mobilisation of stable social groups rather than in transmitted attitudes alone.

articles_hidden.title: Academia as a Mirror of Society: Science in the Age of Capitalist Realism
articles_hidden.authors: Philipp Strasberg
articles_hidden.abstract: Prima facie, the scientific endeavor seems anti-capitalistic par excellence: a collective, non-profit driven effort of humanity to advance its knowledge in which everyone with enough education is free to participate. But a more detailed look reveals that science and its academic system perfectly mirror our late capitalist society: inequality, exclusivity, overproduction, hypercompetition, exploitation, control, self-optimization, burnout and depression are today’s symptoms, here and there. In addition, missing political agency is not only mirrored in academia---it is cultivated there. A common perspective on both, science and society, can offer the chance to change both for good.

articles_hidden.title: Living Arrangements, Going Outdoors, and Well-Being Among Older Persons: Examining Their Associations in a Swedish Population
articles_hidden.authors: Jeanette Melin; Marie-Louise Möllerberg; Marit Preuter; Kristofer Årestedt
articles_hidden.abstract:
Aim: This study examined associations between living arrangement, frequency of going outdoors, and well-being among older persons in Sweden, with particular attention to their interaction.
Methods: Community-dwelling older persons (n = 1,727) across nine Swedish municipalities participated in a cross-sectional survey. Well-being was assessed using the Older Persons’ Well-being Scale (OPWELLS). Linear regression models examined associations and interactions.
Results: Living alone was associated with lower well-being compared to cohabiting, whereas going outdoors more frequently was associated with higher well-being. The association between living arrangement and well-being differed by outdoor frequency.
Conclusions: Frequency of going outdoors was strongly associated with well-being irrespective of living arrangement. However, the association between living alone and well-being varied with outdoor frequency. Thus, living alone should not be considered an isolated indicator of lower well-being in older age and highlights the importance of considering living arrangements within the broader context of older persons’ everyday lives.

articles_hidden.title: From Desktop to Spatial Interfaces: UX Design Implications of Evolving Interaction Paradigms
articles_hidden.authors: Hiromu Tsuruta
articles_hidden.abstract:
This study examines how the transition from screen-based interaction paradigms to spatial
interfaces affects established user experience principles and design considerations. The
study is guided by the following research question: How does the transition from
screen-based interaction paradigms to spatial interfaces affect established UX principles and
design considerations? Apple Vision Pro and visionOS are examined as one case. The
corpus consists of 60 selected Human Interface Guidelines pages, 76 WWDC sessions, the
Apple Vision Pro User Guide, and notes from researcher observation. The HIG and WWDC
materials were analyzed qualitatively and coded using four dimensions: consistency,
feedback, affordance, and information architecture.
The analysis suggests that established UX principles remain relevant in spatial interfaces,
although the way they are implemented changes. This study describes that change through
three categories: retention, adaptation, and extension. Some familiar purposes and
structures remain in place, others are adapted through spatial interaction, and some design
concerns expand to include the user’s body and surrounding environment. Familiar
structures such as windows, controls, and navigation remain important, but visionOS adds
gaze, gesture, depth, distance, sound, anchoring, and immersion as additional design
mechanisms. From this pattern, the study proposes selective spatiality: spatial presentation,
immersion, and embodied interaction are most useful when they support the task, not simply
because they are available on the platform.
In the Vision Pro case, effective spatial UX comes from keeping familiar interaction
structures while adding spatial features only where they are useful. Designers must also
consider comfort, attention, accessibility, environmental awareness, and hardware limits.
Because the study examines one platform and does not include independent user testing, its
findings should be interpreted within that scope.

articles_hidden.title: From Public Dominance to Private Expansion: Changes in Hospital Infrastructure in Spain (1986–2018)
articles_hidden.authors: Mauricio Matus-Lopez; Margarita Vega-Rapún
articles_hidden.abstract: In many countries, the growth of the private hospital sector coincides with a decline in beds per inhabitant. Spain is no exception, showing one of the lowest relative bed provisions in the EU. This study offers an exploratory analysis of the evolution of private hospital bed provision in Spain and its Autonomous Communities between 1986 and 2018. Using historical hospital catalogs from the Ministry of Health, we conducted graphical and cluster analyses to examine trends and classify regions by the share of private hospital beds. Results indicate a national trend toward fewer beds and a growing presence of the private, mainly for-profit, sector, with notable regional differences such as the Catalan model. This research provides comparative and long-term evidence on structural changes in Spain’s hospital system.

articles_hidden.title: Using large-scale supermarket transaction data to understand the environmental sustainability and healthiness of food and drink purchases. Policy Insights from the FIO Food Project.
articles_hidden.authors: Emma Wilkins; Mark Alan Green; Mark S Gilthorpe; Alice Rose Kininmonth; Alexandra Johnstone; Michelle Morris
articles_hidden.abstract: A policy brief summarising recommendations for policy from FIO Food work package 2, which uses large-scale retail transaction data to understand the environmental sustainability and healthiness of food and drink purchases.

articles_hidden.title: Occupational class inequality in non-monetary job quality in Europe, 1995-2024
articles_hidden.authors: Edvin Syk
articles_hidden.abstract:
Occupational class is central to research on inequality, but we have limited knowledge about how it structures non-monetary job quality across countries and over time. 
We examine four dimensions of job quality—autonomy, physical working conditions, work intensity, and work time quality—across eight occupational classes in 14 European countries from 1995 to 2024, using the European Working Conditions Survey. 
We compare class profiles over time, decompose variation into within- and between-class components, and benchmark occupational class against country, country-year, and income. 
Most variation in job quality is within occupational classes, but gradients remain pronounced for physical working conditions and autonomy, while work intensity is only weakly structured by class. Cross-national differences are modest on average but substantially larger among lower-skill than higher-skill classes. 
Occupational class thus remains an important source of inequality in some dimensions of job quality, but captures only part of the broader variation in working conditions.

articles_hidden.title: Behavioural Sociology of Humans and Machines
articles_hidden.authors: Taha Yasseri; Hao Cui; Nico Mutzner
articles_hidden.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly participates in communication, decision-making, and collective action, making the social organisation of human–machine interaction central to Hybrid Intelligence (HI). This chapter reviews the behavioural sociology of humans and machines through an HI lens, examining how interaction and feedback shape the combination of human and artificial capabilities. Drawing on sociology, social psychology, human–computer interaction, organisational studies, collective intelligence, and science and technology studies, it traces processes from individual social perception to cooperation in hybrid groups and organisational and institutional arrangements. Particular attention is given to how machine participation alters familiar mechanisms: social categorisation attaches expectations to designed identities, reciprocity may involve unequal social obligations, and algorithmic recommendations acquire authority through organisational practices. The chapter distinguishes observable machine behaviour from human interpretations of intention, understanding, and moral responsibility. It also considers how behavioural effects can extend beyond direct human–machine encounters, while separating established findings from proposed longer-term consequences. It argues that the benefits of HI depend on how roles, incentives, reliance, and accountability are organised, and identifies priorities for empirical research on these evolving sociotechnical arrangements.

articles_hidden.title: Attribute Relevance in Conjoint Analysis
articles_hidden.authors: Lukas Stoetzer; Asya Magazinnik
articles_hidden.abstract: Researchers often rely on conjoint analysis to understand which attributes drive respondents' decisionmaking, yet standard estimands are not designed to measure attribute relevance. We introduce a novel approach to measuring attribute relevance in conjoint analysis by drawing on causal attribution methods. Our proposed estimand, the average probability of necessary and sufficient causation (APNS), captures the probability that swapping two profiles' levels on an attribute would change a respondent's choice. We establish nonparametric identification under assumptions related to preference heterogeneity, and provide simple difference-in-means estimators that can be applied to existing conjoint data structures. Two empirical applications illustrate the method. A candidate choice experiment in Germany reveals significant preference heterogeneity that leads standard estimands to mask relevance, while under the right assumptions the APNS recovers it. By contrast, in a replication of a prominent refugee experiment, we find that assuming preference homogeneity is unproblematic for many attributes of asylum-seekers.

articles_hidden.title: Using large-scale supermarket transaction data to understand the environmental sustainability and healthiness of food and drink purchases. Policy Insights from the FIO Food Project.
articles_hidden.authors: Emma Wilkins; Mark Alan Green; Mark S Gilthorpe; Alice Rose Kininmonth; Alexandra Johnstone; Michelle Morris
articles_hidden.abstract: A policy brief summarising recommendations for policy from FIO Food work package 2, which uses large-scale retail transaction data to understand the environmental sustainability and healthiness of food and drink purchases.

articles_hidden.title: An Empirical Model of Mobile App Competition: The Role of the Revenue-Source Channel
articles_hidden.authors: Kohei Kawaguchi; Susumu Sato; Toshifumi Kuroda
articles_hidden.abstract: Mobile apps can earn revenue from download fees, in-app purchases, and in-app advertising, and mixed business models coexist within a market, unlike in many familiar markets where firms rely primarily on a single price per product. Because developers choose these revenue sources jointly, a shock to one source can induce adjustments in the others, including the activation or shutdown of a source, a mechanism we call the revenue-source channel. We develop an empirical model of app competition in download prices, usage prices, and advertising intensities, in which developers endogenously determine their business models. The model admits a competition-in-utility formulation that yields a tractable equilibrium characterization and a unified measure of disutility that applies to zero-priced apps. We estimate the model using data on roleplaying apps in the Japanese Google Play market during 2015–2017 and use it to assess how horizontal mergers, changes in platform transaction fees, and changes in advertisement prices affect app developers and consumers. In a merger of a paid app and a free app, a cost synergy at the free app is not passed through to consumers, whereas a quality synergy raises consumer surplus. A lower platform transaction fee can raise the average download price when previously free apps begin charging, while consumer surplus still rises. A higher advertisement price raises advertising intensity and slightly lowers usage prices, while modestly increasing consumer surplus, app profit, and platform revenue. These results demonstrate the importance of zero-priced apps and the revenue-source channel in markets where multiple revenue sources coexist.

articles_hidden.title: An age-old advantage: Evidence for a consistent survival advantage for children of long-lived parents in Sweden 1880-2022
articles_hidden.authors: Ingrid K van Dijk; Niels van den Berg
articles_hidden.abstract: The average lifespan has increased strongly in the past decades, but not everyone has benefited equally. Establishing the degree of intergenerational persistence of survival generates insights into broad inequalities between individuals and families in their likelihood to live to high ages. Using established register-type data for two regions in Northern and Southern Sweden 1880-2022 linked to historical records, we show that even before the rise of the modern social gradient in health in the 1960ies, mortality is lower among descendants from long-lived parents (top survivors of their birth cohort). This shared survival advantage between parents and children persists over time even after considering SES. Mortality among the descendants of top survivors is lower in lifestyle-related causes of death, suggesting that behavioral factors could be a significant factor in explaining the survival advantage. Overall, we find that mortality concentrates in families in patterns that go beyond the influence of SES alone. Similarities between relatives in health and mortality therefore provide an important lens into inequalities in survival and health over time.

articles_hidden.title: Survivors' Perspectives and Experiences of Intimate Partner Violence Perpetrator Intervention Programs and Associated Services: A Qualitative Systematic Review
articles_hidden.authors: Alison Stafford; Chae Rose
articles_hidden.abstract:
This qualitative systematic review synthesises survivors’ perspectives of intimate partner 
violence perpetrator interventions and associated support services. Specifically, it examines 
how different relationship structures, such as intact, co-parenting, or separated 
arrangements, shape these experiences and determines which program features are 
perceived as supporting or compromising safety. Following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, 
electronic databases were searched for peer-reviewed literature published after 1 July 2016. 
Although 13 studies met the initial inclusion criteria for descriptive mapping, the final 
thematic synthesis integrated 11 primary sources containing the specific contextual data 
required for qualitative analysis. The analysis generated three main analytical themes: the 
intervention environment, perpetrator behaviour patterns, and the survivors’ processing 
journey. Findings indicate that relationship structures influence how survivors experience 
these interventions. While individuals navigating ongoing contact or reconciliation attempts 
often report transactional partner compliance driven by child-access pressures or relationship 
motivations, those seeking complete separation report an environment of persistent 
hypervigilance. Survivors report that specialised advocacy and literacy provided by partner 
contact services support safety by deconstructing mutual-blame frameworks and shifting self
blame. Conversely, interventions are perceived as compromising safety when they rely on 
isolated compliance checks and operate separately from substance use and mental health 
services, creating a false impression of behavioural change. Ultimately, the qualitative 
evidence indicates that measuring progress through mere attendance alone provides a 
misleading indicator of risk, suggesting that future policy should prioritise coordinated 
communication across sectors and elevate survivor-defined safety as the key indicator of 
program success.

articles_hidden.title: Electoral systems shape the entry and entrenchment of extremist parties
articles_hidden.authors: Chanuwas Aswamenakul; Tyler Marghetis; Brad L. LeVeck; Paul E. Smaldino
articles_hidden.abstract: Representative democracies aspire to represent voters’ viewpoints through their elected officials. At the same time, they may try to minimize extremist viewpoints that can destabilize democracy itself. Here we show that electoral systems navigate this tension by trading off between two vulnerabilities: extremist entry and extremist entrenchment. Using computational models, we investigate how electoral systems respond to the emergence of ideological extremism arising either through the introduction of a new party or through the gradual radicalization of an established party. Systems that more accurately represent public opinion are more permissive to new parties, including extremist ones. Conversely, systems that suppress extremist entry can also protect incumbent parties as they drift toward increasingly extreme and unrepresentative positions. Electoral systems therefore differ not only in how well they represent voters or how many parties they sustain, but in the vulnerabilities they create: institutional openness increases the risk of extremist entry, while institutional inertia increases the risk of extremist entrenchment. Democracies thus face a fundamental design challenge: The same institutional features that protect a democracy from one extremist risk also expose it to another.

articles_hidden.title: Stabilizing Without Integrating: Ethnopolitical Cartelization and Power-Sharing in Post-Ohrid Macedonia
articles_hidden.authors: Ognen Vangelov
articles_hidden.abstract: This article examines the long-term effects of Macedonia’s post-conflict power-sharing arrangement, introduced by the Ohrid Framework Agreement (2001), on interethnic integration and democratic accountability. While the consociational model is widely credited with stabilizing the state and ensuring minority inclusion, it has also contributed to the institutional entrenchment of ethnic segmentation, shaping the incentives of political competition and governance. The article introduces the concept of ethnopolitical cartelization to describe how consociational power-sharing facilitates the consolidation of dominant ethnic parties as gatekeepers to state institutions, limiting intra-ethnic pluralism while preserving interethnic parity. Drawing on institutional analysis and empirical evidence, the article argues that key features of the Macedonian model, such as ethnic veto mechanisms, proportionality rules, and decentralized governance, have incentivized the monopolization of political representation within ethnic blocs, most clearly exemplified in the long-standing dominance of DUI within the Albanian political segment. This dynamic has enabled the development of vertically integrated party structures that channel access to state resources through identity-based patronage and informal governance. The result is a form of segmented stability in which public administration, education, and language policy operate through parallel structures. The Macedonian case illustrates the broader limitations of consociational design in deeply divided societies: while formal inclusion is achieved, it may come at the expense of shared civic space, horizontal accountability, and democratic responsiveness. By segmenting political authority and embedding elite brokerage into the structure of governance, the system inadvertently entrenches the very boundaries it was designed to overcome.

articles_hidden.title: The Dataset of World Refugee and Asylum Policies (DWRAP): de jure asylum policy for 205 countries, 1951-2022
articles_hidden.authors: Christopher W. Blair; Guy Grossman; Jeremy Weinstein
articles_hidden.abstract: More than two-thirds of the world's refugees and asylum-seekers are hosted in the developing world, yet the national laws governing their reception have never been measured comprehensively across countries or over time. We introduce the Dataset of World Refugee and Asylum Policies (DWRAP), the most expansive coding of de jure asylum and refugee policy assembled to date. DWRAP records every national law pertinent to forcibly displaced populations in 205 countries from 1951 to 2022---951 legal instruments in all. From the text of each law, we hand-code 54 policy provisions, which we aggregate into 14 strands, five fields---access, services, livelihoods, movement, and participation---and a single index of policy liberality, released in three aggregation forms. The result is a country-year panel of 11,484 observations measuring displacement-policy liberality within and across countries over seven decades. Together, these data open the causes and consequences of refugee-policy change to global, historical analysis. They measure law rather than its enforcement---and so make the distance between the two visible and measurable.

articles_hidden.title: Resilience through Pathway Specificity for Managing Climate Shocks. A Review of Evidence from East Africa.
articles_hidden.authors: Mohamed Abdirahman Ibrahim
articles_hidden.abstract:
The study systematically reviews and synthesizes 74 empirical studies from East Africa, covering Ethiopia, Kenya, Somalia, and Somaliland. Using study-level, asset-based thresholds and other complementary indicators, the findings identify that household resilience is non-linear and requires targeted, specific programming. The Pathway-Specific Resilience Framework (PSRF), which the paper validates, divides the target populations into two groups: a resource-deficient group that needs asset assistance and external safety nets (socially supported livelihood resilience pathway) and an asset-based cohort that prioritizes asset protection and market-based interventions. The study found that households with constrained resources face limitations in asset accumulation, which leave them more vulnerable to persistent poverty traps. PSRF proposes poverty graduation that balances immediate protection with long-term resilience through a sequence of protocols. The first “Protocol “A” protects resource-poor (Socially supported pathway) households to prioritize consumption, direct transfers (e.g., assets), and human capital. Once households transition to “Protocol B”, the shift is from survival assistance to access to market, finance, and index-based insurance. Additionally, the PSRF integrates other cross-cutting measures to sustain immediate gains from the protocols and prevent relapses brought by climate shocks. These include basic infrastructure like access to water, healthcare, and education; Connectivity and information such as early warning systems, transport, telecommunications, and adaptation measures including climate-smart technologies. 
Key words: Pathway-Specific Resilience Framework (PSRF), Drought resilience, livelihood pathways, Social protection, East Africa

articles_hidden.title: The 128 Paths to Victory - Swing State Math in the U.S. Presidential Elections
articles_hidden.authors: N. Asger Mortensen; Joel D. Cox
articles_hidden.abstract: In U.S. presidential elections, outcomes are often predictable in most states, with variability primarily introduced by a small number of "swing states". While the specific swing states can fluctuate from one election cycle to the next, they collectively play a critical role in determining the overall result. In the 2024 election, seven key swing states contribute a total of 93 delegates to the electoral college. Without considering mutual correlations, each of the 128 potential electoral outcomes has an equal probability of approximately 0.8%. Due to an uneven distribution of "safe" delegates (219 Republican and 226 Democrat), the Democratic candidate holds a slight statistical advantage. Analysing all possible outcomes for the 2024 election suggests an estimated 55% probability for a Democratic win, compared to 42% for a Republican victory. The odds of a tie are approximately 2.3%, while the likelihood of either party achieving a clean sweep of all swing states is 0.8%. A detailed analysis of the 128 possible election outcomes reinforces the widely held view that securing Pennsylvania is crucial to electoral success. Notably, in 4\% of all possible scenarios, victory is achieved by the narrowest possible margin, and in every such case, it hinges on winning Pennsylvania.

articles_hidden.title: Gene-Environment Interactions: Reconciling Scarr-Rowe and Compensatory Advantage Hypotheses
articles_hidden.authors: Sonia Petrini
articles_hidden.abstract:
Note: Version 3 adds a simulation benchmark accounting for SES differences in completion rates. Versions 1 ans 2 interpreted SES gaps in over- and underachievement as support for both the compensation and Scarr–Rowe hypotheses; this version shows that, with few exceptions, these gaps can be explained by baseline differences in completion rates alone.

Research on gene–environment interactions in education focuses on two main hypotheses: compensatory advantage, where genetic disadvantage is less consequential in resource-rich environments; and Scarr–Rowe hypothesis, where resource-rich environments reinforce ge- netic advantage. Although regression approaches frame these as mutually exclusive, the hypotheses concern differences at the extremes of the genetic distribution, as measured by a polygenic index (PGI). Compensation and reinforcing dynamics are here mapped to socioeconomic (SES) differences in the rate of overachievers (low-PGI individuals who at- tain a degree) and underachievers (high-PGI individuals who do not). Results show that in three representative datasets from the US and UK, high-SES students are indeed more likely to overachieve and less likely to underachieve, a pattern seemingly consistent with both hypotheses. Simulation analyses reveal, however, that gaps of the observed magnitude are, with few exceptions, explainable by SES differences in completion rates alone. This study advances the theoretical framing of compensation and Scarr–Rowe dynamics as co- existing rather than competing, while aligning with recent calls for careful interpretation of gene–environment interactions in the presence of baseline environmental differences.

articles_hidden.title: ‘Building the Internationalist City from Below’: The Role of the Czechoslovak Industrial Cooperative “Interhelpo” in Forging Urbanity in early-Soviet Bishkek
articles_hidden.authors: David Leupold
articles_hidden.abstract:
Abstract
The paper explores the historical trajectory of Interhelpo, an industrial cooperative from Czechoslovakia, and its role in forging urbanization “from below” in early-Soviet town of Pishpek (now Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan). In light of scarce literature available on the success and failures of Western internationalist communes in the early Soviet period, this paper draws from intensive field work in Kyrgyzstan and understudied sources in Czech, Kyrgyz, Slovak and Russian to offer a novel, bottom-up narrative on the socialist city in Central Asia.

Founded 1924 by Czech, Slovak, Hungarian, German internationalists and Ido-learners around the mountaineer and Bolshevik Rudolf Pavlovič Mareček in the Czechoslovakian town Žilina, the cooperative actively shaped urbanization in what would be become known as the capital of Soviet Kyrgyzstan. From 1925 until its liquidation during WWII, the cooperative built from scratch a whole district including the first electric power station of the city, textile and furniture factories, workshops for tailors, shoemakers and joiners, a school, a kindergarten, a tannery, a brewery as well as unique residential district. In the process, the cooperative forged an organic patchwork language referred to as spontánne esperanto to secure translocal collaboration between internationalists from Central Europe, on the one hand, and a heterogeneous mix of workers including Armenians, Kyrgyz, Dungans, Uygurs, Uzbeks, Russians and Ukrainians, on the other.

Transcending a purely historical analysis, the paper ultimately turns to the urban landscape of present-day Bishkek. There it argues that while the district built by Interhelpo corresponds today to an exiled site dislocated by the hegemonic ethno-national memory regime, its materiality harbors relicts of another future capable of mobilizing alternative narratives on the city and her socialist and multi-ethnic past.

articles_hidden.title: A Pipeline for Extracting Data from Videos of Complex Events
articles_hidden.authors: Mirya Holman; Andreas Kuepfer; Tyler Simko
articles_hidden.abstract: Political scientists now regularly use audio, video, and text data to investigate questions about deliberation, representation, and emotion. However, existing research using multimodal data focuses largely on highly professionalized settings with readily available preprocessed data. Although the availability of data from less standardized environments such as campaign events, court hearings, and local government meetings has increased, using recordings of these events for research poses common measurement challenges, including creating transcripts, identifying speakers, and idiosyncratic production styles. In this paper, we present a streamlined and tested pipeline that uses open source tools to automatically transform raw recordings into data formats needed for political science research. The outputs of our pipeline can then be used for a wide range of substantive analyses. We validate our approach through an examination of thousands of hours of local government meetings and state supreme court hearings, showing how we can accurately segment audio, identify speakers, transcribe speech, and detect gender across varying structures and audio/video quality. The flexible open-source pipeline is publicly available and supports both local machines and computing clusters. As an application, we examine participation by gender in over 1,000 hours of school board meeting videos and US state supreme court hearings.

articles_hidden.title: Patriarchal Norms of Reproductive Behavior as an Adaptation to the Demographic Challenges of the Neolithic Transition
articles_hidden.authors: Maksim Sapozhnikov
articles_hidden.abstract:
This article proposes an evolutionary-materialist hypothesis on the origin of three basic
patriarchal norms of reproductive behavior: restriction of divorce, control over female
sexuality, and parental control over the choice of a spouse, which convergently emerge in
societies transitioning to food production. These norms are viewed as an evolutionary
adaptation to the conditions of the Neolithic transition, having emerged at the social level.
Methodologically, the work is structured as a retrospective analysis of specific
demographic conditions that created pressure in favor of such an adaptation. The starting
mechanism is the reproductive strategy of "sex for resources"—the exchange of male-
provided resources for female reproductive access—which arose in the ancestors of
humans in the Paleolithic (or earlier) and was entrenched by sexual selection.
Retrospective analysis shows that the most likely demographic challenges of the Neolithic
transition, creating pressure in favor of the adaptation of reproductive behavioral strategies
at the social level, were: (1) a manifold increase in population density, facilitating the
switching of marital partners (primarily for men) and creating a threat of resource insecurity
for women with children; (2) the emergence or intensification of awareness of the direct
link between sexual intercourse and childbirth, which could reduce women's motivation for
sexual activity due to awareness of reproductive costs; and (3) the dissociation between
the timing of sexual and social maturation in males, as a result of which female hormonal
mechanisms of partner choice (romantic love) continue to target young men who are not
yet able to provide a family with sufficient resources under the new conditions. The
convergent emergence of patriarchal norms of reproductive behavior in isolated cultures
(Mesopotamia, China, the Aztecs, the Incas, and others) serves as evidence of their
reproductive effectiveness compared to possible alternative adaptations. The hypothesis
explains the specific role of older males (fathers) as the main agents maintaining these
norms. The article is theoretical in nature and provides a foundation for further cross-
cultural empirical research.

articles_hidden.title: The Illusion of Precision: Interpreting International Rankings Within Their Measurement Limits
articles_hidden.authors: Milos Kankaras
articles_hidden.abstract: International rankings publish precise country positions. We ask which comparisons the evidence behind five of them supports, by reproducing published tables, optimising weights, applying multiplicity-adjusted rank inference and two source checks, within a framework separating invalid measurement, insufficient validation, normative trade-offs, underrepresentation of uncertainty and misleading communication. In every programme the adjacent ordering is unsupported, each for a different reason: Report Card 19 trades off dimensions in all 35 adjacent pairs; World Happiness Report countries move a median of 30 places when affect replaces life evaluation; 23 of 38 countries can lead the Better Life Index under unrestricted weights; retrospective rescoring moves Global Health Security Index countries a median of seven places within one year; only 4 of 80 adjacent PISA pairs are distinguishable. Broad contrasts survive throughout. Two unrepresented uncertainties are documented: rotated administration behind Report Card 19's social-skills indicator, and unlinked assessment vintages behind the Human Capital Index.

articles_hidden.title: "I don't give a shit anymore" – Future-Oriented Career Agency and Precarity at the Postdoc Stage
articles_hidden.authors: Julian Hamann; Kathia Serrano Velarde; Tim Fenkner; Jonas Gottschalk-Rayling; Sven Boniger; Michi Hügel
articles_hidden.abstract: This paper examines how postdoctoral researchers navigate precarious employment conditions and claim career agency during an uncertain career stage. Drawing on a longitudinal qualitative interview panel of 35 postdocs from particle physics and modern history, the study distinguishes between two forms of agency: empowered strategizing and restricted drifting. Strategizing postdocs actively align short- to mid-term career goals with opportunities arising from fixed-term contracts and grant funding cycles, while drifting postdocs prioritize present research activities over long-term planning. Through in-depth interviews conducted in three waves, the analysis reveals how temporal horizons are compressed by the cyclical nature of academic recruitment and funding. The findings highlight the dynamic interplay between structural constraints and different forms of individual agency. This work contributes a processual perspective on career agency and precarity and adds to career research and studies of precarious working conditions.

articles_hidden.title: Rethinking Revictimization
articles_hidden.authors: Joyce Mok
articles_hidden.abstract: Survivors of childhood abuse have a heightened risk of experiencing adulthood interpersonal violence. Existing theories explain revictimization through the victim’s deficits and past experiences of violence. These theories fail to explain the causes of revictimization, can lead to ineffective interventions, and can harm victims. This article presents a secondary analysis of the qualitative literature inspired by Eve Tuck’s formulation of desire-based research, which originally aimed to address similar narratives in the fields of education research and Indigenous studies. This analysis shows the benefits of a theoretical approach that situates the individual’s motivations within an interpersonal, social, and cultural context.

articles_hidden.title: Research dataset sharing and ethical researcher conduct: A commentary on Ghuge et al. (2026) and Kumar et al. (2026).
articles_hidden.authors: Margaret K. Merga; Saiyidi Mat Roni
articles_hidden.abstract:
This commentary is written for an audience within and beyond academia, as
it concerns a dataset from the international community of school library professionals
(SLPs). After briefly orienting the reader to commentary and data fabrication, we
respond to Ghuge et al. (2026) and Kumar et al. (2026), recent articles with the same
corresponding author. Kumar et al. (2026) strongly imply that amongst other
researchers, there was a fabrication of data in our 2026 article where some SLP
respondents disclosed experiencing significant risk related to their work roles, notably
though not exclusively in the US political context. Kumar et al.’s (2026) “reasonable
evidence” that we fabricated our data is based on our data availability statement and an
opinion poll sent to associates (N=100); this method does not test whether a dataset
exists. Ghuge et al. (2026) cites Kumar et al., (2026) to make a similar though far softer
claim. We consider Kumar et al. (2026) in relation to ethical conduct in research
methods and research respondent risk related to research ecosystem norms. Data
sharing cannot be simply conflated with ethical research conduct. If we cannot
guarantee anonymity where appropriate, at-risk populations will refuse to participate in
social science research.

articles_hidden.title: A Productivity Fixated World in the Age of AI: Investigating The Purpose of Human Art
articles_hidden.authors: Bruce Tan
articles_hidden.abstract: Modern society increasingly prioritizes final products over the creative process, a trend exacerbated by the rapid adoption of generative AI. This study aims to explore the impact of AI integration into the creative process on subjective well-being and fulfillment, and to determine whether these effects differ between individuals creating for leisure versus those creating for a profession. Within this research, a quantitative-focused survey was conducted with 200 adults, categorized using a 2x2 design: acting as either a hobbyist or a professional illustrator, and either utilizing or not utilizing AI. The data reveals a consistent drop in a person’s well-being across both hobbyist and professional groups when AI is utilized. The differences in fulfillment between hobbyist and professional groups were not statistically significant. While a positive correlation was found between a product-focused mindset and satisfaction among professionals using AI, the overall satisfaction for AI users across the board remained significantly lower than for those who didn’t use AI. These findings suggest that AI integration into creative tasks carries measurable psychological costs by separating the creator from the intrinsically beneficial creative process, along with social costs that taint the creator-audience relationship. These findings underscore the value of human creation, suggesting that the ongoing conversation surrounding AI adoption must extend beyond efficiency to account for value within the human process. An avenue for further research lies within AI use in other fields less traditionally considered a “creative” discipline, such as STEM, which show evidence of having similar psychological benefits arising from the process.

articles_hidden.title: Understanding First Nations Disconnection and Reimagining Connection: A yarn between Aboriginal women.
articles_hidden.authors: Cammi Murrup-Stewart; Tess Ryan
articles_hidden.abstract: Connection and belonging are significant processes concerning cultural identity, and for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples in Australia, it has been at the forefront of discussions around the Social and Emotional Wellbeing of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people. One area that needs more investigation is that of those individuals on the margins of society who may find access to communities a complex practice. Furthermore, there has been an emergence of recent practices that move connection and belonging beyond more traditional ways of being towards modernity, which includes inclusiveness, accessibility and flexibility for those involved. Drawing on existing literature, collaborative yarning with Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples and reflective commentary, this article explores the many facets of connection and belonging and the ways in which many Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples navigate between cultural traditions, socio-historical challenges and contemporary realities. We call for a reimagining of community spaces and practices to ensure they are inclusive and responsive to the diversity of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples’ lived experiences.
